item.title: 代码来搭世界、视频模型只负责「渲染」：WorldDraft 问的是这个分工能不能成立 ｜ WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
item.description:
一句话：把 4D 世界的构建与画面生成彻底解耦，视频模型就从「世界生成器」降格成「生成式渲染器」。

要点：

  • 前提：多模态 coding agent 已能把 **4D 世界的构建**与视觉生成解耦，于是视频模型的身份从「世界生成器」变成「生成式渲染器」
  • 分工一变，问题就变得可检验：如果世界由代码搭，视频模型能不能只把它渲染出来？
  • 作者给出两条判据——**世界保持（world preservation）**：必须守住既定的 4D 运动学结构与相机轨迹；以及与之互补的另一项要求

为什么值得看：这是本周「状态外置」主线最锋利的一次表述：如果不要求视频模型维持世界，它就只能当渲染器。引擎侧完全听得懂这句话——几何与动画归场景描述，像素归渲染器。

中文摘要：多模态 coding agent 正在把 4D 世界的构建与视觉生成解耦，这使视频模型的身份从「世界生成器」转变为「生成式渲染器」。分工一旦确立，一个可检验的问题就浮出水面：如果世界由代码搭建，视频模型能否只负责把它渲染出来？作者指出，可靠的生成式渲染器要同时满足两条互补的判据，其中第一条是**世界保持**——必须守住预先给定的 4D 运动学结构与相机轨迹。换句话说，评判标准从「画面好不好看」变成了「有没有按场景描述渲染」。对引擎侧而言，这正是把几何/动画与像素拆开的那套分工。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?

Abstract

Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of 432 strictly paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a 3×3 factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across 12 representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to 64%), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

1 Introduction

Video generation has achieved remarkable progress in visual realism and temporal coherence, yet generating complex, controllable dynamic scenes remains challenging [(Wan et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; HaCohen et al., 2024)]. Since end-to-end models must implicitly infer 4D world evolution from brief text while simultaneously generating pixels, high visual quality often comes at the expense of physical and spatiotemporal reliability. Recently, advances in multimodal coding agents have enabled an alternative paradigm that decouples world construction from visual generation [(Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a; Liang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)]. By programmatically controlling engines such as Blender [(Blender Online Community, 2026)] or MuJoCo [(Todorov et al., 2012)], coding agents can explicitly specify scene layouts, object trajectories, and physical interactions as executable simulation drafts, leaving video generation models to transform these low-fidelity drafts into photorealistic videos.

This emerging division of labor explores repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers, raising a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? We thus argue that a reliable generative renderer hinges on fulfilling two complementary objectives: ❶ world preservation, which demands faithfully retaining the scene geometry, object dynamics, event timing, and camera motion prescribed by the draft without rewriting the underlying world; and ❷ visual realization, which requires accurately generating text-specified target attributes (e.g., color, material) while persistently binding them to the corresponding 4D entities across motion, occlusion, and viewpoint changes.

Formally, generative rendering operates as a conditional video-to-video (V2V) transformation guided by a structural draft and a target text prompt, yet existing benchmarks only partially address its requirements. Early V2V benchmarks [(Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026)] focus on editing real-world videos that already possess rich source textures, whereas recent programmable-world evaluation [(Huang et al., 2026)] primarily examines whether generated videos follow program-logged states and interaction events. Crucially, achieving world preservation does not guarantee faithful visual realization: models frequently retain coarse draft dynamics while failing to generate or temporally bind target appearance, or conversely fulfill appearance prompts at the cost of altering the underlying 4D world. This gap motivates the need for a new benchmark that jointly evaluates both objectives to systematically characterize the capability boundaries of generative renderers.

In this work, we propose WorldDraft, a systematic benchmark designed to evaluate video models as draft-to-video generative renderers through three progressive questions (Figure2). First, ➀ can video models render target appearances without corrupting complex 4D worlds? To test this foundational capability, we curate 48 executable 4D world families spanning ♣ six challenge categories: multi-entity orchestration, multi-stage dynamics, occlusion and reappearance, camera motion, non-rigid deformation, and hybrid interactions. Grounded in explicit simulator references, WorldDraft jointly measures how faithfully a model preserves the prescribed 4D structure and how accurately it realizes and persistently binds target visual attributes over time. Building upon these base worlds, we further probe the capability boundaries of generative renderers along two complementary axes: ➁ how much information must a draft provide to support reliable rendering? We then instantiate each world across ♠ three draft granularity levels (ranging from abstract proxies to detailed previews) to quantify minimal input requirements and the gains from richer structural and visual cues; and ➂ can models disentangle the world structure to preserve from the source appearance to overwrite? We further pair each draft with ♠ three appearance alignment levels (neutral, aligned, and conflicting) under a shared target prompt to evaluate selective adherence to structural versus textual conditions. Crossing both axes across all 48 world families yields a unified 3×3 factorial design of 432 strictly paired test cases.

Through extensive evaluation on WorldDraft, we observe that existing video models struggle to jointly preserve underlying 4D worlds and realize persistent target appearances, especially under coarse draft granularity or conflicting source-target cues (see Figure1). Motivated by these findings, we further propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy designed to enhance frozen video renderers. Unlike existing adaptation pipelines that rely on costly retraining or privileged simulator access [(Li et al., 2026b; Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026)], WorldDraft-Primer operates solely on the input draft and target prompt. Specifically, it injects subtle visual cues into the first draft frame via two complementary strategies: (i) object emphasis, which highlights key or easily overlooked entities to reinforce world preservation; and (ii) attribute cueing, which encodes target colors, textures, and shading cues around entities and supporting surfaces to guide visual realization. Experiments show that WorldDraft-Primer consistently boosts performance across diverse models, serving as both an analytical companion to WorldDraft and a practical solution for improving draft-to-video generative rendering.

To summarize, this work contributes threefold:

  • •

    We propose WorldDraft, a systematic benchmark for draft-to-video generative rendering comprising 432 strictly paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families, organized across six challenge categories and a 3×3 factorial grid of draft granularity and appearance alignment levels.

  • •

    Through extensive experiments across 12 representative video models, our findings highlight that: (i) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (ii) finer draft granularity anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (iii) conflicting source cues cause severe source leakage, exposing fragile source-target disentanglement.

  • •

    We further introduce WorldDraft-Primer, a simple yet effective plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that injects object emphasis and attribute cues into the first draft frame, consistently boosting both world preservation and visual realization across frozen video renderers.

    • 2 Related Work

    Code-for-Vision.

    Emerging works explore executable code as an intermediate representation for 3D reconstruction and scene synthesis [(Yin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2024a)], driving graphics engines to explicitly control geometry, camera parameters, and lighting. Extending this paradigm to dynamic environments, frameworks such as GS-Agent [(Zhang et al., 2026)] and Code as Worlds [(Wang et al., 2026a)] describe 4D physical evolution in code, relying on simulators to govern deterministic trajectories and interaction rules. This approach establishes a modular division of labor: systems like VideoCoCo [(Li et al., 2026b)] and Code Video Model [(Liang et al., 2026)] also employ coding agents to construct simulation drafts, leaving video generation models to synthesize photorealistic outputs. While prior research primarily targets upstream world construction, WorldDraft focuses on the downstream rendering stage, evaluating whether video models can faithfully realize target appearances without corrupting the underlying executable world.

    Evaluation of Video-to-Video.

    V2V evaluation has traditionally focused on text-guided editing, measuring instruction adherence, temporal consistency, and background preservation on natural videos [(Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026)]. With the rise of programmatic generation, recent benchmarks such as PROWBench [(Huang et al., 2026)] check behavioral fidelity and event timelines against engine-logged states while evaluating visual quality through holistic metrics such as CLIP. However, such holistic evaluations overlook whether models can faithfully realize fine-grained target attributes and persistently bind them across dynamic 4D processes. In this work, WorldDraft goes a step further by investigating how varying input conditions govern the interplay between world preservation and appearance realization.

    3 WorldDraft

    3.1 Task Formulation

    Generative Rendering.

    Programmatic video generation decouples physical reasoning from visual generation: upstream engines explicitly govern scene kinematics, leaving downstream video models to act as renderers. Formally, an upstream simulator executes an underlying 4D world W to yield a draft video D={Iₜˢʳᶜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ∈ℝ^T×H×W×3. Given D and a target prompt p, a generative renderer G synthesizes the target video:

    V̂=G(D,p),

    		(1)

    where D provides the 4D spatiotemporal scaffold (e.g., geometry, kinematics, camera), and p dictates target visual attributes (e.g., color, material, lighting). At inference, G strictly accesses (D,p), with W reserved solely for draft generation and ground-truth evaluation references.

    Dual Criteria.

    To determine whether G faithfully executes this conditional transformation, the correctness of generative rendering hinges on two criteria:

  • ❏

    World Preservation, requiring V̂ to faithfully preserve the prescribed 4D kinematics, entity identities, event timelines, and camera motion in D without prompt-countermanded structural hallucinations.

  • ❏

    Visual Realization, requiring V̂ to accurately instantiate target attributes from p and persistently bind them to corresponding entities across dynamic motion, occlusions, and viewpoint changes.

    • Generative rendering thus demands that G disentangle the world structure to preserve from the source appearance to overwrite: a capability fundamentally governed by the draft’s input condition.

    3.2 Executable World Families

    Challenge Taxonomy.

    To evaluate renderers beyond trivial rigid motions, candidate worlds should enforce deterministic physical constraints for world preservation while imposing dynamic stressors for visual realization. Guided by these principles, we first establish 48 executable world families across six primary categories (Figure2):

    These categories serve as primary stressors rather than disjoint splits; each family is classified by its dominant challenge while incorporating secondary dynamics. In particular, multi-entity orchestration focuses on cooperative spatial topology, whereas hybrid interactions stresses dynamic physical coupling between contact processes.

    Construction and Validation.

    For each challenge, we first collect diverse real-world videos as dynamic blueprints, and employ multimodal coding agents (i.e., GPT-6-Astra [(Singh et al., 2025)]) to translate their underlying physical interactions and camera paths into executable MuJoCo [(Todorov et al., 2012)] or Blender [(Blender Online Community, 2026)] scripts. Crucially, the footage serves as world reference rather than a target for pixel-level reconstruction. Execution produces deterministic 4D rollouts while programmatically logging the ground-truth state tuple:

    Wᵢ=(Sᵢ,Tᵢ,𝔼ᵢ,ℂᵢ),

    		(2)

    with 3D geometry Sᵢ, dense trajectories Tᵢ, event timestamps 𝔼ᵢ, and camera poses ℂᵢ. Each world passes a three-tiered admission audit: ➀ numerical stability without divergence, ➁ fidelity to the reference interaction, and ➂ evaluative viability with unambiguous 4D binding stressors, freezing 48 standardized families, as shown in Figure3.

    3.3 Controlled Draft Design

    To further isolate whether rendering failures stem from insufficient structural support or deceptive appearance cues, we then freeze the 4D kinematics and prompt pᵢ for each Wᵢ, and further orthogonally vary drafts across two axes: draft granularity and appearance alignment.

    Prompt Suite.

    A unified prompt pᵢ per family specifies 2∼4 verifiable attributes (e.g., color, material, lighting). To guarantee unbiased evaluation, pᵢ enforces: ➀ observable verification via unambiguous visual criteria; ➁ alignment-invariant references that index entities via spatial/semantic roles (e.g., “leading cube”) rather than volatile appearance tags; and ➂ structural neutrality, strictly omitting trajectories or camera paths so text cannot compensate for draft sparsity. More examples are in AppendixA.

    Draft Granularity (P).

    To investigate minimal input requirements, we instantiate each world across three monotonic information levels P∈{P₀,P₁,P₂}:

  • ❶

    Abstract (P₀): Primitive geometries and flat shading; retains basic semantics and kinematics to test low-scaffold completion.

  • ❷

    Simulation (P₁): Standard physical meshes and basic lighting; serves as the canonical draft-to-video rendering operating point.

  • ❸

    Previs (P₂): Dense meshes, full context, and realistic shadows; quantifies headroom while retaining a synthetic-to-real gap.

    • This axis establishes an information ladder of structural completeness rather than cosmetic image filtering.

    Appearance Alignment (A).

    Rich visual cues can either guide rendering or trigger severe source leakage. Therefore, to evaluate adherence to text over deceptive source cues, each granularity P is paired with three appearance alignment states A∈{A_N,A_A,A_C}:

  • ❶

    Neutral (A_N): Uninformative placeholder shaders (e.g., gray clay), relying solely on text for appearance.

  • ❷

    Aligned (A_A): Source appearances match pᵢ within the precision of the respective granularity level.

  • ❸

    Conflicting (A_C): Contradictory source cues (e.g., blue metal vs. target red plastic) to probe source leakage.

    • Variations affect strictly surface appearance without altering geometry Sᵢ, kinematics Tᵢ, or camera ℂᵢ.

    Crossing both axes yields a unified 3×3 grid of 9 paired inputs Dᵢ^(j,k) for each world, totaling 48×3×3=432 strictly paired test cases. Fixing alignment isolates the marginal gain of draft information (Δ₀₁,Δ₁₂), while fixing granularity isolates conflict sensitivity and source leakage.

    3.4 Evaluation Suite

    Standard video metrics (e.g., FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)]) fail to accurately evaluate both world preservation and visual realization directly. We thus establish an analytical suite across three disentangled dimensions: ➀ world preservation (WP), ➁ rendering fidelity (RF), and ➂ appearance persistence (AP). We report these dimensions separately to preserve diagnostic interpretability, with an additional composite score for overall comparison.

    World Preservation (WP).

    Grounded in Wᵢ=(Sᵢ,Tᵢ,𝔼ᵢ,ℂᵢ), WP independently benchmarks: ➀ Entity & Layout (Sᵢ), using Count Accuracy and trajectory-matched BBox IoU; ➁ Kinematics & Events (Tᵢ,𝔼ᵢ), via Matched Track Coverage, Interaction Success Rate (ISR), and Event Timing Coverage; and ➂ Camera (ℂᵢ), via relative rotation and scale-normalized translation errors against the canonical draft. Metrics evaluate intended topology, ensuring P₀ is not penalized for lacking fine details only introduced in P₂. Details in SectionB.1.

    Rendering Fidelity (RF).

    Adherence to pᵢ is evaluated via attribute-level binary QA (Yes/No) across target colors, materials, and lighting, incorporating balanced affirmative/negated probes. Critically, QA judges receive only the target text and generated video, remaining strictly isolated from source drafts to prevent bias. Standard perceptual scores (e.g., Image Quality, Aesthetic) are reported separately as non-gated references VQ.

    Appearance Persistence (AP).

    Since maintaining an incorrect appearance over time is not always consistency, we therefore establish a correctness-gated persistence metric:

    AP=(100)/(|ℚ_AP|)∑_q∈ℚ_APc_q·s_q,

    		(3)

    where c_q∈{0,1} verifies target attribute realization at an anchor frame, and s_q∈{0,1} checks whether the identical entity retains that attribute across subsequent timestamps. Credit is awarded if and only if both pass (c_q·s_q=1).

    Grid Diagnostics and Aggregation.

    On the full 3×3 grid, we designate (P₁,A_N) as the canonical operating point and derive two diagnostic quantities: (i) Conflict Penalty, CP=RF(A_A)-RF(A_C), measuring performance drop under conflicting cues, and (ii) Source Leakage, SL=N_source_leaked/N_conflict, quantifying the erroneous persistence of conflicting source attributes.

    4 WorldDraft-Primer

    The dual correctness criteria of WorldDraft expose an inherent operational dilemma in generative rendering: how to reliably anchor target attributes without corrupting prescribed kinematics. While prompt engineering might seem intuitive, text prompts are inherently spatially agnostic, frequently inducing attribute cross-contamination across multiple entities. Conversely, modifying all draft frames risks destroying the deterministic kinematics and inducing temporal flickering. Leveraging the fact that video diffusion models naturally propagate initial appearances via spatiotemporal attention [(Fang et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2026)], we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy. WorldDraft-Primer intervenes strictly on the initial frame I₁ˢʳᶜ, producing a cued frame Ĩ₁:

    D̃=(Ĩ₁,I₂ˢʳᶜ,…,I_Tˢʳᶜ), V̂=G(D̃,p),

    		(4)

    leaving the remaining T-1 draft frames untouched to preserve the exact physical evolution.

    Object Emphasis for World Preservation.

    To prevent renderers from dropping small or low-contrast entities, object emphasis introduces sparse, non-intrusive bounding cues. Guided by the prompt p, an open-source VLM (i.e., Qwen3.5 [(Yang et al., 2025)]) identifies K critical entities, while an open-vocabulary grounding model predicts their 2D bounding boxes B={bₖ}ₖ₌₁^K. For each box bₖ, we generate a binary mask Mₖᶜᵒʳⁿᵉʳ∈{0,1}^H×W outlining minimalist corner brackets strictly around the entity periphery. The structural emphasis signal is formulated as:

    ΔI_OE=∑ₖ₌₁^KMₖᶜᵒʳⁿᵉʳ⊙Cₘₒₙₒ,

    		(5)

    where Cₘₒₙₒ is a neutral monochrome tone. Since Mₖᶜᵒʳⁿᵉʳ occupies only narrow peripheral margins without covering entity interiors or physical contact surfaces, it acts purely as a spatial anchor without altering underlying geometry.

    Attribute Cueing for Visual Realization.

    To steer appearance binding, attribute cueing injects non-textual hints across two levels: (i) entity cues (ΔIₑₙₜ), which modulate peripheral brackets with target colors, simplified texture patterns, or coarse specular shading while leaving source interiors visible; and (ii) environment cues (ΔIₑₙᵥ), which introduce soft contact shadows, coarse ground textures, or subtle lighting gradients onto supporting surfaces. The composite initial frame Ĩ₁ is formulated as:

    Ĩ₁=I₁ˢʳᶜ⊙(1-Mₐₗₗ)+(ΔI_OE+ΔIₑₙₜ+ΔIₑₙᵥ)⊙Mₐₗₗ,

    		(6)

    where Mₐₗₗ=∑ₖMₖᶜᵒʳⁿᵉʳ+Mₑₙᵥ is the aggregate cue mask. Cues remain strictly localized to keep source-target conflicts (A_C) uncompromised. To avoid generative noise and pixel blurring from diffusion inpainting, all prompts are synthesized programmatically via SVG, ensuring sub-pixel precision and strictly bounded transparency.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Settings

    Models.

    We benchmark 12 representative video models on WorldDraft, spanning three primary paradigms across 10 open-weight architectures: ➀ Generative Renderers: SolarRenderer-33B [(Fang et al., 2026)], C2R-14B [(Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026)]; ➁ Omni Models: MiniMax-H3-33B [(MiniMax, 2025)], LynnReal-Omni-32B [(Mao et al., 2026)], OmniWeaving-8.3B [(Pan et al., 2026)], VINO-13B [(Chen et al., 2026)], UniVideo-13B [(Wei et al., 2026)]; and ➂ Controllable Generators: Bernini-R-14B [(Team et al., 2026)], Wan2.2-VACE-Fun-A14B [(Jiang et al., 2025)], Wan2.1-VACE-14B [(Jiang et al., 2025)]. We additionally evaluate two leading commercial models: Wan 3.0 [(Wan et al., 2025)] and Seedance 2.5 [(ByteDance Seed, 2025)]. All models take (D,p) as input, ensuring consistent conditioning.

    Evaluations.

    Following Section3.4, we report aggregated dimensional metrics across three core perspectives: ❶ Rendering Performance summarizes overall competence across the full 3×3 grid via World Preservation (WP: Entity, Motion, Camera), Rendering Fidelity (RF), Visual Quality (VQ), and Appearance Persistence (AP); ❷ Granularity Gains measures endpoint gains (Δ₀₂) across draft levels (P₀→P₁→P₂) under neutral appearance A_N; and ❸ Conflict Robustness assesses resilience to conflicting source cues A_C at P₁ via RF_C, AP_C, Conflict Penalty (CP), and Source Leakage (SL). All scores are macro-averaged within each family before aggregating across families on common cohorts. More details in AppendixB.

    5.2 Main Results

    To systematically characterize the capability boundaries of video generative renderers, we first benchmark 12 video models across the 3×3 grid of WorldDraft. Key results in Table1 and Figure1 yield three primary takeaways:

    Takeaway ❶: World preservation and visual realization remain in stark tension.

    Models face an inherent dilemma between retaining 4D physics and realizing target appearance. As shown in the Rendering Performance columns of Table1 and Figure1, dedicated renderers (e.g., SolarRenderer) lead in Preservation (WP=63.28) but lag in Realization (RF=69.97). Conversely, large models (e.g., Wan 3.0) maximize Realization (RF=80.40) at the cost of severe physical corruption (WP=44.37, lowest overall). Remarkably, even prevailing commercial leaders like Seedance 2.5, which dominate conventional video benchmarks, fail to top WorldDraft (Overall: 64.73, edged out by 32B LynnReal-Omni at 64.89), compromised by sub-optimal physical preservation (WP=58.66). This confirms that generic visual scaling does not resolve the dual-correctness challenge.

    Takeaway ❷: Richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but impairs appearance binding.

    Advancing draft granularity (P₀→P₂ under A_N) reliably improves structure but yields negative appearance returns. As reported in the Granularity Gains of Table1 and Figure1, structural gains (gₛ) are consistently positive across open-weight models (e.g., +18.82 for Wan2.1-VACE), confirming that dense meshes suppress physical drift. However, appearance (gₐ) and binding (g_b) gains are negative for 9 out of 10 models (e.g., OmniWeaving drops by -14.47 / -15.95), with Seedance 2.5 as the sole exception (+2.51 / +3.21). Denser drafts introduce synthetic shading biases that actively override text-conditioned cross-attention.

    Takeaway ❸: Conflicting source cues trigger widespread leakage, exposing fragile disentanglement.

    Under contradictory source-target pairs (A_C at P₁), models struggle to separate motion scaffolds from surface appearances. As evidenced by the Conflict Robustness metrics in Table1 and Figure1, open-weight models suffer large Conflict Penalties (up to 10.63 for OmniWeaving) and rampant color leakage (e.g., 64.17% for Wan2.1-VACE and 52.24% for UniVideo). Even top commercial and large models (e.g., Wan 3.0, MiniMax-H3) exhibit ∼28%-30% leakage, revealing that renderers treat draft pixels as rigid visual constraints rather than overwritable scaffolds.

    5.3 Failure Mode Analysis

    To diagnose why state-of-the-art models struggle with generative rendering, Figure4 visualizes representative failure cases from top-performing models ( LynnReal-Omni and Seedance 2.5) on C05 (Occlusion & Reappearance) and A04 (Multi-Entity Orchestration):

    Failure Mode ❶: Prompt-driven structural override.

    When processing dynamic scenes with complex layouts, models frequently sacrifice draft kinematics to satisfy textual semantics. As illustrated in Figure4 (a), both LynnReal-Omni and Seedance 2.5 exhibit near-zero Spatial Preservation (consistently scoring ≤18.8, dipping to 6.2). Instead of adhering to the prescribed camera trajectory and warehouse shelving geometry, the models synthesize entirely ungrounded viewpoints and forklift trajectories conditioned solely on the prompt. This demonstrates that models easily devolve from faithful renderers into unconstrained text-to-video generators.

    Failure Mode ❷: Deficient spatial reasoning and attribute binding.

    Under neutral scaffolds (A_N), models exhibit weak spatial understanding, failing to parse relative coordinate references and topological arrangements. As shown in Figure4 (b) , the prompt specifies an ordered 3×4 color layout across 12 sailboats. Lacking the ability to resolve relative spatial hierarchies (e.g., row depths and left-to-right ordering), the models scramble target colors, causing severe attribute cross-contamination.

    Failure Mode ❸: Previs texture latching and conflicting leakage.

    Richer drafts and conflicting cues severely disrupt appearance synthesis. In Figure4 (b), advancing from simulation (P₁) to previs (P₂) causes Realization scores to collapse for both models (e.g., LynnReal-Omni drops from 73.1 to 46.2 under A_A, and plummets to 17.3 under A_C). Video diffusion models over-attend to the dense synthetic shading and specular highlights of P₂ drafts, treating them as immutable visual priors. Under conflict (A_C), models either persistently reproduce conflicting source colors (source leakage) or hallucinate unprescribed objects (e.g., LynnReal-Omni synthesizing an extra cluster of green sailboats at P₁,A_C) to compensate for text prompts, directly violating draft topology.

    5.4 Results with WorldDraft-Primer

    Motivated by the failure modes above, we further sought to investigate whether a lightweight test-time strategy can unlock frozen video renderers without retraining. To this end, we evaluate WorldDraft-Primer across representative models ( OmniWeaving and MiniMax-H3) against raw baselines and text prompt engineering (Text PE); results are in Table2 and Figures13 and 14.

    WorldDraft-Primer consistently enhances both world preservation and visual realization.

    As shown in Table2, WorldDraft-Primer consistently boosts both world preservation and appearance realization across architectures. For OmniWeaving, WorldDraft-Primer enhances Preservation (+2.99) and Realization (+4.56) while reducing Source Leakage by 3.42%, yielding an Overall gain of +2.51. For MiniMax-H3, it boosts Realization to 80.21 (+3.83) and elevates the Overall score to 65.56 (+1.93), surpassing both LynnReal-Omni (64.89) and the commercial leader Seedance 2.5 (64.73). Conversely, Text PE provides negligible improvements (+0.90 and +1.26), limited by the inherent spatial ambiguity of text. Qualitative results in Figures13 and 14 further confirm these findings: first-frame cues effectively stabilize global camera framing against unprompted zoom-ins, prevent multi-entity attribute cross-contamination (e.g., binding cobalt-blue exclusively to the rightmost ball in B02), and suppress deceptive source color leakage under A_C.

    6 Conclusion

    In this work, we explored the emerging division of labor between code-driven simulation and video generation by proposing WorldDraft, a systematic benchmark of 432 strictly paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families. Extensive evaluations across 12 representative models yield clear answers to our three foundational questions: ➀ world preservation and target appearance realization remain in stark operational tension; ➁ richer draft scaffolding reliably anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and ➂ conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage, exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we introduce WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer establish a foundational stepping stone toward physically grounded generative rendering.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A More Details of WorldDraft

    A.1 Motivation of Each Challenge

    Grounded in the dual objectives of world preservation and visual realization, WorldDraft curates dynamic scenarios that jointly impose deterministic physical constraints and multi-modal binding stressors. Evaluating generative renderers on these scenarios probes spatiotemporal reliability across diverse physical regimes: capabilities that conventional static image metrics fundamentally fail to measure. Below, we detail the design motivations behind our six dynamic challenge categories:

    Each executable world family in WorldDraft is categorized by its primary physical stressor, while naturally incorporating secondary dynamics. SectionA.2 illustrates representative cases and paired draft variants.

    A.2 Data Demonstration

    Figures5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 showcase representative cases across all six challenge categories, visualizing the real-world reference footage, target prompt, and the full 3×3 draft grid (P₀→P₂×A_N,A_A,A_C) for each world.

    Appendix B More Details of Evaluation Suite

    This section details the formal definitions, score normalization, and aggregation protocols underlying the three evaluation perspectives and the composite score in Table1. Formally, let c=(P,A)∈Ω denote an input condition, where Ω={P₀,P₁,P₂}×{A_N,A_A,A_C} represents the full 3×3 grid of 9 paired configurations across 48 executable world families {Wᵢ}ᵢ₌₁⁴⁸. All rate- and accuracy-based metrics are reported on a standard [0,100] scale.

    Shared Temporal & Spatial Protocol.

    To ensure fair cross-model comparisons regardless of native frame rates, all evaluations operate on the first 5 seconds of generated videos using absolute timestamp alignment rather than frame indices:

  • •

    Continuous Tracking & Geometry: Dense geometric evaluation (e.g., bounding boxes, tracks, and 6-DoF camera trajectories) is conducted at 8 Hz across 40 uniformly spaced timestamps (t∈[0,4.875] s).

  • •

    Sparse Attribute & Event QA: Appearance and interaction probes evaluate 8 key timestamps distributed across the 5-second duration. Following [(Huang et al., 2026)], question answering is executed via Qwen3.6-27B [(Yang et al., 2025)]. Visual inputs comprise both full frames and reference-grounded entity crops. To eliminate response bias, all probes incorporate strictly balanced affirmative and literal-negation questions.

  • •

    Strict Pre-registration: No output-dependent spatial alignment, post-hoc warping, or scale re-normalization is performed; models are strictly penalized for spatial drift, aspect distortion, or event desynchronization.

    • Below, we detail the metric composition and normalization for each perspective.

    B.1 Rendering Performance

    The Rendering Performance section in Table1 evaluates foundational generation capability across four dimensional scores: Preservation (WP), Realization (RF), Quality (VQ), and Persistence (AP).

    World Preservation.

    WP quantifies geometric, physical, and camera fidelity against simulator ground truth, hierarchically combining three sub-components:

    WP_c=0.40E_c+0.40M_c+0.20K_c.

    		(7)

    ➀ Entity and Layout (E): We combine Global Count (GC), Local Count (LC), and Bounding Box IoU (BI):

    E_c=0.25 GC_c+0.25 LC_c+0.50 BI_c.

    		(8)

    GC requires exact instance count agreement across all three sampled timestamps T_cnt={0,2.125,5} s, while LC evaluates per-frame count accuracy within reference-defined spatial regions:

    \beginsplitGC=100 𝔼_q[∏_t∈T_cnt1[n̂_q,t=n_q,t]], LC=100 𝔼_q,t[1[n̂_q,t=n_q,t]].\endsplit

    		(9)

    BI evaluates tracked 2D bounding boxes against simulator-projected amodal 3D entity bounds (including deformation). Entities are detected via SAM3 [(Carion et al., 2026)] using attribute-agnostic category prompts and matched across time using global Hungarian assignment (IoU threshold ≥0.05):

    BI=100 𝔼ₑ[(1)/(|Tₑ|)∑_t∈TₑIoU(B_e,t,B̂_a(e),t)].

    		(10)

    Unmatched entities and missing boxes are scored as 0.

    ➁ Motion and Events (M): We assess dynamic continuity and physical causality via Matched Track Coverage (TC), Interaction Success Rate (ISR), and Event Timing Coverage (EC):

    M_c=0.25 TC_c+0.50 ISR_c+0.25 EC_c.

    		(11)

    TC=100 𝔼_e∈O_dyn[(1)/(|Tₑ|)∑_t∈Tₑ1[B̂_a(e),texists]] measures the temporal presence of tracked dynamic entities under the accepted assignment. ISR=100 𝔼_q[1[â_q=a_q] 1[ô_q=o_q]] validates that both the dynamic action (a_q) and its physical outcome (o_q) are simultaneously correct over 12 uniform frames. EC=100·(N_localized/N_expected) reports the fraction of causal events whose temporal boundary intervals [tₛₜₐᵣₜ,t_end] are successfully localized.

    ➂ Camera Kinematics (K): Evaluated across the 8 camera-motion families by estimating 6-DoF trajectories (R(t),t(t)) via ViPE [(Huang et al., 2025)] against the canonical draft. Camera translation is scale-normalized by trajectory peak norm: u(t)=t(t)/(\max_τ∥t(τ)∥₂+10⁻⁹). The camera fidelity score K∈[0,100] maps rotation error Rot∈[0,180^∘] and normalized translation error Trans∈[0,2] to:

    K=100[1-1/2(Rot/180+Trans/2)].

    		(12)

    Rendering Fidelity.

    Rendering Fidelity evaluates compliance with target color, material, texture, environment, and lighting specifications via balanced binary VLM QA on source-blind judges:

    RF=(100)/(|ℚ_RF|)∑_q∈ℚ_RF1[ŷ_q=y_q].

    		(13)

    Each probe evaluates visual evidence at the timestamp where reference entity visibility is maximized.

    Visual Quality.

    Following VBench [(Huang et al., 2024b)], we compute frame-level technical and aesthetic quality across all native frames F in the first 5 seconds using MUSIQ-SPAQ [(Ke et al., 2021)] (IQ∈[0,100]) and LAION [(Schuhmann et al., 2022)] aesthetic predictor on CLIP ViT-L/14 [(Radford et al., 2021)] (AQ=10×Aesthetic∈[0,100]):

    VQ=1/2((1)/(|F|)∑_f∈FIQ(f)+(1)/(|F|)∑_f∈FAQ(f)).

    		(14)

    Appearance Persistence.

    AP measures whether a correctly instantiated target attribute persistently binds to the entity over time:

    AP=(100)/(|ℚ_AP|)∑_q∈ℚ_APc_q·s_q,

    		(15)

    where c_q∈{0,1} verifies attribute realization at a visible anchor frame, and s_q∈{0,1} verifies temporal consistency across subsequent visible timestamps. An incorrect anchor (c_q=0) strictly zeroes out the score.

    Aggregation.

    For any metric X∈{WP,RF,VQ,AP}, we first macro-average per-video scores across its applicable world family cohort I_X for each condition c∈ℂ:

    X_c=(1)/(|I_X|)∑_i∈I_Xs^(X)_i,c.

    		(16)

    The four Rendering Performance columns in Table1 report the mean score over the full 3×3 grid:

    Grid(X)=1/9∑_c∈ℂX_c.

    		(17)

    Across models, each metric is computed strictly over common valid cohorts for uncompromised fairness.

    B.2 Granularity Gains

    To quantify how generative renderers benefit from structural scaffolding without confounding appearance cues, we evaluate the geometric information ladder (P₀→P₁→P₂) strictly under the neutral appearance condition (A_N). For any metric X∈{WP,RF,AP}, the paired marginal change between draft granularities Pₐ and P_b is defined as:

    Δ_ab^X=X_(P_b,A_N)-X_(Pₐ,A_N).

    		(18)

    All comparisons enforce strictly paired world families, keeping underlying metric cohorts fixed before constructing WP.

    As summarized in Table1, we report the net endpoint gains from abstract proxy scaffolds (P₀) to dense preview drafts (P₂) across three corresponding columns:

    \beginsplitgₛ (Structure)=Δ₀₂^WP, gₐ (Appearance)=Δ₀₂^RF, g_b (Binding)=Δ₀₂^AP.\endsplit

    		(19)

    Differences preserve their algebraic signs: positive values signify performance gains enabled by richer structural cues, whereas negative values expose degradation or visual interference. While Table1 focuses on endpoint dynamics Δ₀₂, adjacent transitions (Δ₀₁ and Δ₁₂) and per-level absolute scores are documented in supplementary material to diagnose non-monotonicity and saturation behaviors.

    B.3 Conflict Robustness

    To further evaluate how reliably generative renderers disentangle structural scaffolding from deceptive visual cues, we probe the model’s resistance to contradictory source-target pairs. Fixing the structural scaffold at the canonical simulation operating point (P₁), Table1 reports four complementary metrics:

    \beginsplitAdherence↑&=RF_(P₁,A_C), Retention↑&=AP_(P₁,A_C), Penalty (CP)↓&=RF_(P₁,A_A)-RF_(P₁,A_C), Leakage (SL)↓&=SL_(P₁,A_C).\endsplit

    		(20)

    Adherence and Retention measure absolute target attribute correctness and temporal binding under contradictory conditions (A_C). Conflict Penalty (CP) quantifies the relative fidelity degradation incurred when source cues transition from aligned (A_A) to conflicting (A_C); lower values denote superior immunity to deceptive source distractors.

    Source Leakage.

    SL explicitly tracks the erroneous persistence of conflicting source colors on target entities. For the set of verified source-color probes ℚ_SL and their valid timestamps T_q, it is formulated as:

    SL=(100)/(|ℚ_SL|)∑_q∈ℚ_SL(1)/(|T_q|)∑_t∈T_q1[ŷ_q,t=Yes],

    		(21)

    where ŷ_q,t=Yes indicates the active presence of the contradictory source color. Probes are constructed from audited source materials across 48 world families with explicit color contradictions. Note that low SL does not trivially imply correct target realization.

    B.4 Composite Overall Metric

    To provide a unified ranking across diverse model paradigms, the Overall column in Table1 integrates the three diagnostic perspectives via pre-registered weights:

    Overall=0.50 R+0.25 G+0.25 C_rob,

    		(22)

    allocating 50% to foundational rendering capability, 25% to structural granularity responsiveness, and 25% to source-target conflict disentanglement. All underlying metrics are bounded in [0,100]:

    Rendering Score (R).

    Within each condition c∈ℂ, we combine the macro-averaged dimensional scores using a weighted geometric mean before averaging across the 3×3 grid R=1/9∑_c∈ℂS_c:

    \beginsplitS_c=100·((WP_c)/(100))^0.40((RF_c)/(100))^0.20((AP_c)/(100))^0.30((VQ_c)/(100))^0.10.\endsplit

    		(23)

    The geometric mean strictly penalizes degenerate shortcuts (e.g., preserving kinematics by completely ignoring target prompts, or satisfying prompts by severely corrupting the 4D world), rewarding renderers that achieve balanced dual-correctness.

    Granularity Score (G).

    Since individual endpoint gains g∈{gₛ,gₐ,g_b} lie in [-100,100], we linearly normalize them to a standard [0,100] scale (where 50 denotes zero net change) before computing their unweighted average:

    G=1/3∑_g∈{gₛ,gₐ,g_b}(50+g/2)=50+(gₛ+gₐ+g_b)/(6).

    		(24)

    Conflict Robustness Score (C_rob).

    We unify the four conflict metrics into a higher-is-better index in [0,100]:

    \beginsplitC_rob=1/4[RF_(P₁,A_C)+AP_(P₁,A_C)+ (100-\max(CP,0))+(100-SL_(P₁,A_C))].\endsplit

    		(25)

    Here, the Conflict Penalty CP is clipped at zero to avoid rewarding negative penalties (which arise from statistical variance rather than genuine robustness), while source leakage SL is inverted.

    While the Overall score offers a holistic summary, the underlying gains and penalties are inherently dependent on each model’s baseline operating performance. Therefore, the standalone columns in Table1 remain essential for diagnosing individual failure modes and capability trade-offs.

    B.5 Analysis of Metric-Human Alignment

    To validate the VLM evaluation protocol part of WorldDraft, we compare algorithmic decisions against blind annotations from five independent human judges on randomly sampled test cases, using majority voting as ground truth. As shown in Figure11, automated metrics achieve strong human agreement across all six dimensions, ranging from 87.5% to 94.2% (averaging 91.0%). Appearance probes exhibit the highest concordance (RF:94.2%, SL:92.5%, AP:91.5%), while physical and count metrics remain highly reliable (ISR:90.8%, GC:89.2%, LC:87.5%). This validates our automated benchmark suite as a faithful surrogate for human judgment.

    Appendix C More Details of WorldDraft-Primer

    C.1 Case Demonstration and Analysis

    Figures13 and 14 visualize qualitative rollouts across the 3×3 grid for B02 (Newton’s Cradle) and D02 (Water-Tank Tower). Across both scenarios, WorldDraft-Primer visibly improves adherence to input drafts: it stabilizes global camera framing against erratic zoom-ins, suppresses ball dropouts in B02 while precisely isolating target colors to the rightmost sphere, and preserves surrounding town layouts in D02 while mitigating deceptive A_C roof colors.

    Capacity Dependency and Method Positioning.

    Crucially, WorldDraft-Primer operates as a lightweight visual prompting strategy whose efficacy remains inherently tethered to the underlying base model. On weaker architectures (e.g., OmniWeaving), the model occasionally struggles to assimilate the injected first-frame cues into photorealistic textures, sometimes faintly echoing prompt brackets across subsequent frames. Furthermore, under dense previs drafts (P₂), strong synthetic priors can still bias the renderer toward artificial, plastic-like shading. Ultimately, WorldDraft-Primer serves as an analytical proof-of-concept demonstrating that test-time visual cues can steer frozen video models. Fully overcoming dense prior interference and enabling seamless prompt assimilation remain important challenges for future work.

    C.2 Ablation Study of WorldDraft-Primer

    To dissect the individual contributions of Object Emphasis (ΔI_OE) and Attribute Cueing (ΔIₑₙₜ+ΔIₑₙᵥ), we ablate each component on MiniMax-H3 across the full benchmark. As shown in Figure12, the two mechanisms exhibit remarkable orthogonality and synergy:
