The dataset also includes the shared 3D world representation, world states, and player-action metadata, enabling the community to build proxies tailored to their needs.

  • •

    We achieve state-of-the-art results among the evaluated methods in cross-view player identity and video quality, outperforming Seedance 2.5 and SolarRenderer.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive Generation and Memory.

    Video generation now covers joint audio-video synthesis and long-form, multi-shot narratives [(Hu et al., 2026b; Hu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b)]. Genie learns controllable environments from videos through latent actions [(Bruce et al., 2024)], and GameNGen predicts gameplay observations from previous frames and actions [(Valevski et al., 2025)]. Maintaining a coherent environment over longer interactions requires information beyond the current visual context. WorldMem retrieves historical observations using their associated states [(Xiao et al., 2026)], VMem indexes views by the surface elements they observe [(Li et al., 2025)], and TeleWorld couples generation with 4D reconstruction and persistent memory [(Chen et al., 2025)]. WorldPlay studies geometric consistency in real-time generation [(Sun et al., 2026b)], and SolarWM examines data and training for long-horizon world models [(Huang et al., 2026)]. Cycle-World reduces error accumulation through reverse-prediction cycle consistency [(Su et al., 2026)]. Our setting adds a spatial relation between simultaneous player observations: the same entity can be visible through different cameras within one generated interval.

    Multiplayer and Multiview Generation.

    Solaris jointly models synchronized Minecraft observations and actions [(Savva et al., 2026)]. ShareVerse exchanges features through cross-agent attention [(Zhu et al., 2026)], and Gamma-World uses permutation-symmetric encoding and sparse hub attention to coordinate multiple agents [(Liu et al., 2026)]. Geometric representations provide another source of cross-view information. MultiWorld extracts a 3D-aware global latent state from multiple observations [(Wu et al., 2026)]; Prisma-World combines relative camera geometry, joint attention, and minimap guidance [(Sun et al., 2026a)]; MetaWorld aligns camera and subject trajectories across generation branches [(Hu et al., 2026a)]. Our renderer also couples the generation process, using camera-specific projections of a shared 3D scene as its structural conditions.

    Explicit State and Visual Synthesis.

    MultiGen separates memory, observation, and dynamics, using an external level map and player poses to support multiplayer rollouts [(Po et al., 2026)]. MASS combines a logic engine that updates typed state with a rendering engine that produces camera-specific observations [(Cai et al., 2026)], while PhysOmni and PhysAgent decouples physics simulation from visual synthesis [(Zhang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026)]. EgoSim generates action-conditioned observations and updates a persistent 3D scene state from them [(Hao et al., 2026)]. These methods separate world-state maintenance from appearance synthesis. We adopt this separation at the rendering interface: an external environment supplies scene and entity observations, and a joint video model translates their projections into player views. Our method addresses conditional observation synthesis; learning action-driven state transitions is outside the renderer.

    Structural Conditions and Proxy Rendering.

    ControlNet demonstrates spatial control of pretrained diffusion models using conditions such as depth and pose [(Zhang et al., 2023)]. PoseAnything extends pose guidance to human and non-human subjects [(Wang et al., 2025)], while MotionMaster transfers camera motion without training [(Hu et al., 2024)]. Related controls include camera and object trajectories in SymphoMotion [(Zhang et al., 2026a)], geometry latents in VideoWeave [(Xiang et al., 2026)], and depth trajectories with reference appearance in UniWorld [(Zhang et al., 2026c)]. Code World Model maintains executable state and compiles it into coarse proxy video [(Chen et al., 2026a)], while ProxyUp uses proxy dynamics to guide generated content [(Zhou et al., 2026)]. Seedance 2.5 also supports textureless 3D render references [(ByteDance Seed, 2026)]. SolarRenderer adapts native reference conditioning for video synthesis from structural and appearance inputs [(Fang et al., 2026)]. We extend this rendering formulation to paired observations of a common scene. The structural inputs connect the cameras through map coordinates and entity identities, and the concatenated generation context makes appearance evidence available across views.

    3 Method

    Given two camera trajectories, their proxy videos, and a paired appearance reference, our goal is to generate both players’ observations of the same scene. Figure 2 summarizes the renderer. We first construct paired structural observations from gameplay, then organize the two views in a shared generation context and adapt a pretrained video transformer to this task.

    3.1 Dataset Construction and 3D Proxy–Video Alignment

    Scene Representation.

    We collect two-player GTA V gameplay through a private FiveM server. For each client, we record RGB video, camera parameters, and the identities and poses of players and nearby entities. We export static map geometry in the same coordinate system. The map and persistent entity identifiers connect observations of the same scene across cameras. Dynamic observations retain the states available to each client under local streaming and network updates.

    Let M denote the shared map, 𝔼ₜ⁽ᵖ⁾ the entity observations of player p, and Cₜ⁽ᵖ⁾ its camera pose and projection at time t. The proxy renderer produces

    Pₜ⁽ᵖ⁾=ℝ(M,𝔼ₜ⁽ᵖ⁾,Cₜ⁽ᵖ⁾), p∈{1,2}.

    		(1)

    The map preserves surfaces and obstacles, and simplified character and vehicle geometry represents dynamic entities. Projecting these elements into each camera makes their relative positions, scale, motion, and occlusions available as image-space conditions. The proxy is textureless: its category colors identify coarse entities, while clothing, materials, and scene appearance come from the RGB reference and video prior.

    Paired Supervision.

    We align the two recordings using estimated server timestamps and retain intervals with observations from both players. Each RGB frame is paired with a proxy rendered from its associated camera and entity observations. A training example contains the two RGB video clips, two proxy clips, a joint appearance reference image, and a caption. We take the first RGB frame of each view as its training appearance reference. Captions describe the scene, shared character identities, and the actions and visibility within each view. The paired targets supervise both proxy adherence within a camera and the appearance of shared entities across cameras. Figure 3 summarizes the clip distribution across four gameplay categories and shows paired visual examples.

    3.2 Joint Generation in a Shared Context

    Spatial Organization.

    The proxy specifies geometry but leaves visual detail ambiguous. To make appearance evidence available across cameras, we concatenate the views along image width:

    Vₜ=[Vₜ⁽¹⁾|Vₜ⁽²⁾], Pₜ=[Pₜ⁽¹⁾|Pₜ⁽²⁾],

    		(2)

    where Vₜ⁽ᵖ⁾ is an RGB frame. Player 1 always occupies the left half and player 2 the right half, including in the joint reference I. With V=(Vₜ)ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹, P=(Pₜ)ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹, and caption c, we model

    p_θ,φ(V|P,I,c),

    		(3)

    where θ denotes frozen pretrained parameters and φ the learned adaptation. The two halves preserve their camera-specific content within one prediction task.

    Reference Conditioning.

    We use the native image-and-video reference interface of MiniMax H3. The joint RGB image provides appearance evidence, and the joint proxy video specifies the evolving structure. The backbone encodes these references and the target video into a shared attention context. Full bidirectional attention lets a target region use reference and target features from either player. For example, clothing visible in one reference view can inform synthesis of the same character in the other view. The caption supplies scene and action information that complements the visual conditions.

    The reference segments remain conditioned while the target is denoised. We retain the backbone’s native reference encoding and attention layers, with LoRA applied to the attention projections and feed-forward layers [(Hu et al., 2021)]. Unlike treating each view as a separate training example, the paired canvas exposes both observations to every joint prediction. Cross-view appearance correspondence is learned from the paired RGB supervision; the geometric representation supplies the camera-specific structural constraints.

    3.3 Learning and Inference

    We use the backbone’s flow-matching objective to adapt the renderer [(Huang et al., 2026)]. Let z be the clean latent of the joint RGB clip and ε∼ℕ(0,I) Gaussian noise. For flow time τ∈[0,1], the noised target is z_τ=τz+(1-τ)ε. We optimize the task adapters with

    L(φ)=𝔼 [1/N∥v_θ,φ(z_τ,τ;P,I,c)-(z-ε)∥₂²],

    		(4)

    where v_θ,φ predicts latent velocity and N counts the target latent elements. The loss covers both player regions and excludes the reference segments. The expectation is over training examples, noise, and sampled flow times.

    At inference, the proxy views and appearance reference use the same layout as in training. The reference can specify a visual style different from the source gameplay while the proxy retains its trajectories. We jointly denoise and decode the target canvas, remove spatial padding, and split it into two player videos. The generation process consumes the supplied proxy interval, so each output is conditioned on the recorded motion throughout that interval.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate how well our renderer translates shared gameplay into visually coherent player views across different appearances and environments. We first introduce the benchmark and evaluation protocol, then compare with video generation and rendering baselines, followed by qualitative comparisons and ablations of the proxy representation and generation architecture.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmark.

    We construct a benchmark of 150 two-player cases covering four event categories: exploration, vehicle riding, player fighting, and environment interactions. The proxy trajectories are sampled from GTA V gameplay and provide synchronized structural conditions for the two player views. We use GPT Image 2.5 [(OpenAI, 2026)] to stylize the corresponding reference images, changing player appearances, background environments, and visual styles. Each case pairs these appearance references with the original proxy trajectories, testing whether the renderer can preserve the shared gameplay under appearance and scene changes.

    Evaluation Protocol.

    Following SolarRenderer [(Fang et al., 2026)], we assess visual quality, temporal stability, structural adherence, and reference preservation. DOVER [(Wu et al., 2023)] and the LAION aesthetic predictor measure video quality and frame aesthetics, respectively. DINO Adj. measures temporal appearance stability through the cosine similarity of adjacent-frame DINOv2 embeddings [(Oquab et al., 2024)]. Edge F1 measures agreement between the generated and proxy contours, while First-frame measures DINOv2 similarity between the final second of the generated video and the supplied appearance reference. We evaluate both player views over the same temporal interval, average the view scores within each case, and then average across cases.

    We additionally evaluate whether the same player retains a consistent identity and action across views. The proxy provides player identities, visibility, and spatial correspondences at each second. Whenever a player is visible in multiple views, we use these correspondences to extract synchronized crops of that player from the generated videos. Qwen3.8-27B compares each crop pair and separately judges whether the depicted player identity and action agree, accounting for changes in viewpoint. The paired judgments test player consistency across simultaneous observations.

    4.2 Quantitative and Qualitative Comparison

    Baselines.

    Some multiplayer world models rely on detailed, scene-specific map geometry during training [(Ye et al., 2026)], making direct comparison across the diverse scenes in our benchmark difficult. We therefore select Gamma-World [(Liu et al., 2026)] as a multiplayer baseline: it generates player observations conditioned on initial frames and player action sequences, without requiring an explicit scene map as input. We also compare with two general-purpose video models, MiniMax-H3 [(MiniMaxAI, 2026)] and Seedance 2.5 [(ByteDance Seed, 2026)], each conditioned on the corresponding appearance references and proxy trajectories. SolarRenderer [(Fang et al., 2026)] provides a further baseline that uses a video model as a renderer. Since SolarRenderer supports a single player view, we generate the two views separately from their respective proxies and appearance references. All methods are evaluated on the same benchmark using the same evaluation protocol. To examine an existing multiplayer generation strategy on the same backbone, we adapt MetaWorld’s dual-branch alignment mechanism from its Wan backbone to MiniMax-H3 and fine-tune it on our paired data; Section 4.4 presents this comparison.

    Results.

    Table 1 compares visual quality, structural adherence, appearance preservation, and cross-view player identity. Gamma-World performs substantially worse than the video generation and rendering baselines, with particularly weak reference preservation and cross-view identity consistency. This result highlights the difficulty of transferring existing multiplayer world models to the diverse scenes and appearances in our benchmark. Relative to Seedance 2.5, our renderer improves visual quality and agreement with the proxy structure, together with a higher cross-view identity score. The improvement in identity consistency is particularly relevant to multiplayer rendering, where a player’s appearance must agree across simultaneous observations. Our method also achieves competitive temporal appearance stability and reference preservation compared with Seedance 2.5.

    Qualitative Cross-View Results.

    Figure 4 compares appearance and visibility across views. Seedance assigns inconsistent clothing to the same player in the farm scene and omits the courier from one view in the night-street scene. Our renderer maintains consistent clothing in the former and shows the courier in both views in the latter.

    4.3 Proxy Representation Comparison

    Figure 5 examines three proxy constructions. Raw provides coarse scene and entity geometry. Detail & Lighting adds scene detail and shading, while Skeleton additionally exposes approximate character articulation. Raw’s coarse geometry cannot accurately represent depth relationships, occlusion, and local scene structure in complex environments. The resulting ambiguity is accompanied by blackened image regions, visible around the industrial structures, and weaker following of the proxy’s spatial layout and motion. Adding scene detail and lighting provides more informative contours, depth cues, and shading, improving the rendering of complex surroundings while retaining coarse character control.

    Adding Skeleton makes character pose and limb trajectories more explicit, but this extra precision can overconstrain the video model. It reduces the freedom of the learned video prior to infer natural articulation from the reference appearance and coarse motion. In the corresponding videos, characters tend to copy the proxy’s prescribed limb movements too literally, producing rigid, less natural motion. This limitation is particularly apparent when a human-like skeleton controls a non-human reference character, such as the beagle in the beach example. Based on these observations, we favor detailed environment geometry and lighting with coarse character motion, leaving fine articulation to the video prior.

    4.4 Generation Method Ablation

    We compare our joint generation method with a dual-branch variant inspired by MetaWorld [(Hu et al., 2026a)]. The variant assigns a separate generation branch to each player and uses cross-attention to exchange features between the branches during denoising. Our method generates both views on a concatenated canvas within a shared attention context.

    Figure 6 compares the two methods on a shared courtyard scene, focusing on the same player’s clothing across views.

    5 Discussion and Conclusion

    5.1 Conclusion

    Shared 3D proxies provide a spatial interface between a multiplayer environment and a generative video renderer. Our implementation combines paired camera projections with joint appearance conditioning, adapting a pretrained transformer to synthesize two player views within one context. The evaluation shows higher DOVER, LAION aesthetic quality, edge alignment, and cross-view player-identity consistency than Seedance 2.5 on the recorded appearance-transfer cases, together with remaining adjacent-frame and reference-preservation errors.

    The shared proxy interface could support collaborative virtual environments, with future device–edge–cloud deployment guided by the AI Flow framework [(An et al., 2025; Shao and Li, 2025)]. Extending the renderer to more players requires managing the growing attention context; learned state transitions and sustained interaction remain directions for future work.

    5.2 Limitations

    Our current implementation is limited to two-player generation. The joint generation formulation can in principle extend to N players by concatenating their views within the same context. At fixed per-view resolution and clip length, however, each additional player increases the token sequence and hence the attention computation and memory requirements of the single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT). Scaling to larger player groups therefore requires a more efficient way to manage this shared context.

    Our current renderer uses bidirectional attention with 50 denoising steps. Distilling it to eight steps retains good visual quality in our experiments. Although the proxy can accept inputs in real time, meeting our real-time rendering target requires reducing generation to one or two denoising steps. Our preliminary attempts show that preserving generation quality under such aggressive distillation remains challenging.

    6 Acknowledgment

    We thank Teng Hu for providing advice on the project. We also thank Xinya Wang and Jiahao Yin for collecting the data.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 世界模型不该只模拟物理现实：Duo 把「智能」也当成世界的一部分，做全双工实时交互 ｜ Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction
item.description:
一句话：现有世界模型大多只模拟物理现实，把推理与决策当成外挂控制。

要点：

  • 立场很明确：ReciprocalWorldModel（RWM）把智能与物理现实视为构成「世界」的同等基本要素
  • 批评现有做法：多数世界模型只模拟后者（物理现实），而把推理与决策当成**外部的控制信号**塞进去
  • Duo v1 是一个全双工世界模型：一边持续感知视听输入，一边实时回应用户

为什么值得看：「世界模型要不要包含智能体」是路线问题。把智能放进世界内部、并做成全双工实时交互，是最接近「引擎里跑 NPC 与世界」的形态——比只做视频预测更贴近游戏需要。

中文摘要：这篇提出 ReciprocalWorldModel（RWM）框架与 Duo v1 模型，立场是把「智能」与「物理现实」看作构成世界的同等基本要素：一个世界不只是被模拟的物理场景，也包括在其中推理与决策的主体。作者批评现有世界模型大多只模拟后者，而把推理与决策留作外部的控制输入。Duo v1 因此被设计为全双工（full-duplex）世界模型：一边持续感知视听输入，一边实时对用户作出回应。对游戏而言，这正是「世界与 NPC 同处一个模型」的形态。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction

Abstract

In this report, we introduce the ReciprocalWorldModel (RWM) and present Duov1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audiovisual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duov1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duov1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

Contents

1 Introduction

World models have made rapid progress in simulating the physical side of a world [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Hafner et al., 2025, Brooks et al., 2024)]: given past observations and control signals, they predict how scenes evolve [(Bruce et al., 2024, Valevski et al., 2025, Hu et al., 2023, NVIDIA, 2025)], with increasingly realistic dynamics, appearance, and long-range consistency [(Google DeepMind, 2024, Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025, Robbyant Team, 2026, Gao et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026, Huang et al., 2026a)]. In most of these works, however, intelligence resides outside the world. A user steers the generated world through inputs with limited degrees of freedom, such as keyboard and mouse commands, gamepad actions, or text prompts, but nothing within the world perceives the full state of the user in real time or decides how to respond. Such worlds can be accurate, yet they remain lifeless: there is a world to explore, but no one to talk to.

We argue that intelligence and physical reality are equally fundamental to a world. Building on this view, we introduce the ReciprocalWorldModel (RWM). The RWM generates a world inhabited by living presences and connects it to the real world through full-duplex, real-time interaction. Each side continuously perceives audio and video from the other and can respond, interrupt, or remain silent while the other is still acting. This reciprocal interaction requires two complementary capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audiovisual behavior. These functional roles can be fulfilled by a unified multimodal model or by a modular system combining a multimodal language model with a diffusion model. In this report, we present Duov1, a modular instantiation of the RWM. Interaction proceeds in chunks of 17 video frames, approximately 0.71 s at 24 fps. Three technical designs coordinate Intent and Realization within a single streaming system.

Autoregressive intent for interaction.

In most audio-visual video generative model [(MiniMax, 2026)], a language model serves as an instruction encoder for the diffusion model. In Duov1, the intent module instead reasons over the ongoing interaction autoregressively and makes participation decisions: at every chunk, it emits a action followed by text or a action, conditioned on the user input so far and its own earlier language. Its hidden states, rather than its decoded text alone, carry each decision to the realization module (Sec. 3). Action-aware rebalancing prevents the intent module from collapsing into perpetual waiting, since most chunks contain no new assistant speech, and history perturbations teach it to recover from imperfect earlier responses (Sec. 4).

Causal chunk conditions on a unified timeline.

User speech, user video, intent tokens, and assistant media are synchronized on one timeline, and each chunk is given exactly the conditions that are available at its decision boundary. Module-specific attention masks enforce causality within and across chunks. In the intent module, temporal patches are completed inside each chunk, so no future frame leaks into a decision through the visual frontend. In the realization module, noisy media tokens of a chunk can attend to the reference, intent features, and clean history, but not to their own clean targets or to any later chunk (Sec. 3).

Dual rollout distillation.

Before distillation, the realization module is trained on intent features of recorded assistant text and on recorded media history, whereas in a live exchange both are produced by the system itself. Dual rollout brings inference-time conditioning into distillation: within each training window, the frozen Intent Module autoregressively generates the final assistant turn, and the Realization Module conditions on the resulting intent features and its own generated audiovisual history. Distribution matching distillation on these rollouts yields a four-step streaming generator trained under conditions that match live interaction.

We develop several data construction pipelines and a streaming runtime to support Duov1. The training data combine scripted synthetic video calls and recorded conversations, with audio, video, and text aligned on a shared timeline for causal interaction training (Sec. 5). The streaming pipeline coordinates intent inference, audiovisual generation, and incremental decoding while continuing to capture user inputs (Sec. 6). Speech and vision provide a rich, direct channel between the two worlds, conveying information that keyboard and mouse commands often fail to capture, including tone, timing, expression, and visual details of real objects, actions, and scenes. This richer interface creates opportunities for a wide range of shared activities shaped jointly by real and generated participants.

2 Related Work

World models and persistent interaction.

World Models and Dreamer learn predictive representations for control [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Hafner et al., 2025)], while Genie learns action-controllable environments from video [(Bruce et al., 2024)]. LingBot-World studies a data engine and staged causal adaptation for continuing visual worlds [(Robbyant Team, 2026)]. These works connect learned dynamics to an agent’s actions and subsequent observations.

Full-duplex and multimodal participation.

Moshi represents concurrent user and assistant speech streams [(Défossez et al., 2024)]. Qwen-Omni separates multimodal understanding from streaming speech generation through connected Thinker and Talker components [(Xu et al., 2025a, Xu et al., 2025b)]. Wan-Streamer extends the streaming setting to audio–visual foundation models and their execution schedule [(Huang et al., 2026b)]. ELLSA jointly models full-duplex speech, gesture, and expression, including non-verbal behavior while listening [(Wang et al., 2026)]. These works establish participation timing and visible communicative behavior as closely related modeling problems.

Joint and streaming audiovisual generation.

Ovi, MOVA, and LTX develop synchronized audio–visual generation through coupled modality streams [(Low et al., 2025, SII-OpenMOSS Team, 2026, HaCohen et al., 2026)]. MiniMax-H3 is a reference-conditioned audio–visual generator whose weights can initialize related models [(MiniMax, 2026)]. Audio-driven animation methods such as EMO and OmniHuman realize visible behavior from supplied speech [(Tian et al., 2024, Lin et al., 2025)]. LiveTalk combines a distilled video performer with streaming audio from Qwen-Omni [(Chern et al., 2025)]. These approaches connect speech with visible articulation and motion, with different choices of conditioning and generation order. Streaming joint diffusion further requires audio and video to remain aligned as their generated histories grow. OmniForcing addresses this conversion through asymmetric block-causal alignment, audio-sink stabilization, and joint self-generated rollouts [(Su et al., 2026)]. OmniLiveAvatar combines progressive autoregressive distillation, synchronized audio-video memory, and rolling prompt planning [(Zhu et al., 2026b)].

Causal adaptation and few-step training.

Diffusion Forcing assigns different noise levels across a sequence, and CausVid distills a bidirectional generator into a causal few-step student [(Chen et al., 2024, Yin et al., 2025)]. Self Forcing uses self-generated history during training to reduce the context mismatch with autoregressive inference [(Huang et al., 2025)]. Work on causal-compatible initialization further aligns teacher and student during the transition to few-step generation [(Zhu et al., 2026a, Zhao et al., 2026)]. Consistency models and distribution matching provide complementary tools for reducing sampling steps [(Song et al., 2023, Yin et al., 2024b)], with later distribution-matching work incorporating multistep alignment and adversarial training [(Yin et al., 2024a)].

3 Architecture

Duov1 couples a language-based Intent Module with a causal audiovisual Realization Module (Fig. 2). Hidden states produced by the Intent Module serve as the interface between the two modules, providing semantic guidance for the joint generation of video and stereo audio for the assistant. The two modules process complementary inputs and maintain separate histories, integrating response planning and audiovisual synthesis within a unified architecture. The following subsections describe this design in detail: Sec. 3.1 formalizes the interaction between the two modules, Sec. 3.2 details the Intent Module, Sec. 3.3 describes the audio-visual latent space, and Sec. 3.4 presents the causal joint generator used by the Realization Module.

3.1 The Overview of Reciprocal World Model

RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental components of a world. Their interaction is reciprocal: Intent determines how the system responds to the evolving environment, while Realization expresses that intent through audiovisual behavior, which in turn becomes part of the environment for subsequent interaction. We formalize this process as a chunk-wise, full-duplex interaction.

An interaction is divided into consecutive chunks of fixed duration, and cₖ denotes the chunk at time index k. A chunk is a time interval and need not align with a word, a sentence, or a conversational turn. For each chunk cₖ, let uₖᵛ, uₖᵗ, and uₖᵃ denote the incoming video, speech transcript, and audio, respectively. Let yₖ denote the language output generated by Duov1, either followed by text or . Let hₖ denote the hidden states produced by the Intent Module for this output, and zₖ=(zₖᵛ,zₖᵃ) the latent representations of the generated video and audio. We use the subscript

At each chunk k, Duov1 generates a response cₖ in two steps, where
C^φₖ=(d, xᵛ_u,(1)
yₖ∼p_φ( ·|C^φₖ), hₖ=f_φ(C^φₖ, yₖ).

The model forward pass produces the text output yₖ and hidden states hₖ, which convey the intent to the Realization Module. The Realization Module jointly generates audio and video latents, conditioned on the reference image I_ref, the intent hidden states hₖ, user video embeddings xᵛ_u,
C^θₖ=(I_ref, hₖ, xᵛ_u,(2)
(zᵃₖ, zᵛₖ)∼p_θ( ·|C^θₖ).

The generated latents zᵃₖ and zᵛₖ are decoded into the audio and video of the response chunk cₖ.

This formulation has two properties. First, it is causal. Both modules condition on interaction histories preceding chunk k, and the Realization Module additionally receives the current intent representation hₖ. Neither module accesses future inputs. User inputs received during response generation can be incorporated into subsequent chunks, supporting full-duplex interaction. Second, it supports continuity across chunks. The text output yₖ and generated latents zᵃₖ and zᵛₖ are added to the corresponding histories for subsequent chunks, allowing the system to continue from previous text, audio, and video outputs. Sec. 3.2 describes how the Intent Module implements p_φ, Sec. 3.3 describes the audio-visual latent representations zᵃₖ and zᵛₖ, and Sec. 3.4 describes how the Realization Module implements p_θ.

3.2 Multimodal Intent Module

The Intent Module adapts a pretrained multimodal language backbone [(Bai et al., 2025)] to causal, chunk-wise interaction. Given the context, it generates the text output yₖ and provides hidden states hₖ.

Causal input assembly.

Inputs enter C^φₖ according to when they become available, without requiring all modalities to share a sampling rate. ASR recovers user text uₜ from user audio uₐ, and forced alignment assigns each text token a span on the source audio timeline. A token is admitted only after the end of its aligned span. Video frames and audio samples are mapped to the same half-open chunk intervals using source timestamps.

Assistant text targets are assigned to chunks according to speech onset, while the initial chunk uses a fixed action (Fig. 3). We preserve fine-grained alignment before constructing chunk views, avoiding early rounding of speech boundaries. Each input context therefore contains only information available at the corresponding decision boundary, and different chunk configurations can be derived from the same aligned record. The ASR and alignment tools, together with their quality checks, are described in Sec. 5.3.

Causal visual encoding.

Causality must also hold before attention is applied. Temporal patch construction can combine multiple source frames, so an attention mask cannot remove future information already mixed into a visual token. We therefore form each temporal group entirely within one input chunk. For a native 17-frame chunk with source frames numbered 0,…,16, the final pair is (16,16): the last frame is repeated instead of paired with frame 17 from the next chunk. Each group becomes available at the latest timestamp among its source frames. This preserves the pretrained visual input format while preventing temporal grouping from crossing chunk boundaries.

Participation and language outputs.

The text output yₖ contains either followed by a text body or without new text. Both actions are generated through the standard token prediction path. The explicit action separates the decision to begin speaking from the words of the response, since appropriate content can still be delivered at the wrong time. A output can coexist with ongoing playback and media continuation. Participation supervision, target balancing, and history augmentation are described in Sec. 4.1.

3.3 Variational Autoencoder

To support real-time response generation, we encode audio and video into compact latent representations zᵃ and zᵛ. For audio, each stereo channel is compressed into 40 latent vectors per second, with 32 dimensions per vector. For video, the encoder processes groups of 17 frames, with padding applied when fewer than 17 frames are available. Each group consists of one keyframe followed by four packets of four frames, following a 1-4-4-4-4 temporal arrangement. These 17 frames are encoded into 5 latent frames. Each latent frame has 24 dimensions, with spatial resolution reduced by a factor of 16×16. For input height H and width W, an RGB frame group of shape (17,H,W,3) is therefore encoded into a latent:

z_groupᵛ∈ℝ^5×H/16×W/16×24.

(3)

Before entering the diffusion transformer, the video latents undergo spatial merging over 2×2 patches, producing a video input vector with 2×2×24=96 dimensions. Each audio latent vector has 32 dimensions per channel. The decoding procedure is described in Sec. 6.

3.4 Joint Causal Audiovisual Realization

The Realization Module uses a causal audiovisual diffusion transformer initialized with pretrained weights from [(MiniMax, 2026)]. Causal adaptation and distillation of the pretrained backbone are described in Sec. 4.2. The module jointly generates audio and video in the latent spaces described in Sec. 3.3, implementing the conditional generation process in Eq. (2) through flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2023)]. Starting from random noise, the model generates audiovisual latents conditioned on the intent representation, reference image, available user inputs, and previously generated assistant media. Access to this history supports continuity across response chunks.

Intent conditioning.

A linear projection maps hₖ from the Intent Module to the hidden width of the Realization Module, and a refiner network produces text-conditioning embeddings. An attention mask restricts feature computation to token positions associated with the global instructions d and the current assistant text output yₖ:

xₖᵗ=Refine_θ (Project_θ(hₖ);Mₖ^feat).

(4)

Media conditioning.

User audio and video are encoded by the respective audio and video VAE encoders described in Sec. 3.3, producing conditioning latents zᵃ_u,

Positional embedding.

We use 3D-RoPE to represent temporal and spatial relationships among tokens. The text-conditioning embeddings use only the temporal coordinate, with both spatial coordinates set to zero. Audio tokens use the two extreme spatial position IDs to distinguish the left and right channels.

Temporal coordinates for audio and video are aligned with actual playback times. At 40 latent vectors per second per channel, each audio latent corresponds to 25 milliseconds. The beginning of the user input audio defines the common temporal origin. Each audio token receives a temporal position equal to the offset of its segment start from this origin, divided by 25 milliseconds. Video temporal positions use the corresponding playback times with the same origin and temporal unit. This accounts for the nonuniform temporal mapping from 17 source frames to five video latent frames.

4 Training Strategy

Training proceeds in three stages. Stage 1 trains the Intent Module for causal participation and text prediction through supervised fine-tuning. Stage 2 trains the Realization Module for causal joint audiovisual generation, conditioned on recorded media history and intent features extracted from recorded assistant text by the frozen Intent Module (Fig. 4). Stage 3 distills four-step generation through distribution matching, with dual rollout using predicted text and generated audiovisual history to match inference-time conditioning.

4.1 Stage 1: Intent Training

We adapt the multimodal Intent Module with causal supervised fine-tuning on chunk-aligned conversations. At the start of chunk k, the model predicts the assistant output text yₖ from the global instruction d, the user video uᵥ and ASR text uₜ available through chunk k-1, and earlier assistant language y_ action introduces new text, including continuations of an earlier turn. The action adds no new text and can coexist with ongoing playback or non-verbal behavior. Fig. 3 illustrates this shift, and Sec. 3.2 details the input protocol.

Causal chunk supervision.

Let yₖ be the token sequence of the assistant output in chunk k, and let C^Iₖ=(d,u_v,

Lᵢₙₜₑₙₜ=-𝔼 [(∑_k,jm_k,jw_k,j\logp_φ (y_k,j|C^Iₖ,y_k,

(5)

where y_k,j is the j-th action, content, or structural token, w_k,j is its category-dependent weight, and m_k,j is one for supervised tokens and zero otherwise. The denominator sums the effective weights within each sampled conversation, with a minimum of one. The initial assistant output y₀ is a fixed used as context and excluded from the loss.

Action-aware rebalancing.

Most chunks introduce no new assistant text, so unweighted training can favor waiting. We assign supervision categories offline from recorded assistant events and from whether the user is speaking at the chunk start. This speaking status distinguishes idle waits from waits during user speech and ordinary openings from interruption openings. The assistant annotation distinguishes openings from continuations, and an annotated question in the preceding user turn provides a separate opening tag. We use these labels to subsample targets and weight the loss, with separate action and content weights and adjustments for opening categories. Subsampled targets remain in the conversation history. The model receives only the causal context described above. Validation retains the full set of eligible targets and reports separate token-level metrics for actions, speech, and waits.

Training under imperfect assistant history.

To expose the model to imperfect histories, we truncate or repeat text in selected continuation chunks, mask their losses, and retain supervision on later valid targets. For missed-opening recovery, we replace selected ordinary openings with in the history and mask their losses. In the next chunk of the same assistant turn, only contributes to the loss.

Preserving visual and linguistic grounding.

The training mixture contains examples whose correct answer depends on the user video as well as examples solvable from text alone. We identify visually grounded assistant turns through data inspection and upweight their content-token loss, while retaining the same causal visual input path. Prompt augmentation varies the format, ordering, and completeness of the static assistant/scene description without inventing new facts. Together with source-grouped train/validation splits, these choices discourage the Intent Module from relying on a fixed prompt template or on text-only shortcuts. Optional emotion labels are kept as separately weighted attachments and are admitted only at their annotated causal boundary. We use low-rank adaptation to fine-tune the Intent Module. After this stage, the frozen Intent Module supplies hidden states from its forward passes to condition media training.

4.2 Stage 2: Realization Training

Stage 2 trains the Realization Module for causal joint audiovisual generation while keeping the Intent Module frozen. Training follows the conditional structure in Eq. (2), learning to generate audio and video latents from the current intent representation and available interaction context. The sequence layout and attention mask encode the dependencies among modalities within each chunk and restrict access to preceding interaction history across chunks. We describe this multimodal sequence construction, the joint flow-matching formulation, and the optimization strategy below.

Chunk structure and sequence design.

Each segment of streaming generation spans 17 video frames at 24 fps, or 17/24≈0.708 seconds. The chunk cₖ contains the assistant action for that chunk, represented by the text embedding xₖᵗ obtained from the Intent Module hidden state hₖ, together with the corresponding noised assistant video and audio embeddings:

cₖ=(xₖᵗ,x̃ₖᵛ,x̃ₖᵃ),

(6)

where x̃ₖᵛ and x̃ₖᵃ are the clean media embeddings xₖᵛ and xₖᵃ noised to level τₖ. To align with the timelines used by the audio and video codecs, the number of media embeddings in each chunk corresponds to 5 latent video representations and 2×29 latent audio representations.

During training, we also insert clean audio and video embeddings into the sequence. A carefully designed attention mask prevents noisy media embeddings in each generation chunk from accessing their own clean signals. For each training example, the sequence contains, in order, the assistant reference-media embeddings, the global instruction embeddings, the clean media embeddings for the generation chunks, and the generation chunks themselves:

C^R=(xʳ,xᵈ,x₀ᵛ,x₀ᵃ,…,x_Kᵛ,x_Kᵃ,c₀,…,c_K),

(7)

where xʳ embeds the reference image I_ref, xᵈ embeds the global instruction d, and K+1 is the number of chunks in the sample.

To fit within the context length of the initialized model, we randomly sample a window of consecutive chunks from each training conversation. Because temporal position IDs align with actual video playback times, positional encoding remains closely aligned between training and inference even when the sampled chunk sequence does not start at the beginning of a conversation.

Attention mask design.

Each noisy media embedding can attend to the reference media, global description, historical assistant text, and clean historical media. Clean media related to the current chunk and all content in future chunks are invisible. Noisy media embeddings within the current chunk also have internal content boundaries: video embeddings correspond in order to 5 video-encoder latent representations, while audio embeddings are divided into left and right channels, each corresponding to 25 milliseconds of audio. Nevertheless, all these embeddings are mutually visible within the chunk. The detailed visibility relationships are illustrated in Fig. 5.

Flow-matching velocity prediction.

Flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2023)] supervises the joint media velocity from random noise to clean latent states, with clean time τ=1 and noise time τ=0. For clean media latents z∈{zᵛ,zᵃ} and Gaussian noise ε, we have:

z̃_τ=(1-τ)ε+τznoised input,(8)

4.3 Stage 3: Distribution Matching Distillation

DMD supervision.

DMD [(Yin et al., 2024b)] distills the causal model into a four-step chunk-causal generator G_θ by matching the distribution of its own samples to the data distribution, instead of enforcing agreement between neighboring points on a teacher trajectory as CD does. Two score models provide this supervision: a frozen real-score model μᵣₑₐₗ approximates the conditional data distribution, and a trainable fake-score model μ^ψ_fake tracks the evolving generator distribution. The generator synthesizes a latent window z_gen causally, whereas both score models evaluate the completed window bidirectionally. In our flow convention (τ=0 noise, τ=1 data), each conversation draws one noise level τ from a shifted discrete noise schedule, the window is corrupted once as z̃_gen=τz_gen+(1-τ)ε, and the two models return clean estimates ẑᵣₑₐₗ=μᵣₑₐₗ(z̃_gen,τ) and ẑ_fake=μ^ψ_fake(z̃_gen,τ) under this shared corruption. Since a clean estimate ẑ_∗ determines the score s_∗=-(z̃_gen-τẑ_∗)/(1-τ)², the DMD gradient of the reverse KL divergence reduces to the difference of the two estimates,

∇_θD_KL (p_θ ∥ p_data)≈𝔼_τ,ε [(s_fake-sᵣₑₐₗ)^⊤(∂z_gen)/(∂θ)], s_fake-sᵣₑₐₗ=τ/(1-τ)²(ẑ_fake-ẑᵣₑₐₗ).

(9)

We replace the time-dependent factor by a sample-adaptive scale and realize the update as regression toward a detached target; for one conversation and one modality,

κ=\max (⟨|z_gen-ẑᵣₑₐₗ|⟩_w, ε₀), Δ=(ẑ_fake-ẑᵣₑₐₗ)/(κ), z_DMD=sg [z_gen-Δ],

where sg denotes stop-gradient, ⟨·⟩_w averages over feature dimensions and then over the valid target rows of that conversation and modality, and the floor ε₀ prevents division by a vanishing scale. Assembling the targets across conversations yields the generator loss

L_DMD=1/2∑_m∈{v,a}λₘ WMSE_wₘ (zᵐ_gen,zᵐ_DMD),

(11)

whose WMSE reduction uses the global valid-target normalization of Sec. 4.2. Its gradient with respect to z_gen is proportional to Δ, so the generator is moved along (ẑᵣₑₐₗ-ẑ_fake)/κ through its differentiable outputs.

Because the fake model must follow the generator, it is fitted on detached generated samples by flow matching, L^fake_FM=𝔼[ω(τ) ∥v_ψ(z̃_gen,τ)-(z_gen-ε)∥²], where ω(τ) is a noise-level-dependent weight. The fake model is updated more frequently than the generator, with several fake updates between consecutive generator updates. Each update draws its own window and rollout, so the fake model is always fitted to samples from the current generator.

An optional GAN loss [(Yin et al., 2024a)] adds direct feedback from training media. A lightweight head on middle-block features of the fake-score backbone pools the valid audio and video tokens of each conversation through a learned attention query into a single logit D(·). Its input physically excludes text, Intent Module, reference, and clean-context rows, so the critic judges joint audio–visual realism without requiring generated media to reproduce the recorded transcript. Writing z̃_data and z̃_gen for training-media and generated latents noised to the same level with independent noise, the two trainable roles minimize

L_G=L_DMD+λ_G 𝔼 [softplus (-D(z̃_gen))],(12)
L_F=L^fake_FM+λ_D 𝔼 [softplus (-D(z̃_data))+softplus (D(z̃_gen))],

where the fake backbone and head are frozen but differentiable in the generator update, and generated media are detached in the critic update.

Dual rollout in DMD training.

Dual rollout aligns DMD training with the language and media context encountered during inference (Fig. 6). Before DMD, the Realization Module conditions on features extracted from layer 50 of the Intent Module using recorded assistant text, together with recorded media prefixes. At inference, the Intent Module determines response wording, length, and speaking timing, while the Realization Module continues from its own audiovisual outputs. Each DMD sample therefore undergoes a language rollout by the frozen Intent Module, followed by a media rollout by the Realization Module.

The frozen Intent Module rolls out only the final assistant turn of each training window. Windows may start at any earlier chunk and end at a natural assistant turn boundary rounded up to a codec chunk. Candidates are bucketed by reserved token length, with bucket weights proportional to squared length. Let k₀ be the first chunk within the window containing the final turn. Using only history within the window (Sec. 3.1), the Intent Module replays recorded text before k₀ and greedily predicts participation actions and text thereafter. Recorded tokens of the final turn and all later text are removed, while any recorded prefix from an earlier assistant turn sharing the boundary chunk is retained. With N=4, G_θ⁽ʲ⁾ performs j steps without gradient tracking followed by one differentiable step whose clean estimate becomes the chunk output. The exit j^⋆ is shared across the trajectory. Each detached clean output is processed by a clean forward at τ=1 to update the KV cache. The assembled window z_gen=(ẑₖ)ₖ supplies the targets and losses in Eq. (10) and Eq. (12). DMD can introduce camera-rotation drift that distribution matching does not explicitly penalize. We therefore reweight the video DMD loss using rotations Rᵢ estimated by frozen VGGT [(Wang et al., 2025)] from decoded rollout frames. Let αᵢ denote the geodesic angle between R₀ and Rᵢ, and δᵢ that between consecutive rotations. Sustained deviation and accumulated rotation define

E=1/T₀∫ (([α(s)-α_dz]₊)/(αₛ))²ds+(1/αₚ∑ᵢδᵢ (gᵢ₋₁+gᵢ)/(2))², gᵢ=clip ((αᵢ-α_dz)/(α_g),0,1),(14)

Here, s is playback time, α_dz defines a dead zone, and αₛ, α_g, and αₚ scale deviation, gating, and rotational path length, respectively. The constant T₀ normalizes duration, with weight bounds 0<ρ_\min<1<ρ_\max and strength λᵣₒₜ∈[0,1]. The detached weight ρ scales only the video term in Eq. (11). At λᵣₒₜ=1, stable windows receive weights up to ρ_\max, while strongly rotating windows receive ρ_\min. The metric uses rotation alone, and opposite rotations do not cancel. This weighting rebalances DMD updates without propagating gradients through VGGT or the VAE. Intentional viewpoint changes and unreliable rotation estimates can also affect the weights.

5 Data Construction

Training Duov1 requires temporally aligned user inputs and assistant audiovisual behavior. We combine synthetic and recorded interactions into a unified conversation timeline, preserving natural timing and controlled events. This provides causal supervision for Intent and audiovisual targets for Realization, with additional routes for missing-view reconstruction and recorded-video extensions.

5.1 Synthetic Data

Pipeline overview.

This route generates a two-person video call in which both participants are rendered together. Fig. 7 shows its two stages. Stage I is text only. Control cards are sampled, a LLM writes a structured screenplay under these cards, rule checks reject invalid screenplays, and a template converts each screenplay block into a text prompt [(MiniMax, 2026)]. Stage II feeds these prompts to a t2v model, which generates one split-screen audio-video stream block by block. The left panel is always the user and the right panel the assistant. Generating both panels and the shared audio on a unified timeline preserves the timing of dialogue, reactions, overlaps, and interruptions.

Control cards.

Without explicit constraints, LLM-generated conversations tend to repeat similar topics, relationships, and turn-taking patterns. To improve diversity, we use control cards that define attributes with predefined candidate values. For each screenplay, these values are sampled uniformly and included as explicit requirements in the generation prompt.

  • •

    duration: {30 s, 45 s, 60 s}

  • •

    language: {Chinese, English}

  • •

    persona: {none, relationship, occupation}, e.g., relationship ∈ {“parent-child”, “colleagues”, “doctor-patient”, …} (12 values), occupation ∈ {“firefighter”, “nurse”, “chef”, …} (11 values, per participant)

  • •

    micro-actions: {off, on}, where “on” suggests 24 small reactions, e.g., {“nod”, “raise an eyebrow”, “look away briefly”, …}

  • •

    interaction: {“everyday exchange”, “interruption”, “follow-up / debate”, “proactive inquiry”}

  • •

    emotion: fixed to “follow the topic and the conversation”

  • •

    resolution: {1536×576, 1152×768}, used only by video synthesis

    • Each interaction value carries a written specification. For example, “interruption” requires one speaker to cut in before the other finishes, a brief overlap of voices, and the interrupted speaker yielding the turn.

    Screenplay and t2v prompt synthesis.

    The sampled cards are inserted into a fixed template, and the LLM writes a synopsis followed by a JSON screenplay, shown in Fig. 8 (a). The screenplay describes each participant once (appearance, voice, environment, initial_pose) and then splits the call into blocks of 5-15 s at natural turn boundaries. Each block is an ordered list of events. An event pairs a description of expressions, gestures, and the listener’s reaction with at most one speech entry, so nonverbal reactions need no invented dialogue. A rule-based validator checks the structure, block timing, language, and the absence of capture-device words such as “phone” in the narration, and returns errors to the LLM for up to 3 attempts.

    The validated screenplay is converted into one t2v prompt per block by a template, without further LLM calls (Fig. 8(b)). Screenplay fields fill the slots verbatim. The shaded sentences are fixed for all samples and fall into three groups:

  • •

    Reference roles. Each input is assigned one job: the previous final frame is the starting state, the opening video only sets picture quality, and the opening audio only sets voices and room tone. Without these roles the model tends to replay the reference video or repeat its dialogue.

  • •

    Picture content. Each panel is the participant’s own front camera, which rules out third-person, mirror, and behind-the-back views. Recording devices, UI elements, and subtitles, which otherwise appear frequently in generated calls, are excluded, and content may not cross the center divider, so the two crops stay clean.

  • •

    Causal order. A reaction may start only after its trigger has finished, so the assistant view never responds before the user acts.

    • Video synthesis.

    As shown in Fig. 7, Block 0 receives its prompt and a white layout image whose two panels are separated by a thin black divider. The layout image fixes only the split-screen geometry, and the model creates both participants and backgrounds from the prompt.

  • •

    Previous final frame (orange). The last frame of block i-1 is temporally aligned with the first target frame, preserving pose, expression, and framing across blocks.

  • •

    Opening video (blue). The first 124 frames of block 0 serve as a picture-quality reference for brightness, exposure, color sharpness, and noise.

  • •

    Opening audio (blue). The full block 0 audio anchors both voices and room tone.

    • We preserve generation conditions in their original representations, using VAE latents for the initial video and raw RGB for the final frame. The generated video are then concatenated and split into user and assistant views, both sharing the same synchronized audio track.

    Error accumulation.

    The baseline data synthesis method conditions each block on the final frame of the preceding block, causing visual errors to accumulate over time. Our synthesis method mitigates this drift by using the opening video (block 0) as a fixed reference throughout generation. Fig. 9 compares the two synthesis strategies over a 60 s sequence of ten 6 s blocks. The baseline loses 34.2 luma levels by block 9, with increasingly exaggerated facial textures. Our method stabilizes at approximately 99 luma after a slight initial decline, maintaining consistent facial appearance through block 9.

    5.2 Recorded Data

    As shown in Fig. 10, we organize recorded data into six categories by source and interaction format: single-stream video, synchronous dual-stream video, asynchronous dual-stream video, live streams with audience comments, duplex audio recordings and open datasets. The following common recording standards apply across these categories. Recordings feature real speakers and their original voices, with speaker identities, transcripts, and temporal mappings retained and unrelated audio excluded. For video data, each delivered clip preserves a continuous, uncut half-body or full-body view with accurate audio–visual synchronization, at least 720p effective resolution per view, and no visual overlays. Dual-stream recordings contain at least one complete conversational exchange.

    Single-stream video.

    Fig. 10 (b) illustrates single-stream recordings, such as solo podcasts and single-person presentations. The clips range from 10 to 90 seconds, preserving natural pauses.

    Synchronous dual-stream video.

    Synchronous dual-stream video, illustrated in Fig. 10 (c), keeps both participants visible at the same time and preserves listening behavior, overlapping speech, and reactions.

    Asynchronous dual-stream video.

    Asynchronous dual-stream video shows participants in separate clips that alternate with the speaking turns, as in the interview footage shown in Fig. 10 (d).

    Live streams with audience comments.

    We align timestamped audience questions with presenter responses and reconstruct user videos, converting live streams into synchronized dual-stream conversations.

    Duplex audio recordings.

    This category consists of full-duplex audio recordings of two-person dialogues, which drive the further video synthesis, as illustrated in Fig. 10 (f).

    Open datasets.

    We collected single-stream talking videos from open-source datasets. As depicted in Fig. 10 (g), we filtered the material according to the common recording standards (e.g., resolution requirements) and then applied face detection, video understanding, voice activity detection (VAD), automatic speech recognition (ASR), and language identification to guide further filtering and annotation.

    5.3 Data Processing

    5.3.1 Synthetic Data Quality Control

    Each newly generated video segment undergoes four automatic quality checks.

    First-frame consistency.

    We compare the first frame with the conditioning image, requiring an SSIM of at least 0.90 and a perceptual-hash Hamming distance of at most 4. Conditioning uses the character image initially, then the preceding segment’s processed final frame.

    Unexpected audio.

    We compare the generated audio with the source audio using loudness normalization, waveform residuals, and VAD, rejecting segments with unexplained audio activity lasting at least 0.40 s.

    Camera push-in.

    We track face scale at 4 FPS, using the first valid detection as the baseline. Rejection thresholds for sustained and abrupt enlargement are a smoothed scale of 1.30 times baseline for 0.75 s and a 1.22-fold jump within 0.50 s, respectively.

    Persistent large-area visual changes.

    We sample frames at 4 FPS and measure LAB differences, changed-pixel proportions, and color/brightness histogram distances. Using these metrics, we reject abrupt changes that remain above thresholds relative to the pre-change frame, or cumulative drift from the initial frame exceeding both appearance and histogram thresholds.

    5.3.2 Live-Stream Data Processing

    Collection and initial screening.

    We collect archived live streams and deduplicate source records. Sampled frames are used to check the presence of real participants and visual quality, retaining only suitable material.

    Annotation and filtering.

    We produce transcripts with word- or character-level timestamps by Qwen3-ASR-1.7B and Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B [(Shi et al., 2026)]. And we also use Silero VAD [(Silero Team, 2024)] to identify speech and silence intervals and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B [(Xu et al., 2025a)] to review audio types. Speaker diarization and speaker-count checks combine FSMN-VAD [(Gao et al., 2023)] for speech detection, Paraformer [(Gao et al., 2022)]for transcription, and CAM++ [(Wang et al., 2023)] for speaker embeddings followed by clustering. These checks exclude windows containing singing, whispered or breathy speech, or multiple speakers, producing timestamped candidate material for dialogue construction.

    Dialogue construction and video preparation.

    To obtain the content and timing needed for user-side video synthesis, we match audience comments extracted from real chat logs to the presenter’s responses. When such matching is not possible, we will generate counterpart utterances and schedule their interjections based on the presenter’s original speech and available silence. After reviewing conversational coherence, completeness, and audio-visual correspondence, we extract continuous assistant-side video segments and crop them around the presenter to remove on-screen comments and watermarks. We then synthesize the corresponding user-side videos and pair the two views on a shared timeline. After a final quality check, we deliver clean dual-stream videos together with their transcripts, dialogue timing and source metadata.

    6 Streaming Pipeline and Acceleration

    In this section, we detail our streaming inference design. The system employs an orchestrated scheduling strategy to synchronize the intent module, the realization module and the VAE decoding, ensuring low-latency performance for interactive tasks.

    6.1 Orchestrated Streaming Pipeline

    The front-end device continuously captures user audio and video and forwards them for chunk-wise processing. As shown in Fig. 11, each chunk passes through input acquisition, intent inference, joint latent generation, and streaming decoding, while input capture continues during response generation. The sequential stages of the pipeline can be summarized as:

  • •

    Interaction sampling. At 24 frames per second, each sampling window contains 17 video frames and the corresponding user audio, matching the video VAE grouping described in Sec. 3.3. The window duration is tₛₐₘₚₗₑ=17/24 s≈708 ms.

  • •

    Intent inference. The Intent Module processes the available context, generates a participation and text output, and provides hidden states to the Realization Module. Depending on the input and context length, inference takes tᵢₙₜₑₙₜ=90--160 ms.

  • •

    Joint latent generation. Conditioned on the intent representation and media context, the Realization Module jointly generates audio and video latents. For video generation at 768×576 resolution, this stage takes t_gen=200-450 ms, depending on the context length.

  • •

    Streaming decoding. The generated audio and video latents are decoded incrementally for playback. Decoding a 4-frame group takes approximately t_decode=30 ms.

  • •

    Other overhead. Data movement, transmission to the front-end device, and display processing contribute approximately t_overhead=40 ms.

    • The reported intent inference, latent generation, and overhead terms sum to

    tᵢₙₜₑₙₜ+t_gen+t_overhead≈330--650 ms.

    		(15)

    The delay to the first visible output additionally includes the initial decoding time and any remaining wait for the sampling window to close. An utterance or action ending within a sampling window can incur an additional sampling delay of up to approximately 708 ms. During playback, we post-process the generated frames to maintain visual stability and smooth motion.

    6.2 Causal Latent Decoding

    The original VAE in [(MiniMax, 2026)] decodes 5 latent frames into 17 video frames and requires 2 latent frames of lookahead. This dependency introduces additional waiting at chunk boundaries during streaming playback. We therefore adapt the decoding procedure to process available video latents incrementally.

    After joint generation of a response chunk, its video latents are decoded one at a time. Each latent produces four video frames, followed by temporal alignment to match the original playback schedule and preserve the 17-frame chunk duration. This procedure allows playback to begin from the available chunk without waiting for additional latents from the next chunk.

    At 24 frames per second, the shortest playback interval corresponds to the first latent in each group, which represents one video frame after temporal alignment. This interval is 1/24 s≈41.7 ms. The measured per-latent decoding time is approximately 30 ms, below this interval. The decoder can therefore keep pace with playback provided that generated latents are available on schedule.

    6.3 Inference Acceleration

    The runtime coordinates memory management, stage scheduling, and GPU placement to sustain continuous audiovisual generation. Each input chunk covers 17/24 s of captured audio and video. Sustained playback requires the pipeline to produce output chunks at least as quickly as they are consumed, while keeping memory usage bounded over long interactions. As shown in Fig. 11, the system runs on a single server with eight GPUs. For each response chunk, Intent Module inference precedes joint audiovisual latent generation by the DiT. The remaining VAE decoding steps for one chunk overlap with Intent Module inference for the following chunk, reducing the interval between successive outputs.

    Unified KV Management

    A shared KV cache manager tracks cache ownership and device placement, with sliding-window eviction for the Intent Module and periodic history resets for the Realization Module. For each chunk, four denoising forwards read committed historical KV without committing intermediate noisy states. An additional clean forward processes the generated latents zₖᵃ and zₖᵛ and writes their KV states for subsequent chunks.

    At reset boundaries, the manager discards historical media KV before denoising while retaining reference and shared conditioning. The clean forward then establishes a new history, as illustrated by chunk k+1 in Fig. 11. The reset interval controls retained context, memory use, and context-dependent latency. After a restart, the manager reconstructs the active media cache by replaying completed latents through clean forwards in their original order, following the same reset boundaries and retention policy.

    Chunk-Level Overlap and Deadline Scheduling

    Input capture proceeds independently of computation. As shown in Fig. 11, the Realization Module uses all 8 GPUs for denoising and the clean forward. Between generation phases, GPUs 0-3 run Intent Module inference for chunk k+1, while GPUs 4-7 decode chunk k. Generation resumes once both groups finish. After temporal alignment, each 17-frame chunk is released incrementally as one 1-frame anchor followed by four 4-frame packets, each synchronized with its audio.

    Let t_gen,k include four denoising forwards and the clean forward, t_decode,k^full denote complete chunk decoding, t_intent,k+1 denote the next intent inference, and t_switch,k denote additional transition overhead. When the next input context is available and decoding starts together with intent inference, the cycle time is

    T_cycle,k=t_gen,k+\max {t_intent,k+1,t_decode,k^full}+t_switch,k.

    		(16)

    The target is T_cycle,k≤17/24 s, with margin for stage-time variation. Complete decoding enters the throughput budget, whereas only first-packet decoding enters the initial response path. The scheduler reserves decoding slots, bounds output lead over playback, and admits work using KV windows, available memory, and estimated stage durations.

    Device-Aware Parallel Execution

    The Intent Module uses four-way tensor parallelism (TP), while the Realization Module selects between TP and sequence parallelism (SP). In our SP configuration, each rank holds a complete weight replica and processes part of the token sequence. TP partitions weights and tensor computation. For chunk k, the runtime selects the fastest feasible configuration:

    pₖ^⋆=\arg\min_p∈{SP,TP}Tₖ(p),(17)
    s.t. M_k,g(p)≤B_k,g, g=0,…,7.

    Here, Tₖ(p) denotes profiled runtime, M_k,g(p) peak memory for weights, retained KV, communication buffers, and temporaries, and B_k,g memory remaining after other resident stages. We retain weights when memory permits and prefetch nonresident weights during slack, accounting for transfer and synchronization costs. ASR, input transfers, and packet preparation use pipeline gaps as data dependencies allow.

    7 Evaluation and Showcase

    7.1 Human Evaluation

    Evaluation protocol

    We evaluated the model on 30 real-time duplex interaction cases, each pairing a user’s audio-visual input with the model’s generated audio-visual reply, replayed side by side on a shared timeline. Each reply is judged the way an end user would experience it, at normal playback speed with sound, against six binary criteria: content responsiveness, language adherence, speech intelligibility, visual identity stability, audio-visual synchronization, and audio-visual emotional consistency. Every criterion has written failure conditions, and no partial credit is given.

    Results

    Of 180 checks (30 cases × 6 criteria), 168 passed (93.3%). The clearest strength is generation fidelity: the model passed all 90 checks on language adherence, speech intelligibility, and visual identity stability. Every reply came in the expected language as complete, intelligible speech, and no case showed a visible identity swap, facial or body malformation, or unexplained change in appearance. Cross-modal coherence is nearly as strong. Vocal emotion was consistent with facial expression and body language in 96.7% of cases, and lip movement stayed aligned with speech in 90.0%.

    Where headroom remains

    Content responsiveness, which asks whether a reply substantively addresses what the user has just said and shown, reached 73.3% (22/30). It is the most demanding criterion in the protocol, since a duplex model must settle on a reply while speech and video are still streaming in. The misses fall mainly into two patterns. The first is the long tail of conversation, such as jokes and odd remarks, where a fitting reply requires reading intent beyond the literal words, and doing so in real time. The second is intent that only becomes clear when speech and video are read together. In one case, a user sitting indoors said they had just unlocked a shared bike when it started to rain. Given the indoor setting, this reads as a complaint, yet the model treated it as a request for advice and suggested holding off on riding. Both patterns come down to inferring what the user means from everything they say and show, at conversational speed. This is one of the hardest problems in duplex interaction and the central focus of our next iteration, which builds on a foundation that already passed every language, speech, and identity check.

    7.2 Showcase

    Fig. 12 organizes selected examples: plan revision, visual guidance, collaborative design, social support, and interactive customization. These categories connect language to a change in a shared plan, an observable action, a joint solution, or an affective response. The first four categories use script-conditioned training data, the customization example comes from the user demonstration. Fig. 13 extends the coverage to negotiation, decision support, explanation, and task coordination. Fig. 14 adds collaborative creation, coaching, shared experience, turn negotiation, and supportive responses.

    8 Conclusion

    We introduced the ReciprocalWorldModel and its initial implementation, Duov1, which couples a multimodal Intent Module with a causal audiovisual Realization Module. This report describes the architecture, training procedure, and runtime scheduling used to generate responses while continuing to receive user input. Duov1 remains preliminary and currently supports basic audiovisual conversation. The examples illustrate this functionality, while response timing, consistency over longer sessions, and recovery from misunderstandings still require broader evaluation. Development is ongoing, and an updated version will follow soon.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有世界模型大多只模拟物理现实，把推理与决策当成外挂控制。

要点：

  • 立场很明确：ReciprocalWorldModel（RWM）把智能与物理现实视为构成「世界」的同等基本要素
  • 批评现有做法：多数世界模型只模拟后者（物理现实），而把推理与决策当成**外部的控制信号**塞进去
  • Duo v1 是一个全双工世界模型：一边持续感知视听输入，一边实时回应用户

为什么值得看：「世界模型要不要包含智能体」是路线问题。把智能放进世界内部、并做成全双工实时交互，是最接近「引擎里跑 NPC 与世界」的形态——比只做视频预测更贴近游戏需要。

中文摘要：这篇提出 ReciprocalWorldModel（RWM）框架与 Duo v1 模型，立场是把「智能」与「物理现实」看作构成世界的同等基本要素：一个世界不只是被模拟的物理场景，也包括在其中推理与决策的主体。作者批评现有世界模型大多只模拟后者，而把推理与决策留作外部的控制输入。Duo v1 因此被设计为全双工（full-duplex）世界模型：一边持续感知视听输入，一边实时对用户作出回应。对游戏而言，这正是「世界与 NPC 同处一个模型」的形态。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction

Abstract

In this report, we introduce the ReciprocalWorldModel (RWM) and present Duov1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audiovisual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duov1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duov1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

Contents

1 Introduction

World models have made rapid progress in simulating the physical side of a world [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Hafner et al., 2025, Brooks et al., 2024)]: given past observations and control signals, they predict how scenes evolve [(Bruce et al., 2024, Valevski et al., 2025, Hu et al., 2023, NVIDIA, 2025)], with increasingly realistic dynamics, appearance, and long-range consistency [(Google DeepMind, 2024, Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025, Robbyant Team, 2026, Gao et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026, Huang et al., 2026a)]. In most of these works, however, intelligence resides outside the world. A user steers the generated world through inputs with limited degrees of freedom, such as keyboard and mouse commands, gamepad actions, or text prompts, but nothing within the world perceives the full state of the user in real time or decides how to respond. Such worlds can be accurate, yet they remain lifeless: there is a world to explore, but no one to talk to.

We argue that intelligence and physical reality are equally fundamental to a world. Building on this view, we introduce the ReciprocalWorldModel (RWM). The RWM generates a world inhabited by living presences and connects it to the real world through full-duplex, real-time interaction. Each side continuously perceives audio and video from the other and can respond, interrupt, or remain silent while the other is still acting. This reciprocal interaction requires two complementary capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audiovisual behavior. These functional roles can be fulfilled by a unified multimodal model or by a modular system combining a multimodal language model with a diffusion model. In this report, we present Duov1, a modular instantiation of the RWM. Interaction proceeds in chunks of 17 video frames, approximately 0.71 s at 24 fps. Three technical designs coordinate Intent and Realization within a single streaming system.

Autoregressive intent for interaction.

In most audio-visual video generative model [(MiniMax, 2026)], a language model serves as an instruction encoder for the diffusion model. In Duov1, the intent module instead reasons over the ongoing interaction autoregressively and makes participation decisions: at every chunk, it emits a action followed by text or a action, conditioned on the user input so far and its own earlier language. Its hidden states, rather than its decoded text alone, carry each decision to the realization module (Sec. 3). Action-aware rebalancing prevents the intent module from collapsing into perpetual waiting, since most chunks contain no new assistant speech, and history perturbations teach it to recover from imperfect earlier responses (Sec. 4).

Causal chunk conditions on a unified timeline.

User speech, user video, intent tokens, and assistant media are synchronized on one timeline, and each chunk is given exactly the conditions that are available at its decision boundary. Module-specific attention masks enforce causality within and across chunks. In the intent module, temporal patches are completed inside each chunk, so no future frame leaks into a decision through the visual frontend. In the realization module, noisy media tokens of a chunk can attend to the reference, intent features, and clean history, but not to their own clean targets or to any later chunk (Sec. 3).

Dual rollout distillation.

Before distillation, the realization module is trained on intent features of recorded assistant text and on recorded media history, whereas in a live exchange both are produced by the system itself.
