一句话：一个预测分数混了三样东西：编码器好坏、近未来像不像近过去、预测器自己的贡献。

要点：

  • 现实情况：预训练视频世界模型被当作机器人学习的组件来比较与挑选，主要依据是**未来预测分数**
  • 问题在于这个分数本身不能当作「会预测」的证据——它把编码器质量、近未来与近过去的相似度、预测器自身的贡献混在一起
  • 作者用一个配对对照（matched control）把三者分离，并在 2.7 万次未来检索试验上做了检验（家庭第一人称视频）

为什么值得看：如果分数主要反映「近未来像近过去」，那么高分的世界模型可能只是在做持续性外推。这条直接影响「要不要把某个世界模型当引擎组件」的决策，比再多刷榜都实在。

中文摘要：预训练视频世界模型常被当作机器人学习系统的组件来比较和挑选，主要依据是未来预测分数。这篇指出，单看这个分数并不能作为「模型会预测」的证据：它把三样东西混在了一起——编码器的质量、近未来与近过去的相似程度，以及预测器本身的贡献。作者因此引入配对对照（matched control）把三者分离开，并在来自家庭第一人称视频的 27,000 次未来检索试验上做了检验。结论指向一个工程上很关键的问题：高分可能只是「持续性外推」而非真正预测，这会直接影响世界模型能不能被当作引擎组件。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Prediction or Persistence?
What Future-Prediction Scores Miss
About World Models

Abstract

Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future’s resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor’s own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03–0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.

Keywords: World Models, Evaluation and Benchmarking, Video Representation Learning

1 Introduction

Robot learning increasingly builds on pretrained video world models, such as V-JEPA 2, DINO-WM and the wider latent-predictive line, as components a policy is initialised from, plans against, or is evaluated with [7, 10, 1, 18]. Which one to trust is decided largely by future-prediction score. If that score misleads, the decisions built on it (which model to pretrain from, plan against, or evaluate with) inherit the error. Our probe uses passive video with no robot in the loop: it concerns what the score measures, not control. That is still a question for robot learning, because the model under test and the decision the score informs are the same ones.

A future-prediction score reflects three things at once: an encoder that represents the scene well, a near future that resembles the recent past, and a predictor that anticipates what comes next. Only the last is prediction in the intended sense, yet the score sums all three. A predictor that contributes nothing still scores well on the first two, and a harmful one can still beat chance. The score alone therefore cannot show what the predictive machinery adds.

We separate the three with a matched control. A model must identify a clip’s true continuation among eleven candidates from the same video. It is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, isolating the predictor for one extra forward pass. Score and contribution diverge (Fig. 1). Within the native-video V-JEPA family, V-JEPA 2’s predictors add +0.028 to +0.041 top-1 to scores above 0.42, while V-JEPA 2.1’s adds +0.291 on the identical trials. DINO-WM, measured off-distribution, scores 0.136 against 0.091 chance, yet its persistence baseline reaches 0.315. We therefore offer a diagnostic for reading the score: without the persistence gap, a future-prediction number cannot be interpreted. We do not try to settle whether world models are needed; we show that the score alone cannot settle it, and we measure the predictor’s share directly. Contributions: (i) a persistence control decomposing any future-prediction score into encoder quality, temporal persistence and predictor contribution, for one forward pass and no training; (ii) a 27,000-trial zero-shot future-retrieval probe over 1,094 egocentric videos, sweeping context and horizon independently; (iii) predictor contributions for five models from +0.291 to negative, pooled negatives confined to the two off-distribution models, and a positional envelope fixing in advance where a frozen predictor leaves its trained range.

2 Related Work

Latent-predictive world models predict in representation space: V-JEPA pairs a masked-feature-prediction video encoder with a latent predictor [2, 3], scaled in V-JEPA 2 to over a million hours of video [1] and retrained for dense features in V-JEPA 2.1 [13]. DINO-WM learns an action-conditioned predictor over frozen DINOv2 features [16, 18], and LeWorldModel learns both from pixels [11]. Reconstruction-based models [8, 5] and video simulators [4, 15] are compared by downstream success. Headline scores have repeatedly become interpretable only once paired with a trivial baseline: constant velocity for pedestrians [17], tuned metric-learning baselines [14], copying the present in anticipation [6, 9]. World-model comparisons are mostly reported without one. Our persistence control is the world-model analogue: the same model with one module disabled, so the difference is attributable.

3 Method

The diagnostic has two parts: a retrieval probe that produces a future-prediction score, and a matched control that removes the predictor from it.

Future retrieval.

A trial is τ=(V,t,A,W): the model observes the anchorX_τ=V[t-A, t] and must identify the ground-truth future y^⋆_τ=V[t, t+W] among N=11 candidates, each a W-second window of the same video. Scene recognition is therefore uninformative, and chance top-1 is 1/N=0.0909. With frozen encoder f_θ, frozen predictor g_θ and native training criterion E_θ (lower is more compatible),

\jmatĥ_τ = \argmin_j∈{1,…,N} E_θ ( g_θ(f_θ(X_τ), W) (predicted future), f_θ(cⱼ)).

(1)

Distractors tile outward from the anchor’s start and the ground truth’s end, so none overlaps the anchor. Presentation order and the number preceding it are redrawn per trial, so neither position nor geometry reveals the answer. Each model is scored by its own training criterion over candidates embedded by its own encoder, since an energy is only meaningful in the space its objective was defined over. We compare only the induced ranking (Appendices A, B; worked trials in Fig. 3).

The persistence control.

The control asks whether the explicit predictor adds anything over an encoder that copies the present, that is, whether the predictive structure is doing any work. Egocentric video is temporally continuous, so much of any score needs no prediction. We pair every model with a control identical except that the predictor is replaced by the identity, gᵖᵉʳˢ_θ(z,W)=z: it asks “which candidate most resembles what was just observed?”, under the same encoder, preprocessing and energy. The predictor contribution is the paired difference in top-1 over a common trial set T,

δ_θ = (1)/(|T|)∑_τ∈T[1{\jmatĥ_τ=j^⋆_τ}-1{\jmatĥᵖᵉʳˢ_τ=j^⋆_τ}].

(2)

It attributes to the predictor alone, since encoder, energy and trials are held fixed, and is signed: δ_θ<0 marks a predictor worse than not predicting. Retrieval among candidates tests temporal localisation rather than the content of a predicted future, so a positive δ_θ certifies that the predictor carries future-relevant information beyond its encoder: a prerequisite for, not a demonstration of, usefulness in planning or control. Because trials cluster in videos, every top-1 and δ_θ interval is a 95%video-level cluster bootstrap over the 704 videos (B=10,000, percentile, seeded; Appendix E).

Corpus, envelope and protocol.

Trials are built from 1,094 household egocentric videos (479 h, no action stream), every window inside a span of annotated manipulation. We sweep A∈{1,…,10} s and W∈{1,1.5,…,A} s over 100 cells, separating input budget from horizon. A frozen predictor can only be queried at positions it was trained over. The anticipation wrapper lays context and target tokens end to end, so they consume the positional budget additively: A+W≤uP/φ. For V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-g (P=32, u=2, φ=8 fps) that bound is 8 s. We evaluate inside that envelope and report outside it separately. Every cross-model number uses one pinned intersection of 27,000 trials (704 videos, 25 cells) scored by all nine variants at their own published geometries.

4 Results

The central finding is that score and predictor contribution dissociate. Within the native-video V-JEPA family alone, scores above 0.42 coexist with contributions of +0.03 and +0.04, while V-JEPA 2.1’s predictor adds +0.291, before any off-distribution model is considered.

The contribution is not read off the score.

The dissociation holds within the native-video V-JEPA family and survives dropping V-JEPA 2.1 entirely. V-JEPA 2 ViT-H and ViT-L reach 0.437 and 0.424 top-1, over four times chance, against a shared control at 0.396. Their predictors therefore contribute only +0.0408[+0.0326, +0.0491] and +0.0284[+0.0205, +0.0363]. The claim that a high score need not mean the predictor contributes therefore rests on neither the single 2.1 checkpoint nor any action-conditioned model. V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-g (Fig. 1) widens the spread: 0.736 against 0.444, δ=+0.291[+0.281, +0.302], roughly 10× V-JEPA 2’s. Neither persistence row calls a predictor, so the +0.340 between the two families splits into +0.048 encoder and +0.291 predictor (Table 1), terms a single accuracy cannot separate. Native energy is the stricter readout: it needs no trained probe, so a small or negative δ_θ reflects the predictor under its own training objective rather than a readout we chose.

A predictor can be worse than none.

DINO-WM scores 0.136, above the 0.091 chance rate, which on its own would suggest a working predictor, while its persistence control scores 0.315. Removing the predictor improves retrieval, so scoring above chance was not evidence that it predicts. Its predictor expects actions in PushT’s action space, which passive household video cannot supply, so it is measured off-distribution: we report the direction and treat the magnitude, -0.179[-0.186, -0.172], as illustrative (see Limitations). The same direction appears in-distribution below, where V-JEPA 2 falls under its own control at W=1 s with no embodiment gap. LeWM is off-distribution for the same reason and serves as a domain-mismatch control rather than a peer.

Persistence alone recovers the pretraining ordering.

With every predictor disabled, the four encoders order video- > image- > sim-pretrained, with all four intervals disjoint. Persistence top-1 is 0.444 for ViT-g, 0.396 for ViT-L, 0.315 for DINOv2 and 0.208 for ViT-Ti, trained from scratch in simulation.

Horizon separates anticipating from copying.

Persistence decays with the rollout W (0.554 → 0.308 for the ViT-g encoder, 1–4 s) as the future drifts from the present. V-JEPA 2.1 decays in parallel (0.824 → 0.590), holding +0.27 to +0.31 throughout, so its predictor buys a roughly constant horizon (Fig. 2). V-JEPA 2’s curves are nearly flat (0.452 → 0.361 for ViT-L) and sit below their control at W=1 s, 0.452 against 0.500. At short horizons its predictor is worse than copying. This happens inside the native-video family with no embodiment gap, so it is a counterpart to DINO-WM without that confound.

5 Discussion

A reporting norm.

We suggest that every future-prediction score be reported alongside its own persistence baseline. It costs one forward pass, needs no training, and applies to any encoder–predictor factorisation. Without it, the reported number cannot show whether the predictive structure is doing any work; with it, that share is measured directly. On our passive-video probe the share is substantial for V-JEPA 2.1 and marginal for V-JEPA 2, and the negative values for the two off-distribution models are illustrative. This does not settle whether robots need world models, but it adds a comparison that is usually missing from that discussion.

Limitations

Passive-video scope.

The probe scores predictive representation on passive household video. No claim about control, planning or downstream robot performance follows. Retrieval among eleven candidates tests temporal localisation rather than the content of a predicted future, and it is easier than generation.

Action inputs.

DINO-WM and LeWM are action-conditioned models trained on simulated PushT, and passive video supplies no actions in that space. We evaluate them with zero actions through their own action encoders, so their predictors run outside the regime they were built for. Their persistence controls never call the predictor and are unaffected, but their full-model figures are confounded, so their magnitudes are illustrative and the thesis rests on the V-JEPA models.

Other confounds.

The anchor axis is confounded by lineup geometry and is not interpreted; the corpus is a single household domain; only one V-JEPA 2.1 checkpoint is evaluable, so that result carries no scaling curve. Clustering is not among the confounds: its largest widening (2.12×) falls on V-JEPA 2.1’s top-1, and every claim still holds (Appendix E). Appendix F gives the full discussion and the experiments that would remove each limitation.

AI Usage Statement

The author used generative AI tools for writing and editing assistance. All technical content, experiments, and claims are the author’s own.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Benchmark construction, models and inference

Corpus.

1,094 household egocentric videos, 478.6 h, 242,356 annotated subtasks, passive first-person capture with no action stream. An active run is a maximal contiguous span of annotated manipulation, merging gaps of ≤1.0 s; there are 25,296 such runs covering 425.8 h (89% of the corpus). All lineup geometry must fit inside one active run, so every window shows genuine manipulation rather than idle or transition footage. A trial is labelled by the action in the ground-truth window, not the anchor, so the label describes what has to be predicted.

Lineup geometry.

With margin m and stride s=W+m, and with k distractors drawn per trial to precede the anchor (at least one on each side), the candidate set is

ℂ_τ=\underbrace{[ t-A-m-(i-1)s-W, t-A-m-(i-1)s ]}ᵢ₌₁ᵏ_before the anchor ∪ [ t, t+W ] (y^⋆_τ) ∪ \underbrace{[ t+W+m+(i-1)s, t+2W+m+(i-1)s ]}ᵢ₌₁^N-1-k_after the ground truth,

(3)

presented in a per-trial seeded permutation. We use m=0, giving a contiguous strip. A validator enforces three properties and rejects any lineup that violates them: no distractor overlaps the anchor; presentation order is randomised; and the answer’s index is not a fixed function of the geometry, because k is redrawn per trial. Verified on 40,000 sampled lineups: 0% anchor-overlapping distractors, 0% in raw time order, ground-truth index approximately uniform over all 11 slots. Further construction parameters: anchor stride 0.5 s, minimum anchor separation 2.0 s, at most 3 datapoints per (video, cell), ground truth never at a temporal edge, annotator-confidence floor 0.8, global seed 0.

From construction to the evaluated set.

Construction produced 282,032 lineups; balancing to 400 trials per (task group, cell) retained 204,715 (surplus is marked, not deleted). Of these, 54,481 satisfy A+W≤8 s, and 27,000 were scored by all nine model variants and pinned by id. The 8 s restriction is principled (§3); the further restriction to 27,000 is a wall-clock budget, roughly 2× fewer than could be scored with no new construction. The evaluated set spans 704 videos and 25 cells with 1,041–1,131 trials per cell (median 1,081); composition is in Table 6.

Models and checkpoints.

Each model runs at its own published evaluation geometry: V-JEPA 2 ViT-L/16 (300 M, 256 px, 1024-d) and ViT-H/16 (600 M, 256 px); V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-g/16 (1 B, 384 px, 4×1408=5632-d hierarchical target) [1, 13, 12]; DINO-WM (21 M frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder +20 M predictor, 224 px, 196×384-d) trained on simulated PushT [18]; LeWM (15 M; ∼5 M ViT-Ti/14 encoder trained from scratch, 224 px, 192-d), also on simulated PushT [11]. Two selection points are material to reproducibility. (i) V-JEPA 2 and 2.1 are separate families with different modules, encoder keys and input resolutions. (ii) The released 2.1 ViT-B and ViT-L are distilled: their predictors emit their ViT-G teacher’s 1664-d features, so their native energy is undefined without also running the teacher. ViT-g is used because it is trained with the 2.1 recipe directly and its predictor targets its own EMA encoder. This also means the 2.1 result rests on a single checkpoint, with no scaling curve inside that family.

Action conditioning.

DINO-WM and LeWM are action-conditioned control models, and the corpus is passive video. Actions and proprioception are therefore supplied as zeros through the models’ own action/proprio encoders rather than injected post-embedding, because those layers have biases. Their predictors are conditioned on PushT’s action space, which passive household video cannot supply and which no video-derived surrogate would occupy either, so both models are measured off-distribution here. The mismatch is confined to one arm of each pair: an action is an input to the predictor, not to the encoder, so a control that never calls the predictor never receives an action. In both adapters the zero action is in fact constructed inside the roll-forward method that the control overrides, so the persistence figures are action-free by construction. That makes the control side of each pair clean; it does not make the full-model figure unconfounded, which is why §4 reports those magnitudes as illustrative.

Inference.

Decode once per video at 8 fps and share the frames across models; bfloat16, except LeWM whose encode() casts its input and therefore runs in float32; token-budgeted batching; 4×A100 80 GB, one worker per GPU over a largest-first video-bundle queue. Clip length follows the window’s duration rather than being resampled to a fixed frame count, so one tubelet corresponds to the same physical time in every cell and a horizon in seconds converts to tubelet steps exactly. Top-1 is primary; mean rank and R@k accompany it; intervals are 95% video-level cluster bootstraps (Appendix E), the per-trial normal approximation being retained only as a cross-check on the machinery; model-vs-control differences use the paired form of Eq. (2). All sampling, shuffling and bootstrapping is seeded (\textttseed=0).

Appendix B Native energy

For a prediction ẑ∈ℝ^T×d and candidate tokens h∈ℝ^T×d, the V-JEPA pretraining objective is a LayerNormed ℓₚ regression,

E_θ(ẑ,h) = 1/Td∑_ι=1ᵀ∥ẑ_ι-LN(h_ι)∥ₚᵖ/p, p=1.

(4)

The LayerNorm must be kept, since omitting it compares the prediction against a quantity the model was never trained to match. The V-JEPA 2.1 predictor emits the concatenated features of B=4 encoder blocks, and its training loss normalises each block separately before concatenation, LN_B(h)=[LN(h⁽¹⁾)∥⋯∥LN(h^(B))]; a single LayerNorm over the full Bd width would mix blocks of different scale into one statistic and is not the quantity the predictor was trained against. DINO-WM is scored by its emb_criterion (MSE over the visual token slice) and LeWM by its criterion (MSE summed over features). In every case lower energy denotes greater compatibility.

The degeneracy check.

Each trial is additionally re-ranked using the ground-truth candidate’s own latent as the query. Since that query is a member of ℂ_τ its minimum is a self-distance and it ranks first by construction; the check therefore detects an encoder that collapses distinct moments onto identical latents. It attains 1.000 for every model reported here and should not be read as an achievable-accuracy bound.

Appendix C Additional results

Error structure.

0.264 of top-1 is unreached by the strongest model, and its mistakes are not systematic drift. Candidates are ordered in time, so a signed index offset says whether a model that misses reaches into the past (negative) or overshoots (positive). The mean signed offset is -0.02 steps with a 50/50 past/future split for every model, and only 18% of errors land on a candidate adjacent to the truth. All three are indistinguishable from a uniform guess (-0.02; 0.502/0.498; 0.182). Failures are therefore losses of temporal localisation rather than a bias toward regressing to the past, so closing the remaining gap is not a matter of sharper sub-second timing.

Appendix D Full tables

Appendix E Cluster-robust confidence intervals

The 27,000 evaluated trials are drawn from 704 videos and 4,425 active runs, so roughly 38 trials share each video. Trials from one video share footage, scene, lighting and actor, so their outcomes are correlated and the effective sample size is below 27,000; a per-trial normal-approximation interval is therefore too narrow.

Method.

A video-level cluster bootstrap over the evaluated set. For each of B=10,000 replicates we draw 704 video ids with replacement from the 704 unique ones, gather every trial belonging to the drawn videos (a video drawn twice contributes its trials twice), and recompute the statistic; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicate distribution are the interval. Three properties matter. Resampling is at the video level, never the trial level: all trials from a chosen video stay together, which is what carries the dependence. Pairing is preserved: for a contribution δ_θ the per-trial indicator of Eq. (2) is formed first, then videos are resampled once per replicate and the difference read from that same sample, so a model and its control are never resampled independently. Point estimates are untouched: they come from the full data and only the intervals change. No re-inference is involved: per-trial correctness is read from the stored results. Seeded, so it reproduces exactly.

Is B large enough?

Re-running under 8 seeds gives the Monte-Carlo error of the procedure itself, which is unrelated to the statistical uncertainty being measured. Table 7 reports how far the interval endpoints move between seeds. The intervals themselves are 0.0064–0.0223 wide; at B=10,000 the endpoint jitter is ±0.00029, about 9.1% of the narrowest interval’s half-width, so it affects only the fourth decimal place. B=10,000 is more than sufficient, and even 2,000 would be defensible. Bootstrap bias, |mean of replicates-point estimate|, is ≤0.00007 across all 14 statistics, so plain percentile intervals are appropriate and a BCa or studentised bootstrap would change nothing.

Is the video the right grain?

Trials (27,000) nest in active runs (4,425), runs nest in videos (704), and videos nest in actors (352); every video is its own episode, so there is no hidden level between video and actor. Resampling at each grain (Table 8) separates real dependence from over-correction. Widening from trial to run to video is dependence being captured, up to 2.12×. Widening from video to actor is not: at most 1.13×, and 1.00× on the headline contribution. Video level therefore absorbs nearly all the clustering, and resampling more coarsely only widens the intervals. Every δ_θ still excludes zero even at actor level. As a check on the machinery, the trial-level bootstrap reproduces the analytic normal-approximation interval almost exactly: ±0.0053 against ±0.0053 for V-JEPA 2.1 top-1.

Outcome, and reproduction.

No point estimate changes, no estimate changes sign, and no contribution interval crosses zero; the four persistence intervals remain disjoint, so the video- > image- > sim-pretrained encoder ordering holds under clustering. The intervals in Table 2 are the cluster intervals. The correction applies to those pooled statistics only: bands in the per-cell and per-task-group figures (Figs. 2, 7) remain trial-level, because within a single (A,W) cell or task group too few videos contribute to resample reliably, so those bands show spread rather than cluster-robust uncertainty. The bootstrap (B=10,000, \textttseed=0) runs in ∼35 s from the per-trial scores. Code, the pinned trial ids and the per-trial scores for every model will be released publicly.

Appendix F Extended limitations and the experiments that remove them

Construct validity.

The probe measures predictive representation on passive video, so no claim about control, planning or model-predictive use follows. Retrieval among 11 candidates is strictly easier than generation: a model can rank correctly while its predicted latent is far from the target in absolute terms, and scores here upper-bound nothing about rollout fidelity. Zero-shot native-energy retrieval is a protocol choice; the official V-JEPA evaluation trains a 4-block attentive probe, which measures something related but looser. The degeneracy check is not headroom (Appendix B).

Confounds in the model comparison.

Model families differ on several axes at once (resolution, latent width, pretraining corpus, predictor objective, parameter count), so the persistence controls isolate the predictor’s contribution within a family but cannot attribute the V-JEPA 2 → 2.1 gap to any single change. Only one V-JEPA 2.1 checkpoint is evaluable, so that result carries no scaling curve. LeWM is a domain-mismatch control, not a peer of the video-pretrained models. DINO-WM and LeWM are additionally measured outside the action-conditioned regime they were built for, which is why the thesis is carried by the V-JEPA contributions and their magnitudes are reported as illustrative.

Ranked next steps.

Ordered by priority.

  • 1.

    De-confound the anchor axis. Place distractors at fixed temporal offsets from the ground truth rather than tiling from the anchor’s start, so varying A changes only the amount of context and leaves candidate geometry identical. Table 4 would then become interpretable, and the design could measure how much context a predictive model actually uses.

  • 2.

    Scale to the full in-range pool. The evaluated set is budget-limited, not construction-limited: roughly twice as many in-range lineups already exist and need no new data preparation, which would tighten the small-n task groups.

  • 3.

    Relate to the official probe protocol. Run the standard 4-block attentive probe alongside native-energy retrieval on the same trials. This anchors our numbers to the published V-JEPA results, and the gap between protocols is itself informative: it measures how much of a model’s usable future information is inaccessible without a trained readout.

  • 4.

    Extend past the 8 s bound. In increasing cost: positional interpolation or RoPE scaling at inference; a sliding-context formulation that keeps every query inside the trained range; or continued pretraining at longer context. Any of these would turn the out-of-envelope rows of Table 5 into a tested result about long-horizon prediction.

  • 5.

    Broaden the corpus, and add an action-conditioned split. A second domain tests generalisation. Separately, the only fair evaluation of an action-conditioned world model is the identical future-retrieval lineup built over a robot dataset with native recorded actions: manufacturing surrogate actions cannot escape the embodiment mismatch, so we leave this to future work.

  • 6.

    Stratify by difficulty, and add a human baseline. Label each trial by scene change, motion magnitude and semantic distance between the target and its nearest distractor, then report accuracy by stratum, separating temporal-precision failures from semantic ones. A human baseline on a few hundred trials per stratum would establish whether the 0.264 of top-1 that the strongest model misses is headroom or irreducible ambiguity. This is the most important quantity the study does not yet measure.

    • Reproduction.

    Every trial row stores the full 11-candidate energy vector, so any re-ranking metric can be recomputed without re-running inference. The evaluated set is pinned by id, and all sampling, shuffling and bootstrapping is seeded, so the figures reproduce exactly.

item.title: 别再自回归滚 rollout：PIM 直接预测「交互结果」，一步给出形变而不累积误差 ｜ PIM: A Physical Intuition Model for Low-Latency Prediction of Object Interaction Outcomes
item.description:
一句话：刚体级状态表达不了局部形变，而 rollout 的误差会随预测时程复利累积。

要点：

  • 任务：从初始条件预测物体交互的结果，是数据驱动物理推理的核心问题
  • 现有方法两条短板：用刚体级状态表达不了局部形变；用自回归 rollout 预测演化又会让误差在长时程上累积
  • PIM（Physical Intuition Model）改为**直接预测交互结果**，而不是逐步推演过程，从而做到低延迟

为什么值得看：游戏里大量交互只需要「结果对不对」，不需要逐帧物理过程。把预测目标从「轨迹」换成「结果」，既避开误差累积，也把延迟压下来——这是把物理 AI 用进运行时的正确提问方式。

中文摘要：从初始条件预测物体交互的结果，是数据驱动物理推理的核心问题。现有方法通常依赖刚体级别的状态表示，或通过自回归 rollout 预测演化过程，但前者无法表达局部形变，后者的误差又会随预测时程不断累积。PIM（Physical Intuition Model）因此改变提问方式：不逐步推演交互过程，而是直接预测交互结果，从而做到低延迟。对运行时系统而言，大量交互只关心「结果对不对」而非逐帧过程，这个目标函数的选择本身就是性能优化。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

PIM: A Physical Intuition Model for Low-Latency Prediction of Object Interaction Outcomes

Abstract

Predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions is a central problem in data-driven physical reasoning. Existing methods often use rigid-body-level states or predict the evolution through autoregressive rollouts. Coarse representations cannot represent local deformation, while rollout errors may compound over long prediction horizons. Instead, we introduce PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that directly predicts a physical system’s equilibrium state from its initial mesh geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes. PIM combines local k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) attention to encode intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention to model interactions, and a dual-branch decoder that predicts object-level translations and per-vertex residual displacements. Across MuJoCo scenarios involving both rigid and deformable interactions, PIM achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines. By predicting complete equilibrium states in a single forward pass, PIM substantially reduces latency relative to autoregressive learned models and MuJoCo rollouts under the evaluated protocols, enabling low-latency inference when only the final outcome is required.

1 Introduction

Simulating how objects move, collide, and deform is important in computer graphics, robotics, and embodied intelligence. Conventional physics simulators can resolve collision, contact, friction, and deformation with high fidelity, but numerical time stepping can be computationally expensive when generating large datasets or simulating complex scenes. Learning-based models offer an alternative approach to predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions. Adopting the terminology of prior work on predicting block tower state [1], we use physical intuition to denote the ability to infer the equilibrium state of interacting objects from their initial geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes.

Existing physical AI models use object-, particle-, graph-, or mesh-based representations primarily for stepwise dynamics prediction [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Instead, we present PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that takes the initial scene state as input and directly predicts the equilibrium positions of all mesh vertices. This representation accommodates both rigid-body motion and non-rigid deformation, but requires the model to jointly reason about object geometry, physical attributes, and inter-object interactions across diverse contact phenomena. Throughout this paper, equilibrium state denotes a stationary configuration in approximate static equilibrium, reached after transient motion has decayed and the net forces and torques are balanced up to numerical tolerance. States involving persistent motion, including dynamic equilibria, are outside the scope of this work.

In this work, PIM aims for object interactions. Each object is represented by vertex tokens augmented with object-level and scene-level conditions. Local KNN self-attention captures intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention exchanges information between objects, and a dual-branch decoder separates center displacement from vertex-level residual motion. PIM therefore predicts both global object movement and local geometric change within a unified mesh representation.

We evaluate PIM on four controlled MuJoCo scenarios spanning planar and irregular-surface collisions, structural collapse, and rigid–deformable interaction. Comparisons with direct equilibrium-state predictors and autoregressive rollout baselines, together with controlled ablations and runtime measurements, demonstrate lower equilibrium-state errors and low-latency inference under the evaluated protocols.

The main contributions of this work are:

  • •

    We present a unified physical intuition model that directly predicts object interaction outcomes from initial geometry, kinematic conditions, and physical attributes. By representing these outcomes as equilibrium meshes, the formulation jointly accounts for rigid-body motion and localized deformation while avoiding autoregressive rollouts when only the final interaction outcome is required.

  • •

    We introduce PIM, which takes a vertex-based representation as input and combines local KNN self-attention to encode intra-object geometry with cross-object attention over source anchors selected via farthest point sampling (FPS).     α_p,q=softmax_q∈ℕᵢ(p)(q̄_i,pᵀk̄_i,q),

    π_j,0=0,(4)
    π_j,l=\arg\max_q\min_r

    β_p,q^i←j=softmax_q∈Aⱼ(q̄_i,pᵀk̄_j,q).

    εᵥₜₓ=(1)/(∑ᵢnᵢ)∑_i,p∥ŷ_i,p-y_i,p∥₂,(13)
    ε_cen=1/M∑ᵢ∥ĉᵢ-cᵢ∥₂.

    Here 𝔼ᵢᵗʳⁱ contains unique triangle edges of the shared 642-vertex evaluation mesh for controlled rollout comparisons. Metrics are averaged over test scenes in meters.     PIM has the lowest vertex and centroid errors in all four scenarios (Table 1). Rigid-Pose MLP serves as a rigid-output reference on Deformable. Figures 1 and 7 show representative and randomly sampled predictions.

一句话：刚体级状态表达不了局部形变，而 rollout 的误差会随预测时程复利累积。

要点：

  • 任务：从初始条件预测物体交互的结果，是数据驱动物理推理的核心问题
  • 现有方法两条短板：用刚体级状态表达不了局部形变；用自回归 rollout 预测演化又会让误差在长时程上累积
  • PIM（Physical Intuition Model）改为**直接预测交互结果**，而不是逐步推演过程，从而做到低延迟

为什么值得看：游戏里大量交互只需要「结果对不对」，不需要逐帧物理过程。把预测目标从「轨迹」换成「结果」，既避开误差累积，也把延迟压下来——这是把物理 AI 用进运行时的正确提问方式。

Abstract

Predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions is a central problem in data-driven physical reasoning. Existing methods often use rigid-body-level states or predict the evolution through autoregressive rollouts. Coarse representations cannot represent local deformation, while rollout errors may compound over long prediction horizons. Instead, we introduce PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that directly predicts a physical system’s equilibrium state from its initial mesh geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes. PIM combines local k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) attention to encode intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention to model interactions, and a dual-branch decoder that predicts object-level translations and per-vertex residual displacements. Across MuJoCo scenarios involving both rigid and deformable interactions, PIM achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines. By predicting complete equilibrium states in a single forward pass, PIM substantially reduces latency relative to autoregressive learned models and MuJoCo rollouts under the evaluated protocols, enabling low-latency inference when only the final outcome is required.

1 Introduction

Simulating how objects move, collide, and deform is important in computer graphics, robotics, and embodied intelligence. Conventional physics simulators can resolve collision, contact, friction, and deformation with high fidelity, but numerical time stepping can be computationally expensive when generating large datasets or simulating complex scenes. Learning-based models offer an alternative approach to predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions. Adopting the terminology of prior work on predicting block tower state [1], we use physical intuition to denote the ability to infer the equilibrium state of interacting objects from their initial geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes.

Existing physical AI models use object-, particle-, graph-, or mesh-based representations primarily for stepwise dynamics prediction [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Instead, we present PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that takes the initial scene state as input and directly predicts the equilibrium positions of all mesh vertices. This representation accommodates both rigid-body motion and non-rigid deformation, but requires the model to jointly reason about object geometry, physical attributes, and inter-object interactions across diverse contact phenomena. Throughout this paper, equilibrium state denotes a stationary configuration in approximate static equilibrium, reached after transient motion has decayed and the net forces and torques are balanced up to numerical tolerance. States involving persistent motion, including dynamic equilibria, are outside the scope of this work.

In this work, PIM aims for object interactions. Each object is represented by vertex tokens augmented with object-level and scene-level conditions. Local KNN self-attention captures intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention exchanges information between objects, and a dual-branch decoder separates center displacement from vertex-level residual motion. We evaluate PIM on four controlled MuJoCo scenarios spanning planar and irregular-surface collisions, structural collapse, and rigid–deformable interaction.     Baselines.

    To our knowledge, no publicly available model directly supports our multi-object equilibrium-mesh prediction setting. We therefore construct two direct equilibrium-state baselines: Rigid-Pose MLP predicts object translation and rotation from pooled geometry/physics descriptors, while Vertex Transformer predicts vertex displacements using local attention and a Transformer over pooled object tokens. Both use the same fine meshes, splits and supervised loss as PIM, with the direct-baseline weights given above; they train for 100 epochs using AdamW at an initial 10⁻⁴ and validation-L1 checkpoint selection.

    A controlled Flat comparison evaluates PIM and Small-PIM against HOPNet [14] and our PyTorch reimplementations of FIGNet [6, 39] and MeshGraphNets [5]; -Adapt variants also receive the initial external force. We report mean vertex and centroid errors for the controlled Flat comparison. The direct baselines are additionally evaluated on Jenga and Deformable generalization sets without fine-tuning.

    Evaluation metrics.

    For one scene, omitting batch indices in ℓ, vertex and centroid errors are

    εᵥₜₓ=(1)/(∑ᵢnᵢ)∑_i,p∥ŷ_i,p-y_i,p∥₂,(13)
    ε_cen=1/M∑ᵢ∥ĉᵢ-cᵢ∥₂.

    Using the pairwise distances defined above, edge errors are

    ε_edge=(∑_i,p∑_q∈ℕᵢ(p)|ℓᵖʳᵉᵈ_i,p,q-ℓᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ_i,p,q|)/(∑ᵢnᵢkᵢ),(14)
    εₜᵣᵢ=1/M∑ᵢ(1)/(|𝔼ᵢᵗʳⁱ|)∑_(p,q)∈𝔼ᵢᵗʳⁱ|ℓᵖʳᵉᵈ_i,p,q-ℓᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ_i,p,q|.

    Here 𝔼ᵢᵗʳⁱ contains unique triangle edges of the shared 642-vertex evaluation mesh for controlled rollout comparisons. Metrics are averaged over test scenes in meters. Vertex/KNN errors weight vertices/neighbor pairs; centroid/triangle errors weight objects equally. Edge errors are rigid-motion invariant and diagnostic; rigid outputs, per-step projection, or terminal rigid fitting constrain rollout baselines’ triangle-edge errors, which are excluded from placement ranking.

    4.2 Main results

    PIM has the lowest vertex and centroid errors in all four scenarios (Table 1). Rigid-Pose MLP serves as a rigid-output reference on Deformable. Figures 1 and 7 show representative and randomly sampled predictions.

item.title: 图生 3D 一个资产要几分钟：Sprint3D 不换模型，先 profile 公开管线，看端到端时间浪费在哪 ｜ Sprint3D: Accelerating End-to-End 3D Asset Generation through Pipeline Optimization
item.description:
一句话：以往工作只加速采样，或自己重训生成器；这篇从已经发布的管线里找可省的时间。

要点：

  • 现状：图像到 3D 的生成模型已能产出资产级的带纹理网格，但每个资产要几分钟，迭代慢、部署贵
  • 既有加速工作大多只针对**网络采样**；少数同时优化网格处理的，又自带私有生成器（无法直接复用）
  • Sprint3D 换了个起点：拿一条公开管线做 profile，搞清楚端到端时间里到底哪部分可省

为什么值得看：「不换模型、只重排管线」是最容易在自家资产流水线里复制的优化方式。而且它的方法论比结论更有价值——先测量再优化，而不是先换更大的模型。

中文摘要：图像到 3D 的生成模型已经能产出资产级的带纹理网格，但每个资产耗时数分钟，既不利于迭代也不利于部署。此前的加速工作大多只针对网络采样本身；少数同时优化网格处理环节的方案，又训练了自己的生成器，外部无法直接复用。Sprint3D 选择一个不同的起点：拿一条公开可用的管线做端到端 profile，先弄明白时间到底花在哪里、有多少能省，再做针对性优化。对需要批量产出 3D 资产的团队，这种「先测量再优化」的做法比换模型更容易照搬。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Sprint3D: Accelerating End-to-End 3D Asset Generation through Pipeline Optimization

November 12, 2026

Abstract

Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33×). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7× without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.

1 Introduction

Image-to-3D generation has moved from proof of concept to production. Optimization-based methods introduced for text prompts distill a 2D diffusion prior into one object at a time and take minutes to hours per asset [54, 42, 61]. Novel-view and multi-view diffusion [44, 60, 47] and feed-forward reconstruction from one or a few views [22, 80, 67, 69, 7] brought this down to minutes and then to seconds. Native 3D generation trains a diffusion or flow model directly on a scalable 3D latent representation and now produces textured meshes usable as game and product assets. Recent native generators (Section 2) raise the output resolution and surface detail, generate physically based materials [68] and follow the input image more closely [38].

In production, however, such a generator is rarely run once: creators sample several candidates per input, compare them and re-run with adjusted inputs. The wall-clock time from an uploaded image to an exported asset therefore determines both how quickly they can iterate and how much GPU time each asset costs to serve. On an H200 GPU, the released pipelines that write a textured asset take from about one to more than two minutes per image in our measurements (Appendix Table 9).

Yet work on accelerating these generators has concentrated on the generative networks through few-step distillation, training-free caching and compression of the diffusion transformer, and it reports at most the latency of the accelerated network [32, 94, 8, 83, 34]. Where such work does profile a pipeline stage by stage, the profile stops at the decoded shape [32, 12]. Among the image-to-3D systems we surveyed, only AssetGen [71] breaks down the time from input image to exported asset by stage (Appendix 6).

Meanwhile, the three released pipelines we run that write a textured asset unwrap UVs with xatlas on the CPU [87]: Pixal3D [38], TRELLIS.2 [78] and Hunyuan3D-2.1 [68]. Prior work that also optimizes the steps after the networks does so together with its own generators [7, 71], which leaves open how much of a released pipeline’s end-to-end time can be saved without training a new one. We therefore begin with a measurement and ask: where does the end-to-end time of a state-of-the-art image-to-3D pipeline go, and how much of it can be removed before the networks are touched?

To answer it, we study Pixal3D [38], whose public code and weights allow its end-to-end time to be both measured and changed. Its public implementation runs four rectified flows on the structured latents of TRELLIS.2 [78], conditioned on the input pixels so that the output stays registered to the input view. At its official export (about 1M faces, 4096² texture) it takes more than two minutes per image, and profiled stage by stage it spends most of this time in mesh post-processing and little in its four flows (Figure 1, bottom; Section 3.1). TRELLIS.2 uses the same export code and shows the same split, and the two other released pipelines we timed also spend most of their time outside the sampling of their networks (Appendix Table 9). The latency of such a pipeline is dominated by the work after its networks.

The profile exposes three bottlenecks, each of which limits the latency once the previous one is removed, and our pipeline removes them in turn. The mesh post-processing comes first: it runs on the CPU and on the critical path, and UV unwrapping alone takes longer than all four flows together. We rebuild it on the GPU and take it off the critical path, with a single-pass GPU chart segmentation in place of the CPU unwrap. With the post-processing off the critical path, every network evaluation still has avoidable cost, which we remove by computing the conditioning once, reusing step-invariant keys and values, and using faster attention kernels. What remains is the number of evaluations: each flow takes 12 steps, and three of the four flows are guided. Reducing the steps without retraining degraded the quality. We therefore distill each flow separately and choose the objective and the step count per stage by ablation. Specifically, the coarse- and fine-shape flows are replaced by consistency-distilled students and the structure and texture flows by trajectory students, which reproduce in fewer steps the 12-step sampling trajectory of their teacher, the released flow. Because any of these optimizations can change the asset, we classify every change as output-identical, near-identical or output-changing and measure its effect end to end (Table 1).

The result is Sprint3D, which writes the textured GLB at the official export in 4.05 s at the median, compared with 133 s for Base (Pixal3D), the released pipeline run with its own script (33×; Figure 1). In the order in which the bottlenecks are removed, the speed-up splits into 7.3× for the rebuilt post-processing, 1.2× for the engineering of the unchanged flows and 3.8× for distillation (Table 2). For quality, we follow the protocol of the Pixal3D paper: on 2,653 held-out Toys4K [65] test objects evaluated once, Sprint3D is significantly better than the released pipeline on all ten input-view normal columns, at a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU. Compared with three other open generators, Sprint3D and the released pipeline have the best values in every quality column of this protocol, whereas on the metrics outside it the comparison is mixed. The speed-up comes at the cost of lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail than the 12-step teacher of the texture stage (Section 4.3). Finally, the rebuilt mesh post-processing is not specific to Pixal3D: without the half-resolution remesh it also transfers to TRELLIS.2, where the evaluated metrics do not change detectably (Table 3).

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    An end-to-end profile of a state-of-the-art image-to-3D pipeline (Section 3.1).

  • •

    A pipeline that removes the three bottlenecks in order, with a per-stage distillation cascade at non-uniform step counts. Its mesh post-processing transfers to TRELLIS.2.

  • •

    A decomposition of the end-to-end speed-up against two configurations that keep the 12-step flows at the official export, and an evaluation under Pixal3D’s own protocol with the complete ablation, the measured trade-offs and the techniques we tried and rejected.

    • 2 Related Work

    Native image-to-3D generation and its representations.

    Native generators differ in the latent they denoise. That latent is a set of latent vectors attached to the surface [88, 89, 40, 92, 39], a set of latent vectors anchored to a coarse voxel grid (LATTICE [31], the shape model of Hunyuan3D 2.5 [30]), a triplane [75], sparse voxels [76, 41], or structured latents on a sparse voxel grid [79]. TRELLIS introduced the structured latents, which are generated by a structure flow and then a latent flow over the active voxels and decoded into 3D Gaussians, radiance fields or meshes [79]. Hi3DGen conditions these structured latents on a normal map estimated from the image [85], and TRELLIS.2 learns them from native 3D data with a compact sparse-voxel representation of geometry and material attributes, from which a mesh with material is decoded directly [78]. The released Pixal3D pipeline, which we study, builds on TRELLIS.2 with pixel-aligned conditioning [38]. In contrast to native generation, feed-forward reconstruction returns an asset from one network pass in under a second: TripoSR outputs a vertex-colored mesh and SF3D a UV-unwrapped mesh with estimated material parameters [69, 7].

    Texture and material generation.

    Appearance is generated in two ways, and both end in a UV texture. Multi-view painting renders the mesh from several views, generates or inpaints the views with a 2D diffusion model and back-projects them into a UV texture [56, 1, 9], as Hunyuan3D-2.1 does for its PBR material maps [68]. Native generators instead denoise an appearance latent on the same support as the geometry and bake the decoded attributes into a UV atlas [78]. The released Pixal3D pipeline takes this second route, and its texture resolution is therefore determined by the bake rather than by the generator.

    From generated geometry to an exportable asset.

    Between the decoder and the file lie the steps of classical geometry processing. A surface is extracted from the decoded field [26], simplified to a face budget [15], cut into charts and parameterized [37], packed into an atlas [87], and the attributes are baked into the atlas. GPU formulations exist for these steps: parallel simplification for low-poly modeling (PaMO) [52], real-time charting and packing for texture-space shading (FastAtlas), whose charts are the connected components of the visible triangles, parameterized by perspective projection [70], and interactive GPU atlas packing in rows (TABI) [18]. Alternatively, texture representations defined on the surface itself, such as heat kernel textures, do without a UV atlas [13]. Released pipelines integrate these steps after the generator and differ in how they unwrap. SF3D projects each face onto the cube face chosen by its normal instead of running xatlas, which can take up to 30 s per asset [7], and Hunyuan3D Studio predicts the UV seams with a learned autoregressive model [36]. AssetGen parallelizes xatlas instead and reports the time of each step, as well as the saving from each change in its ablation of the shape branch [71] (Appendix 6).

    Faster sampling: few-step distillation and training-free acceleration.

    The networks themselves are made faster by sampling in fewer steps or by making each step cheaper, and few-step students of a diffusion or flow model are trained in several ways. Progressive distillation halves the sampler’s steps per round by regressing one student step onto two teacher steps [57]. Consistency models map any point of the probability-flow ODE to its endpoint [63], consistency trajectory models extend this to arbitrary time pairs [29], and flow map matching casts all of them as learning the two-time flow map [4]. Distribution-matching objectives match sample distributions instead [86], and classifier-free guidance can be folded into the student [51]. More recently, CrossDistill applies a trajectory-preserving objective at high noise and distribution matching on the student’s own samples at low noise [46]. PDD is a trajectory-based method like the trajectory students used here: it predicts several denoising steps per network evaluation and is trained on the student’s own outputs, as CrossDistill is [59]. In 3D, FlashVDM distills the shape flow of Hunyuan3D-2 from 50 to 5 steps and speeds up its decoder [32], MDT-dist distills both TRELLIS flows to one or two steps each [94], and SAM 3D cuts its geometry flow from 25 to 4 evaluations [8]. AssetGen applies progressive distillation stage by stage, with guidance folded into the shape students and also into the texture student in its faster configuration AssetGen Flash [71]. Seed3D 2.0 also folds guidance into all its geometry and texture transformers and then halves their sampling steps round by round [17]. Outside 3D, TurboT2VA pairs consistency distillation with a quantized, fused inference stack for text-to-video-audio generation [84]. The cost of sampling also falls without training, through higher-order solvers [48], feature caching across steps [50, 83, 12] and token reduction [5, 6, 12], while pruning, quantization and fine-tuning compress the diffusion transformer itself [34]. Finally, FlashAttention-3 [58], CUDA graphs and stream overlap are the standard tools of diffusion serving at the kernel level.

    Relation to this report.

    Against this background, we count the mesh post-processing as part of the latency, as AssetGen does (Section 3.2), and we distill each stage separately, as MDT-dist and AssetGen do (Section 3.4). Unlike AssetGen, which trains its own generator, we keep the released networks frozen and train low-rank adapters only (Section 3.5).

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    The Pixal3D pipeline.

    We study the released implementation of Pixal3D [38], which turns one image into a textured mesh with a cascade of four rectified-flow stages [45, 43] on the structured latents of TRELLIS.2 [78] (Figure 2). In contrast, the model of the Pixal3D paper is built on Direct3D-S2 [76] and generates the geometry only. In the released implementation, the input is cropped to the object and its field of view is estimated by MoGe-2 [73]. A frozen DINOv3 encoder [62] conditions every stage with features sampled where each token’s voxel projects into the input image. Of the four stages, the structure flow denoises a dense 16³ latent that a frozen decoder turns into a 64³ occupancy grid, max-pooled to a 32³ support. Its active voxels become the token set of the coarse-shape flow, and after upsampling they become that of the fine-shape flow. Both shape flows operate on sparse voxels, and the texture flow produces the appearance latent on the same sparse tokens. Frozen VAE decoders turn the shape and texture latents into a dual grid with per-voxel attributes. A mesh path then turns that into a GLB: mesh extraction, remeshing, simplification, UV unwrapping, texture baking and file export. The released code builds this path on the CuMesh library [77] and the nvdiffrast rasterizer [33].

    Sampling.

    Each of the four flows is sampled with 12 Euler steps. The structure flow and the two shape flows use classifier-free guidance [21] at high noise levels (t≥0.6), where a step costs two network evaluations, and the texture flow is unguided. In total, the released sampler performs 76 network function evaluations per image (22+21+21+12 for the four flows). We call the released pipeline run with its public inference script at its defaults Base (Pixal3D) (Section 4.1), and the released flow of one stage sampled in this way the 12-step teacher of that stage.

    Where the time goes.

    To profile Base (Pixal3D), we measure the end-to-end (E2E) time of a request from the input image to the written GLB (Section 4.1). A second in which stages run concurrently is attributed to the stage the request is waiting for, the critical path. Measured this way, Base (Pixal3D) spends most of its time after the networks: in the dedicated timing run, mesh post-processing takes 85% of the mean E2E time and the four flows with their conditioning 14% (Appendix Table 7). Most of that post-processing is spent in a single step, UV unwrapping (a GPU chart clustering followed by the CPU unwrapper xatlas). This step takes 94 s on average, several times as long as the four flows together. The rest of the post-processing consists of the 4096² texture bake, mesh extraction and remeshing with the BVH build, and the WebP export. Among the flows, the fine-shape flow takes the largest share, followed by the texture flow.

    Optimizations and how they are measured.

    Guided by this profile, we remove three bottlenecks in Sections 3.2–3.4, in the order in which they limit the E2E time: the CPU mesh post-processing on the critical path, the per-evaluation cost of the flows and the number of evaluations. Table 1 lists the adopted optimizations in these three groups, each with its output class. An optimization is output-identical (=) when it is designed to leave the output unchanged and near-identical (≈) when its output differs by bf16 accumulation order, rounding or non-deterministic kernels, whereas distilled students, approximate geometry or a different UV chart layout make it output-changing (\blacklozenge). We measure the effects in the cumulative measurement on the 40-object subset of the validation set (80 inputs; Section 4.1, Figure 4). It starts from the re-run of Base (Pixal3D) inside our measurement code and adds the optimizations one at a time in the order of the three groups. In this order, the students are added last, so the released 12-step flows remain until then.

    3.2 Rebuilding the Mesh Post-Processing

    The first bottleneck is the CPU mesh post-processing on the critical path. We therefore replace the released GLB export by the tiled mesh path, add seven optimizations to it and call the result the rebuilt mesh path. Throughout, the networks and the generated latents are untouched, and the seconds quoted in this section are E2E effects from Table 1 unless stated otherwise.

    Tiled mesh path (\blacklozenge).

    The tiled mesh path is the first form of our export and makes two changes to the UV unwrapping, the single step that takes most of the post-processing of the released path. First, we split the export into a geometry half and a bake half, so that the shape is decoded first and unwrapped on a thread while the texture flow samples. Second, we parallelize the unwrap itself: large charts are cut, and the charts are assigned to 16 groups, each unwrapped by its own instance of the CPU unwrapper xatlas [87] and packed into one tile of a 4×4 atlas. With the charts cut and tiled, the UV layout changes. However, the tiled mesh path is an intermediate configuration: Sprint3D replaces its per-tile CPU unwrapping by the single-pass GPU chart segmentation described below, and we keep it here because it is the first step of the cumulative measurement.

    Remeshing and simplification (\blacklozenge, ≈).

    Before the unwrap, the released path remeshes the decoded dual grid with narrow-band dual contouring [26] at full resolution and then simplifies to the face budget by parallel edge collapse with quadric error costs [15, 52], both in CuMesh. To shorten this step, our adaptive half-resolution remesh halves the remesh resolution and thereby changes the intermediate geometry before simplification. The exception is a fine-shape token set that is dense for the grid resolution, as for thin, detailed structures. Because the remesh extracts a thin double-walled shell whose wall is two grid cells thick, the halved grid also doubles the thickness of the never-rendered inner wall. This does not change any rendered metric but lowers the point-cloud alignment scores (Appendix 9.3). The second change here is a faster GPU simplification and chart-clustering kernel, which is non-deterministic but stays within the run-to-run spread of the kernel it replaces.

    BVH and UV atlas (≈, \blacklozenge).

    The released path also builds the bounding-volume hierarchy used for attribute look-ups with cuBVH [66] on the CPU. Instead, we build it on the GPU as a linear BVH [27], which leaves the distances unchanged and changes the nearest face only on exact ties (≈). Since the tiled mesh path leaves the CPU unwrapping on the critical path, we replace its 16-tile CPU unwrapping altogether by a single-pass GPU chart segmentation (Figure 3). It finds the charts in one pass without iterative chart clustering, parameterizes them by a per-chart projection on the GPU and packs them into a single atlas, leaving the geometry unchanged but not the chart layout (\blacklozenge) (Appendix Figure 7). Specifically, each face takes the nearest of a fixed set of directions, and the resulting charts are merged or cut according to their size (steps and parameters: Appendix 6). These parts follow earlier work: the fixed projection directions follow the box projection of SF3D [7], the charts found as connected components follow FastAtlas [70], and the row packing follows the GPU packers of FastAtlas and TABI [18]. The chart segmentation removes 30.5 s, the largest saving after the tiled mesh path itself: the remaining CPU unwrapping leaves the critical path, and the 12-step texture flow becomes the longer branch.

    Baking and export (=).

    In the subsequent bake and export, two changes leave only the file bytes different: the Triton kernel that interpolates attributes into the texture uses a fixed launch configuration instead of autotuning at request time, and a lean GLB writer with parallel PNG encoding replaces the generic exporter. The decoded pixels and the geometry buffer are identical, and each change saves a few seconds (Table 1).

    Worker thread (=).

    Finally, the overlap with the texture flow is not limited to the UV atlas. A worker thread starts as soon as the shape latent is decoded and runs the whole geometry pre-processing (hole filling, BVH build, remeshing, simplification and the GPU atlas) on the GPU while the texture flow samples. This scheduling leaves the arithmetic unchanged.

    Measured effect.

    What each of these optimizations saves depends on what is on the critical path when it is added. With the released 12-step flows, the tiled mesh path alone reduces the median E2E time of the re-run of Base (Pixal3D) from 138.4 to 55.3 s. However, its 16-tile CPU unwrapping hides the 12-step texture flow on most inputs and limits the E2E time. At its position in the order, the adaptive half-resolution remesh lengthens the E2E time (+2.8 s, Table 1) since the CPU unwrapping is still active there and takes longer on the critical path than the mesh stage saves. The same remesh shortens the E2E time (-0.83 s in a control run, Appendix 6) in the rebuilt mesh path, where the GPU chart segmentation has replaced the CPU unwrapping. The worker thread contributes little: switching it off in Sprint3D lengthens the E2E time by only 0.03 s, because the concurrent GPU work slows the texture flow about as much as it hides (Appendix 6).

    3.3 Engineering the Flows

    Once the post-processing is off the critical path, the released 12-step flows limit the E2E time (Table 2). Before shortening them we remove the second bottleneck, the cost that does not depend on the number of steps. All changes below leave the networks unchanged.

    Reuse (=) and attention kernels (≈).

    Part of this cost is repeated work. Since the released pipeline re-encodes the input image for every stage, we run the DINOv3 encoder once for each of the two input resolutions that the stages use, project its features once to the sparse token layout and share the upsampling encoder across the four flows. The conditioning tensors are identical. A second kind of repeated work occurs inside the texture flow: the cross-attention keys and values of the image tokens, and the context projections that produce them, do not depend on the sampling step and are thus computed at the first step and reused. The reuse of the projections can be switched on only together with the structure student and is therefore counted toward the distillation factor. The near-identical changes are the attention kernels: the texture flow and the fine-shape flow use FlashAttention-3 [58] in bf16, an exact-attention kernel whose results differ from the reference implementation only by floating-point rounding, not by the algorithm. The structure and coarse-shape flows keep their attention kernels: the structure stage selects its active voxels by thresholding, so bf16-level perturbations there flip voxels and produce a different sample. Among the shape stages, restricting the changes to the fine-shape flow likewise keeps the active voxels identical and retains most of the gain. FlashAttention-3 gives most of the gain of this section (Table 1).

    Scheduling (=).

    Three scheduling changes complete the flow engineering: texture sampling runs on a side CUDA stream synchronized by events, PNG encoding of the finished texture images starts while baking is still running, and the cache release is deferred to the end of the request. Further re-scheduling and prefetching did not reduce the E2E time (Appendix 11).

    3.4 Per-Stage Distillation

    What remains is the third bottleneck, the number of network evaluations, which we reduce by distilling each of the four flows into a student that takes fewer steps.

    Setting.

    Each stage is a rectified flow: for a clean latent x₀ and Gaussian noise ε the network v_θ(xₜ,t,c) is trained to predict ε-x₀ at xₜ=(1-t) x₀+t ε, t∈[0,1], given the image conditioning c. Sampling integrates dxₜ=v dt from t=1 to 0, and the 12-step teacher takes its Euler steps on a time grid 1=t₀>t₁>…>t₁₂=0 that is shifted toward high noise. Every student is a rank-256 LoRA adapter [24] on the frozen network of its teacher, initialized at zero so that the student equals the teacher at the start of training. An exponential moving average of the adapter is deployed (batch sizes and decay: Appendix 10). We use two objectives.

    Consistency distillation (coarse- and fine-shape flows).

    The first objective is consistency distillation [63] from a guided teacher as in latent consistency models [49], and we use it for the two shape flows in an ODE-anchored variant (the noisy states below are drawn around the guided teacher’s endpoint, not around data). Let f_θ(xₜ,t,c)=xₜ-t v_θ(xₜ,t,c) be the one-jump estimate of the clean latent. For each training view we run the guided 12-step teacher once and keep its endpoint x̂₀. Noisy states are then drawn on the path x_τ=(1-τ) x̂₀+τ ε at the points τₙ₊₁ of a 50-point discretization of [0,1]. The student is trained to be consistent with the teacher’s flow,

    L_CD=𝔼[∥f_θ(x_τₙ₊₁,τₙ₊₁,c)-f_θ⁻(x̂_τₙ,τₙ,c)∥₂²],

    		(1)

    where x̂_τₙ is obtained from x_τₙ₊₁ by one Euler step of the frozen guided teacher over the grid interval 1/50. Here θ⁻ is the moving-average copy of the student. The consistency model is sampled by predicting x₀, re-noising to the next level and repeating, but the deployed coarse- and fine-shape students take a single evaluation from pure noise.

    Trajectory distillation (structure and texture flows).

    With more than one step, consistency distillation trains for a sampler that re-noises between steps rather than for the deterministic sampler that Sprint3D runs (the same observation motivates phased consistency models [72]). Its 4-step structure student indeed agrees less with the 12-step teacher than the trajectory student, and its 4-step texture student agrees less with it than four Euler steps of the released flow (Section 4.5, Appendix 11). We therefore distill these two stages directly onto their deployment grid. Let G={t_g₀=1>t_g₁>…>t_gₖ=0} be a (k+1)-point subset of the 13-point grid of the 12-step teacher, and let xᵀₜ denote the state of the teacher’s own deterministic (guided) trajectory at grid time t, computed once per training view and cached. The student is trained to reproduce, with one Euler step, the teacher’s multi-step transition between consecutive grid points:

    Lₜᵣₐⱼ=𝔼ᵢ[∥xᵀ_t_gᵢ+(t_gᵢ₊₁-t_gᵢ) v_θ(xᵀ_t_gᵢ,t_gᵢ,c)-xᵀ_t_gᵢ₊₁∥₂²],

    		(2)

    with i drawn uniformly over the k segments. The inputs are teacher states (teacher forcing), and re-noising is never used. At deployment the student is run with k plain Euler steps on G without guidance. Specifically, the texture student uses k=2 with t=(1,0.75,0), two segments of 6 teacher steps. The structure student uses k=4 with the non-uniform grid t=(1,0.9,0.75,0.6,0), i.e., segments of 3, 3, 2 and 4 teacher steps. We compute the structure trajectories and deploy the student at the time shift 3.0 of the shape and texture flows rather than the 5.0 of the released structure sampler, so its target is the 12-step teacher at this shift (Appendix 10).

    Relation to prior objectives, and deployment.

    Equation (2) derives from progressive distillation [57]: one round at the non-uniform ratios of the structure grid above instead of 2:1, with the guided teacher’s ODE states as inputs instead of noised data (further relations: Appendix 10). Guidance is folded into the cached teacher states so that the students run conditional-only [51], as AssetGen does for its shape students [71]. The per-stage choice of objective and step count follows the ablation of Section 4.5. At deployment the structure student runs inside a static CUDA graph, which removes launch overhead without changing the arithmetic (counted with the student in Table 1). As with the attention kernels, the adapters of the fine-shape and texture students are folded into the bf16 weights (≈), while the structure and coarse-shape students keep the adapter as a separate branch, because bf16 rounding there would change the active voxels (Section 3.3). Since the students do not use guidance, they take 4+1+1+2 = 8 network evaluations per image.

    Same-step teachers and rejected alternatives.

    To isolate the effect of distillation, we compare every student in Section 4.5 with its same-step teacher, the released flow of its stage sampled with the student’s step count and without guidance. Two alternatives to distillation failed (Appendix 11). Shortening the texture flow without training removes only a few evaluations before the quality degrades, because the discretization error grows as the steps drop, and making the steps cheaper fails because the teacher’s attention is neither local nor low-rank and little is redundant.

    3.5 Training

    Data.

    Under both objectives, we train the students on outputs of the 12-step teachers only, without ground-truth geometry in any loss. The structure student and the two shape students are trained on the 5k set (5,243 objects), which was built first. The texture student is trained on the 10k set, 10,000 objects drawn later from TRELLIS-500K [79] with a stricter metadata filter and better-framed views. Retraining the structure student and the two shape students on the 10k set did not improve them (Section 4.5, Appendix 10), and we therefore keep the 5k-set students. Appendix 7 gives the selection funnel, the views of the two sets and the framing check.

    Schedules.

    On these sets, we trained the structure student with the trajectory objective for 500 updates on one GPU, the coarse-shape student with the consistency objective for 3,000 updates on 16 GPUs, and the texture student with the trajectory objective for 3,000 updates. The fine-shape student was trained like the coarse-shape student and is the checkpoint at 2,000 updates of a run configured for 3,000. Optimizer settings and costs are in Appendix 10, and the selection of every checkpoint in Appendix 7.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Data.

    We evaluate on three sets. The main comparison (Section 4.3) is on the Toys4K test part, 2,653 held-out objects of Toys4K [65] with one fixed view each, evaluated once after the evaluation code had been frozen. The Toys4K development part (500 objects) was evaluated after Sprint3D was fixed, as a check before the test part (block (b) of Appendix Table 10). The validation set consists of 400 objects drawn from the same pool as the training data and disjoint from the 10k set (Section 3.5). Since Sprint3D was selected on this set, the numbers measured on it may be subject to selection bias, which is why the main comparison is on the test part. The ablations, the distillation studies, the timing runs, the qualitative figures and the failure analysis are nevertheless all run on it, and its 40-object subset (two views each, 80 inputs) is used for every timing run and every analysis of Section 4.2. Appendix 7 describes the splits, the views, the selection and the seven validation objects that also occur in the 5k set.

    Baselines.

    We label Sprint3D as Ours in tables and figures and compare it with the released pipeline, with the configurations between the two, and with external baselines. Base (Pixal3D) is the released pipeline run with its own script (Section 3.1), and Base (Pixal3D), re-run is the same pipeline and export run inside our measurement code. Two further configurations keep the released 12-step flows and are named after their rows in Table 2: mesh path rebuilt uses the rebuilt mesh path of Section 3.2, and + flow optimizations adds the optimizations of Section 3.3 that apply to the released networks. As external baselines, we run TRELLIS.2 [78], TripoSG [40] and Hunyuan3D-2.1 [68] at their released defaults. We run every method ourselves and evaluate it with the same code, and we do not copy any number from the Pixal3D paper, because its model differs from the released one (Section 3.1).

    Metrics.

    The main tables follow Table 1 of the Pixal3D paper: the normal map of each output is rendered in the input-image frame and compared with the ground-truth normal map. We report the IoU of the predicted and ground-truth masks, the PSNR, SSIM [74] and LPIPS [90], the mean and median angular error, the mean angular error in a band at the mask boundary (Mean_B) and the accuracy at 11.25^∘, 22.5^∘ and 30^∘. Following the wording of the paper, every metric except the IoU is computed on the overlap of the two masks, the overlap region. However, we compute PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS on the full image outside Table 4 and its validation-set and development-part counterparts unless the overlap region is named. As in the paper, we do not align any output to the ground truth: the external baselines are rendered with the ground-truth camera pose, and Base (Pixal3D) and Sprint3D with their own inference-time projection. The true-camera condition gives the model the ground-truth intrinsics, distance and scale instead of the estimated camera and is used only for analysis (Table 6(a), Appendix 9.1). Throughout, Δ is the mean of a paired per-object difference with its 95% bootstrap CI in brackets. “Significant” refers to a Holm-adjusted sign test and is marked in tables by ∗ (better) and † (worse) against the reference row. Appendix 7 gives the remaining choices and the statistics.

    End-to-end time and export.

    The E2E time (Section 3.1) includes input preparation and the file write but not model loading, and requests run one at a time on one H200 GPU. Unless a caption states otherwise, speed is the median E2E time per input and quality is measured on the 400 validation objects with the inference-time camera of the released script. The official export is the export setting of Base (Pixal3D) (about 1M faces, 4096² texture). Every result uses it except a few analyses in the appendix that name the smaller export (fewer faces and a 2048² texture). Speed ratios thus compare pipelines with the same target face count and texture resolution. However, the assets are not identical: the texture encoding (lossless PNG for ours, lossy WebP for Base (Pixal3D)), the atlas layout and the remesh resolution differ (Section 3). Given identical latents, renders of the two exports agree at 32 dB PSNR (Appendix 6).

    We time the configurations above in two runs. The dedicated timing run gives the main timing result, with one machine per method and requests strictly one at a time: its medians are 133.0 s for Base (Pixal3D) and 4.05 s for Sprint3D, a ratio of 33×. The cumulative measurement (Section 3.1) instead runs all its configurations in one process, so its rows are paired. We therefore compare times only within a run and take every ratio to Base (Pixal3D) in the dedicated timing run. The E2E column of a table likewise serves only the comparison of its rows (Appendix 6).

    4.2 Progressive Design Analysis

    We first attribute the speed-up to the three groups of changes, then apply the rebuilt mesh path to a second pipeline, and finally examine how the quality changes along the cumulative measurement.

    The three groups.

    The attribution is based on the cumulative measurement, which starts from the re-run of Base (Pixal3D) inside our measurement code, i.e., from the released pipeline with its own export. The median of this re-run is consistent with that of Base (Pixal3D) in the dedicated timing run (Table 2), and its time divides between mesh post-processing and the four flows almost as in Base (Pixal3D) (Appendix 6). Thus, the speed-up below is not due to the export or to our measurement code. Of the three groups, the first two shorten the time without a measurable change in the input-view normal quality: up to the row “+ flow optimizations”, every CI of the difference to Base (Pixal3D) includes zero. The third group also changes the quality. Replacing the four flows by the distilled students turns the 15 s pipeline into a 4 s one and raises the normal PSNR by 0.34 dB [+0.18,+0.50] over the 12-step flows of the row above. The mean angular error improves as well, with a CI excluding zero.

    Order of attribution.

    The speed-up factors of these three groups (Table 2) multiply to 34.6×, the ratio from the re-run of Base (Pixal3D) to Sprint3D in the cumulative measurement. However, because the stages overlap and the bottleneck moves, they are not independent contributions and depend on the order in which the changes are applied. In the reverse order the students and the flow optimizations are applied first on the released, serial post-processing. An estimate from the per-input critical paths then gives only 1.15× for these two steps together and 30.1× for the post-processing rebuilt last. In either order, most of the end-to-end factor is due to the mesh post-processing. The split of Base (Pixal3D) is reversed at the end of the measurement: in Sprint3D the neural flows take 59% of the mean critical path and the mesh post-processing takes 34%, mostly the 4096² bake and the file export (dedicated timing run, Appendix Table 7).

    A second pipeline.

    Next, we test whether the mesh optimizations transfer to a second pipeline.
