Analysis of the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 agents yields three observations. Visual understanding of space and camera separates agents. Challenging staging and filming requests remain difficult across capability levels. Agents inspect their renders, but their judgments do not reliably correspond to fewer errors. These observations point to better visual understanding, explicit checks for challenging requests, and verification of renders against the brief. VibePrevisBench makes progress on these capabilities measurable.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Benchmark details

    A.1  Task construction

    Coverage first.

    Two frozen taxonomies tag every task. One covers what a scene holds: places, spaces, layout relations, subjects, actions, camera and editing, and genre, in 67 categories. The other covers how a task is asked: input kind, writing style, information level, organization and length. Each tag and each kind of place has a minimum number of tasks, and the gaps became slots for new tasks, routed to three lanes.

    Scripts.

    Each slot becomes a card fixing genre, writing style, length, places, people, actions and a story seed. Scripts come in seven writing styles, from screenplays and shot lists to ad briefs and novel-like prose, at about 600 to 1,200 words. The hidden GT facts are written before the script: a model (GPT-6.1 Sol) first codes the scene, then writes the script, then the claims, each citing the sentence it comes from and checked to hold in the coded scene. Automatic gates check every task’s scoring and output specification. Two blind readers from the Claude and DeepSeek families, who see only the script, try to recover every claim; a claim both misread is reworded and re-read up to twice, then dropped if still misread.

    Videos and continuations.

    We collected candidate clips ourselves. The screening keeps clips of at least 5 s and 2 fps, with a short edge of at least 480 pixels for local clips and 720 for web videos, and drops clips whose adjacent frames are more than 85% identical. Local clips are cut into windows of 25 to 50 s, a seeded eighth also into 15 s windows, and web videos into 25–45 s video windows and 12 s continuation windows; each source keeps at most three or four windows that overlap by at most 60%. Windows are ranked by subject presence, the number of moving people or vehicles and its changes, motion beyond the camera’s own, camera motion, cuts, person size and duration, and flagged for letterboxing, burned-in text, repeated frames and darkness. We then pre-screened the windows by model ratings of contact sheets (Gemini 4, Claude Sonnet 5.5), and tagged the survivors by place, genre, people, shots and moving vehicles. Human reviewers decided whether a clip becomes a video task, a continuation or neither. Quotas then capped over-represented content such as vehicles, and borders and logos were cropped. A video brief gives an id and a description for each place and subject, and the output must start where the clip starts and cut where it cuts. A continuation brief gives the clip’s opening frame and an account of the next 6 to 20 s, mostly following the clip. Figure10 shows how one clip’s hidden GT facts are built.

    Photos.

    We drew on scan datasets with measured 3D boxes and camera poses, indoors and in street scenes, and used each scene once. Boxes from the hidden GT facts were drawn back onto every photo and checked first by a model and then by a human; candidates whose boxes did not match the photo were rejected. The output must show each photo’s view for 12 frames and then sweep the place for 8 s. One photo task instead uses five keyframes of a real clip, and its hidden GT facts are estimated as for a video.

    Pruning.

    All 11 agents ran the pool, and we dropped tasks that did not discriminate between agents: low item-rest correlation or little spread across agents, never a single agent’s score. Finally we removed tasks with source or licensing problems or an unscorable run.

    Model assistance and fairness.

    Several of the evaluated models help build tasks. GPT-6.1 Sol writes the script specs and scripts; the blind readers come from other families, Claude and DeepSeek; Claude Sonnet 5.5, of the same family as Opus 5.5, pre-screens clips; and Gemini 3.8 and Gemini 4 register and observe the subjects behind the hidden GT facts of videos and continuations, while Gemini 4 also rates web clips. Three safeguards limit their influence. Agents are scored by rule checks on facts, never by similarity to a model’s own output; the hidden GT facts are never edited to make a reader pass; and every brief and its facts are reviewed and corrected by hand. Ranked by Rule-based Scene Check, the agents show no strong self-preference. GPT-6.1 Sol is second on scripts and over all tasks; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is seventh on scripts and over all tasks; and Opus 5.5 is third over all tasks and fourth on videos. The Gemini models rank somewhat higher on the media tasks whose hidden GT facts they helped estimate: Gemini 4 Argon is fourth over all tasks but third on videos and second on continuations, and Gemini 3.8 Flash is eighth over all tasks but sixth on videos. A small preference cannot be ruled out; the judge’s own-family bias is measured separately in Sec.B.4.

    A.2  Task examples

    Figure11 shows one task of each kind, and their prompts are excerpted below.

    Script (excerpt).

    Suitcase Chase Through the Corner Shop. A courier is chased through a shop into a back alley, where a reversing van traps his accomplice… S02 Shop: north of the street’s east part. A west shelf and an east shelf run north–south either side of the aisle from the front door to the back door… P01 person: courier holding O01, west of the planter, facing east. P02 person: pursuer, behind P01, facing east… 0–5 s: P01 runs east with O01, P02 chasing. 5–10.8 s: P01 enters the shop by the front door at 9.5 s; P02 follows at 10.8 s… Shots (lens: wide-angle 24 mm, moderately wide 28 mm, normal 35 mm, slightly long 50 mm)… 5–8 s, hard cut: under the arcade’s east end; eye level, normal, facing west; pans right to the door…

    Photos (prompt).

    Rebuild the place shown in the attached photo as one static 3D proxy blockout, with one camera. Build the place and everything in it at real-world size, and place the camera so that its view matches the photo: position, direction and lens. Output: 12 frames at 24 fps, 640×426… Place: S01 Informal learning lounge. Tag every piece of the place (walls, floor, furniture, fixtures) by class…

    Continuation (excerpt).

    Continue the attached photo as a proxy previs. Frame 1 must reproduce the photo: the camera’s position, direction and lens, and every visible subject and object where it is in the photo… Output: 336 frames at 24 fps (14.00 s)… P01 person: the seated woman beside the bed… P02 person: the standing man to her right… 0.0 s: the close eye-level side view of P01 and P02 pulls back in a dolly move. From 0.3 to 2.2 seconds, P01 stands up from the bed… 4.0 s: Cut to a medium eye-level front view of P01 with P02. The camera orbits toward her side… From 6.4 to 7.1 seconds, P01 turns back toward P02…

一句话：可控视频生成可以条件在灰模预演上，而灰模正需要 agent 在 Blender 里把 4D 场景重建出来。

要点：

  • 链路起点：可控的真实感视频生成可以条件在**渲染出的灰模（graybox）代理视频**上，从而固定布局、运动与相机
  • coding agent 已能在 Blender 里重建 4D 场景来产出这类视频，但此前没有任何基准同时检验**视频本身**与它背后那些长时段、多镜头的场景
  • VibePrevisBench 因此让人把一句话简报变成可执行的 4D 场景，并对场景与渲染结果一起评测

为什么值得看：「让 agent 写脚本搭场景」是引擎里最现实的 AI 落地形态之一。有了灰模这一环，评测就能同时覆盖场景正确性与画面可用性——而不是只看生成视频好不好看。

中文摘要：可控的真实感视频生成模型可以把「灰模（graybox）代理视频」作为条件，从而固定布局、运动与相机路径；而这类灰模视频，正好可以由 coding agent 在 Blender 里重建 4D 场景来生成。但此前没有任何基准同时检验这些灰模视频本身，以及支撑它们的那些长时段、多镜头场景。VibePrevisBench 因此把「把一句话简报变成可执行的 4D 场景」作为任务，并把场景与渲染结果一并评测。对引擎团队，这是少见的「agent 直接操作 DCC 工具产场景」的量化视角。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

 VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding
for 4D Scene Generation in Blender

Abstract

Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

††footnotetext: ∗Equal contribution. †Project lead. ‡Corresponding author.††footnotetext: §This work was conducted during the author’s internship at Kling AI.

1  Introduction

Controllable real-world video generation models now take previsualization (previs), a rough 3D mock-up of a shot, as input and paint the real-world video on top [60, 42, 31, 3]. This input is a graybox proxy video, the untextured render of a 4D scene whose layout, people, actions, cameras and cuts unfold over time. Conditioning on proxy video makes all of these more controllable [30, 20, 44, 4, 36], but building it by hand takes skilled artists and time [23, 67]. Coding agents can build it instead: from a script, photos, a continuation or real footage, they write Blender code, render previews, inspect their frames and revise [34, 7, 8, 36, 32, 10]. We call this task 4D scene generation: the agent writes the executable 4D scene that a brief describes or shows, and renders its proxy video. Figure1(a) shows this pipeline. The agent becomes the director; the real-world video generation model, the renderer.

The proxy video shapes the final real-world video: the real-world video generation model keeps the camera and layout of proxy video, so an agent’s errors carry into the resulted real-world video, as Fig.2 shows. Therefore, it is important to generate the high-quality proxy video. To evaluate the quality of proxy video, we need to check two things. First, is the 4D scene right? In Fig.2(a), the task asks for riders turning at eye level, but the weak agent films them from high above a flat lot. The proxy video looks fine, and the VLM judge even gives it 95.5. Thus, it is necessary to find this error by rule-based scene check in 4D scene. Second, can a viewer see it is right? In Fig.2(b), the car is in frame and turning, so the rules pass it. However, the car is a tiny dot on screen, which can be found by the VLM-based screen check. This happens often: 31% of annotated actions pass the rules but are hard or impossible for a viewer to see in the proxy video, as Sec.C.3 reports.

Existing benchmarks support such an evaluation only in part. Table1 compares them along four dimensions and shows three gaps. (i) Narrow inputs. Benchmarks of dynamic scenes mostly start from text prompts [70, 56] or videos to reconstruct [47, 52, 54]. A director, in contrast, may start from a script, photos of a real location or footage to restage, where each source tests a different skill. (ii) Static content. Scene-building benchmarks mostly target single objects, static scenes or short clips without people [19, 18, 13, 65, 47]. None tests a long, multi-shot scene in which several people’s routes, event timing, camera moves and cuts must hold together. (iii) Screen-only evaluation. Dynamic-scene benchmarks score only proxy or real-world video frames [56, 54], while checks of scene state against ground truth cover only static scenes or short clips [18, 65, 47].

To address these gaps, we introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Figure1b shows what it scores: the 4D scene and its proxy video, both checked against hidden GT facts. VibePrevisBench has three key features that match the three gaps mentioned above. (i) Diverse inputs. Briefs come in four kinds, scripts, photos, continuations and reference videos, across seven scene domains, as Fig.3 shows. (ii) Staged and filmed scenes. Most tasks stage several people in multi-shot scenes of about 40 s, so routes, event timing, camera moves and cuts are tested together. (iii) Two evaluation dimensions.Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the delivered code, exports the 4D scene frame by frame and checks it against hidden GT facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether a viewer can recognize each entity, read each action and follow the story in the proxy video.

We evaluate 11 frontier coding agents, and we make three observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. The gap between the best and the worst agent grows from 12.0 Rule-based Scene Check points on scripts to 19.9 on photos, while weak agents require more rounds facing failed API calls. Second, all agents master only basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. When the reference films from a low angle, 66% of shots come out at eye level, whereas eye-level shots go wrong only 9% of the time. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Even when agents say their renders match the reference, camera-angle errors are just as frequent as in runs without such claims. These observations call for better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    A benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction. VibePrevisBench has 242 tasks over four input kinds: scripts, photos, continuations and reference videos, in seven scene domains. Most tasks stage several people in long, multi-shot scenes, where we can test the moving trajectory of people, the event happening time, the camera moves and cuts together.

  • •

    Two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check tests whether the 4D scene is right by checking it against hidden GT facts, and VLM-based Screen Check tests whether what is right can be seen in the proxy video.

  • •

    A diagnostic study of 11 coding agents. From their scores, trajectories and ablations, three observations show what separates the agents, where they all fail and why they do not correct themselves.

    • 2  Related Work

    Proxy-conditioned real-world video generation. Real-world video generation models follow ever richer conditions, from camera paths [21, 58, 1] and object trajectories [17, 55, 72] to a proxy video [20, 46, 63, 71, 30, 44, 4]. A proxy video is the render of a coarse 4D scene, which previs tools and agents build [23, 11, 67, 32, 43]. It fixes layout, motion and camera at once, so the real-world video inherits the scene’s mistakes. Real-world video generation benchmarks evaluate the real-world video: most score it with learned or VLM judges, including benchmarks that test real-world video generation models as world models [27, 70, 50, 12, 40, 2, 33, 59], and some check it against ground truth for short, single-shot physics or motion [29, 6, 14]. Multi-shot benchmarks rely on judges or detected cuts [56, 48, 57], and others check whether a real-world video generation model renders what a program specifies [28, 45]. All of them evaluate the real-world video, not the 4D scene behind it or the coding agent that builds this scene.

    Understanding a video by rebuilding it. Video understanding benchmarks test perception through answers, groundings or captions [16, 62, 41, 39, 5, 53, 64], and camera benchmarks show that VLMs still misread camera motion [37, 9]. An answer can be right even when the model’s picture of the scene is not, and writing the scene out explicitly exposes such gaps [38, 25]. Rebuilding a video in code takes this furthest, since every object, motion and camera must be written out; existing benchmarks do so for physics clips, indoor scans, embodied demonstrations and short cinematic clips [47, 52, 51, 54]. None of them both rebuilds multi-shot videos of several people and checks the rebuilt scene against ground truth, as the last columns of Tab.1 show.

    Building scenes with code. LLM agents write Blender code for objects, scenes, animation and films [49, 24, 26, 66, 22, 61], and recent code world models already write the 4D scene behind a proxy video as code and leave rendering to a real-world video generation model [34, 7, 8, 36, 15]. Yet benchmarks for such agents mostly target edits, objects or static scenes [19, 18, 13, 65, 69], and camera benchmarks only add cameras to a finished scene [68, 35]. None tests multi-shot scenes in which several people act and the camera moves and cuts.

    As Tab.1 shows, VibePrevisBench fills these gaps: an agent reads a script, photos, a continuation or footage and writes the 4D scene behind a proxy video, which Rule-based Scene Check and VLM-based Screen Check verify against hidden GT facts and on screen. VibePrevisBench thus evaluates the agent that builds the scene, not only its rendered video.

    3  VibePrevisBench

    VibePrevisBench evaluates 4D scene reconstruction along the dimensions in Tab.1. Each of its 242 tasks pairs a brief with hidden GT facts that can be checked one by one. Figure3 shows the four input kinds and seven scene domains they span.

    3.1  Task formulation

    Briefs and deliveries. A task τ=(b,m,E,o) gives an English brief b, optional media m, a list E of places and subjects with ids, and output requirements o: the frame count T, frame rate and resolution of the proxy video. The input kinds differ only in what specifies the scene. A script describes it in prose alone, without distances or angles. Photo and reference video tasks show it in m, as one to five photos or a clip, while b only names the entries of E. A continuation shows the opening frame of a clip and describes the next seconds. The agent answers with a Blender program p. To score it, we run p and read out the 4D scene S=({xₑ(t)}_e∈E, c(t), K): for every place and subject listed in E, its oriented box xₑ(t) at each frame t=1,…,T, together with the camera c(t) and the cut times K. Rendering S gives the proxy video V, with the same T frames.

    Rubric. The hidden GT facts form a rubric F={fⱼ}, where each fⱼ is one checkable statement about the scene. The facts state which subjects exist, where they stand and face, how the places connect, who moves where and when, and how each camera frames, moves and cuts. For example, a fact may require that P01 stops between 3.9 and 4.9 s, within a 1.5 s tolerance. Its score sⱼ(S)∈[0,1] measures how well the agent’s scene S meets fⱼ. A fact met within its tolerance scores 1, and a metric fact loses credit linearly once its error exceeds the tolerance. All tolerances are fixed before any agent is run. Each fact belongs to one of nine dimensions: entities, layout, spaces, picture structure, routes, events, camera, cuts and physical validity. Picture structure compares the depth, normals and segmentation of each shot with the reference frames, so only photo, continuation and video tasks have it; Appendix Tab.3 defines all nine. Appearance is never checked, since the real-world video generation model supplies it. Whatever the input kind, the agent delivers the same kind of program p, which is scored through the same S and V against facts of the same form. Scores thus compare directly across input kinds.

    3.2  Rule-based Scene Check and VLM-based Screen Check

    Rule-based Scene Check asks whether the scene is right, and VLM-based Screen Check whether what is right can be seen. Figure4 follows one task through both, and Sec.B.4 validates them with injected defects, re-scoring, three VLM judges and a human study.

    Delivery and replay. Each delivery must pass three gates: its program runs on its own, renders the full video and reopens in Blender. A delivery that fails a gate scores 0 on both checks. Such failures stay in the average, so an agent gains nothing by failing hard tasks. Every other program is re-run from scratch in a fresh sandbox, which exports S frame by frame and renders V. Scores come only from this replay, never from videos the agent rendered in its own sandbox, so a video cannot show a scene the program does not build.

    Rule-based Scene Check. It binds subjects and places by their tagged ids and matches untagged objects by class. Script facts are relations, since scripts give no coordinates, whereas media facts are metric and are compared after each place is aligned to the ground truth by a similarity transform. The score is then built in three steps. First, the facts of one kind form a block b, whose raw score P_b is the mean of sⱼ over its facts. Second, each block is corrected for chance and for missing entities: Q_b=clip((P_b-R_b)/(1-R_b)) κ_b, where clip bounds the value to [0,1]. The chance rate R_b is the P_b that the agent’s own objects earn when shuffled at random within each place, and κ_b is the share of the block’s facts whose entities exist. A random layout thus scores 0, extra clutter raises R_b along with P_b, and every missing entity lowers κ_b. Third, blocks combine into dimension scores Q_d with weights fixed in advance, and Scene=100·(1)/(|D_τ|)∑_d∈D_τQ_d averages them over the dimensions D_τ that the task exercises. The scorer is deterministic, and Sec.B.2 details the scoring.

    VLM-based Screen Check. A VLM judge, Gemini 4, watches the proxy video at 2 fps, plus an orbit render of the delivered scene on photo tasks, blind to the agent’s name and the object names. Without the brief, it first retells the clip. It then receives the brief, the reference video on video tasks, and checklists from the hidden GT facts, limited to the items the rules passed, and rates each item as no, partial or yes, v_k,i∈{0,1/2,1}. The items fall into four dimensions: recognition, action, visibility and story. Recognition counts as yes only if the blind retelling already named the subject or place, and story asks whether the retelling recounts the story beats. With v̄ₖ the mean verdict of dimension k, Screen=100·(1)/(|K_τ|)∑_k∈K_τv̄ₖ, where photo tasks use recognition only, and the overall score is (Scene+Screen)/2. SectionB.3 gives the judge’s rubric.

    3.3  Construction

    VibePrevisBench is built in the three stages of Fig.5. SectionA.1 details the taxonomies, the screening rules and the pruning.

    Stage 1: Collection and curation. Two frozen taxonomies, of what a scene holds and of how a task is asked, set quotas that new tasks fill. Clips for video and continuation tasks come from over 27k source videos. Keeping a few clips per source with several moving people, camera motion or cuts leaves 1.8k clips, of which 388 pass VLM checks for live action, visible events and distinct subjects. Human reviewers choose among these, and Sec.A.1 describes the steps from these clips to the final video and continuation tasks. Of the 39 photo tasks, 38 draw on scan datasets with measured 3D boxes and camera poses.

    Stage 2: Task construction. Every brief is derived from a fixed scene. For a script, a model builds the scene from a card and then writes the script, each scored claim citing its sentence. Two blind readers from the Claude and DeepSeek families see only the script and write down where everything is and when it happens; a claim that neither recovers is reworded or dropped. A media brief gives each place and subject an id and a description. Human reviewers check and correct every brief and its hidden GT facts.

    Stage 3: Ground truth and checks. Scripts take their hidden GT facts from the built scene, in which every claim is checked to hold, and photo tasks from their scans. For videos, most continuations and one photo task, a pipeline estimates it: it recovers shots, subjects, cameras, depth and bodies and lifts them to 3D, as Appendix Fig.10 shows. Facts the pipeline cannot verify are marked unscorable and never count. All 11 agents then ran the candidates, and tasks that did not separate them were dropped, judged by item-rest correlation and spread rather than by any single agent’s score. Tasks, media, hidden GT facts and scorer are frozen with checksums, so every score can be reproduced from the release.

    3.4  Statistics

    Coverage and scale. VibePrevisBench contains 242 tasks: 94 scripts, 86 reference videos, 39 photo tasks and 23 continuations. As Fig.3 shows, each of the seven domains holds 19 to 46 tasks and each of the 33 places 3 to 13. In Fig.6a, briefs run 153 to 1,200 words with a median of 368: scripts spell out the scene in about 800 words, while media tasks mainly list ids. Outputs run 6 to 60 s with a median of 40 s, as Fig.6b shows.

    Staging demands and checks.Figure6c shows that 88% of tasks have two or more shots, 80% a moving camera, 79% two or more people, 69% hand–object interaction and 61% two or more places, and 71% combine several shots, a moving camera and two or more people. A task carries 20 to 2,175 checks, 408 at the median and 99.0k in all, as Fig.6d shows, and exercises a median of eight of the nine dimensions. Events hold 57% of the checks, since event order is checked pair by pair, but Rule-based Scene Check averages dimensions rather than checks, so they do not dominate the score. SectionA.3 splits them by input kind.

    4  Experiments

    4.1  Setup

    Evaluated agents. We evaluate 11 frontier models as coding agents, each at the reasoning effort given in gray in Tab.2. The GPT models run in the Codex CLI and all other models in Claude Code. An agent writes and runs Blender code, renders previews, inspects its own frames and revises. A small toolkit tags entities and places with the task’s ids, so facts bind to objects without visual matching.

    Protocol. Each run takes place in a sandbox with Blender 5.2, eight CPU cores and no GPU. The agent has a budget of 4 hours and no external assets, network or access to the scorer, so it can rely only on what the brief gives it. Every task is run once, and scores are averaged over tasks with equal weight. Input kinds exercise different dimensions and obtain their hidden GT facts differently, so agents are compared within a kind.

    4.2  Main results

    Table2 reports both checks per input kind; Sec.C.1 adds per-dimension profiles. GPT-6 Astra leads with an overall score of 77.7, ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol at 76.1, Gemini 4 Argon at 75.0 and Opus 5.5 at 74.1. Five of the ten adjacent pairs cannot be separated by a paired bootstrap over tasks, while the overall ranking holds across 18 scoring variants in Sec.B.4, at Kendall τ≥0.85 with GPT-6 Astra always first. The top four lead the rest by at least 3.9 overall points. GPT-6 Astra leads Rule-based Scene Check on every input kind except photos, where Opus 5.5 leads, as Sec.C.2 details. No agent comes close to solving the benchmark. On only 35 of the 242 tasks does any agent reach a Rule-based Scene Check score of 90. The remaining gap is shared, not divided: the best of all 11 agents on every task raises the overall score only to 80.6, and the top four alone already reach 80.5.

    Cost and score come apart. Per-task cost varies 45-fold, from $0.73 for GLM 5.3 Flash to $32.59 for GPT-6 Astra. Five agents sit on the cost–score frontier in Fig.7. GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 98% of the leader’s score at 21% of the cost, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 90% at 6%. Paying more does not buy rank: Kimi K3 is second in cost but seventh in score.

    4.3  Observations and implications

    Three observations show what separates the agents, where they all fail and why they do not correct themselves, and we analyze each and give its implications.

    Observation 1: Multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. The more an input relies on vision, the wider the gap between agents. In Tab.2, the gap between the best and worst agent grows from 12.0 Rule-based Scene Check points on text-only scripts to 19.9 on photos. This gap comes mainly from errors in space and camera. On photos, picture structure and camera account for 63% of the gap between the top four and the other seven, entities and layout for only 9%. The top four score 66–71 on picture structure, the other seven 24–38, as Fig.8b shows. The bottleneck is reading images and videos, not building the scene. Given a text description of the hidden GT facts on five video tasks, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash gains 14.0 points, as Appendix Tab.5 reports, nearly the full 16.7-point gap between the best and the worst agent on videos. Model updates gain here too: in Fig.8a, a newer model of the same family gains 11–14 points on photos but only 3–4 on scripts. A larger tier of the same generation, GPT-6 Astra over GPT-6.1 Sol, gains at most 1.7 points on any input kind. Writing code is not the bottleneck. The three weakest agents often call an API removed in Blender 5, as Fig.9c shows, yet later rounds repair these calls. Within each agent, runs with a failed API call score within 0.1 points of runs without one. Progress on this step thus depends on visual understanding of space and camera, whereas more knowledge of the Blender API saves rounds, not points.

    Observation 2: All agents master only basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Appendix Fig.14a shows that the errors of all 11 agents concentrate on challenging requests, which they turn into the common choice. When the reference films from a low angle, 66% of shots come out at eye level rather than high. Only 4% of orbits around a subject stay orbits, and 47% become sideways moves. Half of the video and continuation runs have more shots than the reference, while only 4% have fewer. Objects mentioned only in prose go missing 35% of the time. The common version of each request, by contrast, mostly succeeds: eye-level shots go wrong 9% of the time, follow and push-in moves 5–8%, and listed objects go missing 11% of the time. Challenging requests are likely scarce in the data agents learn from, so agents fall back on what they know. Two observations fit this reading. The errors lean one way, toward the common choice, whereas a misreading would err both ways. They also barely vary across agents: in Fig.8c, errors in reading the picture fall with the overall score, whereas every agent films 32–41% of shots at the wrong camera height. Agents therefore need explicit checks for challenging requests, such as camera height and move, shot count and objects named only in prose.

    Observation 3: Agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Every agent inspects its renders, viewing 13–40 images per run after its first Blender call, yet more looking does not help. In Fig.9a, the third of runs that looks most views 3.3 times as many images as the third that looks least, yet scores only 0.8 points higher at the median once task difficulty is removed. Removing every image from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash’s context on eight script tasks changes its score by only -0.8 points, as Appendix Tab.5 reports. The reason is that agents cannot tell a wrong render from a right one. In 1,377 of 2,582 runs with comments after a render, the agent states that its render matches the reference or looks right. With agent and task held fixed, these runs get camera angles, camera moves and events wrong as often as the other runs, as Fig.9b and Sec.C.2 show. Only framing and shot count, which show at a glance, are 2–3 points lower. More renders and looking thus do not correct errors; agents need item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

    5  Conclusion

    We introduced VibePrevisBench to evaluate coding agents that build executable 4D scenes and render proxy videos from four kinds of input. Rule-based Scene Check evaluates the scene against hidden GT facts, while VLM-based Screen Check evaluates how clearly those facts read on screen. Analysis of the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 agents yields three observations. Visual understanding of space and camera separates agents. Challenging staging and filming requests remain difficult across capability levels. Agents inspect their renders, but their judgments do not reliably correspond to fewer errors. These observations point to better visual understanding, explicit checks for challenging requests, and verification of renders against the brief. VibePrevisBench makes progress on these capabilities measurable.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Benchmark details

    A.1  Task construction

    Coverage first.

    Two frozen taxonomies tag every task. One covers what a scene holds: places, spaces, layout relations, subjects, actions, camera and editing, and genre, in 67 categories. The other covers how a task is asked: input kind, writing style, information level, organization and length. Each tag and each kind of place has a minimum number of tasks, and the gaps became slots for new tasks, routed to three lanes.

    Scripts.

    Each slot becomes a card fixing genre, writing style, length, places, people, actions and a story seed. Scripts come in seven writing styles, from screenplays and shot lists to ad briefs and novel-like prose, at about 600 to 1,200 words. The hidden GT facts are written before the script: a model (GPT-6.1 Sol) first codes the scene, then writes the script, then the claims, each citing the sentence it comes from and checked to hold in the coded scene. Automatic gates check every task’s scoring and output specification. Two blind readers from the Claude and DeepSeek families, who see only the script, try to recover every claim; a claim both misread is reworded and re-read up to twice, then dropped if still misread.

    Videos and continuations.

    We collected candidate clips ourselves. The screening keeps clips of at least 5 s and 2 fps, with a short edge of at least 480 pixels for local clips and 720 for web videos, and drops clips whose adjacent frames are more than 85% identical. Local clips are cut into windows of 25 to 50 s, a seeded eighth also into 15 s windows, and web videos into 25–45 s video windows and 12 s continuation windows; each source keeps at most three or four windows that overlap by at most 60%. Windows are ranked by subject presence, the number of moving people or vehicles and its changes, motion beyond the camera’s own, camera motion, cuts, person size and duration, and flagged for letterboxing, burned-in text, repeated frames and darkness. We then pre-screened the windows by model ratings of contact sheets (Gemini 4, Claude Sonnet 5.5), and tagged the survivors by place, genre, people, shots and moving vehicles. Human reviewers decided whether a clip becomes a video task, a continuation or neither. Quotas then capped over-represented content such as vehicles, and borders and logos were cropped. A video brief gives an id and a description for each place and subject, and the output must start where the clip starts and cut where it cuts. A continuation brief gives the clip’s opening frame and an account of the next 6 to 20 s, mostly following the clip. Figure10 shows how one clip’s hidden GT facts are built.

    Photos.

    We drew on scan datasets with measured 3D boxes and camera poses, indoors and in street scenes, and used each scene once. Boxes from the hidden GT facts were drawn back onto every photo and checked first by a model and then by a human; candidates whose boxes did not match the photo were rejected. The output must show each photo’s view for 12 frames and then sweep the place for 8 s. One photo task instead uses five keyframes of a real clip, and its hidden GT facts are estimated as for a video.

    Pruning.

    All 11 agents ran the pool, and we dropped tasks that did not discriminate between agents: low item-rest correlation or little spread across agents, never a single agent’s score. Finally we removed tasks with source or licensing problems or an unscorable run.

    Model assistance and fairness.

    Several of the evaluated models help build tasks. GPT-6.1 Sol writes the script specs and scripts; the blind readers come from other families, Claude and DeepSeek; Claude Sonnet 5.5, of the same family as Opus 5.5, pre-screens clips; and Gemini 3.8 and Gemini 4 register and observe the subjects behind the hidden GT facts of videos and continuations, while Gemini 4 also rates web clips. Three safeguards limit their influence. Agents are scored by rule checks on facts, never by similarity to a model’s own output; the hidden GT facts are never edited to make a reader pass; and every brief and its facts are reviewed and corrected by hand. Ranked by Rule-based Scene Check, the agents show no strong self-preference. GPT-6.1 Sol is second on scripts and over all tasks; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is seventh on scripts and over all tasks; and Opus 5.5 is third over all tasks and fourth on videos. The Gemini models rank somewhat higher on the media tasks whose hidden GT facts they helped estimate: Gemini 4 Argon is fourth over all tasks but third on videos and second on continuations, and Gemini 3.8 Flash is eighth over all tasks but sixth on videos. A small preference cannot be ruled out; the judge’s own-family bias is measured separately in Sec.B.4.

    A.2  Task examples

    Figure11 shows one task of each kind, and their prompts are excerpted below.

    Script (excerpt).

    Suitcase Chase Through the Corner Shop. A courier is chased through a shop into a back alley, where a reversing van traps his accomplice… S02 Shop: north of the street’s east part. A west shelf and an east shelf run north–south either side of the aisle from the front door to the back door… P01 person: courier holding O01, west of the planter, facing east. P02 person: pursuer, behind P01, facing east… 0–5 s: P01 runs east with O01, P02 chasing. 5–10.8 s: P01 enters the shop by the front door at 9.5 s; P02 follows at 10.8 s… Shots (lens: wide-angle 24 mm, moderately wide 28 mm, normal 35 mm, slightly long 50 mm)… 5–8 s, hard cut: under the arcade’s east end; eye level, normal, facing west; pans right to the door…

    Photos (prompt).

    Rebuild the place shown in the attached photo as one static 3D proxy blockout, with one camera. Build the place and everything in it at real-world size, and place the camera so that its view matches the photo: position, direction and lens. Output: 12 frames at 24 fps, 640×426… Place: S01 Informal learning lounge. Tag every piece of the place (walls, floor, furniture, fixtures) by class…

    Continuation (excerpt).

    Continue the attached photo as a proxy previs. Frame 1 must reproduce the photo: the camera’s position, direction and lens, and every visible subject and object where it is in the photo… Output: 336 frames at 24 fps (14.00 s)… P01 person: the seated woman beside the bed… P02 person: the standing man to her right… 0.0 s: the close eye-level side view of P01 and P02 pulls back in a dolly move. From 0.3 to 2.2 seconds, P01 stands up from the bed… 4.0 s: Cut to a medium eye-level front view of P01 with P02. The camera orbits toward her side… From 6.4 to 7.1 seconds, P01 turns back toward P02…

item.title: 新视角合成别再每次跑大网络：TTB 把跨视图注意力「烤」进一个小 MLP，渲染时才便宜 ｜ TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
item.description:
一句话：只解码器的大视角合成模型靠 KV-cache 出质量，测试时训练省算力但掉画质——中间还有一条路。

要点：

  • 现状：带 KV-cache 的「只解码器」大视角合成模型（LVSM）不重建 3D 几何、直接用网络回归新视角，质量已达 SOTA
  • 两条加速路线各有代价：测试时训练（TTT）层省算力但牺牲质量，而直接跑全模型又太贵
  • TTB（Test-Time Baking）把跨视图注意力中的全局场景信息「烤」进一个轻量 MLP，于是渲染时不必再付全模型的代价

为什么值得看：「测试时把全局信息烘进小网络」这个模式对引擎很实用：一次性的准备成本换持续的渲染开销下降。比 TTT 更划算的关键在于，它保留跨视图注意力的质量而不重训。

中文摘要：带 KV-cache 的「只解码器」大视角合成模型（LVSM）近来做出了 SOTA 质量——它不显式重建 3D 几何，而是直接由神经网络回归新视角。但代价是渲染时开销大：测试时训练（TTT）层能省算力却牺牲质量，直接跑全模型又太贵。TTB（Test-Time Baking）因此提出一条折中路径：在测试阶段把跨视图注意力中蕴含的全局场景信息「烘」进一个轻量 MLP，使后续渲染不必再付出全模型的计算成本。这种「一次性烘焙换持续渲染开销下降」的模式，与引擎里预计算光照的思路高度一致。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models

Abstract

Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to 23x rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io.

1 Introduction

Our research studies the task of novel-view synthesis conditioned on a set of context images with the powerful Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) [25]. LVSMs have recently emerged with several immediate follow-up improvements [22, 31, 69, 77, 58], achieving state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality across various input conditions [1, 23, 64, 42]. Their geometry-free scene representations and Transformer-based renderers are fully learning-based, making them favorable for scaling with increasing amounts of training data. The minimized 3D inductive bias also shows advantages when scenes are challenging for existing Transformer-compatible geometry-based representations (e.g., 3DGS [29]), such as surfaces with strong mirror reflections or translucent material.

We are especially interested in the decoder-only variant of LVSM [25] for its high-fidelity. DVSM [58] further introduces KV-cache to the cross-view attention layers, showing both quality and efficiency improvement. The KV-cache serves as a global scene state for novel-view queries, but the rendering time is still impractical under dense context view conditions due to the linear complexity per token when attending to the KV-cache. LaCT [77] takes a different approach by replacing cross-view attention layers with Test-Time Training (TTT) [59] layers, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. TTT performs inner-loop optimization to adapt fast-weight MLPs [49] to directly map queries to their values without the quadratic-complexity attention, which can also be interpreted as a variant of linear attention [36]. Despite achieving constant-complexity rendering speed, TTT significantly sacrifices rendering quality. A naive remedy for LaCT is to initialize from pretrained decoder-only model weights, which does improve quality, but the gap to the pretrained model remains significant.

We argue that this quality gap can be minimized by repurposing the fast-weight MLP inner-loop optimization as “baking” the information from cross-view attention, rather than replacing cross-view attention entirely as in TTT. We dub our strategy Test-Time Baking (TTB), illustrated in Fig. 2b. The key motivation is to trade context-view processing time for faster and higher-fidelity novel-view rendering, achieving the Pareto frontier of quality and speed shown in Fig. 1. Specifically, the inner-loop learning target becomes the output tokens from cross-view attention, instead of the raw value tokens used in TTT. This formulation also generalizes beyond the linear-attention interpretation of TTT [36]. In principle, the learning target of our TTB can also be tokens from arbitrarily non-linear layers or tokens enriched with additional scene information.

Furthermore, we identify a modality misalignment issue inherent to the context prefilling of MLP fast-weight for novel-view synthesis. In the reconstruction stage (context prefilling), the fast-weight MLPs are updated using context tokens with both camera and image information. In the rendering stage, however, the updated MLPs take novel-view tokens coming from camera-only input without any image content. This conventional pipeline poses a reconstruction-rendering input modality misalignment challenge.

Our solution to modality misalignment is simple yet effective. As illustrated in Fig. 2c, we pair each context view into i) context ground-truth tokens, derived from input cameras and images that produce the global scene information to be baked, and ii) context rendering tokens, derived from camera-only input that simulates novel-view rendering conditions. At each TTB layer, the fast-weight MLP is optimized to map context rendering tokens to their corresponding context ground-truth tokens, which carry image and cross-view attended information. The optimized TTB-MLP is then shared between context rendering tokens and the downstream novel-view rendering tokens for retrieving scene information, ensuring that their conditioning remains identical across all layers.

Interestingly, TTB draws a natural parallel with traditional implicit radiance and light field reconstruction, where MLPs are optimized to map spatial coordinates to radiance values. In TTB, the fast-weight MLP instead is optimized to map ray-patch latent coordinates to their appearance latent representations, which effectively performs few-step light-field optimization in latent space. This perspective suggests that TTB interpolates appearance latents for novel viewpoints from their ray-patch latent coordinates, motivating a convergence-oriented inner loop over one-shot summarization. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose Test-Time Baking, which retargets the inner-loop optimization of the TTT fast-weight MLP from raw value tokens to cross-view attention outputs, so that the fast-weight MLP collaborates with attention rather than replacing it.

  • •

    We identify a modality misalignment between the reconstruction and rendering stages of MLP fast-weight prefilling, and resolve it via a context pair that disentangles each context view into a ground-truth and a camera-only rendering token.

  • •

    We draw a connection between TTB’s inner loop and light field optimization in latent space, which motivates a convergence-oriented training recipe (multi-step MSE) that we find particularly effective for TTB.

    • 2 Related work

    Per-Scene optimization. Early approaches to novel-view synthesis perform per-scene optimization, fitting differentiable scene representations to observed images via differentiable rendering. Coordinate-based MLPs [41, 2, 4], voxels [56, 15, 8, 43, 57, 34], and the landmark 3DGS [29] as the scene representation have been widely explored. Despite impressive quality, per-scene optimization does not scale with the increasing training scenes and degrades quickly under fewer input views.

    Geometry-based feed-forward models. To overcome the scalability limitations and lengthy procedure of per-scene optimization, learning-based methods train networks to predict 3D representations from images. Early works estimated multi-plane images via cost volumes [73, 68, 17, 72, 16, 40], while NeRF-based generalizable methods [7, 74, 67, 37] extended coverage to wide-angle viewpoints at limited quality. The advent of 3DGS [29] reframed the problem as pixel-aligned GS prediction [6, 71, 10, 60, 62, 24], achieving promising results, and Large Reconstruction Models (LRMs) [21] further demonstrated Transformer scalability across various 3D representations [5, 70, 76]. One fundamental limitation of handcrafted 3D is their degradation on surfaces or materials they are not designed for, whereas the geometry-free representations we study can learn them given data. Furthermore, explicit 3D geometry lacks a compact latent representation, and efforts to manage their linearly growing output size under more input views [12, 11, 63, 45] remain a symptom of this constraint. Our TTB bakes scenes into constant-size MLPs at higher quality.

    Geometry-free feed-forward models. An alternative paradigm sidesteps the limitations of geometry-based models by representing scenes as latent representations and rendering via neural networks. Early methods [13, 55, 54, 53, 46, 47] were constrained by limited network capacity, while Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) [25] broke this barrier by leveraging powerful Transformers. Encoder-decoder and decoder-only LVSM variants are explored. The encoder-decoder LVSM [25] encodes context views into scene tokens and decodes novel views conditioned on the encoded scene, with subsequent works refining scene encoding strategies [22, 31, 69] and extending to generative [1] and uncalibrated camera [23, 78, 64, 42] settings. The decoder-only LVSM [25], on the other hand, uses a single network for both context prefilling and novel-view rendering. Despite higher fidelity, its original form inefficiently processes context views independently for each novel view. DVSM [58] addresses this by prefilling context views into a KV-cache shared across all novel views, achieving state-of-the-art quality under both sparse and dense view settings. However, the linearly growing KV-cache size makes rendering speed impractical for larger numbers of input views. LaCT [77] replaces cross-view attention with Test-Time Training layers to achieve constant rendering complexity, but at a significant quality cost compared to DVSM. Our Test-Time Baking achieves the same constant rendering complexity while substantially closing the quality gap left by LaCT.

    Test-time Training layers. TTT [59] has recently emerged as a popular alternative to attention for its linear time and constant space complexity. We refer interested readers to [36] for an in-depth review and analysis. We are particularly interested in the variant presented in LaCT [77], which has demonstrated success in accelerating various vision and 3D tasks [9, 63, 18, 14, 26], albeit at the cost of quality relative to their attention-based counterparts. Our TTB departs from this paradigm in two ways: rather than replacing attention, TTB learns directly from attention outputs; and rather than performing mere token-to-token information exchange, TTB explicitly learns to map camera-ray tokens to their corresponding image tokens, yielding improved novel-view synthesis quality.

    3 Method

    We start by formally introducing our task and the general pipeline in Sec. 3.1. We detail the decoder-only architecture we build on in Sec. 3.2. Finally, we present Test-Time Baking in Sec. 3.3.

    3.1 Overview

    Given a set of V context images with known poses and intrinsics {Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3,Pᵢ∈SE(3),Kᵢ∈ℝ^3×3}ᵢ₌₁^V, our goal is to synthesize novel views for an arbitrary camera query (P^′,K^′). We focus on reconstruction rather than generation, assuming novel views can be directly regressed from the context views. Approaches to this end generally decompose into two stages:

    S=Recon(I,P,K), Ī=Rend(P^′,K^′,S),

    		(1)

    where Recon(·) processes context views into a method-specific scene representation S, and Rend(·) synthesizes the novel view Ī conditioned on S. Recent feed-forward models instantiate Recon(·) as a Transformer. The Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) [21] family employs a human-defined 3D and renderer, while the Large View Synthesis Model (LVSM) [25] series defines S as a latent state and implements Rend(·) as a neural network. As both Recon(·) and Rend(·) are differentiable, models are trained end-to-end against ground-truth novel views I^′ by:

    J=MSE(Ī,I^′)+λ·Percep(Ī,I^′) ,

    		(2)

    where Percep is the neural perceptual loss [27] and λ balances the photometric objectives.

    3.2 Decoder-only View Synthesis Model

    Our method builds on the Decoder-only View Synthesis Model (DVSM) [58], which uses a shared Transformer decoder for both Recon(·) and Rend(·), and represents the scene S as KV caches. Specifically, the model consists of L repeated blocks, each comprising a sequence of layers:

    X_ℓ=(FFN_ℓ,2∘CrossAttn_ℓ∘FFN_ℓ,1∘IntraAttn_ℓ)(X_ℓ-1) ,

    		(3)

    where IntraAttn(·) and CrossAttn(·) perform intra-view and cross-view attention, respectively, and FFN(·) denotes a fully connected layer. Residual connections [19] and QK-normalization [20] are applied for training stability. During reconstruction, context-view tokens are prefilled into a KV-cache at each CrossAttn(·). During rendering, novel-view tokens query the cached KV to retrieve global scene information from each CrossAttn(·) layer.

    Regarding input tokenization, camera intrinsics and poses are first converted into Plücker ray maps [44] for linear patch embedding. Context-view and novel-view tokens are initialized as:

    X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P,K)+PE⁽ʳᵍᵇ⁾(I)), X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P^′,K^′)) ,

    		(4)

    where PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾ and PE⁽ʳᵍᵇ⁾ are linear patch projections for the Plücker ray maps and context images, respectively, Here, X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀∈ℝ^V×H/p×W/p×D denotes tokens from V context views with patch size p used for KV-cache prefilling, and X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾₀∈ℝ^U×H/p×W/p×D denotes tokens for U novel-view queries, each processed independently. Finally, a shallow model head regresses pixel values as:

    Ī=(PixShuf∘Sigmoid∘Linear∘LayerNorm)(X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾_L) ,

    		(5)

    where PixShuf(·) denotes pixel shuffling [51] and X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾_L is the last-layer tokens out of Eq.3.

    3.3 Test-time Baking

    We present our technical contribution to improve the rendering-time efficiency of DVSM [58] while retaining its high rendering quality. The issue of DVSM is that its KV-cache size grows linearly with the number of context tokens, making it slow and impractical for novel-view queries under high-resolution or dense input context views. A naive strategy is to replace each CrossAttn(·) in Eq. 3 with a Test-Time Training (TTT) [59] layer, achieving constant space and linear time complexity as demonstrated in LaCT [77]. However, we observe significant quality degradation even when finetuning the TTT variant from DVSM pretrained weights. This motivates us to explore a better solution that improves upon TTT. A full model pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 3.

    3.3.1 Repurposing TTT: collaborating instead of replacing attention

    Our motivation is to trade reconstruction (prefilling) computation, which only needs to be performed once per scene, for improved rendering-time speed and quality. The resulting solution is simple yet effective. Rather than entirely replacing cross-view attention with TTT fast-weight MLP as in the LaCT [77], we repurpose TTT to explicitly learn from the input-output pairs out of cross-view attention. Consequently, we no longer need to cache the KV; only the updated MLP fast weights are stored. The space and time complexity of novel-view rendering is therefore identical to that of TTT. We call our strategy Test-Time Baking (TTB), which can be viewed as a generalized form of TTT.

    Formally, the fast-weight update rules of TTT and TTB are:

    θ⁽ᵀᵀᵀ⁾=θ-η∇_θL(f_θ(WₖX),\color[rgb]0.9727,0.5156,0.4727WᵥX),(6a)
    θ^(TTB)=θ-η∇_θL(f_θ(WₖX),\color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406g(X^*)),(6b)

    respectively, where θ is the fast weights of the MLP f(·), η and L are the inner-loop learning rate and objective, Wₖ and Wᵥ are linear projection matrices, and X is the input tokens. The difference between TTT and TTB lies in the mapping target: \color[rgb]0.9727,0.5156,0.4727WᵥX and \color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406g(X^*). In principle, we can employ an arbitrary function g or tokens X^* with additional modality for the mapping target \color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406g(X^*). Note that TTB falls back to TTT when X^*=X and g is a linear projection. In our case, we instantiate g(·) as the CrossAttn(·) from DVSM, which shifts TTB beyond the linear-attention interpretation [36] of TTT. Although this incurs additional reconstruction-time cost, once prefilled, rendering remains identical to TTT with substantially higher quality thanks to the enriched global information from g(·).

    More analysis. We empirically validate that swapping the inner-loop target from \color[rgb]0.9727,0.5156,0.4727WᵥX to \color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406CrossAttn(X) broadens the effective view field of the baked fast-weight MLP. At TTB block 7 with V=16, we measure how much each context image contributes to the TTB output at the novel-view rendering tokens via input-gradient saliency, sorted and averaged across output positions (Fig. 4). The WᵥX variant peaks sharply at top-1 then decays, while CrossAttn(X) flattens the peak and sustains a heavier mid-rank tail. This matches our design intent: CrossAttn(X) already aggregates across all V context views, so each memorized pair inherits a wider receptive field.

    3.3.2 Modality misalignment and context pair

    The baked MLPs via Eq. 6b receive inputs of different modalities between the reconstruction and rendering stages. As defined in Eq. 4, context tokens X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀ used for prefilling contain image content, whereas novel-view tokens X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾₀ are with camera-only information. This modality misalignment poses an unnecessary generalization challenge to the baked MLP.

    We address this by disentangling input context tokens, X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀ from Eq.4, into a paired representation:

    X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P,K)+PE⁽ʳᵍᵇ⁾(I)), X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P,K)),

    		(7)

    where X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾₀ are the context rendering tokens with camera-only input, and X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾₀ are the context ground-truth tokens with additional RGB input. We use X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ to serve TTB mapping target while using X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ to serve TTB input. Specifically, at each TTB layer, the fast-weight MLP is baked to learn the mapping X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾↦CrossAttn(X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾) via the update rule in Eq. 6b. The baked MLP is then shared across both context rendering X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ and the downstream novel-view rendering X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾ tokens to produce feature for the subsequent layers. As visualized in Fig. 2, our context pairing ensures distribution alignment from the early layers, which facilitates feature interpolation. Conversely, the distribution only aligned in the later layers without context pairing due to the modality misalignment between reconstruction and rendering stages. Despite doubling the number of tokens during reconstruction, rendering-stage efficiency remains the same, which aligns with our motivation to trade reconstruction time for rendering-time quality.

    3.3.3 TTB layer details

    The design of our TTB layer is inspired by the TTT layer in LaCT [77]. We remove the asymmetric QK projection and instead use a shared linear projection to produce queries and keys. We adopt SwiGLU-MLP [50] as the fast-weight MLP architecture, and apply an additional linear layer to predict per-token learning rates. For inner-loop optimization, we employ Muon [28] optimizer with weight normalization [48] for a predefined T steps. We find that using MSE as the inner-loop objective for our TTB yields better results than the unnormalized dot-product loss used in LaCT [77]’s TTT. We also find that learning the residual to the mapping target is easier to bake than learning the target directly. Specifically, the final TTB update rule is:

    θₜ₊₁=θₜ-Muon(∇_θₜ∥f_θₜ(WₖX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾)-Wᵥ(CrossAttn(X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾)-X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾)∥₂)~,

    		(8)

    where Muon(·) performs Muon gradient orthogonalization [28], Wₖ and Wᵥ are linear projection matrices for the TTB input and mapping target. The final baked weights θ_T are then applied to update both the context rendering and novel-view rendering tokens and provide feedback to the context ground-truth tokens (the output arrows from the baked MLP in Fig. 3).

    3.3.4 Fast-weight local-duplicate inference

    The baked fast weights have a fixed capacity, causing quality to plateau as the number of context views V grows. We address this at inference time by clustering the context views into K spatially-local groups via k-means on per-view camera poses, with K=V/B for a nominal budget of B views per group. Each group is reconstructed independently by the unmodified model, so that cross-view attention and the inner-loop update only involve the views of that group, yielding per-group, per-layer fast weights {{θ_k,ℓ}_ℓ=1^L}ₖ₌₁^K. At rendering time, each novel view is routed to the group with the nearest centroid and queries only the corresponding copy. Rendering thus remains O(1) per view and each copy only has to absorb about B views, while the stored state grows linearly with K.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation details

    We use 768 latent channels with 12 decoder blocks at patch size 8, replacing each cross-view attention with a TTB layer. We initialize our models from the corresponding DVSM [58] checkpoint. We use AdamW [38] with cosine annealing and perceptual loss weight λ=0.2. Models are trained on DL3DV-10K [35] dataset with 64 A100 GPUs. We first train at 340p for 100K iterations with learning rate 4 × 10⁻⁴, then finetune at 480p, 720p, and 960p for 10K iterations each with learning rate 1 × 10⁻⁵. We randomly sample either 16 or 32 context views per scene with the same number of target views. Ablations use a smaller setup on 8 A100 GPUs at patch size 16 truncated to 720p, with efficiency metrics still reported at patch size 8 for consistency. For evaluation, we use the 140 held-out DL3DV testing scenes and follow previous view sampling [12].

    TTB layer. We use a single-headed fast-weight SwiGLU-MLP [50] with a hidden dimension of 3072, a 4× expansion of the model dimension. The fast weight is updated with the Muon optimizer [28] and we run T = 3 inner-loop update steps. The per-token learning rate is predicted by an additional linear head with base learning rate of 0.01. The inner-loop objective maps context-rendering tokens to the cross-view attention output of context-ground-truth tokens with the MSE loss. Fast-weight local-duplicate inference (Sec. 3.3.4) is turned off except stated otherwise. When enabled, we set B=16. For some experiments we also report a variant denoted TTB– or Ours–, which replaces the cross-view attention target with a linear projection WᵥX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ and thus avoids the quadratic-complexity cross-view attention at reconstruction, making reconstruction time linear in V.

    4.2 Comparisons

    DL3DV. Tab. 1 and Fig. 5 report results on DL3DV with 16, 32, and 64 input views at 960p. TTB substantially closes the quality gap between DVSM [58] and LaCT [77] while rendering at a constant 23 FPS, up to 23× faster than DVSM and 2.3× faster than LaCT. Our model is built on DVSM with 12 blocks while LaCT uses 24 blocks (model size in Tab. 3). The Ours– without cross-view attention is comparable to LaCT quality with less parameters and faster rendering. With local-duplicate inference (Sec. 3.3.4), Ours (duplicate) further closes the residual gap at large V and approaches DVSM quality at the same rendering speed. Fig. 5 confirms these trends qualitatively, where TTB preserves thin and high-frequency structures such as handrails, window grilles, and small text that LaCT and LVSM [25] render with visible blur.

    In-the-wild. We further evaluate the generalization ability on out-of-domain datasets with 16 and 64 context views in Tab. 3. We keep the aspect ratio of the context images and resize to the resolutions preferred by the models. The synthesized novel views are resized to match ground-truth source resolutions for evaluation. Comparisons to LaCT [77] and DVSM [58] are consistent with the in-domain evaluation—our quality is often comparable to DVSM but at a much faster rendering; we use more context prefilling time than LaCT but gaining quality with 2.3× faster rendering. LagerNVS [61] is a very recent work which builds upon VGGT [65] and trains on multiple datasets. We use our intermediate checkpoints at 480p to better align with LagerNVS’s input resolution. Our quality outperforms LagerNVS by a large margin with 3.1–9.5× faster rendering.

    Re10K. We additionally compare on Re10K with two low-resolution context views. This is not our main target scenario as the rendering time gain from cross-view attention becomes marginal. We finetune from the Re10K checkpoint of DVSM [58] with DINO injection. Results are in Tab. 2. Our TTB can reproduce DVSM cross-attention quality in this setup. See supplementary for full results.

    4.3 Ablation studies

    From TTT to TTB. Tab. 4 decomposes the gap between a vanilla LaCT-style TTT replacement [77] and our full TTB into three additive components: context pairing, switching to MSE with T=3 inner steps (yielding TTB–), and replacing the linear-projection target with cross-view attention output. Each contributes meaningfully, and stacking all three closes the quality gap to DVSM [58] while retaining TTT’s ∼ 50 FPS rendering. The reconstruction cost grows quadratically with V due to the in-loop cross-view attention, consistent with our reconstruction time for rendering quality trade-off.

    Inner-loop optimization. Tab. 6 ablates the inner-loop loss and number of update steps T. Switching from LaCT’s unnormalized dot-product loss [77] to MSE consistently improves quality for both TTT and TTB–, with TTB– benefiting more (+0.44 vs +0.27 PSNR). Increasing T brings monotonic but diminishing gains, leading us to adopt T=3 with MSE as a sweet spot between quality and reconstruction cost. This asymmetric response aligns with our light field view—TTB’s inner loop fits a target function and benefits from convergence, while TTT-KVB is closer to a one-shot linear write.

    TTB layer design. Tab. 6 ablates two design choices in our TTB layer. Residual learning reformulates the inner-loop target from the absolute cross-view attention output to its residual against X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾, reducing the magnitude of the regression target and easing the few-step inner-loop optimization. Feedback additionally applies the baked MLP to update the context ground-truth tokens, so that all three token streams propagate through identical operators in subsequent layers. Both designs contribute roughly equally in isolation (+0.43 and +0.44 PSNR) and combine to +0.52.

    Limitations. TTB is constrained by the fixed capacity of its fast-weight MLP, causing quality to saturate at large V; the local-duplicate routing that mitigates this is a heuristic, and learning it during training is left for future work. Its inner-loop cross-view attention also makes reconstruction quadratic in V, a drawback for single-shot scenarios. Finally, TTB is built on reconstruction rather than generation, interpolating within context views without extrapolating to unobserved viewpoints.

    5 Conclusion

    We present Test-Time Baking (TTB), which retargets the TTT inner-loop optimization from raw value tokens to cross-view attention outputs, turning the fast-weight MLP from a replacement for attention into its collaborator. Combined with a context pair that resolves the reconstruction-rendering modality misalignment, TTB bakes DVSM-level scene information into a fixed-size MLP while retaining TTT-level rendering complexity. Across DL3DV, Re10K, and in-the-wild benchmarks, TTB matches DVSM [58] quality at a constant 23 FPS and consistently surpasses LaCT [77]. We hope this baking perspective offers a new way to integrate attention and TTT beyond view synthesis.

    Overview.
