    Appendix A Additional details

    A.1 Common implementation details

    Unless otherwise specified, all of our final models share the configuration described in this section. The decoder consists of 12 blocks with a latent dimension of 768, organized as illustrated in main paper Fig. 3. Optimization is carried out with AdamW [38] using a weight decay of 0.05 and momentum coefficients (0.9,0.95). The learning rate is annealed along a cosine schedule preceded by 2.5k linear warm-up iterations, peaking at 4×10⁻⁴ during the lowest-resolution stage and dropping to 1×10⁻⁵ when finetuning at higher resolutions. The perceptual term in our rendering loss is weighted by λ=0.2. Training runs on 64 A100 GPUs, and we cast the learnable layers to BFloat16 mixed precision during forward propagation.

    Camera information is encoded with the Plücker parameterization [44]: each pixel is associated with a 6-dimensional vector (rₒ×r_d, r_d), where rₒ denotes the camera origin, r_d the unit direction of the corresponding ray, and × the vector cross product. We further normalize the context-view poses following the convention of GS-LRM [76].

    Inside each transformer block, we adopt the pre-norm layout combined with QK-normalization. Each attention layer uses 12 heads, and every fully-connected sublayer expands the hidden dimension by a factor of 4. All linear projections in our architecture are bias-free.

    A.2 TTB layer details

    This section elaborates on TTB layer details that were elided from the main paper for space. We provide the pseudocode of training our TTB model in Algo. 1 as a complementary reference for the descriptions below. The three fast-weight matrices of our SwiGLU-MLP, w₀,w₂∈ℝ^H×dᵢₙ×dₕ and w₁∈ℝ^H×dₕ×dₒᵤₜ, are stored as ordinary learnable parameters and are jointly optimized in the outer loop alongside the rest of the network. Consequently, the inner loop for every scene starts from a common, outer-loop-learned meta-initialization θ₀, which is then advanced by T Muon [28] update steps before being applied to the rendering tokens. When local-duplicate inference is enabled with K>1 groups, every per-group reconstruction starts from the same meta-initialized θ₀ and is specialized only by the views assigned to its group, so all local copies share the same starting point and differ through their inner-loop trajectories.

    We initialize TTB models from the corresponding DVSM [58] checkpoint with strict=False: the patch embeddings, input LayerNorms, Plücker encoding, intra-view attention layers, both FFNs in each block, and the RGB head are inherited directly, while every module inside the TTB layer—including its LayerNorm, query/key and value projections, output projection, per-token learning-rate head, output RMSNorm, and the fast weights w₀,w₁,w₂—is freshly initialized. The cross-view attention projections of DVSM are not reused, since the inner-loop target of TTB is structurally different and warm-starting from the DVSM projections did not yield benefits in our preliminary experiments. To prevent the random-init TTB layer from disrupting the inherited DVSM features at the start of finetuning, we initialize the TTB output projection with a small standard deviation following the residual zero-init trick used in deep transformers, so that the TTB block contributes approximately zero at finetune step 0 and the entire forward pass reduces to the pretrained DVSM model plus an identity TTB layer. This zero-init together with the parameter inheritance above accounts for the +1.02 PSNR gain reported in Tab.  13.

    For the TTB layer micro-architecture, we share a single linear projection between query and key construction: the inner-loop input WₖX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ in main paper Eq. 6 and the rendering-time query WₖX⁽ⁿᵛ⁾ are both produced by passing the input through a single linear layer followed by SiLU and an L₂ unit-norm, which constrains the writes and reads of the fast-weight MLP to a common spherical subspace and removes a magnitude degree of freedom from the inner-loop optimization. The per-token learning rate is predicted by an additional linear head that outputs 3H scalars per token—one for each of the three fast-weight matrices in every head—and reparameterized as softplus(·+softplus⁻¹(0.01)), ensuring strictly positive learning rates and an effective initial value of 0.01 across all heads and matrices.

    The outer loop differentiates fully through all T inner-loop steps without any first-order approximation, so that the rendering loss reflects the exact dependence of the final fast weights on the outer-loop parameters. Each Muon step orthogonalizes the inner-loop gradient with five Newton–Schulz quintic iterations executed in BFloat16; we transpose the gradient before iteration whenever dᵢₙ>dₕ so that the intermediate Gram matrix has size \min(dᵢₙ,dₕ)², which keeps the per-step memory manageable. Even with this optimization, retaining T inner-step activations for backpropagation remains the dominant memory cost of TTB. We mitigate it with two layers of gradient checkpointing: the inner-loop activations of SwiGLU and Muon are recomputed within each step, and the outer-loop checkpointing is applied selectively to the intra-view attention and FFN sublayers but not to the TTB sublayer itself, the combination of which makes our 64-A100 training feasible at 960p resolution with V = 32 context views.

    Finally, our two main paper variants differ only in the inner-loop mapping target. TTB instantiates g(·) in main paper Eq. 6b as the cross-view attention output of X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾, while TTB– replaces this with a linear projection WᵥX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ acting directly on the context ground-truth tokens. Both variants share every other component described above, including the context pair construction, the QK-shared projection, the per-token learning-rate head, the residual target, and the feedback path that propagates the baked MLP output back to X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾.

    A.3 Two-view Re10K specific details

    For the two-view setting, each GPU receives 32 scenes per iteration, with 2 context views and 3 target views per scene. The interval between the two context frames is sampled uniformly between 25 and 192, and target frames are drawn from the union of all intermediate frames between the two context views and the extrapolated frames within 25 frames on either side. We initialize the model from the corresponding DVSM [58] Re10K checkpoint following the strategy detailed in Sec. A.2, and finetune it on Re10K for 100K iterations at 256×256 followed by 10K iterations at 512×512. Note that doubling the context tokens through the context pair (main paper Eq. 7) negligibly affects this two-view setup, so we keep the same per-GPU batch composition as DVSM.

    A.4 Many-view DL3DV [35] specific details

    DL3DV is the main benchmark for our dense-view results in main paper Tab. 1 and Tab. 3, as well as for all the ablations in main paper Sec. 4.3. For training, we adopt a dynamic batching scheme that controls the per-GPU token budget rather than the number of scenes. Each scene draws either 16 or 32 context views uniformly at random, paired with the same number of target views; the number of scenes packed into a GPU is then adjusted on the fly so that the aggregate count of context-pair tokens (i.e., the union of X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ and X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ across all scenes in the batch) stays within a fixed budget. This compensates for the doubled token count introduced by the context pair and keeps the effective compute per iteration comparable to DVSM at the same memory ceiling. The frame interval between two adjacent context views is sampled uniformly from [1,16], and target views are drawn from [\min(ℂ)-2,\max(ℂ)+2]∖ℂ, where ℂ is the index set of the sampled context views. We exclude from training a small subset of scenes whose aspect ratio or native resolution does not match the canonical 16:9960p layout. The resolution curriculum starts from 340p and runs for 100K iterations, after which the model is finetuned for 10K iterations at each of 480p, 720p, and the final 960p (540×960).

    For the controlled ablation setting used in main paper Tab. 4–6 and Tab. 13, we shrink the compute footprint to 8 A100 GPUs by fixing the context view count to 32, raising the patch size to 16 to lower the per-token resolution, and truncating the curriculum to 340p / 480p / 720p with 100K / 10K / 10K iterations respectively. All the design knobs ablated in those tables share this controlled setup; the rendering and reconstruction efficiency reported alongside is measured on a model with patch size 8 to remain consistent with the final main-table configuration.

    A.5 Zero-shot evaluation details

    The in-the-wild numbers in main paper Tab. 3 are produced by the DVSM-initialized 960p TTB model trained on DL3DV with patch size 8, evaluated zero-shot on three out-of-distribution datasets: the 9 scenes of MipNeRF360 [3], the 7 scenes of Free [66], and the 6 stable scenes from Hike [39] as identified by [33]. We hold out every 8th frame on MipNeRF360 and Free and every 10th frame on Hike as target views, and run k-means over the remaining frames to obtain context views. All input images are first resized—preserving their original aspect ratio—so that the total pixel count matches the 540·960=518,400 target used by our model, and predicted novel views are then resized back to the dataset’s native resolution prior to metric computation. We apply the same image preprocessing pipeline to all baselines for a fair comparison. The LagerNVS [61] numbers are produced from our intermediate 480p checkpoint, since LagerNVS operates at 512 pixels along the longer image side and matching its native input resolution is the cleanest comparison.

    A.6 Local-duplicate inference details

    This section gives further details of the local-duplicate inference described in main paper Sec. 3.3.4, which reconstructs the scene as K spatially-local groups of context views at inference time, each with its own copy of the baked fast weights, so that a single fast-weight MLP only has to absorb the views of one local group (about B on average) instead of all V views. It reuses the trained model as is, with no retraining and no additional learned parameters; the per-scene state grows to K sets of fast weights.

    Grouping.

    Each context view i is summarized into a 6-dimensional descriptor fᵢ=[cᵢ;dᵢ]∈ℝ⁶, where cᵢ∈ℝ³ is the camera origin and dᵢ∈ℝ³ is the camera’s unit optical axis, both expressed in the input world frame. The number of groups K is an inference-time hyper-parameter; K=1 falls back to the single-MLP model. Unless stated otherwise we set K=V/B with a nominal budget of B=16 views per group, i.e., K=2 for V=32 and K=4 for V=64. We then run Lloyd’s algorithm for 20 iterations with the Euclidean distance to cluster the V descriptors into K groups. Centroids are initialized with the descriptors of K views whose indices are evenly spaced over [0,V-1]; since our context views are ordered by capture time, this spreads the initial centroids along the camera trajectory. If a centroid attracts no views during an iteration, we leave it unchanged for that round. Group sizes are neither balanced nor capped, and K must stay small relative to V.

    Per-group reconstruction.

    For every group k we run the standard reconstruction pass of our model on its member views only. Inside this pass, all sublayers—intra-view attention, FFN, cross-view attention, and the TTB inner loop—see only the tokens of group k; in particular, the cross-view attention that provides the baking target attends across the views of the group rather than across all V views. The two streams X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ and X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ of a context view are created inside the same pass and are therefore always baked together. Every pass starts from the shared meta-initialization θ₀ and runs the same T inner-loop steps, producing the per-layer fast weights {θ_k,ℓ}_ℓ=1^L of copy k. The K passes are independent of each other and are executed sequentially in our implementation. At the end of context prefilling we cache the fast weights of every group together with the K cluster centroids.

    Rendering.

    At rendering time, we do not re-run k-means. Each novel view computes its own 6-dimensional descriptor in the same input world frame and takes an \arg\min of the Euclidean distance to the cached centroids to select a single group, and all of its tokens are rendered with the fast weights of that group. The switch between copies is hard, without blending. The per-token rendering cost is unchanged and independent of V; routing only adds one nearest-centroid search over K centroids per view, which is negligible. In our implementation every novel view is routed and rendered individually.

    Appendix B Discussion: comparison with related methods

    This section positions TTB within the recent landscape of feed-forward novel-view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction methods. We focus on the LVSM family [25, 58, 22, 77] together with three recent methods that adopt either TTT layers (LongLRM [12], tttLRM [63]) or a 3D-pretrained encoder (LagerNVS [61]), since these are the closest design points to TTB. The discussion is structured around three axes: training settings (Sec. B.1), reconstruction/rendering complexity (Sec. B.2), and architectural composition (Sec. B.3).

    B.1 Training settings across methods

    Tab. 7 compares the training data, compute, and pretraining source across baselines and our method. All listed methods share AdamW as the outer-loop optimizer and a multi-stage resolution curriculum, so we restrict the table to the three axes that most directly affect comparability.

    The compute footprint (64×A100) is broadly shared across the group when reported, so the differences mainly lie in data composition and pretraining strategy. Most LVSM-family methods train scene-only on Re10K or DL3DV, occasionally extending to Objaverse for object-level pretraining; LagerNVS is the outlier that explicitly relies on a multi-dataset mixture of fifteen sources to obtain its in-the-wild generalization. Three methods escape the from-scratch pattern, and they do so along two distinct lines: tttLRM and TTB warm-start from an NVS checkpoint of the same task family (TTT-LVSM and DVSM, respectively), reusing weights that were already optimized for novel-view rendering; LagerNVS instead transfers from VGGT, a model trained for 3D reconstruction, and jointly finetunes both the VGGT encoder and a freshly initialized cross-attention renderer with the rendering loss. TTB sits closer to tttLRM in this taxonomy—both inherit cross-view-attention features from a pretrained NVS backbone and reshape them into a TTT-style fast-weight representation—while LagerNVS represents an orthogonal direction of leveraging 3D-supervised priors.

    B.2 Reconstruction and rendering complexity

    Tab. 8 summarizes per-scene reconstruction and per-token rendering complexity for the methods above. The scene representation column reports the asymptotic memory footprint of the per-scene state that is consumed at rendering time.

    The table makes the design space explicit. The decoder-only LVSM reconstructs nothing offline and pays the full attention cost at every novel-view query; LVSM enc.-dec. and Efficient-LVSM amortize the cost into a one-time encoding stage but the rendering cost remains linear in the number of context tokens. DVSM further removes the encoder-decoder decoupling but at the price of quadratic cross-view attention during prefilling. LagerNVS occupies the same asymptotic regime as LVSM enc.-dec. but with a heavier V-dependence because its VGGT encoder runs alternating frame-wise and global self-attention over all V·L tokens, yielding O(V²·L²) encoding and O(V·L) per-token rendering through cross-attention to the encoder output. LaCT pushes both axes to their constant-complexity limits via TTT layers, whereas TTB occupies a previously empty cell on this map: it preserves DVSM’s quadratic reconstruction cost—necessary because cross-view attention provides the inner-loop target—while inheriting LaCT’s O(1) rendering and fixed-size scene representation. TTB– in turn shows that, when the cross-view attention target is replaced by a linear projection, reconstruction collapses back to linear in V, recovering LaCT’s complexity profile but with the rest of the TTB design choices retained. LRM-style baselines such as LongLRM and tttLRM occupy a different regime altogether, since their per-scene state is an explicit 3D Gaussian set rendered by a rasterizer rather than a neural module; we list them for completeness but do not directly compare O-rendering with them.

    B.3 Architectural composition

    Tab. 9 compares the per-block composition and the total decoder depth. We restrict the table to depth, latent dim, and the cross-view sublayer type, since these are the most consequential differences relative to TTB. For LagerNVS we report depth in two parts since its model is composed of a 24-block VGGT encoder operating at 1024-dim and a 12-block cross-attention decoder operating at 768-dim.

    A consistent pattern across the methods is a 24-block decoder for from-scratch models, while methods that initialize from a pretrained backbone are able to reduce decoder depth. DVSM and our method use a 12-block decoder by sharing weights between reconstruction and rendering stages; LagerNVS reaches the same 12-block decoder width and depth (768, 12 blocks) by offloading representational capacity to a 24-block, 1024-dim VGGT encoder. TTB inherits the 12-block depth directly from DVSM: every TTB layer additionally houses a fast-weight MLP whose inner loop is supervised by the cross-view attention output, but the surrounding intra-view attention and FFN sublayers are unchanged from DVSM. The net effect is that TTB matches or surpasses both 24-block from-scratch baselines and the much heavier LagerNVS on DL3DV (main paper Tab. 1, Tab. 3) while operating with comparable parameter counts to DVSM (244M for TTB– and 271M for TTB, against 163M for DVSM, 379M for LaCT, and over 1B for LagerNVS due to the included VGGT encoder). We attribute this efficiency to the combination of a shallow shared decoder and the inheritance of pretrained DVSM weights, which Sec. A.2 discusses in detail.

    Appendix C Additional results

    C.1 Few-view lower-resolution results

    We additionally train and evaluate our models on 2-view setup at a lower resolution. This is not our intended scenario as the rendering FPS speedup by replacing cross-view attentions with our baked MLPs become marginal: 64→72 at 256×256 and 45→52 at 512×512.

    We follow previous works to train and test on Re10k [30] dataset. We start from the most capable pretrained checkpoint from DVSM [58] which employs DINO [52] injection and patch size of 8. We first train at 256×256 resolution for 100K iterations with learning rate 4 × 10⁻⁴, and then finetune at 512×512 resolution for 10K iterations with learning rate 1 × 10⁻⁴. In each iteration on a GPU, we sample 32 scenes with 2 context views and 3 target views. The distance between the 2 views is randomly sampled between 25–192 frame skips following previous works.

    The results comparison is presented in Tab. 16. Under such few views, our TTBs can faithfully reproduce the cross-view attentions results, as reflected by the comparable results with our pretrained DVSM.

    C.2 In-the-wild generalization at 16 input views

    We complement the 64-view in-the-wild evaluation in main paper Tab. 3 with a 16-view counterpart in Tab. 10, covering the same three out-of-domain datasets (MipNeRF360 [3], Free [66], Hike [39]) at both 960p and 512-pixel longer-side settings. The trends mirror our in-domain DL3DV results: TTB closely matches DVSM [58] quality across all three datasets while consistently surpassing LaCT [77] and LVSM [25], and outperforms LagerNVS [61] by a clear margin under the 512-pixel setting. Efficiency-wise, TTB retains its constant-FPS rendering at 16 views just as at 64 views, confirming that the rendering speedup is independent of context view count. These results indicate that TTB’s quality and speed advantages generalize beyond the dense-view regime to fewer-view, out-of-domain scenarios.

    C.3 Inference at scale on DL3DV.

    A single fast-weight MLP per TTB layer has fixed capacity, which becomes a bottleneck as the number of context views V grows. Tab. 11 compares this single-MLP baseline against our local-duplicate variant, which maintains K local copies of the per-layer fast-weight state, each updated only by views routed to its spatially-local group via k-means over per-view camera features (results reported with our ablation model at 720p). Up to V=32, the two variants are indistinguishable and both match DVSM [58]. Beyond V=64, the single-MLP variant saturates and plateaus around 25.8 PSNR, while the local-duplicate variant continues to scale and reaches 27.74 at V=256, on par with DVSM’s 27.56. Throughout, rendering FPS stays in the 67 to 72 range, in stark contrast to DVSM’s drop from 63.6 at V=16 to 12.6 at V=256. Local duplication thus resolves the capacity ceiling of a single fast-weight MLP without compromising the constant-complexity rendering that motivates TTB.

    C.4 Capacity scaling

    Tab. 12 studies the two knobs that set the capacity of the baked state. Sweeping K jointly with V shows that the best K is always V/16, so local duplication is governed by a single scene-independent budget of B=16 views per copy rather than a per-scene heuristic; we use this budget for all Ours (duplicate) entries in Tab. 1, and the K=1 column and the K=V/16 diagonal reproduce the two TTB rows of Tab. 11. Widening the fast-weight MLP closes the gap as well and reaches DVSM at 16× width, indicating that the remaining gap is a capacity limit rather than a limitation of baking. Since width enlarges the model and requires retraining, we keep the 4× width and scale capacity through K.

    C.5 Effect of pretraining.

    Tab. 13 compares three frameworks trained from scratch versus initialized from a DVSM [58] checkpoint (results reported with our ablation model at 720p). The PSNR gain from pretraining grows monotonically with cross-view attention preservation: smallest for TTT (no cross-view attention), larger for TTB– (linear target), and largest for our full TTB (cross-view attention target), confirming that preserving cross-view attention is key to re-using decoder-only pretrained weights. Notably, TTB from scratch already surpasses pretrained TTT, indicating that its advantage is structural.

    C.6 Efficiency analysis

    We provide a detailed efficiency comparison in Tab. 14, reporting parameter counts, per-scene reconstruction time, per-view rendering FPS, and peak GPU memory at both inference and training time. All numbers are measured at 544×960 resolution with V=32 input views.

    End-to-end time.

    Since TTB shifts computation from rendering to reconstruction, Tab. 15 reports the total time to reconstruct a scene and render N novel views. TTB overtakes DVSM after only 5–7 views at every V, a threshold that any interactive viewer or trajectory rendering exceeds, while TTB– leads from the first view at the quality cost reported in Tab. 1.

    C.7 Scene representation size

    We further quantify the memory footprint of the per-scene state that must be retained between reconstruction and rendering at 544×960 resolution. Fig. 7 compares the KV-cache of DVSM [58] against the baked fast-weight state of TTB as the number of context views V grows. The DVSM KV-cache scales linearly with V, reaching tens of GBs at V=256, whereas TTB’s scene representation is a fixed-size set of fast-weight matrices whose footprint is independent of V (324 MB across all L blocks in FP32). At V=64 this is an 85× reduction over DVSM, growing to 340× at V=256; local-duplicate inference stores K=V/16 copies and stays a constant 21× smaller than the KV-cache at every V. This compact, V-independent state is what enables TTB’s O(1) per-token rendering and is also a practical advantage for deployment scenarios with limited GPU memory.

    Appendix D Qualitative results

    This section provides additional qualitative results that complement the quantitative comparisons in the main paper. We include in-domain comparisons on DL3DV [35] (Sec. D.1), two-view comparisons on Re10K [30] (Sec. D.2), and zero-shot comparisons on three in-the-wild datasets [3, 66, 39] (Sec. D.3).

    D.1 In-domain results on DL3DV

    Fig. 8 extends the comparison in main paper Fig. 5 to additional held-out DL3DV scenes spanning input view counts of V=16, 32, and 64, complementing the three-column quantitative results in main paper Tab. 1. TTB consistently preserves thin geometric structures and high-frequency texture where LaCT [77] blurs and LVSM [25] loses detail.

    D.2 Two-view results on Re10K

    Fig. 9 compares TTB against DVSM [58] and LVSM [25] under the two-view setting, complementing main paper Tab. 2. TTB matches DVSM’s quality at the same rendering speed-up regime, and outperforms LVSM in regions involving moderate viewpoint extrapolation.

    D.3 Zero-shot results on in-the-wild datasets

    Figs. 10–12 report zero-shot results on MipNeRF360 [3], Free [66], and Hike [39], all using the DL3DV-trained TTB model with V=64 input views. These figures complement the in-the-wild numerical results in main paper Tab. 3. Despite a clear domain gap from DL3DV, TTB recovers fine details such as small text and thin structures that LaCT [77] and LVSM [25] blur out.

    Appendix E Broader impacts

    TTB shares its broader impacts with feed-forward novel-view synthesis methods in general. What is more specific to TTB is the methodological perspective it offers: rather than replacing attention with a test-time-trained fast-weight MLP as in prior TTT-style architectures, TTB shows that the fast-weight MLP can be supervised to collaborate with attention by baking its outputs into a constant-size state. This baking perspective is potentially applicable beyond novel-view synthesis, in any setting where a powerful but expensive attention module needs to be amortized into a state of fixed size. Long-context language models, where attention KV-caches grow linearly with sequence length, could similarly benefit from baking attention outputs into a fixed-capacity fast weight to enable constant-memory inference. World models and video generators that maintain a long temporal context face the same memory-growth issue and may adopt analogous baking strategies for the temporal-attention component. Physical 3D perception systems that operate on streaming sensor inputs, such as embodied agents and autonomous driving stacks, could likewise use a baked fast-weight state to maintain a compact running memory of the environment without unbounded KV growth. We hope the baking perspective inspires further exploration of how attention and test-time training can be combined across these domains.

    Appendix F Declaration of LLM usage

    Large language models were used as writing and editing aids during manuscript preparation—paraphrasing, grammar correction, and improving readability. We additionally used Claude Code as a coding assistant during the development of our training and evaluation pipeline; all code generated with its help was reviewed and tested by the authors before being incorporated into the final implementation. LLMs did not contribute to the research ideation, model design, experimental protocol, or analysis of results.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：只解码器的大视角合成模型靠 KV-cache 出质量，测试时训练省算力但掉画质——中间还有一条路。

要点：

  • 现状：带 KV-cache 的「只解码器」大视角合成模型（LVSM）不重建 3D 几何、直接用网络回归新视角，质量已达 SOTA
  • 两条加速路线各有代价：测试时训练（TTT）层省算力但牺牲质量，而直接跑全模型又太贵
  • TTB（Test-Time Baking）把跨视图注意力中的全局场景信息「烤」进一个轻量 MLP，于是渲染时不必再付全模型的代价

为什么值得看：「测试时把全局信息烘进小网络」这个模式对引擎很实用：一次性的准备成本换持续的渲染开销下降。比 TTT 更划算的关键在于，它保留跨视图注意力的质量而不重训。

中文摘要：带 KV-cache 的「只解码器」大视角合成模型（LVSM）近来做出了 SOTA 质量——它不显式重建 3D 几何，而是直接由神经网络回归新视角。但代价是渲染时开销大：测试时训练（TTT）层能省算力却牺牲质量，直接跑全模型又太贵。TTB（Test-Time Baking）因此提出一条折中路径：在测试阶段把跨视图注意力中蕴含的全局场景信息「烘」进一个轻量 MLP，使后续渲染不必再付出全模型的计算成本。这种「一次性烘焙换持续渲染开销下降」的模式，与引擎里预计算光照的思路高度一致。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models

Abstract

Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to 23x rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io.

1 Introduction

Our research studies the task of novel-view synthesis conditioned on a set of context images with the powerful Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) [25]. LVSMs have recently emerged with several immediate follow-up improvements [22, 31, 69, 77, 58], achieving state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality across various input conditions [1, 23, 64, 42]. Their geometry-free scene representations and Transformer-based renderers are fully learning-based, making them favorable for scaling with increasing amounts of training data. The minimized 3D inductive bias also shows advantages when scenes are challenging for existing Transformer-compatible geometry-based representations (e.g., 3DGS [29]), such as surfaces with strong mirror reflections or translucent material.

We are especially interested in the decoder-only variant of LVSM [25] for its high-fidelity. DVSM [58] further introduces KV-cache to the cross-view attention layers, showing both quality and efficiency improvement. The KV-cache serves as a global scene state for novel-view queries, but the rendering time is still impractical under dense context view conditions due to the linear complexity per token when attending to the KV-cache. LaCT [77] takes a different approach by replacing cross-view attention layers with Test-Time Training (TTT) [59] layers, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. TTT performs inner-loop optimization to adapt fast-weight MLPs [49] to directly map queries to their values without the quadratic-complexity attention, which can also be interpreted as a variant of linear attention [36]. Despite achieving constant-complexity rendering speed, TTT significantly sacrifices rendering quality. A naive remedy for LaCT is to initialize from pretrained decoder-only model weights, which does improve quality, but the gap to the pretrained model remains significant.

We argue that this quality gap can be minimized by repurposing the fast-weight MLP inner-loop optimization as “baking” the information from cross-view attention, rather than replacing cross-view attention entirely as in TTT. We dub our strategy Test-Time Baking (TTB), illustrated in Fig. 2b. The key motivation is to trade context-view processing time for faster and higher-fidelity novel-view rendering, achieving the Pareto frontier of quality and speed shown in Fig. 1. Specifically, the inner-loop learning target becomes the output tokens from cross-view attention, instead of the raw value tokens used in TTT. This formulation also generalizes beyond the linear-attention interpretation of TTT [36]. In principle, the learning target of our TTB can also be tokens from arbitrarily non-linear layers or tokens enriched with additional scene information.

Furthermore, we identify a modality misalignment issue inherent to the context prefilling of MLP fast-weight for novel-view synthesis. In the reconstruction stage (context prefilling), the fast-weight MLPs are updated using context tokens with both camera and image information. In the rendering stage, however, the updated MLPs take novel-view tokens coming from camera-only input without any image content. This conventional pipeline poses a reconstruction-rendering input modality misalignment challenge.

Our solution to modality misalignment is simple yet effective. As illustrated in Fig. 2c, we pair each context view into i) context ground-truth tokens, derived from input cameras and images that produce the global scene information to be baked, and ii) context rendering tokens, derived from camera-only input that simulates novel-view rendering conditions. At each TTB layer, the fast-weight MLP is optimized to map context rendering tokens to their corresponding context ground-truth tokens, which carry image and cross-view attended information. The optimized TTB-MLP is then shared between context rendering tokens and the downstream novel-view rendering tokens for retrieving scene information, ensuring that their conditioning remains identical across all layers.

Interestingly, TTB draws a natural parallel with traditional implicit radiance and light field reconstruction, where MLPs are optimized to map spatial coordinates to radiance values. In TTB, the fast-weight MLP instead is optimized to map ray-patch latent coordinates to their appearance latent representations, which effectively performs few-step light-field optimization in latent space. This perspective suggests that TTB interpolates appearance latents for novel viewpoints from their ray-patch latent coordinates, motivating a convergence-oriented inner loop over one-shot summarization. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose Test-Time Baking, which retargets the inner-loop optimization of the TTT fast-weight MLP from raw value tokens to cross-view attention outputs, so that the fast-weight MLP collaborates with attention rather than replacing it.

  • •

    We identify a modality misalignment between the reconstruction and rendering stages of MLP fast-weight prefilling, and resolve it via a context pair that disentangles each context view into a ground-truth and a camera-only rendering token.

  • •

    We draw a connection between TTB’s inner loop and light field optimization in latent space, which motivates a convergence-oriented training recipe (multi-step MSE) that we find particularly effective for TTB.

    • 2 Related work

    Per-Scene optimization. Early approaches to novel-view synthesis perform per-scene optimization, fitting differentiable scene representations to observed images via differentiable rendering. Coordinate-based MLPs [41, 2, 4], voxels [56, 15, 8, 43, 57, 34], and the landmark 3DGS [29] as the scene representation have been widely explored. Despite impressive quality, per-scene optimization does not scale with the increasing training scenes and degrades quickly under fewer input views.

    Geometry-based feed-forward models. To overcome the scalability limitations and lengthy procedure of per-scene optimization, learning-based methods train networks to predict 3D representations from images. Early works estimated multi-plane images via cost volumes [73, 68, 17, 72, 16, 40], while NeRF-based generalizable methods [7, 74, 67, 37] extended coverage to wide-angle viewpoints at limited quality. The advent of 3DGS [29] reframed the problem as pixel-aligned GS prediction [6, 71, 10, 60, 62, 24], achieving promising results, and Large Reconstruction Models (LRMs) [21] further demonstrated Transformer scalability across various 3D representations [5, 70, 76]. One fundamental limitation of handcrafted 3D is their degradation on surfaces or materials they are not designed for, whereas the geometry-free representations we study can learn them given data. Furthermore, explicit 3D geometry lacks a compact latent representation, and efforts to manage their linearly growing output size under more input views [12, 11, 63, 45] remain a symptom of this constraint. Our TTB bakes scenes into constant-size MLPs at higher quality.

    Geometry-free feed-forward models. An alternative paradigm sidesteps the limitations of geometry-based models by representing scenes as latent representations and rendering via neural networks. Early methods [13, 55, 54, 53, 46, 47] were constrained by limited network capacity, while Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) [25] broke this barrier by leveraging powerful Transformers. Encoder-decoder and decoder-only LVSM variants are explored. The encoder-decoder LVSM [25] encodes context views into scene tokens and decodes novel views conditioned on the encoded scene, with subsequent works refining scene encoding strategies [22, 31, 69] and extending to generative [1] and uncalibrated camera [23, 78, 64, 42] settings. The decoder-only LVSM [25], on the other hand, uses a single network for both context prefilling and novel-view rendering. Despite higher fidelity, its original form inefficiently processes context views independently for each novel view. DVSM [58] addresses this by prefilling context views into a KV-cache shared across all novel views, achieving state-of-the-art quality under both sparse and dense view settings. However, the linearly growing KV-cache size makes rendering speed impractical for larger numbers of input views. LaCT [77] replaces cross-view attention with Test-Time Training layers to achieve constant rendering complexity, but at a significant quality cost compared to DVSM. Our Test-Time Baking achieves the same constant rendering complexity while substantially closing the quality gap left by LaCT.

    Test-time Training layers. TTT [59] has recently emerged as a popular alternative to attention for its linear time and constant space complexity. We refer interested readers to [36] for an in-depth review and analysis. We are particularly interested in the variant presented in LaCT [77], which has demonstrated success in accelerating various vision and 3D tasks [9, 63, 18, 14, 26], albeit at the cost of quality relative to their attention-based counterparts. Our TTB departs from this paradigm in two ways: rather than replacing attention, TTB learns directly from attention outputs; and rather than performing mere token-to-token information exchange, TTB explicitly learns to map camera-ray tokens to their corresponding image tokens, yielding improved novel-view synthesis quality.

    3 Method

    We start by formally introducing our task and the general pipeline in Sec. 3.1. We detail the decoder-only architecture we build on in Sec. 3.2. Finally, we present Test-Time Baking in Sec. 3.3.

    3.1 Overview

    Given a set of V context images with known poses and intrinsics {Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3,Pᵢ∈SE(3),Kᵢ∈ℝ^3×3}ᵢ₌₁^V, our goal is to synthesize novel views for an arbitrary camera query (P^′,K^′). We focus on reconstruction rather than generation, assuming novel views can be directly regressed from the context views. Approaches to this end generally decompose into two stages:

    S=Recon(I,P,K), Ī=Rend(P^′,K^′,S),

    		(1)

    where Recon(·) processes context views into a method-specific scene representation S, and Rend(·) synthesizes the novel view Ī conditioned on S. Recent feed-forward models instantiate Recon(·) as a Transformer. The Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) [21] family employs a human-defined 3D and renderer, while the Large View Synthesis Model (LVSM) [25] series defines S as a latent state and implements Rend(·) as a neural network. As both Recon(·) and Rend(·) are differentiable, models are trained end-to-end against ground-truth novel views I^′ by:

    J=MSE(Ī,I^′)+λ·Percep(Ī,I^′) ,

    		(2)

    where Percep is the neural perceptual loss [27] and λ balances the photometric objectives.

    3.2 Decoder-only View Synthesis Model

    Our method builds on the Decoder-only View Synthesis Model (DVSM) [58], which uses a shared Transformer decoder for both Recon(·) and Rend(·), and represents the scene S as KV caches. Specifically, the model consists of L repeated blocks, each comprising a sequence of layers:

    X_ℓ=(FFN_ℓ,2∘CrossAttn_ℓ∘FFN_ℓ,1∘IntraAttn_ℓ)(X_ℓ-1) ,

    		(3)

    where IntraAttn(·) and CrossAttn(·) perform intra-view and cross-view attention, respectively, and FFN(·) denotes a fully connected layer. Residual connections [19] and QK-normalization [20] are applied for training stability. During reconstruction, context-view tokens are prefilled into a KV-cache at each CrossAttn(·). During rendering, novel-view tokens query the cached KV to retrieve global scene information from each CrossAttn(·) layer.

    Regarding input tokenization, camera intrinsics and poses are first converted into Plücker ray maps [44] for linear patch embedding. Context-view and novel-view tokens are initialized as:

    X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P,K)+PE⁽ʳᵍᵇ⁾(I)), X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P^′,K^′)) ,

    		(4)

    where PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾ and PE⁽ʳᵍᵇ⁾ are linear patch projections for the Plücker ray maps and context images, respectively, Here, X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀∈ℝ^V×H/p×W/p×D denotes tokens from V context views with patch size p used for KV-cache prefilling, and X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾₀∈ℝ^U×H/p×W/p×D denotes tokens for U novel-view queries, each processed independently. Finally, a shallow model head regresses pixel values as:

    Ī=(PixShuf∘Sigmoid∘Linear∘LayerNorm)(X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾_L) ,

    		(5)

    where PixShuf(·) denotes pixel shuffling [51] and X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾_L is the last-layer tokens out of Eq.3.

    3.3 Test-time Baking

    We present our technical contribution to improve the rendering-time efficiency of DVSM [58] while retaining its high rendering quality. The issue of DVSM is that its KV-cache size grows linearly with the number of context tokens, making it slow and impractical for novel-view queries under high-resolution or dense input context views. A naive strategy is to replace each CrossAttn(·) in Eq. 3 with a Test-Time Training (TTT) [59] layer, achieving constant space and linear time complexity as demonstrated in LaCT [77]. However, we observe significant quality degradation even when finetuning the TTT variant from DVSM pretrained weights. This motivates us to explore a better solution that improves upon TTT. A full model pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 3.

    3.3.1 Repurposing TTT: collaborating instead of replacing attention

    Our motivation is to trade reconstruction (prefilling) computation, which only needs to be performed once per scene, for improved rendering-time speed and quality. The resulting solution is simple yet effective. Rather than entirely replacing cross-view attention with TTT fast-weight MLP as in the LaCT [77], we repurpose TTT to explicitly learn from the input-output pairs out of cross-view attention. Consequently, we no longer need to cache the KV; only the updated MLP fast weights are stored. The space and time complexity of novel-view rendering is therefore identical to that of TTT. We call our strategy Test-Time Baking (TTB), which can be viewed as a generalized form of TTT.

    Formally, the fast-weight update rules of TTT and TTB are:

    θ⁽ᵀᵀᵀ⁾=θ-η∇_θL(f_θ(WₖX),\color[rgb]0.9727,0.5156,0.4727WᵥX),(6a)
    θ^(TTB)=θ-η∇_θL(f_θ(WₖX),\color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406g(X^*)),(6b)

    respectively, where θ is the fast weights of the MLP f(·), η and L are the inner-loop learning rate and objective, Wₖ and Wᵥ are linear projection matrices, and X is the input tokens. The difference between TTT and TTB lies in the mapping target: \color[rgb]0.9727,0.5156,0.4727WᵥX and \color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406g(X^*). In principle, we can employ an arbitrary function g or tokens X^* with additional modality for the mapping target \color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406g(X^*). Note that TTB falls back to TTT when X^*=X and g is a linear projection. In our case, we instantiate g(·) as the CrossAttn(·) from DVSM, which shifts TTB beyond the linear-attention interpretation [36] of TTT. Although this incurs additional reconstruction-time cost, once prefilled, rendering remains identical to TTT with substantially higher quality thanks to the enriched global information from g(·).

    More analysis. We empirically validate that swapping the inner-loop target from \color[rgb]0.9727,0.5156,0.4727WᵥX to \color[rgb]0.0977,0.7148,0.6406CrossAttn(X) broadens the effective view field of the baked fast-weight MLP. At TTB block 7 with V=16, we measure how much each context image contributes to the TTB output at the novel-view rendering tokens via input-gradient saliency, sorted and averaged across output positions (Fig. 4). The WᵥX variant peaks sharply at top-1 then decays, while CrossAttn(X) flattens the peak and sustains a heavier mid-rank tail. This matches our design intent: CrossAttn(X) already aggregates across all V context views, so each memorized pair inherits a wider receptive field.

    3.3.2 Modality misalignment and context pair

    The baked MLPs via Eq. 6b receive inputs of different modalities between the reconstruction and rendering stages. As defined in Eq. 4, context tokens X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀ used for prefilling contain image content, whereas novel-view tokens X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾₀ are with camera-only information. This modality misalignment poses an unnecessary generalization challenge to the baked MLP.

    We address this by disentangling input context tokens, X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁾₀ from Eq.4, into a paired representation:

    X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P,K)+PE⁽ʳᵍᵇ⁾(I)), X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾₀=LayerNorm(PE⁽ʳᵃʸ⁾(P,K)),

    		(7)

    where X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾₀ are the context rendering tokens with camera-only input, and X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾₀ are the context ground-truth tokens with additional RGB input. We use X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ to serve TTB mapping target while using X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ to serve TTB input. Specifically, at each TTB layer, the fast-weight MLP is baked to learn the mapping X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾↦CrossAttn(X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾) via the update rule in Eq. 6b. The baked MLP is then shared across both context rendering X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ and the downstream novel-view rendering X⁽ⁿᵛ⁾ tokens to produce feature for the subsequent layers. As visualized in Fig. 2, our context pairing ensures distribution alignment from the early layers, which facilitates feature interpolation. Conversely, the distribution only aligned in the later layers without context pairing due to the modality misalignment between reconstruction and rendering stages. Despite doubling the number of tokens during reconstruction, rendering-stage efficiency remains the same, which aligns with our motivation to trade reconstruction time for rendering-time quality.

    3.3.3 TTB layer details

    The design of our TTB layer is inspired by the TTT layer in LaCT [77]. We remove the asymmetric QK projection and instead use a shared linear projection to produce queries and keys. We adopt SwiGLU-MLP [50] as the fast-weight MLP architecture, and apply an additional linear layer to predict per-token learning rates. For inner-loop optimization, we employ Muon [28] optimizer with weight normalization [48] for a predefined T steps. We find that using MSE as the inner-loop objective for our TTB yields better results than the unnormalized dot-product loss used in LaCT [77]’s TTT. We also find that learning the residual to the mapping target is easier to bake than learning the target directly. Specifically, the final TTB update rule is:

    θₜ₊₁=θₜ-Muon(∇_θₜ∥f_θₜ(WₖX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾)-Wᵥ(CrossAttn(X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾)-X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾)∥₂)~,

    		(8)

    where Muon(·) performs Muon gradient orthogonalization [28], Wₖ and Wᵥ are linear projection matrices for the TTB input and mapping target. The final baked weights θ_T are then applied to update both the context rendering and novel-view rendering tokens and provide feedback to the context ground-truth tokens (the output arrows from the baked MLP in Fig. 3).

    3.3.4 Fast-weight local-duplicate inference

    The baked fast weights have a fixed capacity, causing quality to plateau as the number of context views V grows. We address this at inference time by clustering the context views into K spatially-local groups via k-means on per-view camera poses, with K=V/B for a nominal budget of B views per group. Each group is reconstructed independently by the unmodified model, so that cross-view attention and the inner-loop update only involve the views of that group, yielding per-group, per-layer fast weights {{θ_k,ℓ}_ℓ=1^L}ₖ₌₁^K. At rendering time, each novel view is routed to the group with the nearest centroid and queries only the corresponding copy. Rendering thus remains O(1) per view and each copy only has to absorb about B views, while the stored state grows linearly with K.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation details

    We use 768 latent channels with 12 decoder blocks at patch size 8, replacing each cross-view attention with a TTB layer. We initialize our models from the corresponding DVSM [58] checkpoint. We use AdamW [38] with cosine annealing and perceptual loss weight λ=0.2. Models are trained on DL3DV-10K [35] dataset with 64 A100 GPUs. We first train at 340p for 100K iterations with learning rate 4 × 10⁻⁴, then finetune at 480p, 720p, and 960p for 10K iterations each with learning rate 1 × 10⁻⁵. We randomly sample either 16 or 32 context views per scene with the same number of target views. Ablations use a smaller setup on 8 A100 GPUs at patch size 16 truncated to 720p, with efficiency metrics still reported at patch size 8 for consistency. For evaluation, we use the 140 held-out DL3DV testing scenes and follow previous view sampling [12].

    TTB layer. We use a single-headed fast-weight SwiGLU-MLP [50] with a hidden dimension of 3072, a 4× expansion of the model dimension. The fast weight is updated with the Muon optimizer [28] and we run T = 3 inner-loop update steps. The per-token learning rate is predicted by an additional linear head with base learning rate of 0.01. The inner-loop objective maps context-rendering tokens to the cross-view attention output of context-ground-truth tokens with the MSE loss. Fast-weight local-duplicate inference (Sec. 3.3.4) is turned off except stated otherwise. When enabled, we set B=16. For some experiments we also report a variant denoted TTB– or Ours–, which replaces the cross-view attention target with a linear projection WᵥX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ and thus avoids the quadratic-complexity cross-view attention at reconstruction, making reconstruction time linear in V.

    4.2 Comparisons

    DL3DV. Tab. 1 and Fig. 5 report results on DL3DV with 16, 32, and 64 input views at 960p. TTB substantially closes the quality gap between DVSM [58] and LaCT [77] while rendering at a constant 23 FPS, up to 23× faster than DVSM and 2.3× faster than LaCT. Our model is built on DVSM with 12 blocks while LaCT uses 24 blocks (model size in Tab. 3). The Ours– without cross-view attention is comparable to LaCT quality with less parameters and faster rendering. With local-duplicate inference (Sec. 3.3.4), Ours (duplicate) further closes the residual gap at large V and approaches DVSM quality at the same rendering speed. Fig. 5 confirms these trends qualitatively, where TTB preserves thin and high-frequency structures such as handrails, window grilles, and small text that LaCT and LVSM [25] render with visible blur.

    In-the-wild. We further evaluate the generalization ability on out-of-domain datasets with 16 and 64 context views in Tab. 3. We keep the aspect ratio of the context images and resize to the resolutions preferred by the models. The synthesized novel views are resized to match ground-truth source resolutions for evaluation. Comparisons to LaCT [77] and DVSM [58] are consistent with the in-domain evaluation—our quality is often comparable to DVSM but at a much faster rendering; we use more context prefilling time than LaCT but gaining quality with 2.3× faster rendering. LagerNVS [61] is a very recent work which builds upon VGGT [65] and trains on multiple datasets. We use our intermediate checkpoints at 480p to better align with LagerNVS’s input resolution. Our quality outperforms LagerNVS by a large margin with 3.1–9.5× faster rendering.

    Re10K. We additionally compare on Re10K with two low-resolution context views. This is not our main target scenario as the rendering time gain from cross-view attention becomes marginal. We finetune from the Re10K checkpoint of DVSM [58] with DINO injection. Results are in Tab. 2. Our TTB can reproduce DVSM cross-attention quality in this setup. See supplementary for full results.

    4.3 Ablation studies

    From TTT to TTB. Tab. 4 decomposes the gap between a vanilla LaCT-style TTT replacement [77] and our full TTB into three additive components: context pairing, switching to MSE with T=3 inner steps (yielding TTB–), and replacing the linear-projection target with cross-view attention output. Each contributes meaningfully, and stacking all three closes the quality gap to DVSM [58] while retaining TTT’s ∼ 50 FPS rendering. The reconstruction cost grows quadratically with V due to the in-loop cross-view attention, consistent with our reconstruction time for rendering quality trade-off.

    Inner-loop optimization. Tab. 6 ablates the inner-loop loss and number of update steps T. Switching from LaCT’s unnormalized dot-product loss [77] to MSE consistently improves quality for both TTT and TTB–, with TTB– benefiting more (+0.44 vs +0.27 PSNR). Increasing T brings monotonic but diminishing gains, leading us to adopt T=3 with MSE as a sweet spot between quality and reconstruction cost. This asymmetric response aligns with our light field view—TTB’s inner loop fits a target function and benefits from convergence, while TTT-KVB is closer to a one-shot linear write.

    TTB layer design. Tab. 6 ablates two design choices in our TTB layer. Residual learning reformulates the inner-loop target from the absolute cross-view attention output to its residual against X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾, reducing the magnitude of the regression target and easing the few-step inner-loop optimization. Feedback additionally applies the baked MLP to update the context ground-truth tokens, so that all three token streams propagate through identical operators in subsequent layers. Both designs contribute roughly equally in isolation (+0.43 and +0.44 PSNR) and combine to +0.52.

    Limitations. TTB is constrained by the fixed capacity of its fast-weight MLP, causing quality to saturate at large V; the local-duplicate routing that mitigates this is a heuristic, and learning it during training is left for future work. Its inner-loop cross-view attention also makes reconstruction quadratic in V, a drawback for single-shot scenarios. Finally, TTB is built on reconstruction rather than generation, interpolating within context views without extrapolating to unobserved viewpoints.

    5 Conclusion

    We present Test-Time Baking (TTB), which retargets the TTT inner-loop optimization from raw value tokens to cross-view attention outputs, turning the fast-weight MLP from a replacement for attention into its collaborator. Combined with a context pair that resolves the reconstruction-rendering modality misalignment, TTB bakes DVSM-level scene information into a fixed-size MLP while retaining TTT-level rendering complexity. Across DL3DV, Re10K, and in-the-wild benchmarks, TTB matches DVSM [58] quality at a constant 23 FPS and consistently surpasses LaCT [77]. We hope this baking perspective offers a new way to integrate attention and TTT beyond view synthesis.

    Overview.

    This supplementary material expands on the main paper with implementation details (Sec. A.1–A.6), a method-level comparison with related decoder-only LVSM and TTT-based methods (Sec. B), additional quantitative results (Sec. C), and additional qualitative comparisons (Sec. D).     Appendix A Additional details

    A.1 Common implementation details

    Unless otherwise specified, all of our final models share the configuration described in this section. The decoder consists of 12 blocks with a latent dimension of 768, organized as illustrated in main paper Fig. 3. Optimization is carried out with AdamW [38] using a weight decay of 0.05 and momentum coefficients (0.9,0.95). The learning rate is annealed along a cosine schedule preceded by 2.5k linear warm-up iterations, peaking at 4×10⁻⁴ during the lowest-resolution stage and dropping to 1×10⁻⁵ when finetuning at higher resolutions. The perceptual term in our rendering loss is weighted by λ=0.2. Training runs on 64 A100 GPUs, and we cast the learnable layers to BFloat16 mixed precision during forward propagation.

    Camera information is encoded with the Plücker parameterization [44]: each pixel is associated with a 6-dimensional vector (rₒ×r_d, r_d), where rₒ denotes the camera origin, r_d the unit direction of the corresponding ray, and × the vector cross product. We further normalize the context-view poses following the convention of GS-LRM [76].

    Inside each transformer block, we adopt the pre-norm layout combined with QK-normalization. Each attention layer uses 12 heads, and every fully-connected sublayer expands the hidden dimension by a factor of 4. All linear projections in our architecture are bias-free.

    A.2 TTB layer details

    This section elaborates on TTB layer details that were elided from the main paper for space. We provide the pseudocode of training our TTB model in Algo. 1 as a complementary reference for the descriptions below. The three fast-weight matrices of our SwiGLU-MLP, w₀,w₂∈ℝ^H×dᵢₙ×dₕ and w₁∈ℝ^H×dₕ×dₒᵤₜ, are stored as ordinary learnable parameters and are jointly optimized in the outer loop alongside the rest of the network. Consequently, the inner loop for every scene starts from a common, outer-loop-learned meta-initialization θ₀, which is then advanced by T Muon [28] update steps before being applied to the rendering tokens. When local-duplicate inference is enabled with K>1 groups, every per-group reconstruction starts from the same meta-initialized θ₀ and is specialized only by the views assigned to its group, so all local copies share the same starting point and differ through their inner-loop trajectories.

    We initialize TTB models from the corresponding DVSM [58] checkpoint with strict=False: the patch embeddings, input LayerNorms, Plücker encoding, intra-view attention layers, both FFNs in each block, and the RGB head are inherited directly, while every module inside the TTB layer—including its LayerNorm, query/key and value projections, output projection, per-token learning-rate head, output RMSNorm, and the fast weights w₀,w₁,w₂—is freshly initialized. The cross-view attention projections of DVSM are not reused, since the inner-loop target of TTB is structurally different and warm-starting from the DVSM projections did not yield benefits in our preliminary experiments. To prevent the random-init TTB layer from disrupting the inherited DVSM features at the start of finetuning, we initialize the TTB output projection with a small standard deviation following the residual zero-init trick used in deep transformers, so that the TTB block contributes approximately zero at finetune step 0 and the entire forward pass reduces to the pretrained DVSM model plus an identity TTB layer. This zero-init together with the parameter inheritance above accounts for the +1.02 PSNR gain reported in Tab.  13.

    For the TTB layer micro-architecture, we share a single linear projection between query and key construction: the inner-loop input WₖX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ in main paper Eq. 6 and the rendering-time query WₖX⁽ⁿᵛ⁾ are both produced by passing the input through a single linear layer followed by SiLU and an L₂ unit-norm, which constrains the writes and reads of the fast-weight MLP to a common spherical subspace and removes a magnitude degree of freedom from the inner-loop optimization. The per-token learning rate is predicted by an additional linear head that outputs 3H scalars per token—one for each of the three fast-weight matrices in every head—and reparameterized as softplus(·+softplus⁻¹(0.01)), ensuring strictly positive learning rates and an effective initial value of 0.01 across all heads and matrices.

    The outer loop differentiates fully through all T inner-loop steps without any first-order approximation, so that the rendering loss reflects the exact dependence of the final fast weights on the outer-loop parameters. Each Muon step orthogonalizes the inner-loop gradient with five Newton–Schulz quintic iterations executed in BFloat16; we transpose the gradient before iteration whenever dᵢₙ>dₕ so that the intermediate Gram matrix has size \min(dᵢₙ,dₕ)², which keeps the per-step memory manageable. Even with this optimization, retaining T inner-step activations for backpropagation remains the dominant memory cost of TTB. We mitigate it with two layers of gradient checkpointing: the inner-loop activations of SwiGLU and Muon are recomputed within each step, and the outer-loop checkpointing is applied selectively to the intra-view attention and FFN sublayers but not to the TTB sublayer itself, the combination of which makes our 64-A100 training feasible at 960p resolution with V = 32 context views.

    Finally, our two main paper variants differ only in the inner-loop mapping target. TTB instantiates g(·) in main paper Eq. 6b as the cross-view attention output of X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾, while TTB– replaces this with a linear projection WᵥX⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ acting directly on the context ground-truth tokens. Both variants share every other component described above, including the context pair construction, the QK-shared projection, the per-token learning-rate head, the residual target, and the feedback path that propagates the baked MLP output back to X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾.

    A.3 Two-view Re10K specific details

    For the two-view setting, each GPU receives 32 scenes per iteration, with 2 context views and 3 target views per scene. The interval between the two context frames is sampled uniformly between 25 and 192, and target frames are drawn from the union of all intermediate frames between the two context views and the extrapolated frames within 25 frames on either side. We initialize the model from the corresponding DVSM [58] Re10K checkpoint following the strategy detailed in Sec. A.2, and finetune it on Re10K for 100K iterations at 256×256 followed by 10K iterations at 512×512. Note that doubling the context tokens through the context pair (main paper Eq. 7) negligibly affects this two-view setup, so we keep the same per-GPU batch composition as DVSM.

    A.4 Many-view DL3DV [35] specific details

    DL3DV is the main benchmark for our dense-view results in main paper Tab. 1 and Tab. 3, as well as for all the ablations in main paper Sec. 4.3. For training, we adopt a dynamic batching scheme that controls the per-GPU token budget rather than the number of scenes. Each scene draws either 16 or 32 context views uniformly at random, paired with the same number of target views; the number of scenes packed into a GPU is then adjusted on the fly so that the aggregate count of context-pair tokens (i.e., the union of X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ and X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ across all scenes in the batch) stays within a fixed budget. This compensates for the doubled token count introduced by the context pair and keeps the effective compute per iteration comparable to DVSM at the same memory ceiling. The frame interval between two adjacent context views is sampled uniformly from [1,16], and target views are drawn from [\min(ℂ)-2,\max(ℂ)+2]∖ℂ, where ℂ is the index set of the sampled context views. We exclude from training a small subset of scenes whose aspect ratio or native resolution does not match the canonical 16:9960p layout. The resolution curriculum starts from 340p and runs for 100K iterations, after which the model is finetuned for 10K iterations at each of 480p, 720p, and the final 960p (540×960).

    For the controlled ablation setting used in main paper Tab. 4–6 and Tab. 13, we shrink the compute footprint to 8 A100 GPUs by fixing the context view count to 32, raising the patch size to 16 to lower the per-token resolution, and truncating the curriculum to 340p / 480p / 720p with 100K / 10K / 10K iterations respectively. All the design knobs ablated in those tables share this controlled setup; the rendering and reconstruction efficiency reported alongside is measured on a model with patch size 8 to remain consistent with the final main-table configuration.

    A.5 Zero-shot evaluation details

    The in-the-wild numbers in main paper Tab. 3 are produced by the DVSM-initialized 960p TTB model trained on DL3DV with patch size 8, evaluated zero-shot on three out-of-distribution datasets: the 9 scenes of MipNeRF360 [3], the 7 scenes of Free [66], and the 6 stable scenes from Hike [39] as identified by [33]. We hold out every 8th frame on MipNeRF360 and Free and every 10th frame on Hike as target views, and run k-means over the remaining frames to obtain context views. All input images are first resized—preserving their original aspect ratio—so that the total pixel count matches the 540·960=518,400 target used by our model, and predicted novel views are then resized back to the dataset’s native resolution prior to metric computation. We apply the same image preprocessing pipeline to all baselines for a fair comparison. The LagerNVS [61] numbers are produced from our intermediate 480p checkpoint, since LagerNVS operates at 512 pixels along the longer image side and matching its native input resolution is the cleanest comparison.

    A.6 Local-duplicate inference details

    This section gives further details of the local-duplicate inference described in main paper Sec. 3.3.4, which reconstructs the scene as K spatially-local groups of context views at inference time, each with its own copy of the baked fast weights, so that a single fast-weight MLP only has to absorb the views of one local group (about B on average) instead of all V views. It reuses the trained model as is, with no retraining and no additional learned parameters; the per-scene state grows to K sets of fast weights.

    Grouping.

    Each context view i is summarized into a 6-dimensional descriptor fᵢ=[cᵢ;dᵢ]∈ℝ⁶, where cᵢ∈ℝ³ is the camera origin and dᵢ∈ℝ³ is the camera’s unit optical axis, both expressed in the input world frame. The number of groups K is an inference-time hyper-parameter; K=1 falls back to the single-MLP model. Unless stated otherwise we set K=V/B with a nominal budget of B=16 views per group, i.e., K=2 for V=32 and K=4 for V=64. We then run Lloyd’s algorithm for 20 iterations with the Euclidean distance to cluster the V descriptors into K groups. Centroids are initialized with the descriptors of K views whose indices are evenly spaced over [0,V-1]; since our context views are ordered by capture time, this spreads the initial centroids along the camera trajectory. If a centroid attracts no views during an iteration, we leave it unchanged for that round. Group sizes are neither balanced nor capped, and K must stay small relative to V.

    Per-group reconstruction.

    For every group k we run the standard reconstruction pass of our model on its member views only. Inside this pass, all sublayers—intra-view attention, FFN, cross-view attention, and the TTB inner loop—see only the tokens of group k; in particular, the cross-view attention that provides the baking target attends across the views of the group rather than across all V views. The two streams X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ᵍᵗ⁾ and X⁽ᶜᵗˣ⁻ʳᵉⁿᵈ⁾ of a context view are created inside the same pass and are therefore always baked together. Every pass starts from the shared meta-initialization θ₀ and runs the same T inner-loop steps, producing the per-layer fast weights {θ_k,ℓ}_ℓ=1^L of copy k. The K passes are independent of each other and are executed sequentially in our implementation. At the end of context prefilling we cache the fast weights of every group together with the K cluster centroids.

    Rendering.

    At rendering time, we do not re-run k-means. Each novel view computes its own 6-dimensional descriptor in the same input world frame and takes an \arg\min of the Euclidean distance to the cached centroids to select a single group, and all of its tokens are rendered with the fast weights of that group. The switch between copies is hard, without blending. The per-token rendering cost is unchanged and independent of V; routing only adds one nearest-centroid search over K centroids per view, which is negligible. In our implementation every novel view is routed and rendered individually.

    Appendix B Discussion: comparison with related methods

    This section positions TTB within the recent landscape of feed-forward novel-view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction methods. We focus on the LVSM family [25, 58, 22, 77] together with three recent methods that adopt either TTT layers (LongLRM [12], tttLRM [63]) or a 3D-pretrained encoder (LagerNVS [61]), since these are the closest design points to TTB. The discussion is structured around three axes: training settings (Sec. B.1), reconstruction/rendering complexity (Sec. B.2), and architectural composition (Sec. B.3).

    B.1 Training settings across methods

    Tab. 7 compares the training data, compute, and pretraining source across baselines and our method. All listed methods share AdamW as the outer-loop optimizer and a multi-stage resolution curriculum, so we restrict the table to the three axes that most directly affect comparability.

    The compute footprint (64×A100) is broadly shared across the group when reported, so the differences mainly lie in data composition and pretraining strategy. Most LVSM-family methods train scene-only on Re10K or DL3DV, occasionally extending to Objaverse for object-level pretraining; LagerNVS is the outlier that explicitly relies on a multi-dataset mixture of fifteen sources to obtain its in-the-wild generalization. Three methods escape the from-scratch pattern, and they do so along two distinct lines: tttLRM and TTB warm-start from an NVS checkpoint of the same task family (TTT-LVSM and DVSM, respectively), reusing weights that were already optimized for novel-view rendering; LagerNVS instead transfers from VGGT, a model trained for 3D reconstruction, and jointly finetunes both the VGGT encoder and a freshly initialized cross-attention renderer with the rendering loss. TTB sits closer to tttLRM in this taxonomy—both inherit cross-view-attention features from a pretrained NVS backbone and reshape them into a TTT-style fast-weight representation—while LagerNVS represents an orthogonal direction of leveraging 3D-supervised priors.

    B.2 Reconstruction and rendering complexity

    Tab. 8 summarizes per-scene reconstruction and per-token rendering complexity for the methods above. The scene representation column reports the asymptotic memory footprint of the per-scene state that is consumed at rendering time.

    The table makes the design space explicit. The decoder-only LVSM reconstructs nothing offline and pays the full attention cost at every novel-view query; LVSM enc.-dec. and Efficient-LVSM amortize the cost into a one-time encoding stage but the rendering cost remains linear in the number of context tokens. DVSM further removes the encoder-decoder decoupling but at the price of quadratic cross-view attention during prefilling. LagerNVS occupies the same asymptotic regime as LVSM enc.-dec. but with a heavier V-dependence because its VGGT encoder runs alternating frame-wise and global self-attention over all V·L tokens, yielding O(V²·L²) encoding and O(V·L) per-token rendering through cross-attention to the encoder output. LaCT pushes both axes to their constant-complexity limits via TTT layers, whereas TTB occupies a previously empty cell on this map: it preserves DVSM’s quadratic reconstruction cost—necessary because cross-view attention provides the inner-loop target—while inheriting LaCT’s O(1) rendering and fixed-size scene representation. TTB– in turn shows that, when the cross-view attention target is replaced by a linear projection, reconstruction collapses back to linear in V, recovering LaCT’s complexity profile but with the rest of the TTB design choices retained. LRM-style baselines such as LongLRM and tttLRM occupy a different regime altogether, since their per-scene state is an explicit 3D Gaussian set rendered by a rasterizer rather than a neural module; we list them for completeness but do not directly compare O-rendering with them.

    B.3 Architectural composition

    Tab. 9 compares the per-block composition and the total decoder depth. We restrict the table to depth, latent dim, and the cross-view sublayer type, since these are the most consequential differences relative to TTB. For LagerNVS we report depth in two parts since its model is composed of a 24-block VGGT encoder operating at 1024-dim and a 12-block cross-attention decoder operating at 768-dim.

    A consistent pattern across the methods is a 24-block decoder for from-scratch models, while methods that initialize from a pretrained backbone are able to reduce decoder depth. DVSM and our method use a 12-block decoder by sharing weights between reconstruction and rendering stages; LagerNVS reaches the same 12-block decoder width and depth (768, 12 blocks) by offloading representational capacity to a 24-block, 1024-dim VGGT encoder. TTB inherits the 12-block depth directly from DVSM: every TTB layer additionally houses a fast-weight MLP whose inner loop is supervised by the cross-view attention output, but the surrounding intra-view attention and FFN sublayers are unchanged from DVSM. The net effect is that TTB matches or surpasses both 24-block from-scratch baselines and the much heavier LagerNVS on DL3DV (main paper Tab. 1, Tab. 3) while operating with comparable parameter counts to DVSM (244M for TTB– and 271M for TTB, against 163M for DVSM, 379M for LaCT, and over 1B for LagerNVS due to the included VGGT encoder). We attribute this efficiency to the combination of a shallow shared decoder and the inheritance of pretrained DVSM weights, which Sec. A.2 discusses in detail.

    Appendix C Additional results

    C.1 Few-view lower-resolution results

    We additionally train and evaluate our models on 2-view setup at a lower resolution. This is not our intended scenario as the rendering FPS speedup by replacing cross-view attentions with our baked MLPs become marginal: 64→72 at 256×256 and 45→52 at 512×512.

    We follow previous works to train and test on Re10k [30] dataset. We start from the most capable pretrained checkpoint from DVSM [58] which employs DINO [52] injection and patch size of 8. We first train at 256×256 resolution for 100K iterations with learning rate 4 × 10⁻⁴, and then finetune at 512×512 resolution for 10K iterations with learning rate 1 × 10⁻⁴. In each iteration on a GPU, we sample 32 scenes with 2 context views and 3 target views. The distance between the 2 views is randomly sampled between 25–192 frame skips following previous works.

    The results comparison is presented in Tab. 16. Under such few views, our TTBs can faithfully reproduce the cross-view attentions results, as reflected by the comparable results with our pretrained DVSM.

    C.2 In-the-wild generalization at 16 input views

    We complement the 64-view in-the-wild evaluation in main paper Tab. 3 with a 16-view counterpart in Tab. 10, covering the same three out-of-domain datasets (MipNeRF360 [3], Free [66], Hike [39]) at both 960p and 512-pixel longer-side settings. The trends mirror our in-domain DL3DV results: TTB closely matches DVSM [58] quality across all three datasets while consistently surpassing LaCT [77] and LVSM [25], and outperforms LagerNVS [61] by a clear margin under the 512-pixel setting. Efficiency-wise, TTB retains its constant-FPS rendering at 16 views just as at 64 views, confirming that the rendering speedup is independent of context view count. These results indicate that TTB’s quality and speed advantages generalize beyond the dense-view regime to fewer-view, out-of-domain scenarios.

    C.3 Inference at scale on DL3DV.

    A single fast-weight MLP per TTB layer has fixed capacity, which becomes a bottleneck as the number of context views V grows. Tab. 11 compares this single-MLP baseline against our local-duplicate variant, which maintains K local copies of the per-layer fast-weight state, each updated only by views routed to its spatially-local group via k-means over per-view camera features (results reported with our ablation model at 720p). Up to V=32, the two variants are indistinguishable and both match DVSM [58]. Beyond V=64, the single-MLP variant saturates and plateaus around 25.8 PSNR, while the local-duplicate variant continues to scale and reaches 27.74 at V=256, on par with DVSM’s 27.56. Throughout, rendering FPS stays in the 67 to 72 range, in stark contrast to DVSM’s drop from 63.6 at V=16 to 12.6 at V=256. Local duplication thus resolves the capacity ceiling of a single fast-weight MLP without compromising the constant-complexity rendering that motivates TTB.

    C.4 Capacity scaling

    Tab. 12 studies the two knobs that set the capacity of the baked state. Sweeping K jointly with V shows that the best K is always V/16, so local duplication is governed by a single scene-independent budget of B=16 views per copy rather than a per-scene heuristic; we use this budget for all Ours (duplicate) entries in Tab. 1, and the K=1 column and the K=V/16 diagonal reproduce the two TTB rows of Tab. 11. Widening the fast-weight MLP closes the gap as well and reaches DVSM at 16× width, indicating that the remaining gap is a capacity limit rather than a limitation of baking. Since width enlarges the model and requires retraining, we keep the 4× width and scale capacity through K.

    C.5 Effect of pretraining.

    Tab. 13 compares three frameworks trained from scratch versus initialized from a DVSM [58] checkpoint (results reported with our ablation model at 720p). The PSNR gain from pretraining grows monotonically with cross-view attention preservation: smallest for TTT (no cross-view attention), larger for TTB– (linear target), and largest for our full TTB (cross-view attention target), confirming that preserving cross-view attention is key to re-using decoder-only pretrained weights. Notably, TTB from scratch already surpasses pretrained TTT, indicating that its advantage is structural.

    C.6 Efficiency analysis

    We provide a detailed efficiency comparison in Tab. 14, reporting parameter counts, per-scene reconstruction time, per-view rendering FPS, and peak GPU memory at both inference and training time. All numbers are measured at 544×960 resolution with V=32 input views.

    End-to-end time.

    Since TTB shifts computation from rendering to reconstruction, Tab. 15 reports the total time to reconstruct a scene and render N novel views. TTB overtakes DVSM after only 5–7 views at every V, a threshold that any interactive viewer or trajectory rendering exceeds, while TTB– leads from the first view at the quality cost reported in Tab. 1.

    C.7 Scene representation size
