    To pick a random light position for a given pixel px, we use different strategies depending on the characteristics of the scene. For smaller scenes, we uniformly pick among our recorded path segments for that pixel, and then choose a random point uniformly on that segment. This implicitly importance samples positions that have higher contribution to the image (e.g., are closer to the camera or strongly reflected by objects), and avoid positions that do not contribute to any pixel in the image (e.g., lights within closed objects). However, some of our tested production scenes are gigantic in scale and only a tiny fraction is directly visible from the camera. In such cases, segment-based sampling can produce suboptimal training candidates, causing the network to allocate capacity to regions where lights are unlikely to be placed during inference. As a practical remedy for such scenes, we instead sample uniformly within the bounding box of all positions visible from the camera. More sophisticated sampling schemes could be explored in future work.

    Loss function

    We use the relative mean squared error loss of Müller et al. [MRNK21] to account for the high dynamic range of the data, assigning equal importance to errors across dark and bright regions:

    L_HDR(Î,I)=1/Nₚₓ∑ₚₓ((Îₚₓ-Iₚₓ)²)/(sg(Îₚₓ)²+ε),

    		(4)

    where Îₚₓ is the predicted value at pixel px, Iₚₓ is the denoised reconstructed value, ε is a small constant (we always set it to 0.01) and sg(·) is a stop-gradient operation.

    5 Evaluation

    We evaluated our system across several academic and production scenes at different sampling rates to measure scalability. All our trainings and experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32 GB VRAM).

    5.1 Path-based Sampling

    Our method trains on path data from a light-agnostic rendering pass from which arbitrary light configurations can be evaluated on-the-fly. This allows the network to see a far greater variety of lighting conditions than any pre-rendered image dataset of comparable size. To validate this advantage, in Figure 5, we compare against an image-based baseline where networks are trained on datasets of rendered images with NEE and multiple importance sampling, using light configurations sampled from the same distribution as our method. We evaluate two settings: (1) a varying number of 1 spp images (64 to 1024), and (2) a constant rendering budget of 1024 total sampled paths per pixel, distributed across different numbers of images (e.g., 32 images at 32 spp, 512 images at 2 spp). Note that our path-based approach uses 64 spp, so the constant-budget setting represents a 16× higher render time.

    We report the PSNR in tonemapped space, averaged across three scenes and evaluated on 500 validation images whose light configurations are sampled from the same distribution used during training. Our method outperforms all image-based configurations by a significant margin. Even with 1024 training images, the image-based baseline remains 2.8 dB below ours. The constant-budget ablation further shows that redistributing a larger rendering budget across fewer, higher-quality images does not close the gap. This confirms that the key advantage of our approach is not the total rendering cost, but the ability to reuse path data across many light configurations during training, providing the network with far richer supervision over the light transport distribution of the scene than a fixed dataset of images can offer.

    5.2 Training & Network Architecture

    Increasing spp for path data.

    We evaluate the effect of samples per pixel (spp) in the training path data. Figure 6 shows prediction quality and the denoised reconstruction from the GatherLight pass across four metrics, averaged over three scenes. Increasing spp improves both reconstruction and prediction quality. Notably, at low spp (32 and 64), the network outperforms the denoised reconstruction. Since the denoiser operates independently per frame, it introduces temporal flickering across light configurations. The network, trained under many lighting conditions, learns a temporally smooth approximation of the scene’s light transport. At higher spp, reconstruction noise diminishes and the denoised reference surpasses the network, whose finite capacity limits its ability to capture all high-frequency detail.

    Component ablation.

    Table 2 reports the effect of three components, which is visualized in an example in the supplemental material: auxiliary features (albedo, normals, depth), denoising the reconstruction targets at training, and a hashgrid encoding for pixel coordinates. Auxiliary features substantially improve all metrics by providing geometric and material information complementary to path throughput weights. The denoiser alone does not yield significant gains, as the network already smooths noise through exposure to many light configurations. The hashgrid encoding alone degrades performance by enabling overfitting to high-frequency noise patterns. However, combining the encoding with denoised targets resolves this: Clean supervision allows the encoding to faithfully capture spatial detail without noise overfitting. The full configuration (Aux. + Enc. + Den.) achieves the best results across all metrics.

    Network size.

    Figure 7shows the effect of network capacity on prediction quality, evaluated on 2k random validation images for both Mitsuba scenes (averaged over three scenes) and a production scene. Increasing the network size consistently improves quality, but with diminishing returns beyond 256 × 8 (8 layers of 256 neurons). Conversely, the bottom of Table 1 shows that inference time keeps growing with network size, even where prediction quality has already plateaued. We therefore adopt 256 × 8 as a good compromise between inference speed, memory footprint, and prediction quality. These conclusions hold across scenes of varying complexity, including those with caustics and volumes.

    5.3 Light Optimization

    We evaluate the differentiability of NRP by optimizing light parameters for sphere lights, i.e., center position ℓᵢ∈ℝ³, radius rᵢ∈ℝ_>0, and color Eᵢ∈ℝ_>0³, to match a target image.

    Optimization formulation.

    For each pixel px, the predicted image is computed as the sum of contributions from N lights:

    Îₚₓ=∑ᵢ₌₁^NEᵢ·ℕₛₚₕₑᵣₑ(px, ℓᵢ, rᵢ),

    		(5)

    where ℕₛₚₕₑᵣₑ is the pre-trained NRP for sphere lights. Here, ℕₛₚₕₑᵣₑ denotes a trained instance of ℕ_type from Equation 2, specialized to sphere lights. The loss is the mean squared error on Reinhard-tonemapped values against the target I^*ₚₓ:

    L=(1)/(|S|)∑_px∈S∥T (Îₚₓ)-T (I^*ₚₓ)∥², where T(I)=I/1+I,

    		(6)

    and S is the set of evaluated pixels (the full image, or a stochastic subset as described in Mini-batch SGD).

    Light parameters are reparameterized to unconstrained space: position and radius via the logit function σ⁻¹(x)=\log(x/(1-x)) mapping from their respective bounded domains [ℓ_\min,ℓ_\max] and [r_\min,r_\max], and color via the inverse softplus \log(eˣ-1) mapping from ℝ_>0. Optimization is performed with Adam in unconstrained space and constrained values are recovered via the sigmoid and softplus functions at each step. For multi-light scenes, gradients are accumulated sequentially per light to bound GPU memory.

    Comparison against baselines.

    In order to evaluate our method in inverse rendering tasks for lighting, we compare it against Mitsuba 3 [JSR∗22], an academic differentiable renderer, and ZeroGrads [FR24], a neural proxy method for black-box renderers. Note that Mitsuba 3 is a general-purpose differentiable renderer with gradients computed from the proper light transport of the scene. This evaluation does not intend to claim a superiority over real physically-based inverse renderers, but just to validate our method as an alternative when these renderers are not available, like in the context of complex production path tracers that drive our problem.

    We perform 50 optimization runs per scene (Cornell Box, Bedroom, and Kitchen) with a single light and randomly sampled initial and target parameters. All methods run for 500 iterations with Adam (lr=0.05). Mitsuba uses a progressive spp schedule, starting at 8 spp for the first 100 iterations, increasing to 16 spp for iterations 100–299, and 32 spp for iterations 300–499, to reduce gradient variance as the optimization converges. ZeroGrads uses a fixed 8 spp throughout, training its neural proxy on-the-fly with a proxy learning rate of 0.001 and batch size 4. For both baselines, we use DrJIT’s @dr.freeze decorator to eliminate JIT recompilation overhead and report only the effective computation time.

    Our method does not require samples per pixel as it uses a pre-trained NRP, whereas Mitsuba 3 requires progressively increasing spp for variance reduction, and ZeroGrads requires additional hyperparameters for proxy learning. In contrast to our method, which operates on a finite set of precached paths, ZeroGrads can be run in a streaming fashion, progressively increasing accuracy at the expense of additional computation. Being non-progressive is a deliberate design choice in our approach that avoids loading bulky production scenes; incorporating progressive streams remains a promising direction for future work. Figure 8 shows convergence plots and error maps for representative optimization runs.

    Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD).

    We ablate the optimization of light parameters with our method under different configurations. Note that due to our decomposition into individual light sources (Equation 3), our method requires evaluating each light individually and the evaluation time therefore scales linearly with the number of light sources. To support scenarios with many lights to some limited extent, we propose to evaluate the loss on a random pixel subset S of size K=⌊α·H·W⌋, drawn uniformly without replacement at each iteration. We ablate pixel fractions α∈{1.0, 0.50, 0.25, 0.05, 0.01, 0.001}, ranging from the full image down to ∼462 pixels per step for a 680×680 resolution, which means a 1000× reduction in per-iteration computation. The stochastic subset provides an unbiased estimate of the full-image gradient, analogous to mini-batch SGD where pixels play the role of data samples. We run this ablation on N∈{1,3,5,20} lights per scene with 5 optimization runs per configuration, and show quantitative results in Table 3. Our ablation shows good robustness of the optimization at small pixel fractions, showing our method can still be performant in (modest) many light scenarios.

    6 Applications

    Differentiable NRPs can be leveraged for many lighting paradigms. We demonstrate three applications enabled by the compact, differentiable nature of NRPs.

    6.1 Interactive relighting

    First, NRP is immediately applicable in relighting applications: Given a lighting configuration, the NRP predicts the contribution of each light source to the final image pixels. As demonstrated in our experiments, the NRP network provides more accurate renderings compared to generative image-based relighting networks (Figure 4). NRPs scale gracefully to production scenes (Figure 3) with complex geometry and radiometry. Our method supports relighting of volumes with spectrally non-varying extinction coefficients, and supports virtual spherical lights and virtual quad lights (Figure 12).

    Second, since the NRP network is compact, unlike most neural methods, separate NRPs for different views can be loaded simultaneously into memory. This is particularly useful in production multi-view setups, where several cameras capture the same scene from different viewpoints. Traditionally, every lighting edit would need to be applied and re-rendered independently for each view. With NRPs, however, each light edit can be applied interactively and consistently across all views simultaneously (see Figure 9). Similar applications for simultaneous lighting editing across entire sequences are thinkable, but have not been explored in this work.

    Third, our approach can be seamlessly combined with compositing workflows; separate NRPs can be trained on separately rendered layers of a scene, allowing us to edit the lighting of individual layers without affecting other layers (Figure 10).

    6.2 Art-directed edits

    The differentiability of NRPs admits their use in optimization-based lighting edits, such as image-space shading target matching (see Figure 8) and art-directed “light scribbling” (see Figure 11, left). In this workflow, artists paint color scribbles directly onto the rendered image to indicate desired lighting changes, and the optimizer adjusts the underlying light parameters to match them. Constraint masks can be applied to preserve existing pixel values in regions the artist does not wish to modify, ensuring that only the targeted areas are affected. This combination of intuitive painting controls and automatic parameter recovery enables rapid iterative workflows, particularly suited for live sessions between lighting supervisors and lighting artists.

    6.3 Optimization with generative targets

    Generative image models can produce compelling lighting variations, but their outputs are not guaranteed to be physically plausible and do not provide the underlying light parameters needed for integration into a production pipeline. By using a generated image as an optimization target, our method recovers a close physically plausible lighting configuration along with its explicit parameters, bridging the gap between generative creativity and physically-based rendering. Figure 11 (right) presents qualitative results demonstrating this capability, utilizing target images generated by Qwen-Image-Edit [WLZ∗25].

    7 Limitations and Future Work

    While our model in principle generalizes to arbitrary types of light sources, their respective parameter counts directly impact the training convergence and accuracy of our neural render proxy. We therefore leave complex light sources, such as textured lights or area lights of arbitrary shapes, as future work.

    Another limitation is that our approach assumes that the light transport between any objects remains constant after rendering. Commonly used tools in the arsenal of lighters, like non-physical light-attenuation between objects or light-exclusivity for certain objects, cannot be changed after the NRP was trained. While per-layer NRPs can be used to somewhat mimic light-exclusivity, it comes at the price of training multiple NRPs.

    Additionally, our training relies on a light-agnostic path sampling strategy. We currently employ material-based sampling, which produces training data with similar throughput weight to the camera. However, this can lead to under-sampling in occluded regions where a user might later wish to place a light source. For instance, in Figure 13, the region inside the lamp shade is under-sampled since no NEE was used during path sample generation, which leads to inaccurate predictions. Investigating different sampling strategies during data generation that deliberately increase the sampling density of locations where a user might add light sources could yield significant improvements in quality.

    Finally, our training pipeline is constrained by the available GPU memory, as all path-sample data is pre-loaded. While this enables on-the-fly generation of denoised training targets, it limits the number of samples and the quality of our training data. Future research could investigate out-of-core training schedules that allow on-demand loading of path data from disk during training, or partitioning of the predicted image.

    8 Conclusion

    Interactive, physically grounded lighting design on production scenes has been limited by the cost of path tracing, trapping artists in a slow cycle of parameter adjustment and re-rendering. The neural render proxy removes this bottleneck: A single light-agnostic rendering pass produces a compact, differentiable model that enables real-time forward relighting with full parametric precision, independent of scene complexity. Its differentiability further unlocks a new mode of creative control that production pipelines have traditionally lacked: Image-space objectives from art direction, paint-overs, or generative models are translated via gradient descent into the lighting parameters that produce them. Production scenes thus become interactively relightable and inversely designable through a single representation, with every edit grounded in a physical, editable, and reusable set of light configurations.

    Acknowledgment

    We thank Violaine Fayolle and Doriano van Essen for the lighting design on the showcased scenes, Charlotte Zhu and Daniel Teece for providing the production scenes, and Karl Li and André Mazzone for their support since the early stages of the project. We are also grateful to Christian Döring for his help with Mitsuba 3 function freezing, and to Yotam Erel for running the relighting comparisons.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 腾讯混元开源 HY-Motion 1.0：用流匹配做 3D 动作生成，直接出 .fbx；还有视频转动作的 FlowHMR 能在 12GB 显卡上跑 ｜ Tencent-Hunyuan/HY-Motion-1.0: Scaling Flow Matching Models for 3D Motion Generation
item.description:
一句话：输出是 .fbx——不是一堆点位，而是能直接进 DCC 与引擎的动作资产。

要点：

  • 核心是一个用**流匹配（flow matching）**扩展出来的 3D 动作生成模型，从文本/提示产出人体动作
  • 落点很实际：产出的是 **`.fbx` 动作序列**，意味着能直接进 DCC 与引擎，而不是停在点云或骨架数组
  • 额外一条线：**FlowHMR** 是建立在 HY-Motion-1.0 之上的 Video2Motion 模型，把人体动作视频转成 3D 动作，能在单张消费级显卡（12GB+，如 RTX 5080）上运行

为什么值得看：「输出 .fbx」这三个字决定了它是资产管线里的工具，而不是论文里的 demo。加上视频转动作能在 12GB 显卡上跑，等于把动捕的门槛从「专用棚」降到「一张消费卡」。

中文摘要：腾讯混元开源了 HY-Motion 1.0，核心是用流匹配（flow matching）方法扩展的 3D 人体动作生成模型。它值得关注的地方在输出形态：生成结果是 `.fbx` 动作序列，可以直接进入 DCC 工具与引擎，而不是停留在骨架数组或点集这种需要二次加工的形式。仓库同时提到 FlowHMR——一个构建在 HY-Motion-1.0 之上的 Video2Motion 模型，能把人体动作视频转换成高质量 3D 动作序列，并且能在单张 12GB 以上显存的消费级显卡上运行。对动作管线来说，这两件事合起来把「文本/视频 → 引擎可用动作」的链路打通了。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：GitHub·Tencent-Hunyuan（English）

中文阅读

HY-Motion 1.0: Scaling Flow Matching Models for 3D Motion Generation

🔥 News

  • Oct 30, 2026: FlowHMR — A Video2Motion (V2M) model built on HY-Motion-1.0 that converts human motion videos into high-quality 3D motion sequences (.fbx) and runs on a single consumer GPU with 12+ GB of VRAM (e.g., RTX 5080).
  • Jan 29, 2026: 📊 We released the evaluation prompts and code for SSAE (Structured Semantic Alignment Evaluation), a VLM-based metric designed to assess the semantic alignment of generated videos. Check the 
    ssae
    directory for usage details!
  • Dec 30, 2025: 🤗 We released the inference code and pretrained models of HY-Motion 1.0. Please give it a try via our HuggingFace Space and our Official Site!

    • Introduction

    HY-Motion 1.0 is a series of text-to-3D human motion generation models based on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and Flow Matching. It allows developers to generate skeleton-based 3D character animations from simple text prompts, which can be directly integrated into various 3D animation pipelines. This model series is the first to scale DiT-based text-to-motion models to the billion-parameter level, achieving significant improvements in instruction-following capabilities and motion quality over existing open-source models.

    Key Features

  • State-of-the-Art Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in both instruction-following capability and generated motion quality.

  • Billion-Scale Models: We are the first to successfully scale DiT-based models to the billion-parameter level for text-to-motion generation. This results in superior instruction understanding and following capabilities, outperforming comparable open-source models.

  • Advanced Three-Stage Training: Our models are trained using a comprehensive three-stage process:

  • Large-Scale Pre-training: Trained on over 3,000 hours of diverse motion data to learn a broad motion prior.

  • High-Quality Fine-tuning: Fine-tuned on 400 hours of curated, high-quality 3D motion data to enhance motion detail and smoothness.

  • Reinforcement Learning: Utilizes Reinforcement Learning from human feedback and reward models to further refine instruction-following and motion naturalness.

    • 🎁 Model Zoo

    HY-Motion 1.0 Series

    ModelDescriptionDateSizeHuggingfaceVRAM (min)
    HY-Motion-1.0Standard Text2Motion Model2025-12-301.0BDownload26GB
    HY-Motion-1.0-LiteLightweight Text2Motion Model2025-12-300.46BDownload24GB

    Note: To reduce GPU VRAM requirements, please use the following settings: 

    --num_seeds=1
    , text prompt with less than 30 words, and motion length less than 5 seconds.
    Note: This table does not includes GPU VRAM requirements for LLM-based prompt engineering feature. If you have sufficient VRAM to run HY-Motion-1.0 model but gradio fails with a VRAM-related error, Run the Gradio application with prompt engineering disabled by setting the environment variable like this: 
    DISABLE_PROMPT_ENGINEERING=True python3 gradio_app.py

    🤗 Get Started with HY-Motion 1.0

    HY-Motion 1.0 supports macOS, Windows, and Linux.

  • Code Usage (CLI)
  • Gradio App

    • 1. Installation

    First, install PyTorch via the official site. Then install the dependencies:

    git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/HY-Motion-1.0.git
cd HY-Motion-1.0/
# Make sure git-lfs is installed
git lfs pull
pip install -r requirements.txt

    2. Download Model Weights

    Please follow the instructions in ckpts/README.md to download the necessary model weights.

    Code Usage (CLI)

    We provide a script for local batch inference, suitable for processing large amounts of prompts.

    # HY-Motion-1.0
python3 local_infer.py --model_path ckpts/tencent/HY-Motion-1.0

# HY-Motion-1.0-Lite
python3 local_infer.py --model_path ckpts/tencent/HY-Motion-1.0-Lite

    Common Parameters:

  • --input_text_dir
    : Directory containing 
    .txt
    or 
    .json
    prompt files.
  • --output_dir
    : Directory to save results (default: 
    output/local_infer
    ).
  • --disable_duration_est
    : Disable LLM-based duration estimation.
  • --disable_rewrite
    : Disable LLM-based prompt rewriting.
  • --prompt_engineering_host
    / 
    --prompt_engineering_model_path
    : (Optional) Host address / local checkpoint for the Duration Prediction & Prompt Rewrite Module.
  • Download: You can download the Duration Prediction & Prompt Rewrite Module from Here.
  • Note: If you do not set these parameter, you must also set 
    --disable_duration_est
    and 
    --disable_rewrite
    . Otherwise, the script will raise an error due to host unavailable.

    • Gradio App

    You can host a Gradio web interface on your local machine for interactive visualization:

    python3 gradio_app.py

    After running the command, open your browser and visit 

    http://localhost:7860

    Prompting Guide & Best Practices

  • Language & Length: Please use English. For optimal results, keep your prompt under 60 words. For other languages, please use the Text2MotionPrompter to rewrite the prompt.

  • Content Focus: Focus on action descriptions or detailed movements of the limbs and torso.

  • Current Limitations (NOT Supported):

  • ❌ Non-humanoid Characters: Animations for animals or non-human creatures.
  • ❌ Subjective/Visual Attributes: Descriptions of complex emotions, clothing, or physical appearance.
  • ❌ Environment & Camera: Descriptions of objects, scenes, or camera angles.
  • ❌ Multi-person Interactions: Motions involving two or more people.
  • ❌ Special Modes: Seamless loop or in-place animations.
  • Example Prompts:
  • A person performs a squat, then pushes a barbell overhead using the power from standing up.
  • A person climbs upward, moving up the slope.
  • A person stands up from the chair, then stretches their arms.
  • A person walks unsteadily, then slowly sits down.

  author={Tencent Hunyuan 3D Digital Human Team},
  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2512.23464},
  year={2025}
}

一句话：输出是 .fbx——不是一堆点位，而是能直接进 DCC 与引擎的动作资产。

要点：

  • 核心是一个用**流匹配（flow matching）**扩展出来的 3D 动作生成模型，从文本/提示产出人体动作
  • 落点很实际：产出的是 **`.fbx` 动作序列**，意味着能直接进 DCC 与引擎，而不是停在点云或骨架数组
  • 额外一条线：**FlowHMR** 是建立在 HY-Motion-1.0 之上的 Video2Motion 模型，把人体动作视频转成 3D 动作，能在单张消费级显卡（12GB+，如 RTX 5080）上运行

为什么值得看：「输出 .fbx」这三个字决定了它是资产管线里的工具，而不是论文里的 demo。加上视频转动作能在 12GB 显卡上跑，等于把动捕的门槛从「专用棚」降到「一张消费卡」。

中文摘要：腾讯混元开源了 HY-Motion 1.0，核心是用流匹配（flow matching）方法扩展的 3D 人体动作生成模型。它值得关注的地方在输出形态：生成结果是 `.fbx` 动作序列，可以直接进入 DCC 工具与引擎，而不是停留在骨架数组或点集这种需要二次加工的形式。仓库同时提到 FlowHMR——一个构建在 HY-Motion-1.0 之上的 Video2Motion 模型，能把人体动作视频转换成高质量 3D 动作序列，并且能在单张 12GB 以上显存的消费级显卡上运行。对动作管线来说，这两件事合起来把「文本/视频 → 引擎可用动作」的链路打通了。

HY-Motion 1.0: Scaling Flow Matching Models for 3D Motion Generation

🔥 News

  • Oct 30, 2026: FlowHMR — A Video2Motion (V2M) model built on HY-Motion-1.0 that converts human motion videos into high-quality 3D motion sequences (.fbx) and runs on a single consumer GPU with 12+ GB of VRAM (e.g., RTX 5080).
  • Jan 29, 2026: 📊 We released the evaluation prompts and code for SSAE (Structured Semantic Alignment Evaluation), a VLM-based metric designed to assess the semantic alignment of generated videos. Check the 
    ssae
    directory for usage details!
  • Dec 30, 2025: 🤗 We released the inference code and pretrained models of HY-Motion 1.0. Please give it a try via our HuggingFace Space and our Official Site!

    • Introduction

    HY-Motion 1.0 is a series of text-to-3D human motion generation models based on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and Flow Matching. It allows developers to generate skeleton-based 3D character animations from simple text prompts, which can be directly integrated into various 3D animation pipelines. This model series is the first to scale DiT-based text-to-motion models to the billion-parameter level, achieving significant improvements in instruction-following capabilities and motion quality over existing open-source models.

    Key Features

  • State-of-the-Art Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in both instruction-following capability and generated motion quality.

  • Billion-Scale Models: We are the first to successfully scale DiT-based models to the billion-parameter level for text-to-motion generation. This results in superior instruction understanding and following capabilities, outperforming comparable open-source models.

  • Advanced Three-Stage Training: Our models are trained using a comprehensive three-stage process:

  • Large-Scale Pre-training: Trained on over 3,000 hours of diverse motion data to learn a broad motion prior.

  • High-Quality Fine-tuning: Fine-tuned on 400 hours of curated, high-quality 3D motion data to enhance motion detail and smoothness.

  • Reinforcement Learning: Utilizes Reinforcement Learning from human feedback and reward models to further refine instruction-following and motion naturalness.

item.title: 厚的介质重建要算多次散射的导数：用神经算子预测散射场，再对它做微分，省掉可微路径追踪的噪声采样 ｜ Learning the Missing Derivative: Neural Multiple-Scattering Operators for Inverse Volume Rendering
item.description:
一句话：冻结光源的层析丢掉了「灭绝对散射的导数」，而可微路径追踪又贵又噪。

要点：

  • 物理前提：要从照片重建光学厚介质，必须建模**多次散射**以及它对消光系数变化的响应
  • 两条现成路线都不理想：冻结光源的层析（frozen-source tomography）把这一项导数直接丢掉；可微路径追踪则用昂贵且带噪的采样去估它
  • 这篇改用神经算子预测多次散射场，并在逆渲染过程中对它求导，透射率另行计算

为什么值得看：体积介质的逆渲染一直卡在「要么不准要么太贵」。把散射场交给神经算子、并把导数穿过它，相当于用学习到的代理替换掉采样估计——这是「神经算子进渲染管线」的具体形态。

中文摘要：要从照片重建光学厚介质（烟、云、参与介质），必须建模多次散射，以及它对消光系数变化的响应。现有两条路线都不理想：冻结光源的层析方法直接丢弃了这一项导数；可微路径追踪则用昂贵且高噪声的采样去估计它。这篇改用神经算子来预测多次散射场，并在逆渲染过程中直接对该场求导，而透射率另行计算。这样就把「靠采样估导数」换成了「对一个学到的算子求导」，是神经算子真正落进体积渲染管线的一种形态。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Learning the Missing Derivative: Neural Multiple-Scattering Operators for Inverse Volume Rendering

Abstract

Reconstructing optically thick media from photographs requires modeling multiple scattering and its response to changes in extinction. Frozen-source tomography discards this derivative; differentiable path tracing estimates it through expensive, noisy sampling. We instead predict the multiple-scattering field with a neural operator and differentiate through it during inverse rendering, while computing transmittance and single scattering directly. A further challenge arises during optimization: an operator that predicts the field accurately on held-out media can still produce poor derivatives at the density states visited by the optimizer. We address this by fine-tuning on states generated during inversions driven by the operator, using Monte Carlo scattering-field supervision. On held-out optically thick clouds, our method improves relighting over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing given substantially more time. Training on inversion trajectories also improves derivative alignment at visited states and reduces optimization drift.

1 Introduction

“Light travels in a straight line.” This simple principle has shaped modern 3D reconstruction. NeRF [36] and 3D Gaussian Splatting [20] reconstruct scenes by accumulating contributions along camera rays, typically without explicitly modeling multiple scattering. But in optically thick media such as clouds and smoke, light changes direction repeatedly before reaching the camera. A pixel can therefore depend on light scattered far outside its camera ray.

A reconstruction may fit the input views yet contain errors in its interior extinction that only become visible under new lighting. To reconstruct these media from photographs and relight them under new illumination, we must account for multiple scattering. For gradient-based inverse rendering, we must also differentiate this transport with respect to the medium’s density.

Computing this derivative is a central bottleneck. In optically thick media, the multiple-scattering response to density changes can be substantially larger than the camera-side response. Differentiable path tracing estimates the full gradient through sampled light paths [48, 38], but the computation is expensive and subject to Monte Carlo noise [38, 25, 39]. Frozen-source tomography takes a cheaper approach [27]: it periodically updates the scattered-light field but treats it as constant when optimizing density (Fig.2). This approximation omits the nonlocal multiple-scattering derivative, potentially producing incorrect interior density even when the observed images are well matched. Such errors become apparent when the reconstructed medium is rendered under new lighting (Fig.1). Can we obtain an accurate multiple-scattering derivative without repeatedly performing expensive Monte Carlo differentiation?

Our approach predicts the multiple-scattering source with a neural operator and differentiates through that prediction during inversion. The resulting derivative captures how the scattered-light field responds to changes in density. Transmittance and single scattering remain physically computed; the neural operator supplies the expensive light-side response (Fig.3).

Accurate field prediction does not guarantee accurate derivatives, especially inside an inversion loop. Each approximate gradient determines the next density state, which in turn becomes the next input to the operator. As optimization proceeds, these states may depart from the training distribution, allowing derivative errors to accumulate and redirect subsequent updates. The operator must therefore remain accurate along the trajectory its own gradients induce.

To address this problem, we train the operator on the states visited by inversions that use the operator itself. Starting from a pretrained operator, we collect intermediate density states generated during inversion, obtain Monte Carlo supervision for their scattering fields, and fine-tune the operator on these states. This improves derivative accuracy on visited states and reduces optimization drift.

On 12 held-out optically thick clouds, our method improves relighting over frozen-source tomography on every medium, with a median gain of 6.8 dB after two minutes. It also outperforms differentiable path tracing after thirty minutes (Sec.4.2), while training on inversion-visited states substantially improves optimization stability (Sec.4.4).

Our contributions are twofold:

  • •

    Learning the missing derivative. We introduce a neural multiple-scattering operator that supplies the otherwise expensive light-side derivative through automatic differentiation, enabling efficient gradient-based inverse volume rendering.

  • •

    Learning the operator for inversion. We identify the limitations of conventional operator accuracy for inverse rendering and introduce training on inversion-visited states to improve derivative reliability and optimization stability.

    • 2 Related Work

    Differentiable volume rendering and cloud tomography.

    Inverse rendering of participating media requires differentiating volumetric light transport. Monte Carlo methods, including adjoint transport and path replay backpropagation (PRB), estimate the full gradient by tracing light paths [14, 48]. Variance reduction and path reuse reduce the cost [38, 10], but reconstructing dense scattering volumes remains expensive.

    Early cloud tomography methods reconstruct cloud extinction using an SHDOM forward model while holding the in-scattered source fixed during differentiation [27]. This frozen-source approximation has since been used with both deterministic and Monte Carlo transport models [28, 15]. Later methods also differentiate single scattering or full light paths [29, 33], and learned inverses map images to extinction directly [46, 43, 44]. Yet freezing the scattered source removes its nonlocal response to density changes, which dominates the camera-side response in optically thick media. We learn this missing response instead of repeatedly sampling it or discarding it.

    Neural multiple scattering and neural operators.

    Neural networks have been used to predict in-scattered radiance for cloud rendering, including models that generalize to unseen media [19, 16]. Other approaches, such as NRPM, photon field networks, and radiance caches, fit or store light transport for individual scenes [50, 4, 37].

    Neural operators [30] have been trained to predict fluence and radiance fields, including from noisy Monte Carlo labels [6, 7]. A related approach in photoacoustic tomography uses a pretrained neural operator to predict light fluence, but holds that field fixed when updating absorption [32]. Our method instead differentiates the predicted multiple-scattering field with respect to extinction and uses its Jacobian directly in inverse rendering. The learned field is not merely a faster forward model; its derivative drives the reconstruction.

    Learned surrogates for inverse optimization.

    A surrogate used inside an optimizer influences the states at which it will be evaluated next. Model-management methods correct surrogate values and gradients during optimization [3], while solver-in-the-loop and rollout-based training expose learned models to states produced by their own predictions [47, 5]. Adaptive and derivative-informed neural operators further improve surrogate accuracy where it matters for optimization [13, 41]. Neural operators can also be trained directly on optimization trajectories using supervision on the objective gradient [8].

    We take an operator-in-the-loop approach to inverse volume rendering: the operator supplies the multiple-scattering derivative while the camera-side and direct-light terms remain physically computed. Following the idea of DAgger [45], we collect the density states visited by inversions driven by the operator and fine-tune it using Monte Carlo scattering-field labels.

    3 Method

    We reconstruct a heterogeneous participating medium from photographs taken under known directional illumination, with the goal of relighting it from novel views and light directions.

    3.1 Image Formation and Gradient Decomposition

    The unknown is the extinction field σₜ(x) in the unit cube, represented on a voxel grid. The albedo α and Henyey–Greenstein phase-function parameter g are known, and the scattering coefficient is σₛ=ασₜ. For light propagating along ωₗ, the direct-beam transmittance at x is Tₗ(x)=e^-τₗ(x), where τₗ(x)=∫₀^∞σₜ(x-sωₗ) ds. A camera ray xₜ=o+td observes

    I=∫₀^∞T_cam(t) σₛ(xₜ)[Tₗ(xₜ) p_g(ωₗ · ωₒ)+S(xₜ,ωₒ)] dt,

    		(1)

    where ωₒ=-d, p_g is the phase function, and T_cam is transmittance along the camera ray. The first term in brackets accounts for light scattered once toward the camera. The source S collects light that has already scattered and is scattered again toward ωₒ; its dependence on extinction requires solving multiple-scattering transport. Its angular integral is given in the supplement. In contrast, transmittance and single scattering are computed by deterministic ray marching.

    We optimize the log-extinction parameters θ, with σₜ=\min(e^θ,2000). Let I(θ)∈ℝ^P contain the rendered values of P rays and r=I-y their residuals. The image Jacobian splits according to the three ways in which extinction enters Eq.1:

    J=(∂I)/(∂θ)=J_cam+J_direct+Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ.

    		(2)

    J_cam differentiates the local scattering coefficient and camera transmittance while holding the bracket of Eq.1 fixed; J_direct accounts for the effect of extinction on the incoming direct beam; and Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ describes how a density change redistributes the multiple-scattering field. Frozen-source tomography keeps only J_cam, whereas differentiable path tracing estimates the full gradient J^⊤r by Monte Carlo. Our method retains J_cam and J_direct and learns the expensive Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ term.

    3.2 Neural Multiple-Scattering Operator

    Operator and representation.

    We learn the multiple-scattering source rather than the rendered image. A neural operator G_φ takes the medium and illumination as input and predicts angular coefficients of the source field throughout the volume. A single predicted field is shared across all camera rays and views; only its evaluation direction changes. The input includes extinction, albedo, light transmittance, and analytic single- and forward-scattering features. The backbone is a 3D U-Net [9], conditioned on the phase-function parameter g and light direction ωₗ through FiLM [42].

    We represent the angular dependence using a basis B containing real spherical harmonics (SH) through degree 4 (25 functions) and 12 additional light-aligned zonal harmonics of degrees 5–16. Under Henyey–Greenstein scattering, harmonics of degree ℓ have eigenvalue g^ℓ (Funk–Hecke, as in MRBNN [31]), so the source is reconstructed from angular moments c_b of the radiance that has scattered at least once:

    S(x,ω)=∑_b∈Bg^ℓ(b) c_b(x) b(ω).

    		(3)

    Here ℓ(b) denotes the degree of basis function b. The zonal terms resolve the forward-scattering lobe without the 264 additional coefficients required by full SH through degree 16. The network predicts a light-aligned zonal component and a world-frame SH residual, which are mapped to the coefficients in Eq.3; the exact basis and mapping are in the supplement.

    Learning and differentiating the field.

    The generic operator is trained on 1.2×10⁵ procedural media, covering optical depths 1–100, albedos 0.8–0.999, g∈[0,0.9], and varying light directions. Monte Carlo transport supplies noisy field labels. We write S_φ(σₜ,τₗ) for the predicted source, with the other physical parameters understood. Since τₗ itself depends on σₜ, automatic differentiation through the light sweep, operator, and camera ray marcher supplies J_multi,φ^⊤r without explicitly forming a Jacobian. The transmittance and single-scattering derivatives remain physically computed. Figure4 compares the resulting directional derivative with Monte Carlo in accuracy and online cost.

    3.3 Differentiable Inverse Rendering

    We reconstruct extinction at 64³ resolution, with known albedo, phase function, light, and cameras. At each iteration, we sample training-view rays ℝ and minimize their squared image residuals, L=|ℝ|⁻¹∑_p∈ℝ(Iₚ-yₚ)². The light sweep gives τₗ and Tₗ; the operator predicts S_φ; and ray marching evaluates Eq.1. We use the corrected forward source S=S_φ(σₜ,τₗ)+Δ, where Δ is held constant during differentiation. The resulting update uses

    ∇_θL=(2)/(|ℝ|)(J_cam+J_direct+J_multi,φ)^⊤r,

    		(4)

    with r restricted here to the sampled rays. Adam updates θ using this gradient.

    Monte Carlo correction.

    Every 30 iterations, a new Monte Carlo estimate S_MC updates Δ by an exponential moving average with weight β=0.25 of the stop-gradient difference S_MC-S_φ. This anchors the forward values without replacing the operator’s learned Jacobian. The correction is initialized from the current Monte Carlo–operator difference at the first refresh and after each coarse-to-fine resolution change; otherwise it uses the moving average. It can lag as density changes, making operator accuracy along the trajectory important.

    Gradient baselines and output.

    Frozen Source uses periodically refreshed Monte Carlo source fields but holds the entire light-side term fixed during differentiation, retaining only J_cam. Detached Operator uses the same anchored source values as ours but likewise retains only J_cam; our method additionally differentiates the direct beam and the operator-predicted multiple scattering. Every 25 iterations we evaluate four held-out views and retain the best checkpoint. The inversion uses a coarse-to-fine warm start and runs at approximately 17 iterations per second at 64³. The full procedure and baseline protocols are in the supplement and Sec.4.1.

    3.4 Learning the Operator for Inversion

    The operator must predict useful derivatives at the density states encountered during reconstruction, not just at media drawn from its training distribution. Inversion can create transient, speckled, or sharply peaked density fields; derivative errors on these states redirect subsequent updates, which in turn change the states seen by the operator. We therefore train on the distribution induced by inversion itself (Fig.3b).

    Training has three stages. Generic pretraining covers a broad range of media and illumination (Sec.3.2). Scope fine-tuning specializes the operator to strongly scattering media using 4000 procedural and Cloudy [26] training volumes (optical depths 30–120, albedos 0.99–0.9999, and g∈[0.6,0.9]), mixed equally with generic data. Trajectory fine-tuning uses the scope operator to reconstruct separate training media, collects the density states visited during these inversions, labels their scattering fields with Monte Carlo, and fine-tunes on these states together with the earlier data. This follows the data-aggregation principle of DAgger [45].

    The new labels supervise scattering-field values, not Jacobians. Sampling states along an inversion trajectory also constrains the predicted field’s changes along the displacements that the optimizer actually makes. The resulting improvements in derivative alignment and optimization stability are measured in Sec.4.4. Each fine-tuning stage uses 4×10⁴ training steps; equal-steps controls isolate the effect of the added data from additional training time. Implementation and data-collection details are in the supplement; the reconstruction loop is summarized in Algorithm1.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Data and task.

    We evaluate on held-out, optically thick clouds with maximum column optical depth 40–100, albedo 0.99–0.999, and g∈[0.7,0.9]. Half are procedural cumulus and half come from Cloudy [26]; none are used for training or development. Our main evaluation contains 12 media rendered by Mitsuba 3 [17] at 128³ resolution, while all methods reconstruct extinction at 64³. The observations therefore differ from every method’s reconstruction model. The protocol and success criteria were fixed before generating these test media (supplement). A separate 12-medium controlled set, rendered at 64³ by our path tracer, supports comparisons and ablations; the supplement also reports a broader optical-depth study.

    Each medium is observed in 32 views of 128² pixels under one directional light. We evaluate reconstruction quality by rendering three novel light directions from two unseen views. Our primary metric is relighting PSNR against reference images, corrected for the Monte Carlo noise in both images (supplement). We also report voxel-wise extinction error and projected-optical-depth error.

    Baselines and timing.

    Frozen Source [27] uses periodically refreshed Monte Carlo source fields [15] but retains only the camera-side derivative. The Detached Operator uses our corrected operator source with the same detached derivative, isolating the contribution of differentiating through the operator. PRB [48] estimates the full gradient in Mitsuba 3. All methods use the same density parameterization, optimizer, 10-s warm start, and visual hull. We select the best checkpoint using four held-out views, except that PRB returns its current iterate. Frozen Source and PRB use the best of their evaluated configurations for each medium and budget, including two smoothness priors; ours and the Detached Operator use one fixed configuration. PRB uses no Russian roulette on the main evaluation and Mitsuba’s default roulette on the controlled set; budget-specific tuning is detailed in the supplement.

    We compare equal wall-clock budgets of 30 s and 2, 8, and 16 min on one NVIDIA B200, including warm start and checkpoint selection. PRB is additionally run to 30 min. After 2 min, Frozen Source performs 1.7–1.8 times as many iterations as ours, while PRB completes 0.15–0.23 times as many. Unless stated otherwise, we report medians across media and bootstrap 95% intervals for median paired differences.

    4.2 Reconstruction and Relighting

    Relighting under new illumination.

    Differentiating through the learned multiple-scattering source improves relighting on every main-evaluation medium at every tested budget (Tab.1). After 2 min, ours reaches a median of 42.5 dB, compared with 35.1 dB for Frozen Source, 32.8 dB for the Detached Operator, and 28.4 dB for PRB. The median paired gain over Frozen Source is 6.8 dB [5.5, 10.7] (12/12 media), and remains 4.0 dB after 16 min. PRB reaches 33.4 dB after 30 min; ours after 2 min still leads on all 12 media, by a median paired 9.0 dB [8.1, 9.9]. The controlled set gives the same result with the scope-trained operator: at 2 min ours gains 6.6 dB over Frozen Source, and it exceeds PRB after 30 min by 12.0 dB with roulette (10.7 dB without roulette, post hoc), each on all 12 media.

    The relighting examples in Figs.1 and 5 expose the weakness of camera-side gradients. Camera-side gradients can fit the observed images while placing extinction incorrectly inside the cloud; the error is revealed by a new light. With the learned light-side derivative, the reconstruction retains the structure needed for relighting.

    Recovered extinction.

    The density slices show corresponding reconstruction errors (Fig.6). Without the multiple-scattering derivative, extinction tends toward smooth interior ramps; PRB’s noisy updates produce speckled density, whereas ours recovers more of the underlying clumps. The gap is larger in projected optical depth: after 2 min its median relative error is 0.20 for ours, versus 0.42–0.68 for the two Frozen Source priors, 0.53 for the Detached Operator, and 0.31–0.36 for PRB after 30 min (Fig.S4). The voxel-wise extinction errors are closer (ours 0.55; other methods 0.55–1.29). Ours has the lowest voxel-wise error on 6 of 12 main-evaluation media among the shown methods; PRB is lower on five Cloudy media and Frozen Source on one.

    4.3 The Contribution of the Learned Derivative

    An accurate nonlocal response at low cost.

    On the held-out cloud of Fig.1, the predicted multiple-scattering source differs from Monte Carlo by 2.9% (σₛ-weighted relative field error; Tab.S3). Along a localized density increase, its directional derivative agrees with the Monte Carlo central-difference reference (cosine 0.99, relative error 0.16); Fig.4 shows the response extending well beyond the perturbed region. Outside two standard deviations of the perturbation, 31% of the angular-mean response’s squared norm lies, with cosine 0.99. Evaluating this directional derivative takes 77 ms for the operator versus 23 min for Monte Carlo at comparable reference-relative error. Across the 12 main-evaluation media, source-field errors are 2.2–4.9% and derivative cosines 0.95–0.99 (post hoc; supplement). In rendered-image responses, the frozen-source derivative captures only 0.1–18.1% of the true change’s norm (median 1.2%), while ours preserves its direction (cosine 0.91–0.99; Tab.S3).

    The multiple-scattering term dominates.

    For four density perturbations on development clouds, ∥Jₘᵤₗₜᵢv∥ is 2.9–4.8 times ∥J_camv∥, while ∥J_directv∥ is only 0.24–0.34 times ∥J_camv∥ (the decomposition uses the generic operator; supplement). The direct-light response opposes the multiple-scattering response: upstream extinction blocks the direct beam but also redirects scattered light. As optical depth increases from 5 to 60, the frozen-source gradient’s cosine with the full gradient drops from 0.95 to 0.58.

    The derivative, not just the field values.

    The Detached Operator shares our corrected source values but omits both J_direct and J_multi,φ. It trails ours by 10.2 dB after 2 min on the main evaluation (12/12 media; Tab.1). On the controlled set, detached operator values perform almost identically to the Monte Carlo values used by Frozen Source (median difference -0.03 dB at 2 min, post hoc), while enabling the learned derivative improves relighting by 7.1 dB. Replacing the learned operator with a classical P1 diffusion model under the same correction yields 26–36 dB on eight development media, 13.8 dB below our operator and below Frozen Source after 2 and 8 min.

    4.4 Learning on Inversion Trajectories

    Accuracy where the optimizer goes.

    The operators in Tab.2 have generic-media field errors within 7% of each other, yet their behavior inside inversion differs sharply. The trajectory operator and the equal-steps scope+ control have nearly identical generic errors (0.0216 and 0.0214), but the trajectory operator has lower error on held-back inversion states (0.0446 versus 0.0597). On drifted states, its derivative along the next optimization step aligns much better with Monte Carlo (cosine 0.51 versus 0.13–0.15 for the other measured operators; Fig.S3). The visited-state data, rather than more training steps alone, account for this improvement.

    Less drift, better final iterates.

    Trajectory training also reduces final-iterate drift. After 16 min, its current-iterate density error on the main evaluation is lower than that of scope and scope+ on all 12 media (median per-medium error ratios 0.28 and 0.41). Without held-out checkpoint selection, the scope and scope+ operators diverge on 11 of 12 media, versus 4 of 12 for trajectory. Figure7 shows one such case: the scope operator accumulates density spikes, while trajectory training preserves a more faithful reconstruction.

    At the final iterate, without selection, the trajectory operator’s median paired gain over scope is 4.5 dB after 8 min (11/12 media) and 8.7 dB after 16 min (12/12), and over scope+ 5.0 and 8.0 dB. With held-out checkpoint selection, the improvement is smaller: 0.70 dB averaged over main-evaluation media and budgets (t-interval [0.26, 1.14]; controlled set: 0.44 dB). Trajectory training primarily stabilizes inversion, while checkpoint selection remains useful for the residual drift.

    4.5 Ablations

    The multiple-scattering derivative carries the improvement. On the controlled set, removing J_direct changes relighting by only 0.1–0.3 dB in favor of the variant without it, with every interval including zero. Dropping J_multi,φ as well, as in the Detached Operator, reduces relighting by 7.1 dB after 2 min (Tab.S15). Removing the Monte Carlo correction costs 0.8–0.9 dB from 2 min onward, though it gains 0.5 dB at 30 s because no correction refresh is needed.

    Dependence on optical thickness.

    The benefit is strongest when multiple scattering dominates. On moderate development media (τ=7.6–24), ours with the scope operator and Frozen Source are tied after 2 min (median -0.01 dB). Within the controlled set, the 2-min median gain is 7.8 dB on eight media with τ≥50, versus 1.5 dB on the other four (τ<50; post hoc). This agrees with the increasingly poor frozen-source gradient alignment at larger optical depths (supplement, Sec. E.3).

    Architecture and zonal-basis ablations are reported in the supplement.

    5 Conclusion and Future Directions

    A neural operator can supply the costly multiple-scattering derivative needed for inverse volume rendering. Differentiating its predicted scattering field avoids repeated Monte Carlo gradient estimation while retaining the nonlocal response omitted by frozen-source tomography. Training the operator on inversion-visited states further improves the reliability of its derivatives and substantially reduces optimization drift. On held-out thick clouds, these choices improve reconstruction and relighting within short compute budgets.

    Future work includes smoke, joint recovery of illumination and material parameters, and reconstruction from captured images. Differentiating learned physical fields may also benefit inverse problems with costly gradients.
