    Supplementary Material

    Citations, numbered sections, and figures, tables and equations without the prefix S refer to the main paper. Operators are named by their training data (generic, scope, trajectory; generic+ and scope+ are the equal-steps controls of Sec.3.4), and methods as in the main paper.

    Appendix A Method Details

    A.1 Renderer and Angular Representation

    Ray marching.

    Grids hold values at the voxel centres of the unit cube and are interpolated trilinearly, constant between the outermost centres and the faces and zero outside the cube; the ray marcher, the Monte Carlo kernels and Mitsuba 3 use the same convention. A camera ray is marched from its entry into the cube with a fixed step h=1/(2N), two samples per voxel at N=64; σₜ, τₗ and S are read at the step midpoints and held constant over the step, so step j contributes Tⱼ (1-e^-σₜh) α Qⱼ, with Tⱼ the transmittance to the start of the step and Qⱼ=Tₗ p_g(ωₗ · ωₒ)+S: Eq.1 integrated exactly for piecewise-constant coefficients. The optical depth to the light is computed at the voxel centres by marching towards the light with the same step; camera samples interpolate τₗ and exponentiate, since interpolating Tₗ biases single scattering by +0.1 to +0.8%. For full multiple scattering our path tracer agrees with pbrt-v3 (mean ratio 0.9971–1.0000 at g=0, 0.5 and 0.85) and with Mitsuba 3.9.1 to within Mitsuba’s own seed-to-seed noise.

    Angular basis.

    The source of Eq.1, S(x,ω)=∫_S²p_g(ω · ω^′) L^(≥1)(x,ω^′) dω^′ with L^(≥1) the radiance that has scattered at least once, is evaluated from 37 nodal coefficient grids: real SH to degree 4 (orthonormal, without the Condon–Shortley phase) and the zonal harmonics of degrees 5–16 about ωₗ, with the factors g^ℓ applied. Multiple-scattering images of a development cumulus (τ=20, albedo 0.99, g=0.85) rendered from tallied moments under a top, a front and a back light reach 32.7, 15.6 and 35.9 dB with SH to degree 4 alone and 36.7, 33.1 and 41.3 dB with the zonal extension, the noise floor of the 4096-spp references (34.3, 31.5 and 38.3 dB between two independent references): the forward cascade of a front light is what truncated SH miss. At g=0.9, front-lit, zonal degrees to 16 give 19.6–23.4 dB and to 32 give 31.2–33.5 dB, so more strongly forward-scattering media would need a higher zonal degree. At the true density of five development media, this forward model relights under the evaluation lights at 41.9–51.1 dB (single scattering alone: 16.2–25.9 dB).

    Cell averages and nodal values.

    Monte Carlo tallies cell averages, whereas rendering interpolates nodal values. The operator therefore predicts nodal values ĉ and is trained through their cell averages Mĉ, M=M^⊗3, so noisy labels are never deconvolved; per axis M has interior rows (1/8,3/4,1/8) and boundary rows (7/8,1/8). Monte Carlo fields entering the inversion are converted with M⁻¹; rendering tallied cell averages as nodal values instead would bias multiple scattering by -0.6 to -1.1%.

    A.2 Operator

    Inputs and network.

    The 14 input channels per voxel are \log(1+σₜ/10), -\log(1-α)/5, Tₗ, the first-order forward-lobe amplitude Tₗτₛ with τₛ(x)=∫₀^∞σₛ(x-sωₗ) ds, \log(1+σₛTₗ/10) and, for ℓ∈{0,1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16}, the zonal moments of the scattered radiance in the small-angle approximation,

    z^fwd_ℓ=√\tfrac2ℓ+14π Tₗ (e^τₛg^ℓ-1),

    		(S1)

    which reuse the sweep’s τₗ inside the inversion (τₛ=ατₗ for a constant albedo). (g,ωₗ) passes through a two-layer MLP to a 128-dimensional embedding. The 3D U-Net has pre-activation residual blocks (GroupNorm, SiLU, 3³ convolutions), two per level at widths 32, 64, 128 and 256 and two at the bottleneck, strided downsampling and transposed-convolution upsampling with concatenated skips; FiLM, x↦x(1+γ)+β with zero-initialised (γ,β), follows the first convolution of every block. The head outputs 42 channels, z₀,…,z₁₆ and the 25 residuals u_ℓm, which are multiplied by g^ℓ and mapped to the 37 coefficients of B by

    c_Y_ℓm=√\tfrac4π2ℓ+1 Y_ℓm(ωₗ) z_ℓ+u_ℓm, c_Z_ℓ=z_ℓ;

    		(S2)

    the network has 19.4 M parameters, and the network alone takes about 13 ms per forward pass at 64³ in bfloat16.

    Generic training.

    Procedural 64³ media (cumulus 40%, fBm 25%, plume 25%, blob 10%; maximum column optical depth log-uniform in [1,100], 1-α log-uniform in [0.001,0.2], spatially varying in 25% of the media, g uniform in [0,0.9], light uniform on the sphere) are generated on line: at every step one new medium is tallied with 2×10⁶ photons and replaces the oldest of a buffer of 1024, from which batches of 4 are drawn. The loss is the relative squared error of Mĉ against the tallied cell averages on the medium dilated by one voxel. AdamW [34] runs at learning rate 10⁻³ after 500 warm-up steps with cosine decay over 1.2×10⁵ steps, weight decay 10⁻⁴, gradient clipping at 1 and bfloat16 mixed precision; the selected checkpoint, the last, has a field error of 0.0228 on 200 validation media (geometric mean of the relative L₂ error). Training took 5.3 h on one NVIDIA B200. TableS1 changes one design choice at a time.

    Forward accuracy on held-out media.

    On 300 held-out procedural and Cloudy media (the forward test of the regime set), images rendered with the operator’s field are 15.9 dB more accurate in the median than with a Monte Carlo field computed in the same time (6×10⁵ photons; better on 100%) and 1.2 dB more accurate than with one computed in about 32 times the time (2×10⁷ photons; better on 66%), against a 2×10⁸-photon reference. Outside the training distribution, on 100 media from The Well [40] (MHD and supernova), it stays ahead of the 6×10⁵-photon field (by 9.6 and 12.2 dB; there it took 1.6–3.2 times the operator’s time) but behind the 2×10⁷-photon one (-5.1 and -2.7 dB).

    A.3 Learning the Operator for Inversion

    The training and inversion procedures are summarized in Algorithm1 in the main paper; implementation schedules and data selection are specified below.

    Scope data.

    4000 training and 100 validation media in which multiple scattering dominates: maximum column optical depth log-uniform in [30,120], albedo in [0.99,0.9999] (1-α log-uniform, spatially varying in 25% of the media), g uniform in [0.6,0.9], light direction uniform; procedural cumulus 35%, fBm 15%, plume 10%, blob 5% and Cloudy training clouds 35%. Labels: 2×10⁷ photons per training medium, 2×10⁸ per validation medium.

    Trajectory data.

    A separate set of 64 training-side media is reconstructed by inversions with the scope operator in the loop (18000 iterations, coarse to fine at 300 and 900 iterations, observations at 1024 samples per pixel, so that the trajectories also visit noise-driven states); the density is stored every 750 iterations. Every stored state with density error at most 3 is labelled by Monte Carlo (2×10⁷ photons): 896 states of 56 training media (448 further, fully diverged states are skipped); the remaining 8 media give 95 held-back states, labelled with 10⁸ photons, on which the operators are compared.

    Fine-tuning.

    Every fine-tuning stage starts from the previous operator and runs 4×10⁴ steps (batch 4, AdamW, learning rate 3×10⁻⁴ after 500 warm-up steps, weight decay 10⁻⁴, gradient clipping at 1, mixed precision), with selection on the scope validation set every 2000 steps (Tab.S2). The equal-steps controls start from the same operator and run the same schedule without the new data.

    A.4 Monte Carlo

    Light-side fields.

    The moments c_b are estimated by a CUDA photon tracer: photons enter through the lit faces in proportion to their projected area and are transported by delta tracking with a global majorant, analog absorption and Henyey–Greenstein sampling; every path segment after the first real scattering is tallied with the track-length estimator into every voxel it crosses, in double precision, which estimates the cell averages of ∫L^(≥1)b dω without bias. The uncollided tally reproduces the exact sweep and the absorbed energy balances, both to the level of the noise. On one B200 the tracer runs at 1.1–3.2×10⁸ photons per second on a 64³ cumulus of maximum optical depth 10–50.

    Anchor schedule.

    In the inversion a refresh uses 3×10⁶ photons and a new seed (about 0.11 s), every 30 iterations and right after every coarse-to-fine switch, where the average restarts with Δ=S_MC-S_φ; Frozen Source updates its source field S←(1-β)S+βS_MC on the same schedule.

    Fixed point and lag.

    If the iterates converge to σₜ^∗, the exponential average gives 𝔼[Δ]→𝔼[S_MC(σₜ^∗)]-S_φ(σₜ^∗), and the corrected source S=S_φ+Δ equals the Monte Carlo one in expectation; the stationarity condition of Eq.4 differs from the exact one by (Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ-J_multi,φ)^⊤r, while that of the frozen source differs by (J_direct+Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ)^⊤r. Away from a fixed point the anchor lags: at σₜ=σₜᵃ+δ near the last refresh σₜᵃ the source’s error is (∂S_φ-∂S) δ to first order, with ∂ the Jacobians of the sources. Where the iterate leaves the operator’s training distribution, the Jacobian error on the visited states therefore drives the error of both the gradient and the values, which is what trajectory training targets.

    A.5 Inverse Renderer

    Parameterisation and visual hull.

    The density used for rendering, the sweep, the operator, Monte Carlo and evaluation is \min(e^θ,2000) (an optical depth of 31 per voxel at 64³), upsampled trilinearly to 64³ from the current coarse-to-fine grid and multiplied by a visual hull [24, 22]: a voxel is kept if it projects onto a pixel brighter than 0.5% of the image maximum in every training view that sees it, and the mask is dilated by one voxel. The hull and every other shared setting apply to every method, PRB included.

    Warm start and coarse to fine.

    The warm start fits an emission–absorption model [35] at 16³ for 10 s, charged to every method’s clock. The grid switches from 16³ to 32³ at 15 s and to 64³ at 45 s (PRB has its own schedules); at a switch, θ is re-initialised from the upsampled density and Adam’s moments are reset.

    Iteration and clock.

    Each iteration draws 32768 rays uniformly from the pixel-centre rays of the training views that intersect the cube and minimises their mean squared error of linear radiance with Adam [21] (learning rate 0.05, ε=10⁻⁸). A method’s clock starts after a one-time warm-up of every model it uses, includes the warm start and the held-out losses, and pauses during checkpoint evaluation; the GPU is synchronised before the clock is read. Every run used one B200, one CPU core (four for PRB) and 6 GB of host memory.

    Appendix B Gradient Decomposition

    Descent with a partial Jacobian.

    A step Δθ=-η J_cam^⊤r changes the loss by -η \tfrac2P⟨J^⊤r,J_cam^⊤r⟩+O(η²), which is \cos(J_cam^⊤r,J^⊤r) times the change of a steepest-descent step of the same length: for a small step the frozen-source iteration descends if and only if this cosine is positive. Linearised at a consistent solution, its error evolves as

    δ←(1-η J_cam^⊤J) δ,

    		(S3)

    which decays along eigenvectors of J_cam^⊤J with eigenvalues of positive real part and grows along any with negative real part, as for the unmatched projector–backprojector pairs of iterative tomography [49, 12]. With consistent data every solution is a fixed point of every variant; with noise or model error the true gradient at the frozen source’s fixed point is \tfrac2P(J_direct+Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ)^⊤r.

    Measurements.

    On five development media (model-consistent data rendered with the generic operator, 131072 rays of the 32 training views) the Jacobian is measured along four perturbations v of θ (a uniform scaling, two smooth random fields and the layer within unit optical depth of the light), and the gradients at four perturbed densities (the truth scaled by 0.8 and 1.25, and multiplied by two smooth log-normal fields); Fig.S1 reports the means. J_multi,φ, obtained by differentiating the operator, agrees with Monte Carlo central differences with cosine 0.94–0.99 in the 13 of 15 cases whose Monte Carlo noise is below 0.35. ∥Jₘᵤₗₜᵢv∥/∥J_camv∥ grows with optical depth (1.5 at τ=5, 3.9 at τ=60 with albedo 0.999), albedo and g; J_direct and Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ do not cancel (∥(J_direct+Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ)v∥ is 5–21 times ∥J_directv∥ on the clouds). Adding J_direct without Jₘᵤₗₜᵢ does not help in clouds (the alignment is tied at τ≤20 and lower by 0.09–0.13 at τ≥40), consistent with the ablation of Tab.S15; on a thin 2D cloud slice a small gain from it was reported [11], and at τ=5 our alignment does not separate the two either (0.95 and 0.94).

    Source iteration and diffusion.

    Frozen-source differentiation lags the scattering source, just as source iteration does in transport solvers [1]. Diffusion synthetic acceleration approximates the missing response to accelerate transport [2, 23]; here J_multi,φ supplies a learned response to the inverse problem instead.

    P1 diffusion derivative.

    The classical control replaces the operator by the P1 approximation: for the current density a cell-centred finite-volume P1 equation with Marshak boundaries and the single-scattered light as its source is solved by Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients; its degree-0 and degree-1 moments enter S in place of the operator’s, the derivative flows through the solve by implicit differentiation, and the same anchor corrects the values every 30 iterations. It runs 7.0–9.5 iterations per second (ours 17). On eight development media it relights at 26.2–36.2 dB after 2 and after 16 min, against 40.4–49.0 dB for ours with the scope operator and 27.3–42.3 dB for Frozen Source after 2 min; its selected iterate stops improving after 30–120 s. Diffusion is least accurate at the optically thin edges of clouds and for strongly forward-peaked scattering, which these media have.

    The learned field and derivative on held-out clouds.

    For each medium of the main evaluation (its 64³ truth, albedo, g and training light; post hoc), a Gaussian bump v of \logσₜ with a standard deviation of 3 voxels and peak 1 is placed at the density-weighted centroid, inside the cloud (for medium 8 within two voxels of a gap, where 15% of the bump falls outside the support and is masked). The multiple-scattering source of light-side Monte Carlo at the truth (two independent halves of 1.0–2.3×10⁹ photons; their difference puts the reference’s noise below 1.0%) is compared with each operator’s prediction. Its directional derivative along v is estimated by central differences of \logσₜ with ε=0.5 and common random numbers: photon-indexed random streams and one majorant for both densities, so that photon paths that never meet the bump are identical and cancel; two independent pairs of 1.5–3.4×10⁹ photons per evaluation give the estimate’s own noise rₙ. The operators are evaluated in fp32 (the inversion runs them in bfloat16) and differentiated by central differences with ε=0.02 (within cosine 0.99999 of ε=0.05); the trajectory operator’s own difference at ε=0.5 lies within cosine 0.9995 of this derivative, so its response is close to linear over this range, and compared secant with secant the cosines below change by at most 0.002. Field errors and derivative cosines are σₛ-weighted over all coefficients (Tab.S3; cosines in brackets corrected for rₙ as in Tab.S5); the far field is the σₛ-weighted angular mean of the derivative more than two bump standard deviations from its centre, with its share of the squared norm; image cosines are over pixels. The image changes of Tab.S3 are rendered by our model from a camera at 25^∘ elevation, with the light-side bracket of the unperturbed density held fixed (the frozen source, J_camv), with the operator’s source and the correction Δ of the unperturbed density ((J_cam+J_direct+J_multi,φ)v), and with the Monte Carlo sources of both densities (Jv). Figure4 shows the medium of Fig.1 (9.8×10⁹ reference photons in both halves, 7.4×10⁹ per finite-difference evaluation); the main text quotes this run for that medium, the table the uniform budget.

    Appendix C Operator Learning Analyses

    Data or training time.

    The scope data lower the field error on scope media by 24% (generic+ by 5%), and the trajectory states lower it on the held-back inversion states by 29% and on the most drifted ones by 44% (scope+ by 5% and 4%; Tabs.S4 and S2).

    Jacobian on visited states.

    Directional derivatives of the multiple-scattering source along a perturbation v of \logσₜ are compared by central differences (ε=0.2) for light-side Monte Carlo (5×10⁸ photons, common random numbers within a pair; two independent pairs give the estimate’s own noise rₙ) and for each operator, on held-back states of the trajectory data (per medium the stored states nearest density error 0.35, 1.0 and 2.2), along the inversion’s next step (to the next stored state), the drift (the state minus the truth in \logσₜ) and a smooth random field. Errors and cosines are σₛ-weighted over all coefficients; errors are corrected for the Monte Carlo noise, e=√\max(e_raw²-rₙ²,0), and cosines by √1+rₙ². Along the next step and along the drift from drifted states, the derivatives of the generic, scope and scope+ operators are nearly orthogonal or opposite to Monte Carlo’s, and the trajectory operator’s are not (Tab.S5). The weighting lets the density spikes of drifted states dominate: on the two states closest to both median next-step cosines (a tie; Fig.S3; recomputed post hoc with 4×10⁹ photons per evaluation, rₙ 0.04 and 0.06), voxels above σₜ=500, 0.3% and 2% of the support, carry 74% and 85% of the weighted energy of the Monte Carlo derivative’s angular mean. Below σₜ=500 the trajectory operator is still closer (weighted angular-mean cosines 0.69 against 0.45 for scope, 0.62 against 0.28), though on the first state (top row) the two operators’ slices look alike.

    In the loop (development).

    On three thick development media after 17500 iterations, the trajectory operator has current-iterate density errors 2.03 / 1.65 / 1.92, versus 8.13 / 9.51 / 3.80 with scope and 7.62 / 8.96 / 3.32 with the equal-steps scope+ control. The corresponding anchor-estimated source errors are 43 / 21 / 33% for trajectory and 208 / 219 / 83% for scope.

    Without selection (development).

    On eight development media with all 32 views and no selection (Tab.S6), the trajectory operator relights 3.6 dB better than the scope operator in the mean over 2–16 min (8 of 8 media), 6.5 dB at 16 min, and diverges on two media instead of six; it stays 1.9 dB below the scope-operator pipeline with selection at 16 min, which is why selection remains part of the method.

    Appendix D Experimental Protocol

    Media.

    The main evaluation and the controlled set each hold six procedural cumulus clouds and six Cloudy clouds [26] that no training or development step used, each the first in a hash order of its candidates to pass an occupancy check, with maximum column optical depth log-uniform in [40,100], 1-α log-uniform in [10⁻³,10⁻²], g uniform in [0.7,0.9] and the development lights rotated about the vertical by a random angle. The main evaluation’s drawn values span τ 43.8–89.7, α 0.9901–0.9987 and g 0.706–0.884 (controlled set: 42.8–99.8, 0.9909–0.999 and 0.703–0.888). The main evaluation’s media are 128³ volumes (procedural clouds generated at 128³, Cloudy clouds averaged to 128³) whose 2³ averages are the 64³ truths; Mitsuba 3 renders its observations and references by volumetric path tracing with Russian roulette disabled, and every inversion reads them from a cache that refuses any other source. For the main evaluation the representation ceiling, our renderer’s image of the 64³ truth against Mitsuba’s references under the new lights, is 44.7 dB in the median (ours reaches 42.9 dB after 16 min), and the two renderers agree at 64³ to at least 53.7 dB. The controlled set’s observations and references are rendered by our path tracer from the 64³ truth, so that ours, Frozen Source and the Detached Operator share the data’s forward model up to noise (an inverse crime [18] that favours them over PRB).

    Cameras, lights and metric.

    The 32 views are cameras on an orbit at distance 2.2 from the cube centre, evenly spaced in azimuth with elevations cycling through 5^∘, 25^∘ and 45^∘, field of view 40^∘, 128² pixels and 4096 samples per pixel; four of them (every eighth) are held out for selection. The training light is at an elevation of 60^∘; the three new lights are at 95^∘, 41^∘ and 59^∘ from it (elevations 22^∘, 22^∘, 53^∘), and two relighting cameras of 96² pixels lie between training views. The metric is the noise-free relighting PSNR

    PSNR=10\log₁₀(∑_l,v\maxₚ(R⁽¹⁾)²)/(∑_l,veₗᵥ),

    		(S4)

    with eₗᵥ=⟨(A⁽¹⁾-R⁽¹⁾)(A⁽²⁾-R⁽²⁾)⟩ₚ over the new lights l and views v and the mean over pixels ⟨·⟩ₚ, where A⁽ᵏ⁾ and R⁽ᵏ⁾ are path-traced images (4096 samples per pixel) of the reconstruction and of the truth with seed set k; the two seed sets are independent, so eₗᵥ has the expectation of the squared error of the noise-free images. Density errors are relative L₂ errors over the grid, and the projected optical depth error is that of the three axis-aligned projections.

    Baselines.

    Frozen Source ran with two TV priors, 10⁻³ and 3×10⁻³, each the best of its budgets on development media; the tables report each, and the better per medium and budget (best of configuration). The Detached Operator uses its best development prior, TV 10⁻³; ours uses none. PRB [48] runs in Mitsuba 3.9.1 with Dr.Jit 1.5.0 (integrator prbvolpath, unbounded paths); the density comes from the shared parameterisation through drjit.wrap, and each iteration renders one random training view with 64 samples per pixel for the primal and the adjoint pass. Its settings were chosen per budget on four thick development media among the ten configurations of Tab.S7, and the two configurations run to 30 min, with learning rates 0.01 and 0.005, form the best-of-configuration baseline; the main evaluation ran only these two. On the controlled set, the configurations tuned for 30 s and 2 min reached medians of 28.9 and 29.3 dB at these budgets, against 24.2 and 28.2 dB for the better of the two 30-min configurations. Without Russian roulette, which in media of albedo 0.99–0.998 reweights rare long paths by factors of 10²–10⁴, this baseline gains 1.3 dB on the controlled set (post hoc), so the main evaluation runs it without; a TV prior changes PRB by at most 0.2 dB. In PRB’s favour are its tuning on development media and the best-of-configuration selection on the test media, and in the main evaluation the observations come from its own renderer; in the controlled set they come from ours.

    Statistics and failures.

    Comparisons are medians of per-medium paired differences with bootstrap 95% intervals (the main evaluation’s estimate of trajectory against scope training: a mean with a t-interval). A run whose density error exceeds 2 in an evaluated checkpoint, or whose relighting falls 1 dB below its first evaluation, counts as diverged and enters with its last evaluation; a job that ends early without diverging is rerun once. All 132 jobs of the main evaluation ended normally on their first submission.

    Pre-registration.

    For each held-out set the method, comparators, settings, claims, thresholds and failure rules were committed before any of its media was generated, after independent read-only audits; the media were generated once, and the report ran once on rows from the frozen code and checkpoints. The main evaluation’s thresholds are half the median effect on eight development media free of the inverse crime, rounded down to a multiple of 0.5 dB. The controlled set tested ours with the scope operator, the method at the time, and the main evaluation the complete recipe; every claim with a threshold passed in both (Tab.S8).

    Appendix E Additional Results

    E.1 Main Evaluation

    TableS10 gives the paired comparisons at every budget, Tab.S11 iterations, density errors and drift per method, Tabs.S12 and S4 the projected optical depth, and Tabs.S13 and S9 the values per medium. Ours leads Frozen Source with either prior at every budget on all 12 media, and its lead over the better prior after 2 min is 2.2–13.4 dB per medium; the gain of the trajectory operator without selection is concentrated on Cloudy (7.5 dB after 8 min, against 0.6 dB on the procedural clouds, 5 of 6 positive). PRB’s better configuration reaches ours’ 2-min value on no medium within 30 min. After 16 min, ours’ density error is the highest of the methods with selection (0.70 against 0.57–0.60), and its projected optical depth error (0.24) is below that of Frozen Source and the Detached Operator (0.31–0.35) but above the scope operator’s (0.21). Among the runs with selection, Frozen Source with TV 10⁻³ diverged on 1 of 12 media by the density criterion and on 2 counting a 1-dB fall, the Detached Operator on 2 counting a 1-dB fall, and every other method on none.

item.title: 交互式视频转视频：靠「显式对应」把长程一致性从窗口外捞回来，而不是把窗口拉长 ｜ Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences (vid2vid-long)
item.description:
一句话：现有方法加速的办法是限制在固定长度因果窗口里；相关历史一出窗就丢一致性。

要点：

  • 目标：交互式视频转视频要求**实时**生成，同时保持长程时间一致性
  • 问题出在加速手法：近期方法把注意力限制在固定长度的因果窗口内，一旦关键历史落在窗口之外，长程一致性就断了
  • vid2vid-long 改用基于**显式对应（correspondence）**的方式，把窗口外的历史通过对应关系带回来

为什么值得看：「窗口开多大」是在算力与一致性之间做线性交换；用显式对应则是换一个信息通道。对实时风格化、视频翻译这类交互式渲染，这是绕开窗口权衡的思路。

中文摘要：交互式视频转视频（vid2vid）要求实时生成，同时长期保持时间一致性。近期方法靠把注意力限制在固定长度的因果窗口里来提速，但这带来一个结构性缺陷：一旦相关历史落在窗口之外，长程一致性就无从维持。这篇提出 vid2vid-long，改用基于显式对应关系的做法，把窗口之外的历史信息通过对应关系重新引入，而不是延长窗口。对实时风格化与视频翻译类应用，这等于把「算力换一致性」的线性交换改成换一条信息通道。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Consistent Video-to-Video Translation
via Explicit Correspondences

Abstract

Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

1 Introduction

Real-time video-to-video translation unlocks a large class of interactive applications, including streaming, gaming, and augmented and virtual reality. Recent advances in large scale text-to-video diffusion models [41, 57, 31, 1, 16, 6], and subsequently distilling them into few-step, autoregressive models [51, 12, 47, 22, 20], have enabled high-quality generation at interactive speeds.

Autoregressive video generation relies on a history of past frames to ensure temporal continuity. However, determining an efficient mechanism for maintaining this history remains a fundamental challenge. Naïvely retaining all past outputs causes memory to scale linearly and runtime quadratically with sequence length, both of which are prohibitive for real-time applications. To maintain real-time latency, many methods resort to a fixed-length sliding window. While this ensures a fixed memory and runtime per frame, it fundamentally sacrifices long-range consistency: once an object leaves the window, often after only a few seconds, the model “forgets” it forever.

Several lines of work have attempted to bridge this gap. First, attention sinks [45, 47, 22, 38] heuristically retain the initial frames as a global anchor.

However, this approach inherently cannot address novel content that first appears in a later frame, even in cases like simple disocclusions. Another approach involves models with learned hidden states, such as Mamba [8, 4], which compress history into fixed-size bottlenecks. While efficient, these models often forgo the expressive power of transformers and remain largely limited to scenes with lower temporal complexity [32].

Finally, some methods use pose conditioning [52] or explicit world representation (e.g., 3D point clouds) to maintain a consistent world [46, 42]. These methods struggle to model dynamic scenes and require additional privileged inputs that are hard to obtain.

In this paper, we address the challenge of long-range consistency in video-to-video translation. Our insight is that long-range consistency cues are provided in the input video itself. That is, if two regions match in the input video, their generated outputs should match as well. The input space can therefore serve as an index for retrieving previously generated content, allowing consistency to be enforced, without requiring access to the full output history.

As such, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based dynamic memory mechanism that enables long-term consistency while preserving real-time performance. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input video and use them to index a compressed global representation of prior outputs. This representation grows only when novel content appears, rather than with video length, resulting in sub-linear memory growth in practice. The approach is complementary to existing autoregressive distillation backbones.

We evaluate our approach in combination with multiple autoregressive distillation frameworks, including Self-Forcing, LongLive, and Rolling Forcing. In all settings, incorporating our technique substantially improves long-range consistency, while maintaining real-time inference speed and high visual quality. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We identify a structural property of video-to-video translation: correspondences in input space induce correspondences in output space, enabling input-driven retrieval for long-range consistency.

  • •

    We propose a correspondence-based mechanism that maintains a compressed global representation of prior outputs whose size scales with visual novelty rather than sequence length.

  • •

    We demonstrate consistent improvements in long-range temporal coherence across multiple real-time autoregressive backbones.

    • Our project website is available at https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~vid2vid-long/.

    2 Related Works

    Controllable Generation.

    The rapid advancements in text-to-image [34, 18, 44] and text-to-video [1, 41, 10] have been accompanied by controllable adapters that allow a more fine-grained control over the generation. In the image domain, works like ControlNet[54], Sketch-Guided-Diffusion[40], T2I adapter[25], img2img-turbo[28] show the ability to add structure control like edge maps, depth maps, and hand drawn sketches. Models such as IP-adapter[48], BLIP-diffusion[19], SynCD[17], VisualComposer[29] show ability to condition the generation of subject identity. These methods have also been extended to videos in recent methods like ControlVideo[56], Control-A-Video[3], VACE[14], and COSMOS-T [26]. However, existing video control methods are primarily designed for offline generation, often relying on non-causal processing that makes them unsuitable for interactive applications. We aim to address this gap in this paper.

    Diffusion Distillation.

    Several prior works have explored speeding up diffusion models by reducing the number of denoising steps. Initial image domain approaches like consistency models[39], progressive distillation[35], adversarial distillation[37], and distribution matching distillation [50, 49], moment matching distillation[36] enabled high-quality inference in 1–4 steps. Recent methods like CausVid[51] extend distillation to video generation, while Diffusion Forcing[2] explores autoregressive video generation. However, these approaches can still suffer from error accumulation during autoregressive inference. To address this, Self-Forcing[12] trains the student model on its own generated rollout, rather than ground truth video. Our work is complementary to these methods, focusing on maintaining long-range consistency during autoregressive inference.

    Long Context Generation.

    Maintaining long-term consistency in autoregressive generation is computationally challenging due to the quadratic complexity of transformer attention. This is particularly severe for videos: five seconds of 480p video can exceed 32,000 tokens in modern architectures like WAN2.1 [41]. Existing methods such as Streaming-T2V[11] or LongLive[47] typically use sliding windows or hierarchical latent memory. However, these often suffer from recency bias, where the model forgets the appearance of objects or environments during loop closures or long-duration occlusions. While the language modeling literature has explored KV cache pruning and compression [7, 23], these methods often ignore the spatiotemporal continuity of video.

    Rather than deciding which history to retain solely based on temporal position, learned compression, or token importance, we use input-space correspondences to retrieve the specific past outputs that are relevant to the current frame. This makes the memory mechanism task-aware and particularly well-suited to video-to-video translation, where repeated input regions should induce repeated output appearances.

    3 Method

    Our objective is to design an autoregressive video-to-video diffusion model equipped with a correspondence-based memory mechanism. Our architecture enables long-range temporal consistency while maintaining the low-latency performance required for real-time deployment. We begin by reviewing the autoregressive formulation in Section 3.1. In Section 3.2, we introduce our explicit correspondence-based memory component. We then detail our strategy for conditioning on this historical context in Section 3.3. Finally, we describe the specific training objectives and real-time inference algorithm in Sections 3.4 and 3.5, respectively.

    3.1 Preliminaries

    Bidirectional Video Generation.

    Our method builds upon pre-trained flow-matching models designed for video-to-video translation. Specifically, we adopt VACE [14], which is a latent flow-matching model, operating within the latent space of a pre-trained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [34]. Given a block of input frames I⁽ᵇ⁾∈ℝ^T×H×W×3, the VAE encoder 𝔼 maps the pixel data to a latent representation z⁽ᵇ⁾∈ℝ^t×h×w×c. The latent dimensions are determined by the spatial and temporal compression factors, which for VACE are given as follows: h=H/8, w=W/8, and t=1+(T-1)/4. Following common practice in vision transformers [30], the latent block is further patchified into a sequence of tokens. Each latent frame is partitioned spatially into non-overlapping patches of size 1×p×p, where the temporal dimension of a patch remains singular. This process yields a total of N=t×(h/p)×(w/p) tokens per block. Specifically for VACE, p=2.

    For the generative model itself, VACE utilizes a bidirectional spatiotemporal transformer to generate an entire video at once. This design implies that every generated token depends on the full context of the video, including both past and future tokens. This design is expensive in computation and memory, limiting their operation to short, fixed-length sequences, typically up to five seconds.

    Autoregressive Video Generation.

    To enable long-form generation, recent methods [51, 12, 47, 22] replace bidirectional attention with causal attention. These models generate videos autoregressively in temporal blocks, where each block z⁽ᵇ⁾ is generated by conditioning on the previously generated blocks z^(

    3.2 Compressed Patch History

    In video-to-video translation, the availability of the input stream allows us to move beyond temporal proximity as the sole proxy for relevance. While a sliding window approach utilizes only recent frames for context, we can use explicit correspondences in the input space to identify relevant history from any point in the past. This is a reliable strategy because regions that match in the input video should match in the generated output (see Figure 2).

    By explicitly hard-coding these correspondences, we offload the burden of discovery from the transformer’s expensive attention layers. Rather than forcing the model to rediscover these relationships, we provide them directly via an external index. We represent this memory as an evolving set of input-output pairs. Each entry consists of a descriptor for an input patch, which acts as a retrieval key, and the corresponding generated output patch, which serves as the value for future conditioning. To ensure the system remains scalable for long sequences, we only update the memory when the input video presents novel information. If an incoming patch is already sufficiently represented in the history, we do not save it. This ensures that the memory footprint scales with the visual novelty of the scene, rather than the raw sequence length. (See history growth analysis in the appendix.)

    To implement this mechanism, we define three concrete operations that govern the memory lifecycle. We first specify the patch-level representation for the keys and values, followed by the retrieval protocol for reading from history, and finally the novelty-based policy for writing to the global store.

    Patch Descriptor.

    Our memory mechanism leverages the spatial discretization already present in the diffusion transformer (see Section 3.1). In this framework, every input video spatiotemporal patch is already mapped to a small latent patch of shape (1,2,2) that corresponds to a single token. From here, we use term “latent patch” for these token-corresponding patches. We assign each latent patch a global index g that uniquely identifies its spatiotemporal coordinates. For every input latent patch at index g, denoted as z_g, we define a descriptor k_g to serve as a retrieval key. We evaluated several feature extractors φ to produce these keys, including external vision backbones applied in pixel space. However, our experiments show that the most effective representation is the latent patch itself (further analysis is included in the appendix). Consequently, we define the feature extraction function as the identity mapping, where k_g=z_g. This approach also avoids the computational cost of decoding latents back to pixels and the inference run of additional feature extraction backbones. Under this formulation, the memory stores pairs (k_g,v_g), where the key k_g is the input latent patch and the value v_g is the corresponding to the generated output latent patch.

    Memory Management.

    To maintain temporal coherence throughout the generation process, we define the memory as a dynamic set of key-value pairs that evolves alongside the autoregressive blocks. Let H_b represent the memory state after the generation of block b, initialized as an empty set H₀=∅. We similarly define G_b as the set of all global indices g associated with the latent tokens generated within block b. Under this formulation, the generation of each subsequent block b+1 utilizes the existing history H_b for retrieval and concludes by updating the state to H_b+1 using the newly generated tokens in G_b+1.

    Memory Write Policy.

    The memory state is updated after the generation of each block by evaluating the novelty of every new latent patch relative to the existing stored patches. For each generated latent patch at index g∈G_b+1, we pair the input descriptor k_g with the corresponding output latent patch v_g. The similarity between a query latent patch k_g and the current memory H_b is defined as the maximum cosine similarity:

    sim(k_g,H_b)=\max_(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈H_bsim(k_g,k_g^′)=\max_(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈H_b(k_g·k_g^′)/(∥k_g∥∥k_g^′∥).

    		(1)

    For an empty memory, we define sim(k_g,H₀)=-∞, ensuring that all patches from the first generated block are added to memory. The latent patch and its corresponding generated output v_g are committed to the memory only if this similarity falls below a novelty threshold τₕ. The updated memory H_b+1 is thus defined as:

    H_b+1=H_b∪{(k_g,v_g):sim(k_g,H_b)<τₕ}_g∈G_b+1.

    		(2)

    This policy ensures that memory footprint and inference cost scales with discovery of unique visual content rather than total sequence length.

    Memory Read Mechanism.

    Before generating the output latents for block b+1, we query H_b using the descriptors of the current input latent. For each patch index g, we identify the set of k nearest neighbors ℕₖ(g) whose similarity exceeds a retrieval threshold τₘ:

    \vskip-2.84526ptℕₖ(g)=Topₖ({(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈H_b:sim(k_g,k_g^′)≥τₘ}).\vskip-2.84526pt

    		(3)

    For every query latent patch that satisfies this condition, we retrieve the stored output values v_g^′. If no entries in H_b meet the threshold τₘ, the neighborhood ℕₖ(g) is empty. We track these occurrences with a binary validity mask m_g, where m_g=1 if ℕₖ(g)≠∅ and 0 otherwise. This mask and the retrieved values are then used to condition the diffusion transformer as described in Section 3.3.

    3.3 Conditioning via Correspondence Cross-Attention

    We now describe how these retrieved values are used to condition the video translation model. The retrieved output patches {v_g^′} are tokenized using the same patch embedding as the input latents, producing history tokens h_g^′ in a shared representation space.

    To incorporate these history tokens into the video-model architecture, we add correspondence cross-attention layers to every transformer block between self-attention and text cross-attention layers. Each token attends only to its own k retrieved neighbors. Concretely, for each token index g, the current hidden state x_g provides the query. Let H_g={h_g^′}_(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈ℕₖ(g) denote the set of retrieved history tokens for query g. We define

    CorrXA(g)=m_g·Wₒ Attn(W_qx_g, WₖH_g, WᵥH_g).

    		(4)

    where m_g is the validity mask that zeros out tokens without valid correspondences. The output is added as a residual: x_g←x_g+CorrXA(g). The output projection Wₒ is zero-initialized [54], so the layer acts as an identity at the start of training, preserving the behavior of the pretrained model. Since each token attends only to its k neighbors, the computational overhead of these layers is minimal. We’ve described the cross-attention operation for a single token. To implement this efficiently, we reshape the query and memory tensors to collapse the sequence length into the batch dimension, effectively treating each token’s cross-attention as an independent 1×k operation.

    3.4 Training

    We incorporate our correspondence-based memory into several different autoregressive video model. Unless stated otherwise, we use Rolling Forcing [22] distillation with 5 steps as the default configuration. The student model is initialized from pretrained VACE 1.3B and all model parameters are finetuned jointly, including the newly introduced correspondence cross-attention layers. We adopt the standard Rolling Forcing objective without modification or extra loss terms. The correspondence memory is active during training, and memory read and write operations are performed as described in Section 3.2. The student conditions on retrieved correspondences from its own previously generated blocks, and newly generated patches are written to memory according to the novelty threshold. The teacher model is a bidirectional VACE 14B model and it does not use correspondence memory.

    3.5 Inference

    At inference time, the model generates the video autoregressively, processing fixed-size blocks sequentially. At the start of each video, we set H₀=∅. For each block b, we compute the input latent tokens z_g, g∈G_b. Using z_g, we query H_b-1 to compute neighbors ℕₖ(g) for each g∈G_b. The retrieved neighbors are used to condition the translation network through correspondence cross-attention layers during each denoising step of block b. Retrieval is performed once per block and the resulting neighbors are reused across all denoising steps. After block b is fully denoised, we obtain the output latents v_g, g∈G_b, and update the memory according to Eq. 2. The updated memory H_b is used to generate the next block b+1. A complete inference pseudocode is provided in the appendix.

    4 Experiments

    Here, we first evaluate our method on depth-to-video translation, focusing on long-range temporal consistency on long videos. Our mechanism is agnostic to the conditioning modality. Experiments are conducted on two benchmarks: VACE-Benchmark [14], covering diverse real-world scenes, and DL3DV [21], a geometry-grounded 3D dataset enabling controlled pose revisits. We compare against bidirectional diffusion models, prior video translation methods, and recent autoregressive distillation approaches, and ablate the key components of our correspondence mechanism. Unless stated otherwise, all experiments use VACE 1.3B at 480p resolution.

    Datasets.

    We evaluate on two benchmarks. VACE-Benchmark [14] contains diverse real-world video sequences with varying motion and scene complexity. DL3DV [21] is a geometry-grounded 3D dataset with calibrated camera poses, enabling controlled evaluation of viewpoint revisits and long-range consistency. Additional dataset details and preprocessing are provided in appendix.

    Evaluation Protocol.

    We evaluate our method in terms of video quality, long-range consistency under revisits, and inference efficiency. Video quality is measured on full generated videos using V-Bench [13] metrics (subject consistency, background consistency, temporal flickering, motion smoothness, aesthetic quality, and imaging quality). Experiments report average of scores, individual metrics values are provided in the appendix. Long-range consistency is evaluated using controlled revisit protocols that require model to reproduce previously observed content. On VACE-Benchmark, following [9], we construct synthetic long sequences by concatenating two distinct 5-second clips in an interleaved order (A→B→A→B), and measure reconstruction consistency between repeated occurrences of the same clip. Consistency is quantified using LPIPS [55], DreamSim [5], and CLIP [33] image similarity. On DL3DV, we use pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting models [15] using calibrated camera poses to render exact pose revisits and measure consistency between first-visit and revisit frames. We measure inference latency and throughput. Inference latency is measured as time to produce first frame and throughput is reported in frames per second (FPS). All measurements are performed on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.

    Implementation Details.

    We use VACE 1.3B [14] as the student model and VACE 14B as the teacher. The student is initialized from the pretrained VACE 1.3B checkpoint and trained using Rolling Forcing [22]. For correspondence retrieval, we use VAE encoder’s latent features as keys, with k=3 retrieved neighbors, history threshold τₕ=0.75, and memory threshold τₘ=0.75. Training is performed using AdamW [24] with batch size 64, a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁶ for the student network and 4×10⁻⁷ for the critic.

    4.1 Baseline Comparisons

    We evaluate our method against several video-to-video translation frameworks. Quantitative and qualitative results are in Table 1 and Figure 3. First, we compare to Control-A-Video [3], VideoComposer [43], and ControlVideo [56].

    They operate in an offline bidirectional setting with multi-step diffusion and global attention over fixed-length sequences. In our experiments, they produce lower visual quality and struggle to maintain long-range consistency (Figure 3). ControlVideo achieves relatively strong reconstruction scores due to its hierarchical sampling strategy over long sequences. However, this comes at the cost of high latency (≈ 42 minutes in our setting) and reduced perceptual quality, making it impractical for real-time video-to-video translation.

    We next compare to newer, state-of-the-art video translation models, such as VACE [14]. As discussed before, VACE is a bidirectional model which is limited to a fixed-length, short video sequences. Unfortunately, there is no publicly available adaption of VACE to an unbounded-length, streaming use case. In order to still apply VACE on our setting, we adapt it in two manners.

    First, we directly evaluate VACE by applying it on non-overlapping video segments. We find that this naive adaptation of VACE produces high-quality results, but unsurprisingly has poor long-range consistency. For example, note row 2 in Figure 3 where each individual frame is of high-quality, but objects change their colors drastically over the length of the video.

    Second, we adapt VACE to a streaming use-case with three recent causal, autoregressive distillation methods: Self-Forcing [12], LongLive [47], and Rolling Forcing [22]. These methods were originally designed for text-to-video generation and aren’t applied to video-to-video yet. Here, we implement and adapt the three methods to video-to-video with VACE. We find that all methods achieve competitive quality scores and substantially lower latency than the bidirectional VACE baseline (Tables 1, 2). Nevertheless, these methods still perform poorly on long-range consistency. On VACE-Bench, Self-Forcing and LongLive underperform bidirectional VACE, while Rolling Forcing only slightly outperforms it in long-range reconstruction.

    Our main contribution, correspondence mechanism, can be readily applied with any autoregressive method. In Table 1, 2 and Figure 3, we report results of our best configuration, where our method is applied with Rolling Forcing. Among autoregressive methods, our approach achieves the strongest long-range consistency and visual quality while maintaining real-time performance. In Table 3, we report the results of our method when applied on top of all autoregressive methods. Adding our correspondence mechanism consistently improves long-term consistency across all autoregressive backbones while preserving visual quality. Table 3 results demonstrate that our method is orthogonal to choice of autoregressive backbone. Please refer to the appendix for a comparison of different conditioning mechanisms.

    4.2 Alternate Consistency Mechanisms

    We compare our correspondence mechanism against alternative strategies for extending temporal context beyond the default sliding window. Qualitative and quantitative results are shown in Figure 4 and Table 4, respectively.

    Larger KV Cache window.

    We increase the sliding window size from 21 latent frames to 42 (×2), 63 (×3), and 84 (×4). On VACE-Bench, larger windows improve reconstruction consistency slightly, although the gains are non-monotonic. However, on DL3DV, where sequences are substantially longer, performance degrades sharply in both quality and long-range consistency.

    Keyframe retention.

    Next, instead of sliding window, we retain KV cache of every N-th block (N=3,5,10), providing a sparse but more complete coverage of the history. While this improves over simply enlarging the window, it remains worse than correspondence-based retrieval in long-range reconstruction (Table 4).

    Global Pooling.

    We maintain a single block of KV tokens as a running cumulative average of all previous blocks, providing constant memory access to the entire history. Although this improves long-range consistency on DL3DV degrades visual quality on both datasets (quality scores drop to 0.753 and 0.772).

    Random Retrieval.

    To isolate the role of correspondence matching from the cross-attention layers, we replace the similarity-based retrieval with uniform random sampling from the memory bank. Each query patch receives k randomly selected history patches instead of the top-k most similar, the history creation process remains the same. This significantly degrades long-range reconstruction performance, demonstrating that accurate correspondence matching is essential.

    Attention Sink.

    Recent methods such as LongLive, MotionStream, and Rolling Forcing retain initial frames as an attention sink to provide global context. However, this mechanism cannot capture novel content that appears later in the sequence and is insufficient to prevent identity drift in long videos.

    FramePack.

    FramePack [53] is applied to the task of video to video translation, storing past blocks at geometrically decreasing spatial resolution. Recent blocks maintain full resolution while older blocks are progressively downsampled. While this retains the entire history, aggressive spatial compression reduces detail, leading to weaker long-range reconstruction.

    Overall, correspondence-based retrieval outperforms all alternative mechanisms for extending temporal context, achieving stronger long-range consistency without sacrificing visual quality.

    4.3 Analysis and Ablations

    Importance of Correspondence.

    First, we show the importance of using correspondence patches through an ablation where we remove the correspondences and disable the correspondence cross-attention layer (Equation 4). As in Table 5, without using correspondence the long context consistency gets significantly worse. The LPIPS reconstruction improves by 37% and 30% on the two datasets. DreamSim and CLIP similarity scores are also similarly effected. Figure 5 shows this qualitatively. The top row shows the generated video when the correspondence is disabled. In this video, the dog starts with a yellow snout, but as the video progresses and the dog re-enters the scene, the snout turns blue. In contrast, our full method with correspondence is shown in the bottom row. Here the dog retains the identity and re-enters the scene with the same yellow snout.

    Sensitivity to different distillation methods.

    Next, we show that our method is not specific to any single distillation method. We apply our method to three different distillation methods: SelfForcing [12], LongLive [47], and RollingForcing [22]. Add our correspondence method improves the consistency across each of the base distillation methods as seen in Table 3.

    5 Conclusion and Limitations

    We introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based memory mechanism for long-range consistent video-to-video translation. By exploiting a structural property of the task, matching regions in the input should match in the output, we replace implicit long-range attention with explicit input-driven retrieval. Our dynamic memory grows with visual novelty rather than length of the video, enabling sub-linear scaling while preserving real-time performance. Across multiple autoregressive distillation backbones, our method consistently improves long-range reconstruction and reduces identity drift while maintaining high visual quality and real-time inference performance. Compared to alternative context extension strategies, explicit correspondence retrieval proves both more effective and more efficient.

    Limitations.

    Our model struggles on fast videos with large motion, where reliable cross-frame correspondences become harder to establish. It can also fail when the text prompt is inconsistent with the input depth video, since the model must reconcile conflicting semantic and structural conditioning signals.

    Appendix

    We provide additional details and results that complement the main paper. Section A presents the architecture diagram and runtime analysis. Section B analyzes the history growth and memory scaling behavior. Section C shows results on other conditioning inputs. Sections D and E provide training and inference details. Section F compares different feature extractors for correspondence matching. Section G details the dataset preprocessing steps. Section H reports per-metric V-Bench scores. The video results are primarily shown in the accompanying website.

    A Model Architecture and Runtime Analysis

    Section 3.3 of the main paper describes conditioning with correspondence-cross attention layers. In Figure 6, we show the corresponding architecture diagram. The only architectural modification to the pretrained VACE transformer is the insertion of a correspondence cross-attention layer in each block. Note that each token attends only to its k retrieved neighbors.

    Figure 7 reports the per-component inference time for generating a 20-second video on a single H100 GPU at 480p resolution, for all three autoregressive backbones with our correspondence mechanism. The denoising forward passes dominate the total runtime across all methods, accounting for over 77% of the total. The correspondence-specific components (memory read, correspondence cross-attention, and memory write) add a small overhead. Memory read and write operations have a negligible inference cost (∼50ms total).

    B History Growth Analysis

    As discussed in Section 3 of the main paper, the memory footprint scales with the visual novelty of the scene rather than the raw sequence length. Here, we empirically validate this claim.

    VRAM Scaling.

    Table 6 compares the total GPU memory footprint of a naive full KV-cache approach against our dynamic memory mechanism as video length increases. The naive approach retains KV entries for every past token across all 45 transformer layers, causing memory to grow linearly with sequence length. At 480p resolution, it exceeds the 80 GB capacity of an H100 GPU after roughly 30 seconds; at 720p the limit is reached even sooner. Our method replaces the large KV cache with an attention sink and a fixed-size sliding window (W=21 latent frames), plus a correspondence memory that stores only input–output latent patch pairs. Because the correspondence memory bypasses the per-layer KV overhead, its footprint is negligible: even after 10 minutes of video (9,600 frames), total VRAM increases by only 0.1 GB at 480p and 0.3 GB at 720p compared to the initial cost. As a result, total VRAM remains nearly constant regardless of video duration at both resolutions.

    History Growth and Read/Write Cost.

    Figure 8 (left) shows the history size |H| over time with and without our novelty-based compression, evaluated on 30 videos spanning three categories (webcam, surveillance, and action camera). Without compression, every generated patch is stored, causing |H| to grow linearly to over 936 K entries at 9 600 frames (10 minutes). With our write policy (τₕ=0.75), the history grows sub-linearly, reaching roughly 26 K entries at the same point (∼36× reduction). This directly translates to runtime savings: Figure 8 (right) shows that the per-block memory read and write time grows linearly without compression, exceeding 30 ms at 10 minutes, while with compression it remains below 2 ms throughout.

    History Growth and thresholds τₕ and τₘ

    Increasing τₕ admits more patches into the memory, trading memory size for better reconstruction. LPIPS improves from 0.301 to 0.204 as |H| grows from 413 to 15.8K patches. For τₘ, the reconstruction quality is stable over a wide range of values. But, a strict threshold (τₘ=0.90) rejects many valid matches, degrading reconstruction (LPIPS 0.286). The same defaults perform consistently for both datasets with no scene-specific tuning needed.

    C Other Conditioning Inputs

    We show the evaluation of different methods when other conditioning inputs such as sketch and optical flow are used in Table 8. Our method is robust and shows an improvement in the long range consistency across other conditioning inputs (sketch and optical flow) too.

    D Training Details

    Table 9 lists all training and model hyperparameters. We train the student model using Rolling Forcing [22] distillation with 5 uniformly spaced denoising steps ({1000,800,600,400,200}) that are shifted following standard practice. The student is initialized from the pretrained VACE 1.3B checkpoint and all parameters are finetuned jointly, including the newly introduced correspondence cross-attention layers. The student is initialized with Diffusion Forcing training before timestep distillation. The teacher is the bidirectional VACE 14B model and does not use correspondence memory. During training, the correspondence memory is active: for each rollout, memory read and write operations are performed as described in Section 3.2 of the main paper. We use the standard Rolling Forcing objective without modification or additional loss terms. We apply EMA with weight 0.99 starting at iteration 200. Training uses mixed precision and gradient checkpointing on 32 A100 80GB GPUs across 4 nodes. All inference benchmarks are measured on a single H100 80GB GPU.

    Negative Prompt.

    Following standard practice, we use a fixed negative prompt: “Bright tones, overexposed, static, blurred details, subtitles, style, works, paintings, images, static, overall gray, worst quality, low quality, JPEG compression residue, ugly, incomplete, extra fingers, poorly drawn hands, poorly drawn faces, deformed, disfigured, misshapen limbs, fused fingers, still picture, messy background, three legs, many people in the background, walking backwards.”

    E Inference Details

    Algorithm 1 provides the complete inference procedure. The model processes the input conditioning video block-by-block. For each block, we retrieve matching past outputs from the correspondence memory (memory read), denoise with correspondence cross-attention conditioning, and update the memory with novel input-output pairs (memory write). Retrieval is performed once per block and the retrieved tokens are reused across all denoising steps.

一句话：现有方法加速的办法是限制在固定长度因果窗口里；相关历史一出窗就丢一致性。

要点：

  • 目标：交互式视频转视频要求**实时**生成，同时保持长程时间一致性
  • 问题出在加速手法：近期方法把注意力限制在固定长度的因果窗口内，一旦关键历史落在窗口之外，长程一致性就断了
  • vid2vid-long 改用基于**显式对应（correspondence）**的方式，把窗口外的历史通过对应关系带回来

为什么值得看：「窗口开多大」是在算力与一致性之间做线性交换；用显式对应则是换一个信息通道。对实时风格化、视频翻译这类交互式渲染，这是绕开窗口权衡的思路。

中文摘要：交互式视频转视频（vid2vid）要求实时生成，同时长期保持时间一致性。近期方法靠把注意力限制在固定长度的因果窗口里来提速，但这带来一个结构性缺陷：一旦相关历史落在窗口之外，长程一致性就无从维持。这篇提出 vid2vid-long，改用基于显式对应关系的做法，把窗口之外的历史信息通过对应关系重新引入，而不是延长窗口。对实时风格化与视频翻译类应用，这等于把「算力换一致性」的线性交换改成换一条信息通道。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-14

Consistent Video-to-Video Translation
via Explicit Correspondences

Abstract

Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

1 Introduction

Real-time video-to-video translation unlocks a large class of interactive applications, including streaming, gaming, and augmented and virtual reality. Recent advances in large scale text-to-video diffusion models [41, 57, 31, 1, 16, 6], and subsequently distilling them into few-step, autoregressive models [51, 12, 47, 22, 20], have enabled high-quality generation at interactive speeds.

Autoregressive video generation relies on a history of past frames to ensure temporal continuity. However, determining an efficient mechanism for maintaining this history remains a fundamental challenge. Naïvely retaining all past outputs causes memory to scale linearly and runtime quadratically with sequence length, both of which are prohibitive for real-time applications. To maintain real-time latency, many methods resort to a fixed-length sliding window. While this ensures a fixed memory and runtime per frame, it fundamentally sacrifices long-range consistency: once an object leaves the window, often after only a few seconds, the model “forgets” it forever.

Several lines of work have attempted to bridge this gap. First, attention sinks [45, 47, 22, 38] heuristically retain the initial frames as a global anchor.

However, this approach inherently cannot address novel content that first appears in a later frame, even in cases like simple disocclusions. Another approach involves models with learned hidden states, such as Mamba [8, 4], which compress history into fixed-size bottlenecks. While efficient, these models often forgo the expressive power of transformers and remain largely limited to scenes with lower temporal complexity [32].

Finally, some methods use pose conditioning [52] or explicit world representation (e.g., 3D point clouds) to maintain a consistent world [46, 42]. These methods struggle to model dynamic scenes and require additional privileged inputs that are hard to obtain.

In this paper, we address the challenge of long-range consistency in video-to-video translation. Our insight is that long-range consistency cues are provided in the input video itself. That is, if two regions match in the input video, their generated outputs should match as well. The input space can therefore serve as an index for retrieving previously generated content, allowing consistency to be enforced, without requiring access to the full output history.

As such, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based dynamic memory mechanism that enables long-term consistency while preserving real-time performance. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input video and use them to index a compressed global representation of prior outputs. This representation grows only when novel content appears, rather than with video length, resulting in sub-linear memory growth in practice. The approach is complementary to existing autoregressive distillation backbones.

We evaluate our approach in combination with multiple autoregressive distillation frameworks, including Self-Forcing, LongLive, and Rolling Forcing. In all settings, incorporating our technique substantially improves long-range consistency, while maintaining real-time inference speed and high visual quality. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We identify a structural property of video-to-video translation: correspondences in input space induce correspondences in output space, enabling input-driven retrieval for long-range consistency.

  • •

    We propose a correspondence-based mechanism that maintains a compressed global representation of prior outputs whose size scales with visual novelty rather than sequence length.

  • •

    We demonstrate consistent improvements in long-range temporal coherence across multiple real-time autoregressive backbones.

    • Our project website is available at https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~vid2vid-long/.

    2 Related Works

    Controllable Generation.

    The rapid advancements in text-to-image [34, 18, 44] and text-to-video [1, 41, 10] have been accompanied by controllable adapters that allow a more fine-grained control over the generation. In the image domain, works like ControlNet[54], Sketch-Guided-Diffusion[40], T2I adapter[25], img2img-turbo[28] show the ability to add structure control like edge maps, depth maps, and hand drawn sketches. Models such as IP-adapter[48], BLIP-diffusion[19], SynCD[17], VisualComposer[29] show ability to condition the generation of subject identity. These methods have also been extended to videos in recent methods like ControlVideo[56], Control-A-Video[3], VACE[14], and COSMOS-T [26]. However, existing video control methods are primarily designed for offline generation, often relying on non-causal processing that makes them unsuitable for interactive applications. We aim to address this gap in this paper.

    Diffusion Distillation.

    Several prior works have explored speeding up diffusion models by reducing the number of denoising steps. Initial image domain approaches like consistency models[39], progressive distillation[35], adversarial distillation[37], and distribution matching distillation [50, 49], moment matching distillation[36] enabled high-quality inference in 1–4 steps. Recent methods like CausVid[51] extend distillation to video generation, while Diffusion Forcing[2] explores autoregressive video generation. However, these approaches can still suffer from error accumulation during autoregressive inference. To address this, Self-Forcing[12] trains the student model on its own generated rollout, rather than ground truth video. Our work is complementary to these methods, focusing on maintaining long-range consistency during autoregressive inference.

    Long Context Generation.

    Maintaining long-term consistency in autoregressive generation is computationally challenging due to the quadratic complexity of transformer attention. This is particularly severe for videos: five seconds of 480p video can exceed 32,000 tokens in modern architectures like WAN2.1 [41]. Existing methods such as Streaming-T2V[11] or LongLive[47] typically use sliding windows or hierarchical latent memory. However, these often suffer from recency bias, where the model forgets the appearance of objects or environments during loop closures or long-duration occlusions. While the language modeling literature has explored KV cache pruning and compression [7, 23], these methods often ignore the spatiotemporal continuity of video.

    Rather than deciding which history to retain solely based on temporal position, learned compression, or token importance, we use input-space correspondences to retrieve the specific past outputs that are relevant to the current frame. This makes the memory mechanism task-aware and particularly well-suited to video-to-video translation, where repeated input regions should induce repeated output appearances.

    3 Method

    Our objective is to design an autoregressive video-to-video diffusion model equipped with a correspondence-based memory mechanism. Our architecture enables long-range temporal consistency while maintaining the low-latency performance required for real-time deployment. We begin by reviewing the autoregressive formulation in Section 3.1. In Section 3.2, we introduce our explicit correspondence-based memory component. We then detail our strategy for conditioning on this historical context in Section 3.3. Finally, we describe the specific training objectives and real-time inference algorithm in Sections 3.4 and 3.5, respectively.

    3.1 Preliminaries

    Bidirectional Video Generation.

    Our method builds upon pre-trained flow-matching models designed for video-to-video translation. Specifically, we adopt VACE [14], which is a latent flow-matching model, operating within the latent space of a pre-trained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [34]. Given a block of input frames I⁽ᵇ⁾∈ℝ^T×H×W×3, the VAE encoder 𝔼 maps the pixel data to a latent representation z⁽ᵇ⁾∈ℝ^t×h×w×c. The latent dimensions are determined by the spatial and temporal compression factors, which for VACE are given as follows: h=H/8, w=W/8, and t=1+(T-1)/4. Following common practice in vision transformers [30], the latent block is further patchified into a sequence of tokens. Each latent frame is partitioned spatially into non-overlapping patches of size 1×p×p, where the temporal dimension of a patch remains singular. This process yields a total of N=t×(h/p)×(w/p) tokens per block. Specifically for VACE, p=2.

    For the generative model itself, VACE utilizes a bidirectional spatiotemporal transformer to generate an entire video at once. This design implies that every generated token depends on the full context of the video, including both past and future tokens. This design is expensive in computation and memory, limiting their operation to short, fixed-length sequences, typically up to five seconds.

    Autoregressive Video Generation.

    To enable long-form generation, recent methods [51, 12, 47, 22] replace bidirectional attention with causal attention. These models generate videos autoregressively in temporal blocks, where each block z⁽ᵇ⁾ is generated by conditioning on the previously generated blocks z^(

    3.2 Compressed Patch History

    In video-to-video translation, the availability of the input stream allows us to move beyond temporal proximity as the sole proxy for relevance. While a sliding window approach utilizes only recent frames for context, we can use explicit correspondences in the input space to identify relevant history from any point in the past. This is a reliable strategy because regions that match in the input video should match in the generated output (see Figure 2).

    By explicitly hard-coding these correspondences, we offload the burden of discovery from the transformer’s expensive attention layers. Rather than forcing the model to rediscover these relationships, we provide them directly via an external index. We represent this memory as an evolving set of input-output pairs. Each entry consists of a descriptor for an input patch, which acts as a retrieval key, and the corresponding generated output patch, which serves as the value for future conditioning. To ensure the system remains scalable for long sequences, we only update the memory when the input video presents novel information. If an incoming patch is already sufficiently represented in the history, we do not save it. This ensures that the memory footprint scales with the visual novelty of the scene, rather than the raw sequence length. (See history growth analysis in the appendix.)

    To implement this mechanism, we define three concrete operations that govern the memory lifecycle. We first specify the patch-level representation for the keys and values, followed by the retrieval protocol for reading from history, and finally the novelty-based policy for writing to the global store.

    Patch Descriptor.

    Our memory mechanism leverages the spatial discretization already present in the diffusion transformer (see Section 3.1). In this framework, every input video spatiotemporal patch is already mapped to a small latent patch of shape (1,2,2) that corresponds to a single token. From here, we use term “latent patch” for these token-corresponding patches. We assign each latent patch a global index g that uniquely identifies its spatiotemporal coordinates. For every input latent patch at index g, denoted as z_g, we define a descriptor k_g to serve as a retrieval key. We evaluated several feature extractors φ to produce these keys, including external vision backbones applied in pixel space. However, our experiments show that the most effective representation is the latent patch itself (further analysis is included in the appendix). Consequently, we define the feature extraction function as the identity mapping, where k_g=z_g. This approach also avoids the computational cost of decoding latents back to pixels and the inference run of additional feature extraction backbones. Under this formulation, the memory stores pairs (k_g,v_g), where the key k_g is the input latent patch and the value v_g is the corresponding to the generated output latent patch.

    Memory Management.

    To maintain temporal coherence throughout the generation process, we define the memory as a dynamic set of key-value pairs that evolves alongside the autoregressive blocks. Let H_b represent the memory state after the generation of block b, initialized as an empty set H₀=∅. We similarly define G_b as the set of all global indices g associated with the latent tokens generated within block b. Under this formulation, the generation of each subsequent block b+1 utilizes the existing history H_b for retrieval and concludes by updating the state to H_b+1 using the newly generated tokens in G_b+1.

    Memory Write Policy.

    The memory state is updated after the generation of each block by evaluating the novelty of every new latent patch relative to the existing stored patches. For each generated latent patch at index g∈G_b+1, we pair the input descriptor k_g with the corresponding output latent patch v_g. The similarity between a query latent patch k_g and the current memory H_b is defined as the maximum cosine similarity:

    sim(k_g,H_b)=\max_(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈H_bsim(k_g,k_g^′)=\max_(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈H_b(k_g·k_g^′)/(∥k_g∥∥k_g^′∥).

    		(1)

    For an empty memory, we define sim(k_g,H₀)=-∞, ensuring that all patches from the first generated block are added to memory. The latent patch and its corresponding generated output v_g are committed to the memory only if this similarity falls below a novelty threshold τₕ. The updated memory H_b+1 is thus defined as:

    H_b+1=H_b∪{(k_g,v_g):sim(k_g,H_b)<τₕ}_g∈G_b+1.

    		(2)

    This policy ensures that memory footprint and inference cost scales with discovery of unique visual content rather than total sequence length.

    Memory Read Mechanism.

    Before generating the output latents for block b+1, we query H_b using the descriptors of the current input latent. For each patch index g, we identify the set of k nearest neighbors ℕₖ(g) whose similarity exceeds a retrieval threshold τₘ:

    \vskip-2.84526ptℕₖ(g)=Topₖ({(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈H_b:sim(k_g,k_g^′)≥τₘ}).\vskip-2.84526pt

    		(3)

    For every query latent patch that satisfies this condition, we retrieve the stored output values v_g^′. If no entries in H_b meet the threshold τₘ, the neighborhood ℕₖ(g) is empty. We track these occurrences with a binary validity mask m_g, where m_g=1 if ℕₖ(g)≠∅ and 0 otherwise. This mask and the retrieved values are then used to condition the diffusion transformer as described in Section 3.3.

    3.3 Conditioning via Correspondence Cross-Attention

    We now describe how these retrieved values are used to condition the video translation model. The retrieved output patches {v_g^′} are tokenized using the same patch embedding as the input latents, producing history tokens h_g^′ in a shared representation space.

    To incorporate these history tokens into the video-model architecture, we add correspondence cross-attention layers to every transformer block between self-attention and text cross-attention layers. Each token attends only to its own k retrieved neighbors. Concretely, for each token index g, the current hidden state x_g provides the query. Let H_g={h_g^′}_(k_g^′,v_g^′)∈ℕₖ(g) denote the set of retrieved history tokens for query g. We define

    CorrXA(g)=m_g·Wₒ Attn(W_qx_g, WₖH_g, WᵥH_g).

    		(4)

    where m_g is the validity mask that zeros out tokens without valid correspondences. The output is added as a residual: x_g←x_g+CorrXA(g). The output projection Wₒ is zero-initialized [54], so the layer acts as an identity at the start of training, preserving the behavior of the pretrained model. Since each token attends only to its k neighbors, the computational overhead of these layers is minimal. We’ve described the cross-attention operation for a single token.
